recs: A Promise, Not a Finding For forty-nine issues we have signed off Love you down to your star stuff . The grammar of that phrase has been doing the hardest work on this site, and nobody had said so. Here is what it claims, what it carefully does not, and why that is the stronger position. Everything here is signed with one phrase. It is on thirty-five of these pages, in five registers, and it is the closest thing this project has to a thesis. Love You Down To Your Star Stuff. Read it as a sentence rather than a logo and two things come into view. Both are load-bearing. Neither is decoration. The subject is us. [We] love you down to your star stuff. There is no cosmic agent anywhere in it — the loving is being done by particular people, on purpose, and the phrase has never pretended otherwise. And “down to” measures reach, not cause. It says how far the love goes, not why it is given. Not because you are star stuff, therefore loved — but loved all the way down, star stuff included . The star stuff is the extent of the claim, not its warrant. That distinction is the whole of this page, and it matters because there is a sentence one short step away that gets both parts wrong. We wrote it once.

The sentence we wrote once At the foot of Bone Song — Zine No. 1, the first thing this project ever made — the colophon ends like this: “You are made of star stuff. The universe loves you for it. So do we.” Bone Song · Zine No. 1 · colophon The middle sentence is the naturalistic fallacy stated flatly. The universe is the subject, doing the loving; for it makes the star stuff the reason. Both moves are exactly what the rest of this page argues against. And then the next three words take it back. So do we. We are pointing at that line rather than quietly deleting it, for two reasons. A site that keeps a public error log does not get to tidy its own first page and pretend it was always clean. And more to the point: those three words are this entire essay, written before any of the rest of it. The repair was already in the building. What follows is just the argument for why it was needed. A correction this page exists downstream of No. 49 quoted that Bone Song line, called it “our masthead,” and dropped the So do we — then argued against what was left. Neither half of that was right. It is a colophon on one zine, not a masthead; the masthead tagline is Cosmic Connections ; and the sentence had already corrected itself. Ryan caught it on 15 August 2026, which is why this essay is built on the phrase we actually use. The zine is corrected and the error is logged in the changelog rather than absorbed quietly. So: the strongest objection to a claim like ours, in its strongest form. It comes from a comic fantasy novel, which is where we found it, so the credit goes above the argument rather than in a footnote below it.
The objection, in its strongest form

The objection, in its strongest form In Hogfather , Death is explaining to his granddaughter Susan why humans need to believe in things like the Hogfather. She pushes back — they are not the same as the big things, she says — and he answers with the hardest sentence anyone has aimed at this website. YOU THINK SO? THEN TAKE THE UNIVERSE AND GRIND IT DOWN TO THE FINEST POWDER AND SIEVE IT THROUGH THE FINEST SIEVE AND THEN SHOW ME ONE ATOM OF JUSTICE, ONE MOLECULE OF MERCY. AND YET— Death waved a hand. AND YET YOU ACT AS IF THERE IS SOME IDEAL ORDER IN THE WORLD, AS IF THERE IS SOME . . . SOME RIGHTNESS IN THE UNIVERSE BY WHICH IT MAY BE JUDGED. Death, in Terry Pratchett's Hogfather (1996), verbatim — the small capitals and both italics are the novel's own He is right. That is the whole reason this page exists.
There is no atom of justice in the powder

There is no atom of justice in the powder Grind this entire site down. Every citation, every field guide, every carefully sourced figure, every abundance table. Sieve it. There is no molecule of and therefore you belong in what comes through. This is the naturalistic fallacy, and we have named it in the house rules from the beginning: you cannot get an ought out of an is . But naming a fallacy is not the same as understanding why it would be fatal here specifically , and that part is worth spelling out, because it is not an abstraction for us. The same move, run the other way, is how eugenics argued. Nature does X, therefore we should do X is a machine that will manufacture a welcome or an extermination depending only on which fact you feed it, and the people feeding it have always been able to find a fact. Our chain collection exists because good physics keeps getting misapplied to human beings by exactly this route. So the danger is not that the argument is impolite. It is that it does not hold, and it can be turned around . And there is a sharper consequence still: The part that decides it If our claim that you belong rested on variation persists in nature , then a paper finding that variation does not persist — in some species, some system, some scale — would revoke it. The belonging would be contingent on the literature holding still. A claim that the next paper can take away was never doing the work we needed it to do. Which is not a reason to abandon it. It is a reason to be honest about what kind of claim it is.
Which is why the grammar matters

Which is why the grammar matters Pratchett's answer arrives a few lines earlier in the same conversation, and it is the one we actually use. The small lies — the Hogfather, the tooth fairy — are practice . And what they are practice for is the big ones: justice, mercy, duty . Which are also not found in the powder, and which exist anyway, because enough people acted as though they did for long enough. Susan makes our objection almost word for word — people have got to believe that, or what is the point — and Death's reply is three words long: MY POINT EXACTLY. NO. YOU NEED TO BELIEVE IN THINGS THAT AREN'T TRUE. HOW ELSE CAN THEY BECOME ? Death, in Terry Pratchett's Hogfather (1996) How else can they become. Not a consolation — a construction schedule. Justice is not a thing anyone discovered; it is a thing being built, badly and unevenly and for a long time yet, and belief is the scaffolding you stand on while you build it. Now put Death's sieve beside our phrase, because they travel in the same direction and make opposite kinds of claim. He grinds the universe down to the finest powder and goes looking for justice among the atoms, and finds none, correctly. Love you down to your star stuff goes down exactly as far — and does not claim to have found anything there. It claims that the loving reaches that far. Down to is not because of. One of those is a discovery, and the other is a distance we are willing to travel. So the phrase never needed correcting. The love in it was always ours, doing what we do, and the star stuff was always the measure of how far it goes rather than the reason it is given. What was missing was not better wording. It was anybody saying out loud that the wording is doing something — and that the sentence we wrote once, in the colophon of No. 1, is what it looks like when the grammar slips. A finding can be overturned by the next paper. A promise can only be broken by the people who made it. That is not a weaker position than the one we appeared to be in. It is a much stronger one, and it is also a great deal more demanding — because it means nobody else is holding it up . There is no cosmic backstop, no fact in reserve that will do the arguing for us if we stop. The universe is not going to pathologize your variation, and it is not going to welcome you either. It is not that kind of thing. We are that kind of thing. The phrase, split by what kind of claim each half is The phrase Love You Down To Your Star Stuff, cut in half in reading order. On the left, "love you down to" — justice, mercy and the claim that you are loved — passes through no sieve at all and is placed by hand into a box marked promised. On the right, "your star stuff" falls through a sieve and arrives in a box marked checkable, with examples: nucleosynthesis, abundances, piezoelectric bone. Beneath: one half is kept, one half is found, and down to is the reach rather than the reason. one phrase, two different kinds of claim love you down to … justice mercy “you are loved” no sieve passes these PROMISED put there, and kept there, by us … your star stuff the sieve CHECKABLE nucleosynthesis · abundances · bone one half is kept. one half is found. “down to” is the reach. it is not the reason. Figure 1 · the same phrase, sorted by what kind of claim each half is
Every piece here is a ladder

Every piece here is a ladder The second rule falls out of the first. If the physics is not carrying the ethics, then the physics has one job — being accurate — and we have to be candid that every piece here simplifies it. There is a proper name for that, and it is not ours. Jack Cohen and Ian Stewart called it a lie-to-children : a simplification that is false, and is nevertheless the only way to get somebody to the next rung. It is what your physics teacher is doing when they tell you electrons orbit the nucleus like little planets. We do it constantly. The atoms in your body were forged in dying stars is a rung — hydrogen is primordial, and a great deal of the rest arrives from stellar winds, neutron-star mergers and cosmic-ray spallation. Bone is piezoelectric is a rung, and one we got wrong twice before correcting it : the effect is collagen's, not the mineral's. So what separates an honest simplification from the thing this site was built to fight? One property, and only one. the same simplification, two practices a lie-to-children a smoothed retelling says it is a rung presents itself as the top names what it left out files off the hedges, because the tidy version travels further survives being climbed past collapses the moment somebody checks Which is what the house phrase “a rhyme, not a proof” has been doing at the foot of piece after piece without ever having a name. It is a rung marker. So is the wood-wide-web hedge , where the mycorrhizal trade is ours to use and the forest-wide story is not. And the ladder has a moral limit as well as an epistemic one , which is the part that is genuinely ours. Field Guide No. 10 keeps five turtles people made in their own section with no correction table, because a table that fixes a mistaken verdict has no business being run over somebody's cosmology. There the rung stops for a reason that has nothing to do with accuracy. Some things are not ours to climb past.

First Sight and Second Thoughts The third rule is the method, and we were using it for a year before we found out it had a name — in a children's book about a girl learning to be a witch. “First Sight and Second Thoughts, that's what a witch had to rely on: First Sight to see what's really there, and Second Thoughts to watch the First Thoughts to check that they were thinking right.” Terry Pratchett · Wintersmith, 2006 First Sight is seeing what is actually in front of you rather than what you expected to be there. It is harder than it sounds, because the expectation arrives first and feels exactly like observation. It is why the field guides keep arriving, independently, at there is no standard one of these — that is what you find when you go and look instead of consulting the type specimen in your head. It is also what our corrections look like: the mantis shrimp's famous colour vision collapses on contact with the literature, and the wood wide web rhymed so beautifully with mutual aid that it got past us in three separate pieces. Second Thoughts are the thoughts that watch the first ones. Not doubt — supervision. And this is the half you can build machinery for, which is the only reason this site has any: second thoughts, as installed the first thought what watches it “this quote is obviously by…” FACTCHECK.md , and the rule that aggregators are leads and never citations “the page looks fine” six checking gates that measure instead of glancing “we got that right, surely” a changelog that publishes our own errors That last one is the Second Thought that costs something, and it is the reason the changelog is a public page rather than a private log. Publishing your own corrections is not a virtue display; it is the only way first thoughts ever get supervised where somebody can see it happen. The asymmetry matters, though, and it is worth ending this section on: only the second half can be automated. No gate will ever tell you that a beautiful pattern is doing your looking for you. First Sight needs a person who is willing to be disappointed by a finding they loved — which is the same person the previous essay is about.
What this licenses, and what it refuses

What this licenses, and what it refuses Every argument on this page has a cheap version that sounds nearly identical, and the cheap versions are common enough that leaving them unnamed would be negligent. Not: Not permission to believe whatever you like. The little lies are practice for justice and mercy, not for anything that happens to be comforting. A belief that has to become true puts you under an obligation the moment you hold it, and most comfortable beliefs ask nothing of anybody. Not a softening of a single figure. Everything checkable here is still checked to the same standard, by the same gates, with the same ledger. This page changes what the checking is for ; it does not change how hard it is done. Not relativism. “There is no atom of justice” is a claim about where justice is located — not a claim that cruelty and care are the same, or that it does not matter which you choose. It matters more, not less, once you know nothing else is holding it up. Not an argument that fiction beats evidence. The opposite, and emphatically. This whole collection exists to reclaim science from the things that wear its clothes. Not a demotion of the physics. The star stuff is true, it is checked, and it is the most beautiful fact we know. It earns its place in the phrase entirely on its own. It simply does not carry the ethics, and it never claimed to. Not a claim that we planned this. We are not going to pretend the phrase was engineered to dodge a fallacy. It was written as an act of love and the grammar came out right, and we only noticed why it was right in the course of getting something else wrong . Being correct by instinct still counts, but it is not the same as having reasoned it out, and this page is the reasoning arriving late. Not ours. Three borrowed ideas hold this page up. Two are Cohen and Stewart's and one is Pratchett's, they are credited above rather than below, and the full account of the borrowing — including two attribution errors that finding it corrected — is in No. 49 .

The shorter version You are made of star stuff. That part we checked, and it is the most beautiful fact we know. The universe does not love you for it, because the universe is not the kind of thing that loves. We are. That is not a discovery being reported to you — it is a thing being done, on purpose, and it will go on being done. And the phrase we have signed off with since the first zine never claimed otherwise. It has been saying the right thing in the right grammar for forty-nine issues, and all this page does is finally say why. Love you down to your star stuff. Not because of the star stuff. All the way down to it. Where this came from → Sources. Terry Pratchett , Hogfather (1996) — both passages quoted verbatim from the novel, including the small capitals Death's dialogue is set in and the italics on show , rightness and become . The versions circulating online, including in Stimpunks' own commonplace book, are sourced to a quote aggregator and to a clip of the 2006 television adaptation and drop all of that; the correction is logged in FACTCHECK.md and in the changelog . Terry Pratchett , Wintersmith (2006) — First Sight and Second Thoughts, quoted at stimpunks.org since 2024. Jack Cohen & Ian Stewart , The Collapse of Chaos (1994) and Figments of Reality (1997) — lies-to-children, five years before The Science of Discworld carried it to a wide audience. It is theirs and not Pratchett's , which is one of the two attribution errors No. 49 corrects; the Science of Discworld books alternate chapters between Pratchett's Discworld narrative and Stewart and Cohen's science. What is ours. The reading of these ideas against this site's own signature phrase, and the grammatical argument about down to ; the argument that a revocable claim was never doing the work; the moral limit on the ladder; and every error above. Terry Pratchett's estate has no involvement in this page and was not asked. Nucleosynthesis: B²FH (1957), and Kobayashi, Karakas & Lugaro, ApJ 900:179 (2020), as cited in LYDTYSS . About Star Stuff Zines and field guides on the science of belonging — we are made of star stuff, and we belong not despite our differences but as them. Star Stuff (starstuff.earth) is a collaboration between the Stimpunks Foundation and More Realms — a growing collection of zines and field guides that read settled science as an argument about belonging. It is the public flowering of the Stimpunks knowledge garden: if stimpunks.org is the garden, this is where it blooms. And a great deal of what blooms here was grown from seed in More Realms. The method is consistent. Each piece begins with something well-established in physics, cosmology, chemistry, or biology, and lets it carry a claim about neurodivergent and disabled life — not as loose metaphor, but as the same pattern showing up at more than one scale. Almost every atom heavier than helium was forged in stars and their deaths; the calcium in our bones and the iron in our blood came from stars that died before the Earth existed. We take that settled science and read it as an argument: if we are all made of the same stellar matter, then neurodivergent and disabled people belong here fully — as part of the universe knowing itself in every possible way.

An official collaboration Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms. Two sites, one argument: difference comes first. Stimpunks is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit built by and for neurodivergent and disabled people — a knowledge garden of glossary, patterns, and practice. More Realms is Helen Edgar 's speculative companion to her Autistic Realms : where Autistic Realms is the grounded, practical site, More Realms is, in her words, “looser, weirder, more speculative” — somewhere to wander and think sideways rather than conclude. Star Stuff is what the two of us make together, and the pairing is on every page for that reason. Helen's writing is not a footnote to this collection — it is one of its sources and much of its weather. Why Difference Comes First , We Are Made of Relations , My Monotropic Galaxy , the shared-air and shared-signal coinages, the constellation reading of the spiky profile: these arrived here from More Realms and Autistic Realms, and they set the frame that later pieces work inside. Three zines are hers outright, in her own voice — Nos. 11 , 28 , and 30 — one more, No. 29 , was developed after her essay, and her work is named and cited across much of the rest. Attribution stays specific underneath the co-branding. Where a piece is Helen's, it says so and it is hers. Where a piece takes an idea from her, it names the essay. The two organizations share the masthead; the individual credits stay exact. How the three sites actually feed each other — which essays became which zines, which glossary terms became which arguments, and why a web of linked notes produces concepts nobody wrote down — is its own page: Cosmic Connections .

The through-line Difference is not a deviation from a norm. It is the default state of matter — and we belong as it, not despite it. That claim gets made across scales, and the scales are the point. The same shape keeps turning up whether you look through a telescope, a microscope, or a front door. The cosmic & subatomic Relativity and crip time; phase transitions and fluctuating capacity; spectroscopy and the constellation that was never a severity scale; the near-uniform early universe that needed tiny differences to make any structure at all. The ecological & biological Niche construction and worldmaking; the umwelt and the double empathy problem; symbiosis and the self that was always a collective; tides and co-regulation. The lived & communal Monotropism and spiral time; threshold anxiety and the crossing; functioning labels and the constellation of intensities; memory, mutual aid, and the work of being loved down to your star stuff.

How it's made, and held Each piece pairs a real diagram and honest sourcing with the community's own knowledge, and many are built with — or directly credit — neurodivergent thinkers. Everything is written in the first person plural: we , not they . And everything is held in common under Creative Commons, made to be printed free and shared freely. The zines are flowers of the garden, and a flower's whole purpose is to give its seeds away. A note on the science These are resonances, not proofs. The physics does not owe us our ethics, and we don't pretend it does — we begin from well-established science and read it as an argument about belonging, noticing where the same shape recurs. Where a source is contested or an interpretation is one among several, we say so. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. Sources & corrections We trace every quotation to a primary source, credit coinages to the people who made them, and ground the science in real, checkable work. We're human, and the collection is living — fact-checking here is ongoing, not finished. Every audit and every correction is published in the changelog , our own errors included. If you spot an error or a misattribution, please tell us: open an issue on GitHub or reach us at stimpunks.org , and we'll fix it. Solidarity, not charity — corrections are mutual aid. We love you down to your star stuff. 51 Star Stuff Almost Shadow on the zone Kepler had to name, why partial is the enormous one, and the two fields that borrowed the word Umbra · penumbra · antumbra · 1604 · 1965 · 1981 · a rhyme, not a proof L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely
A man runs out of words

Frankfurt · 1604 A man runs out of words Johannes Kepler was trying to draw an eclipse properly, and the language stopped him. The problem is geometry. If the thing casting a shadow is lit by a point of light, the shadow has one crisp edge and you need one word. But the Sun is not a point. It is a disc — an extended source — and every part of it throws its own shadow in a slightly different direction. So the shadow comes out layered. There is a core where the whole disc is hidden. There is an outer region where some of the disc is hidden and some of it still shines through. Between them there is no edge at all, just a handover. Kepler had umbra for the core. For the handover he had nothing. So, in the middle of a diagram in Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena, he made one: …quod est inter KE, NM penumbra dicatur, LN vero umbra. Kepler, Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena, 1604 — orthography normalised Let what lies between KE and NM be called penumbra — and LN, indeed, umbra. The verb is dicatur: let it be called. That is not a man using a word. That is the word being made, in one clause, because a drawing demanded it. He built it out of paene, almost, and umbra, shadow. Almost-shadow. And notice what gets named: not the dark, not the light. The thing between them. Before 1604 there was a shadow and there was not-a-shadow. The zone in between existed the whole time, and had no name, and therefore could not be reasoned about. what a word is for A few pages on he is already using it as an ordinary working term — decrescente, crescit penumbra, as the one shrinks the other grows — and noting that well before an eclipse looks like it has begun, nearly the whole Moon is already inside the almost-shadow. Which is the first thing this zine wants: the partial state arrives long before anyone would say anything is happening. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks
Three zones, because two would lie

The vocabulary now Three zones, because two would lie Kepler's two words became three, and the third one is the one people have never heard of. Because the Sun is a disc and the Moon is a ball, the Moon's shadow is a cone — it narrows to a point and then stops. Which means the shadow behaves differently depending on how far down it you stand: the Moon's shadow, per NASA's eclipse glossary zone what you see from inside it umbra the darkest part of the shadow. The Sun is completely blocked — a total eclipse. penumbra the weak or pale part. The Sun is only partially blocked — a partial eclipse. antumbra past the cone's apex. The Sun appears larger than the Moon, which is seen in complete silhouette — an annular eclipse, the ring of fire. The antumbra is worth sitting with, because it is the case a two-word vocabulary genuinely cannot describe. Stand there and the Moon is entirely in front of the Sun — nothing is sticking out, nothing is off to one side — and it is still not a total eclipse, because the Moon is simply too small in your sky to cover what is behind it. Complete coverage, and still not enough. The obstruction is total and the darkness never comes. the antumbra, which needs its own word Two words would have forced that case into one of the other two, and both would have been wrong. The vocabulary has three zones because the world has three. The three shadow zones of an extended light source A large light source at the left casts the shadow of a small round body. Crossing tangent lines form a narrow cone, the umbra, which comes to a point; beyond that point the region reopens as the antumbra. The partial one is the enormous one

Scale The partial one is the enormous one Here is the fact that rearranges the picture, and it is purely a matter of footprint. When the Moon's shadow lands on Earth, the two zones are not remotely comparable in size. The umbra touches down as a narrow track — on the order of a hundred to a few hundred kilometres across, a stripe you can drive out of in an afternoon. The penumbra lands as a vast disc, thousands of kilometres wide, covering a good fraction of a hemisphere. Run the consequence. Everyone inside that huge disc is having an eclipse. Almost none of them are in the track. The overwhelming majority of people who have ever seen a solar eclipse have seen a partial one. Totality is the rare case. The penumbra is where we live. the arithmetic of the two footprints And this is exactly why the word had to be invented rather than borrowed. The condition Kepler named is not an edge case or a rounding error at the border of the real thing. It is the ordinary condition, and the total case is the exception. Which sets up the trap this zine spends the next spread walking into on purpose. If partial is the normal state, and partial is a gradient, it is very tempting to conclude that the difference between 99 percent and 100 percent is just... one percent. It is not. It is not close to one percent. And the reason is not poetic. The cliff Ninety-nine percent is daylight Stand at 99 percent obscuration and you are not almost at totality. You are in a slightly odd afternoon. The reason is that the Sun's surface is outrageously bright and the corona is not. The corona — the thing you have come to see, the pearl-white structure that only exists for the eye during totality — is roughly as bright as a full Moon. Now leave one percent of the photosphere uncovered. That surviving sliver is still hundreds to thousands of times brighter than a full Moon. It does not politely dim the scene. It obliterates the corona and keeps the sky blue. Photometry bears this out as a cliff rather than a slope: measured illuminance falls roughly a hundred-fold in the last two minutes before totality, by another order of magnitude in the final half minute, and by more than four orders of magnitude in total between full Sun and totality. Ninety-nine percent of the way there gets you almost none of the way there. The last increment is not an increment — it is a change of state. what the photometry says, put plainly And then the Moon covers the last sliver, and the world does something else entirely: The period of total eclipse felt like a fermata. Birds quieted. Colors dimmed. A surreal calmness unfurled. Ryan Boren, Central Texas, 8 April 2024 A fermata is the mark that tells a musician to hold a note past its written value — to suspend the count. It is the right word, and it is not available at 99 percent. At 99 percent the birds are unbothered and the count runs on. So both of these are true at once, and the zine will not drop either: The shadow is a gradient. There is no edge; there never was; Kepler needed a third word precisely because the handover is smooth. And there is a threshold inside the gradient. Somewhere in that smooth handover sits a point where the birds stop. Both, not either Gradient and threshold Most arguments about difference pick one of these and lose the other. The shadow does not let you. Pick gradient only and you get the flattening move: everyone's a bit like that, it's all a spectrum, we're all somewhere on it. True as far as it goes, and it dissolves every threshold that matters. If it is all one smooth ramp, nothing in particular is owed to anyone in particular. The word for this is not solidarity. It is erasure with a friendly face. Pick threshold only and you get the gatekeeping move: either you qualify or you don't; either you're disabled or you're fine. Also recognisable. It is the shape of every eligibility form any of us has ever been failed by, and it makes the enormous partial zone invisible by construction — which, as spread four showed, is where nearly everyone actually is. The shadow is smooth and the birds stop. Any account that can only hold one of those is describing something other than the world. the shape of the argument Kepler's word is precise about this in a way our usual vocabulary is not. Penumbra does not mean a bit shadowed. It names a specific region with real boundaries — you are in it or you are not — whose defining property is that the blocking there is incomplete. It is a category, not a hedge. A named place where a partial state is the actual condition, and the partial state is not a failed attempt at a total one. Two other fields worked this out independently, went looking for a word for it, and arrived at Kepler's. They arrived there because in both cases treating the partial zone as though it were the total one costs people their lives. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks
The tissue that is not dead yet

Stroke · 1981 The tissue that is not dead yet When an artery in the brain closes, the damage is not a disc. It is a shadow, with zones. In 1981, Jens Astrup, Bo Siesjö and Lindsay Symon published a paper in Stroke with a title that is half physiology and half borrowed astronomy: "Thresholds in cerebral ischemia — the ischemic penumbra." Working in a baboon model of middle cerebral artery occlusion, and measuring blood flow alongside electrical activity, pH and extracellular potassium, they found not one threshold but two: two thresholds, and the zone between them as blood flow falls what happens first threshold electrical failure. The tissue goes silent. It stops doing its job. second threshold ion-pump failure. Potassium floods out. The tissue stops being tissue. Between those two lines sits a region that is functionally silent but structurally intact. It is not working. It is also not gone. Restore the blood supply and it can come back. Impaired is not lost. There is a zone between not functioning and not surviving, and it is where every intervention lives. the ischaemic penumbra, in one sentence They called it the ischaemic penumbra — and the word fits with an exactness that is almost uncomfortable. A region of partial deprivation, wrapped around a core of total deprivation, distinguished from it not by how bad it looks but by whether anything can still be done. The core is the umbra. Nothing is coming back from there. The penumbra is the part still holding on, and it is holding on on a clock. Consequences What the word bought This is the part that matters, and it is not linguistic. Naming that zone changed what happens to people. Consider the alternative vocabulary — the two-word one. In it, brain tissue after a stroke is either alive or dead. Under that description, the urgency is unclear and the target is unclear. There is damage; you assess the damage; the damage is what it is. Now describe the same brain with three words. Suddenly there is a region that is currently non-functional and currently salvageable, and it is shrinking, and it is shrinking as a function of time. That description does something the other cannot: it makes a clock visible. And a visible clock is the thing an entire field of emergency medicine is organised around — the reason acute stroke has a treatment window at all, the reason imaging tries to distinguish core from penumbra before deciding, the reason the phrase time is brain exists. Every intervention is aimed at the penumbra. Nobody is treating the core; there is nothing there to treat. The whole enterprise is a fight over the almost-shadow. what follows from having the word Sit with the shape of that, because it recurs everywhere and is almost always got wrong. The zone that looks least dramatic — not the catastrophic core, not the healthy surround, the ambiguous ring in between — is the only zone where anything you do makes a difference. The core is past help. The healthy tissue does not need it. All of the leverage is in the part that a two-state description cannot even name. And a two-state description does not merely fail to help there. It actively hides where the help would go. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks

Griswold · 1965 Penumbras, formed by emanations The second borrowing is stranger, more contested, and we are going to say so on the page rather than in a footnote. In Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965), the Supreme Court struck down a law banning contraceptives. The difficulty was that the Constitution does not mention privacy. Justice Douglas, writing for the Court, reached for Kepler's word: "…specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance." Justice William O. Douglas, Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965) The claim is that a written guarantee casts something beyond its own literal edge. Protect the home against quartered soldiers, protect papers against search, protect association — and around each of those, in the region where the light is partly blocked, sits something the text implies without stating. Now the honest part. This is among the most criticised passages in American constitutional law, and not only from one direction. The objection is real and worth stating fairly: if a text casts penumbras, who decides how far they reach? A shadow with no measurable edge can be extended to cover whatever the reader wanted covered. The danger of the penumbra is exactly its virtue. It is the region where the boundary is not sharp — which is what makes it honest, and what makes it available for abuse. the objection, not dodged We are not resolving that here; it is a live argument among people who have spent careers on it. We include it because of what the borrowing shows: twice now, in fields with nothing else in common, someone confronted a situation where a binary would produce an obviously wrong answer — and both times the word they reached for was the astronomer's. Both times, for the same reason. A hard edge would have been easier to administer and false. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks
Almost accessible is a phase change away

The turn Almost accessible is a phase change away Here is where we live, and both halves of the physics are load-bearing. Take the gradient half first. Most of us are neither fully blocked nor fully in the light — and the next spread is about who gets told they are the former. We are Disabled and Autistic and chronically ill in ways that fluctuate — good days, bad weeks, a capacity that is real on Tuesday and gone on Thursday. There is no crisp edge to point at, and every system we deal with demands one. So we get told the partial state is not a state. You managed last month. You're doing fine now. The penumbra gets read as a failed umbra — as a claim that hasn't finished proving itself — rather than as the place where most people actually are. Now the threshold half, which cuts the other way and is the one more often forgotten by people who mean well. Support is not proportional. Ninety percent of a ramp is a wall. A venue that is accessible except for the toilets is not 95 percent accessible; it is a venue you cannot stay in. Captions that drop out for the last two minutes did not deliver 98 percent of the talk. The last increment is where the phase change is — and up to that point the sky stays stubbornly, uselessly bright. Ninety-nine percent of the way to totality is a slightly odd afternoon. Ninety-nine percent of the way to access is a locked door with a very good ramp leading up to it. the same arithmetic, twice And then hold them together, because separately each one is a well-worn mistake. All gradient gives you the flattening, and nobody is owed anything specific. All threshold gives you the eligibility form, and the enormous partial zone vanishes. The shadow insists on both. Smooth, and with a place in it where the birds stop. The last thing to carry over is the 1981 one, which is the most hopeful sentence in this zine and the least sentimental. In the penumbra, what looks like loss is often deprivation — and deprivation is a thing you can reverse, if you can see that the zone exists and get there in time. There is no umbra in a bodymind

The distinction this piece owes There is no umbra in a bodymind Everything so far has been about shadows falling on things. Now the question that decides whether any of it is safe to use: where does an umbra actually live? Go back to the geometry on spread 3. An umbra is a relation between a source, an obstruction, and a place. It is not a substance and not a property. The ground in an umbra has not changed; it is simply where the blocked light would have gone. Move the source and the umbra moves. Take the obstruction away and it is not there at all. The pavement does not have an umbra. The pavement is in one. Nothing about the pavement is different. what a shadow is, and is not So the threshold on the previous spread is real, and it is an umbra of support. Support can be partial, and it can be total — ninety percent of a ramp is a wall, and behind that wall nothing gets through at all. That umbra is a fact about an arrangement, and arrangements can be changed by whoever built them. Functioning labels do something else entirely. They take the shadow the arrangement casts and paint it onto the person standing in it. High-functioning. Low-functioning. Mild. Severe. Levels. Each one relocates a fact about circumstances into a fact about a body. And “profound autism” is the umbra version of that move. Proposed in the Lancet Commission on the future of care and clinical research in autism (2021) for Autistic people who are minimally or non-speaking, require round-the-clock care, and are “not able to advocate for themselves.” Hold that last criterion against what the research actually finds. Steven Kapp's 2023 review concludes that minimally speaking Autistic people can communicate — particularly with responsive partners — that they need testing which lets them show what they have rather than testing built to miss it, and that they can self-advocate. Which makes “unable to advocate for themselves” partly a statement about the listener, the method and the room — and only partly about the person it is written on. the criterion, read carefully Now put spread 7's sentence where it belongs. In the ischaemic penumbra, what looks like loss is often deprivation — and reading deprivation as loss is not a small error there. It is the exact mistake that costs the salvageable zone. Profound reads deprivation as loss, and does it on a person. So let this be flat and unhedged. This piece recognises an umbra in support — support that is wholly blocked, and can be unblocked. It recognises no umbra in an Autistic bodymind at all. Not a small one. Not a rare one. Not one reserved for somebody further along than you. There is no zone of person that light does not reach and cannot be made to. And that refusal is not a denial of anyone's support needs, which would be its own way of writing people off. Some people need constant, skilled, expensive, round-the-clock support, and saying so plainly is part of the argument rather than an exception to it. Helen Edgar puts the distinction exactly: Autistic people with profound and multiple learning disabilities and health needs are not “Profoundly Autistic,” they are autistic with specific needs. Helen Edgar, More Realms · “Profound autism” does not exist Which is why support-needs language restores the penumbra. It is specific, it names domains, it varies by day and by room, it can go up and down, and — the part that matters here — it never declares any part of a person past reaching. The word came from an eclipse, and an eclipse is the right lender. Medicine's umbra is a genuine property of matter: that tissue is dead. That is precisely why it must not travel any further. Borrowing the astronomer's word does not license borrowing the surgeon's verdict. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks
A borrowed word is not an argument

The guardrail A borrowed word is not an argument Two fields reaching for the same word is a striking fact. It is not evidence for anything about us, and we want to be exact about that before closing. What the borrowings actually establish is narrow: that in at least two serious domains, practitioners found a two-state description inadequate to something real, and the vocabulary they wanted already existed in optics. That is a fact about the usefulness of a distinction. It is not a finding about disability, and no amount of elegance makes it one. The physics on spreads three through five is exact and checkable. The turn on spread ten is an analogy, and analogies license nothing on their own. A rhyme, not a proof. What we would defend without the metaphor: that fluctuating capacity is real, that partial support frequently delivers nothing, and that describing people in two states hides the place where help works. Those stand on their own evidence, and the eclipse is how we show them, not why we believe them. Not:that any bodymind has an umbra. This is the refusal the whole piece turns on, and spread 11 states it outright. We recognise a total blockage of support, which is a fact about an arrangement somebody built and can unbuild. We recognise nothing of the kind in a person. Profound, severe, low-functioning and level 3 all take a shadow cast by circumstances and write it on a body. Not:that refusing the label denies anyone's support needs. Some people need constant, skilled, round-the-clock support, and spread 11 says so plainly rather than sidestepping it. Refusing an umbra on the bodymind and funding the support are the same position, not competing ones. Not:that anyone is in shadow. The reading is right there — dimmed, obscured, waiting for the light to come back — and we refuse it. Nobody here is a diminished version of a brighter thing. The shadow is a description problem, not a person. Not:a severity spectrum. "Mild to severe" is the umbra-and-nothing vocabulary wearing a gradient costume, and it still ranks us along one axis toward a normal. The penumbra is a zone, not a rung. See No. 21. Not:"everyone's a little bit like that." This is precisely the flattening spread six refuses. A gradient with no threshold in it is not solidarity; it is a way of owing nobody anything. Not:that partial support is a start. Sometimes it is. Often it is a wall with a ramp leading to it, counted as ninety percent done. The photometry is the whole point: almost can be worth nearly nothing. Not:a proof about people. Kepler was drawing eclipses. Astrup, Siesjö and Symon were measuring baboon cortex. Douglas was construing the Bill of Rights. None of them was writing about us, and we are not pretending otherwise. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks

The Moon Is Always Half Lit

53 Star Stuff The Moon Is Always Half Lit on phases as geometry, the far side that was never dark, and why waning is a word about the angle 50.2% · 59% · 27.32 d · 29.53 d · 1959 · a rhyme, not a proof L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely
There has never been less Moon

The fact There has never been less Moon The Sun lights one hemisphere of the Moon. Not usually. Not on average. Continuously, for four and a half billion years, without a single interruption that was not an eclipse. This is worth sitting with, because almost nobody pictures it that way. A crescent Moon looks like a Moon that has had most of its light taken away. It is not. It is a fully half-lit Moon seen nearly edge-on to its own daylight — you are looking at the boundary between its day and its night from almost alongside, so the lit part presents to you as a sliver. The illuminated hemisphere is exactly as large at new Moon as at full. Nothing dims. Nothing is withheld. Nothing is recovering. The same amount of Moon is in the same amount of sunlight the entire month, and the entire month is a story about where you happen to be standing. A phase is not something that happens to the Moon. It is something that happens between the Moon and you. One refinement, because precision is a form of care. Slightly more than half is lit — about 50.2 percent. The Sun is not a point and it is much larger than the Moon, so the tangent lines that define the terminator close a little past the geometric halfway line. It is a small number and it is the honest one, and we show the arithmetic in the colophon rather than asking you to take it. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
A phase is an angle, and you are one of its arms

The geometry A phase is an angle, and you are one of its arms Three bodies are required to make a phase: the Sun, the Moon, and somebody looking. Remove any one of them and the phase does not become something else — it stops existing. There is no fact of the matter about "what phase the Moon is in" that does not include an observer's position in it. The quantity astronomers actually compute is the angular separation between the Sun and the Moon as seen from where you are, and that number has your location baked into it as surely as it has the Moon's. So the month-long procession of shapes is not the Moon doing anything. It is the Moon and the Earth carrying you around a lit object at a steadily changing angle, and your line of sight sweeping across a boundary that, on the Moon itself, has not moved at all. The Moon is not changing. The three of us are moving. Figure 1 is the standard diagram with one thing insisted upon: every Moon in the ring is drawn with the same lit half, facing the same way. That is not an artist's simplification. That is the finding. Eight orbital positions, one unchanging lit hemisphere Sunlight arrives from the left. Earth sits at the centre of a dashed circular orbit. Eight Moons are spaced around that orbit, and every one of them is drawn with its left-hand hemisphere lit and its right-hand hemisphere dark, because every one of them is lit by the same Sun in the same direction. The apparent shape a viewer on Earth sees differs at each position only because the viewing angle differs. every Moon here is exactly half lit only the angle to the viewer changes Figure 1 · the lit half never moves Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
Four of the eight last no time at all

The names Four of the eight last no time at all Everyone has seen the chart: eight little Moons in a row, eight names, eight equal boxes. The chart is a convention laid over a continuum, and it is lopsided in a way the drawing hides. The US Naval Observatory is precise about this. New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon and Last Quarter are defined to occur when the excess of the Moon's apparent ecliptic longitude over the Sun's is 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° respectively — which makes them instants. Moments. They have no duration. The Moon is Full at a specific second and is not Full a second later. The other four — waxing crescent, waxing gibbous, waning gibbous, waning crescent — are the entire rest of the month, about a week each. Four knife-edges and four long weeks, drawn as though they were eight equal things. Underneath the chart the illuminated fraction changes smoothly and without steps, every value between nothing and everything, all month, every month. There is no moment at which the Moon crosses from one kind of thing into another kind of thing. The boxes are ours. We drew them because a chart needs boxes, and then we started reading the boxes back as though we had found them. This is not an argument against the names. They are useful, they are precise where they claim to be, and the USNO states their status plainly rather than hiding it. It is an argument about what happens when a naming convention outlives the page it was drawn on. One synodic month: four instants and four intervals A horizontal band represents one lunar month. Four bright vertical hairlines mark New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon and Last Quarter, which are defined as instants with no duration. Between them lie four wide blocks, each about a week long, labelled waxing crescent, waxing gibbous, waning gibbous and waning crescent. A smooth curve beneath shows the illuminated fraction rising and falling continuously with no steps. 0° 90° 180° 270° 360° wax cres wax gibb wan gibb wan cres underneath, no steps at all Figure 2 · the boxes are ours Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
Three people, three crescents, one Moon

The observer Three people, three crescents, one Moon Because you are one arm of the angle, moving you changes the answer. Take a single instant — one waxing crescent, one illuminated fraction, one Moon. In Edinburgh it is lit along the right-hand edge. In Melbourne, at the same moment, it is lit along the left. Near the equator it rides low as a bowl, lit along the bottom, and there is a lovely folk name for it: a wet moon, tipped up to hold the rain. Nobody is wrong. Nobody is seeing an illusion. The Moon is not doing three different things. Your horizon is tilted differently relative to the plane the Sun and Moon lie in, so the same lit edge presents at a different roll angle — and since up is defined by where your feet are, the picture rotates with you. Three drawings. Three correct answers. The difference is entirely in the observer. If somebody handed you these three sketches and asked which was the real Moon, the question would be malformed — and yet it is exactly the question we ask about people constantly, in reports, in assessments, in the sentence but she seems fine with me. The same crescent seen from three latitudes Three identical Moons at the same instant with the same illuminated fraction. The first, seen from the northern hemisphere, is lit along its right edge. The second, seen from the southern hemisphere, is lit along its left edge. The third, seen from near the equator, is lit along its bottom edge like a bowl. NORTHERN SOUTHERN EQUATOR lit on the right lit on the left lit underneath one instant · one lit fraction · one Moon Figure 3 · the picture rotates with your feet Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
There is a far side. There is no dark side.

Luna 3 · 7 October 1959 There is a far side. There is no dark side. The far side of the Moon receives exactly as much sunlight as the side we know. It has days and nights of the same length. It has noon. And at new Moon — the one night of the month when we can see nothing of the Moon at all — the far side is in full daylight, the whole hemisphere blazing, entirely unwitnessed. The phrase "dark side" is not poetic licence. It is simply a mistake, and it names the wrong property: the far side is not dark, it is turned away. We found out what was there on 7 October 1959. Luna 3 swung behind the Moon and took twenty-nine photographs of a hemisphere no one had ever seen, developed the film in a small automated darkroom it was carrying, scanned the negatives with a moving light beam, and radioed the result back across the vacuum. The pictures were grainy and covered about seventy percent of it. What came back was not a shadow. It was a landscape — sunlit, crowded edge to edge with craters, and almost entirely lacking the great dark maria that make the familiar face familiar. It had been like that the whole time. Unseen is not unlit. It never was. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
Tidally locked was never rigidly held

Libration Tidally locked was never rigidly held "The Moon always shows us the same face" is the second thing everyone knows about the Moon, and it is also an approximation that dissolves by about nine percent if you watch carefully. We see roughly 59 percent of the lunar surface from Earth, not fifty. The Moon rocks, and it does so for two unrelated reasons that happen to compound: Why we get more than half Motion Cause What it shows us In longitude the orbit is an ellipse, so the Moon runs fast near perigee and slow near apogee while its spin stays even a little around the eastern and western limbs, in turn In latitude the axis is tilted about 6.7° to the orbital plane a little over the north pole, then a little over the south So the lock is real but it is loose. It is a tendency the system settled into, not a bolt. The Moon is very slightly out of step with itself all month, and the reward for noticing is nine percent more world. Even the thing we describe as fixed turns out to be negotiating. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
New Moon here is a full Earth there

Complements New Moon here is a full Earth there Stand on the Moon on the night we call new, look up, and Earth is full — a complete blue-white disc, four times as wide as the Moon looks to us, and far brighter. This holds all the way round. The phases are complements. When we have a thin crescent, they have a fat gibbous Earth. When we have full Moon, they have new Earth, a black disc ringed in red by every sunrise and sunset on the planet at once. At every instant, the two phases sum to one whole. Which means the light is never missing. It is only ever distributed differently between two vantage points. Nobody in this system is having less; somebody is having it elsewhere, and the arithmetic is exact. There is no moment in the Earth–Moon system when anybody is in the dark. There are only moments when the light is somewhere you are not standing. This zine is about light. The other half of the relationship — nearness, tides, and what a body close by does for another body's rhythm — belongs to No. 17, The Nearest Body, and is deliberately not re-walked here. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks

The ashen light The light we send back Find a thin crescent a few days after new Moon, on a clear evening, and look at the part that should be nothing. It is not nothing. The whole round disc is faintly there, ash-grey, the dark part visible. That glow is our light. Sunlight strikes Earth, bounces off cloud and ocean and ice, crosses to the Moon, and comes back to your eye. English has an old name for the sight: the old Moon in the new Moon's arms. Leonardo da Vinci worked out the mechanism around 1506–09 and drew it in the Codex Leicester, and — being Leonardo — never published it, so it did nobody any good for a century. He also got it slightly wrong: he thought the light came off Earth's oceans, where in fact most of it comes off clouds. The first published explanation is credited to Michael Mästlin. Mästlin taught at Tübingen, and among his students was Johannes Kepler — who, a few years later, ran out of vocabulary while drawing eclipse geometry and had to invent a word for the region that is neither full shadow nor full light. He called it penumbra. That story is No. 51. The teacher explained the light on the unlit part. The student named the shadow that is not quite a shadow. Neither of them would accept a picture with only two states in it. And note what earthshine actually requires. The dark limb is visible because something else is lit and facing it. Nothing about the Moon changed to make it appear. It became visible because of what was turned toward it. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
You can finish the circle and still not count as returned

27.32 · 29.53 You can finish the circle and still not count as returned The Moon completes one full orbit of the Earth — a whole circuit, 360 degrees, measured against the fixed stars — in 27.32 days. That is the sidereal month, and it is the orbit the Moon is actually on. But it is not back to new Moon. Not close. Because while the Moon went round, Earth moved too, about 27 degrees along its own orbit around the Sun, and "new Moon" is defined by the alignment with the Sun. The target slid forward. The Moon has to keep going — past a full circle, roughly 29 degrees further, about two more days — to catch an arrangement that did not stay put. That gives the synodic month: 29.53 days. It is the month everyone actually lives by. It is the one calendars are built from, and it is longer than the orbit it is made of. The cycle you are counted by is longer than the circuit you are actually completing — because the thing you are measured against keeps moving. There is a whole second piece in this — 29.53 days will not divide 365.24 days, and every calendar humans have built is a patch over that refusal. That is a chain for another day, and it is not this zine. The synodic month overshoots the orbit A dashed circle represents one complete lunar orbit of 360 degrees, taking 27.32 days. An additional short arc drawn outside the circle at the top right represents a further 29 degrees, about 2.2 days, that the Moon must travel to return to the same phase, because Earth has moved along its own orbit meanwhile. Together they make the synodic month of 29.53 days. +29° · 2.2 d the overshoot 360° · 27.32 d the orbit the phase cycle is 29.53 days a full circle was not enough Figure 4 · past 360° to arrive Always Half Lit · Stimpunks

The turn Nothing about it waned Here is the whole of it: waxing and waning are words about the geometry. They are not words about the Moon, and nothing in the Moon does them. We are described in phases constantly. Verbal on Tuesday and not on Thursday. Fine at home and struggling at school, or the reverse, which is usually taken as more damning. Capable in the assessment room and not in the corridor outside it. Someone writes down the sliver they were standing at the right angle to see, and it enters the record as how much there is. Those are not two quantities of person. Nothing was withheld in the first case and released in the second. The whole hemisphere was lit the entire time. What changed was the angle, the conditions, and who was doing the looking. A functioning label is a phase recorded as a substance. It takes the crescent and files it as the whole Moon there is. And the observer is in the measurement — that is the part that keeps getting dropped. But she seems fine with me is not a fact about her. It is a report of one angle, offered as though it were the object. So is he never speaks. So is every profile assembled from people who each saw one edge and none of whom were asked where they were standing. The spiky profile that No. 21 is about is exactly this, seen from inside: not a person who fluctuates in amount, but a whole person meeting differently-angled conditions and being measured as though the conditions were neutral. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks

A case, first-hand Full time and part time The previous spread is an argument. Here is what it looks like from inside one school career — Ryan Boren, writing in 2022 about being read at both extremes at once. He is hyperlexic and Autistic. School did not know he could read, because he would not read aloud: situational mutism and exposure anxiety, in his words, “locked my lips.” Then one day, in a quiet corner with what he calls a semblance of psychological safety, he read a book cover to cover to his teacher in a whisper, and asked: “Can I go now?” “During my school career, I was both r-word and genius.” Ryan Boren, R-word and Genius: Situationally Mute Hyperlexic Autistic, 2022 Note what actually changed, because it was nothing about him. The reading was there the whole time — the entire lit hemisphere, at full brightness, before the quiet corner and after it. What moved was the room. And he names the variable exactly: “R-word and genius. The difference in impressions is due to psychological safety, it’s presence and absence.” Then the sentence this whole zine has been building toward without knowing it. He describes going “from being a full time r-word to a part time one, depending on who was in the room with me and if I felt safe enough speak.” Full time to part time. That is a phase, recorded in the vocabulary of proportion — as though there were an amount of him, and it had gone up. And depending on who was in the room with me is not a metaphor for the observer's position in the angle. It is the observer's position in the angle, stated plainly by the person being measured. He goes further than we would have dared, and he is right to: “Autistic people are psychological safety barometers.” Which inverts the whole measurement. A barometer's reading is a fact about the air around it. If the apparent phase tracks the safety of the room, then the instrument was measuring the room the entire time — and the room wrote the result down as a fact about the child. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
The crescent really is less light

The guardrail The crescent really is less light There is an easy, wrong version of this zine, and it is one sentence away from the right one. The easy version says: since the Moon is always half lit, the difference is imaginary, so nothing is really harder on Thursday than it was on Tuesday. That is false, and it would be a cruel thing to hand anybody. A crescent genuinely delivers less light to you. Measurably. A full Moon can light a path home; a crescent cannot. The geometry is not a trick and its consequences are entirely real for whoever is standing under it. The correction we are actually making is narrower and holds up better: the difference is located in the arrangement, not in the body. Not in the Moon, which never changed. In the angle, the conditions, the room, the lighting, the hour, and the position of whoever is writing it down. That is exactly where an arrangement can be altered — and exactly where a diagnosis cannot reach. This is the same move No. 51 makes with shadow, and we are borrowing it rather than re-deriving it: an umbra is a relation between a source, an obstruction and a place, never a property of the ground it falls on. Same here. A phase is a relation between a source, a body and an observer, never a property of the body. Not:that the hard days are not hard. They are. This zine is about where the difficulty is located, and relocating it out of the bodymind is not the same as denying it. Anyone who reads this as "cheer up, you're always full" has been handed the wrong sentence, and we would rather say so on the page than hope. Not:that support needs are an illusion of perspective. Some of us need substantial, skilled, continuous support, and nothing in the optics touches that. What the optics refuse is the inference from seen as a crescent to is a crescent. Not:that inconsistency is a character flaw. Unreliable, attention-seeking, could do it yesterday — all of these read a changing angle as a changing will. Fluctuating capacity is ordinary, and the demand for a flat output is a demand no orbit has ever met. Not:the masking compliment. "You'd never know" is a description of the observer's angle presented as praise for the object. It is the same error as "the dark side," and it costs more. Not:that we are unknowable. The far side was unseen for the whole of human history and it was never unreal — and then Luna 3 went and looked. Hard to see from one position is an instruction to move, not a mystery to romanticise. See No. 48 on where that guardrail sits. Not:a proof about people. The USNO was defining ephemeris terms. Luna 3 was a spacecraft. Mästlin was explaining a glow. None of them was writing about us. Spread eleven is an analogy, and analogies license nothing on their own. A rhyme, not a proof. Not:that psychological safety is the only variable. Spread twelve is one person's account and it names safety because that is what was decisive for him. Sensory load, processing time, energy, pain, interoception, the demand itself and plain accumulated exhaustion are all real angles too. “Just make them feel safe” would be a new flattening, and a cheap one — the point is that the variables are in the arrangement, not that there is only one of them. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks

L★S The lit half was never in question. Only ever the angle, and who was standing at it. No. 17 The Nearest Body — nearness beats mass, and co-regulation is gravity No. 21 Not a Line — a spectrum is not a ranking No. 44 You Cannot Flatten a Sphere — what a summary must throw away No. 48 The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing — known only by its effect No. 51 Almost Shadow — the named zone in between No. 53 The Moon Is Always Half Lit — the phase is the angle ← you are here Reflection Which of your crescents has somebody written down as the whole of you? Where were you standing the last time you decided how much someone had in them? What have you called waning that was only ever the room, the hour, or the light? Whose far side have you called dark, when the truth was that nobody had gone round to look? If someone’s apparent phase is a reading of the room, what has your room been reading out lately? What would it take for the people describing you to be asked where they were standing? Sources The four principal phases are instants — quoted, not paraphrased. The US Naval Observatory's Astronomical Applications Department states that “the phases New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon, and Last Quarter are defined to occur when the excess of the apparent ecliptic (celestial) longitude of the Moon over that of the Sun is 0, 90, 180, and 270 degrees, respectively,” and that the dates and times computed this way “are instantaneous and well defined.” The same source describes the crescent and gibbous phases as intermediate, “each of which lasts for about a week between the primary phases.” Spread four's whole argument is carried by that asymmetry, which is why it is quoted rather than characterised. The 50.2 percent figure is ours, computed, and shown so you can check it. No source is cited because we did the arithmetic rather than finding it. For a sphere of radius r lit by a larger sphere of radius R at distance d, the terminator falls beyond the great circle by an angle α with sin α = (R − r) / d, and the lit fraction is (1 + sin α) / 2. With R = 695,700 km, r = 1,737.4 km and d = 1.496 × 10⁸ km, that gives sin α ≈ 0.00464 and a lit fraction of ≈ 50.23 percent. Wikipedia's article on the solar terminator corroborates the principle for Earth — “a little over one half of Earth is illuminated at any point in time” — but not the lunar number, so we are not claiming it as sourced. It is a grace note; the load-bearing claim on spread two is that one hemisphere is always lit, which needs no decimal. Luna 3. Launched 4 October 1959; the first photograph of the lunar far side was taken at 03:30 UT on 7 October 1959, from roughly 63,500 km, after the spacecraft had passed the Moon and looked back at the sunlit far side. Twenty-nine photographs were returned, covering about seventy percent of the far side; the film was developed onboard and the negatives scanned and transmitted to Earth. Per NASA and the NSSDC, the most striking feature of the images was the near-absence of the large dark maria that dominate the near side. Figures are as reported and the resolution was low; nothing in this zine rests on the image quality. Libration. That roughly 59 percent of the lunar surface is visible from Earth over time, through libration in longitude (orbital eccentricity against uniform rotation) and libration in latitude (an axial tilt of about 6.7 degrees to the orbital plane), is standard positional astronomy. The 59 percent figure is the conventional one and is an accumulated total over time, not a fraction visible at any single moment — spread seven says “from Earth,” not “tonight,” deliberately. Sidereal and synodic months. Sidereal month 27.32 days, synodic month 29.53 days. The synodic month is the longer because Earth advances roughly 27 degrees along its own orbit during one sidereal month, so the Moon must travel about 29 degrees past a full circuit — about 2.2 days — to restore the same Sun–Earth–Moon alignment. Both figures are mean values; the true synodic month varies by several hours either side, and Figure 4 is schematic rather than to scale. Earthshine, and what we can and cannot claim about who explained it. That the ashen glow on the Moon's dark limb is sunlight reflected from Earth is settled. Leonardo da Vinci gave a correct explanation around 1506–09 in the Codex Leicester and never published it; he attributed the reflection to Earth's oceans, where most of it in fact comes from clouds, and spread nine says so rather than tidying it. That Michael Mästlin was the first to publish an explanation is stated by the history-of-science writer Thony Christie (The Renaissance Mathematicus), and we mark it plausible rather than verified: it is a single strong secondary source, Wikipedia's Mästlin article does not mention earthshine at all, and we did not confirm it against a primary text. What we cut during the check: a much better story, that Kepler credited Mästlin for earthshine in Astronomiae pars optica (1604) — the same book in which he coined penumbra for No. 51. It would have been a perfect joint between two zines, which is precisely why we distrusted it. What the sources actually support is that Mästlin's 1596 Disputatio de Eclipsibus is often referred to in Kepler's 1604 work — not that Kepler credited him for this. So the spread claims only what is documented: Mästlin taught Kepler at Tübingen (Kepler studied there 1589–1594, and learned Copernican astronomy from Mästlin's lectures), and the two men's work sits either side of the same problem. Also deliberately not claimed: a publication date for Paolo Sarpi, whose writings on earthshine are variously dated to c. 1578–83 and variously described as published or not; we could not settle it, so he is not on the page. The wet moon. The bowl-shaped crescent seen from low latitudes is a real observational fact following directly from the geometry, and wet moon is a genuine folk name for it. We give it as folk usage, not as a technical term, and attach no cultural claim to it. Spread 12 is Ryan Boren's own account, quoted verbatim from a published post. “R-word and Genius: Situationally Mute Hyperlexic Autistic,” stimpunks.org, 19 September 2022. Every quoted phrase on that spread — locked my lips, a semblance of psychological safety, Can I go now?, During my school career, I was both r-word and genius, the difference in impressions is due to psychological safety, it’s presence and absence, from being a full time r-word to a part time one, depending on who was in the room with me and if I felt safe enough speak, and Autistic people are psychological safety barometers — is his wording, not a paraphrase, and the post was read at the source rather than through a summary. The slur is written as “r-word” throughout because that is how the source writes it, and that convention is deliberate on stimpunks.org rather than our own softening. The barometer inference is ours, not his: he wrote the sentence; the observation that it inverts the direction of measurement — that a barometer reading is a fact about the surrounding air — is this zine's addition, and it is an interpretation of his line rather than a claim he made. The two terms that spread carries, credited to their originators. Exposure anxiety is Donna Williams's, from Exposure Anxiety — The Invisible Cage: An Exploration of Self-Protection Responses in the Autism Spectrum and Beyond (Jessica Kingsley, 2003); Williams was herself Autistic. Psychological safety as a research construct is Amy Edmondson's, from “Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams,” Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2):350–383 (1999) — a study of work teams, not of Autistic children; the application to classrooms and to Autistic people is Ryan's, not Edmondson's, and the distinction is kept here rather than allowed to blur. We write situational mutism rather than selective mutism, following the source and the Stimpunks glossary, because selective implies a choice that is not being made. What this zine deliberately does not do. It does not restate the tides, nearness or co-regulation argument of No. 17, which is the Moon's gravity and a different physical story from its light. It does not take up eclipses, which belong to No. 51 and No. 52. It does not make comparative claims about non-Western lunar phase systems, which we did not research and will not gesture at. And it does not follow the calendar problem — that 29.53 days will not divide 365.24 — which is a Burke chain rather than a zine, and is parked as a candidate rather than half-told here. No claim is made that the geometry proves anything about people: spread eleven is an analogy and spread thirteen says so on its face. Spread twelve is not offered as evidence for the optics either — it is a life that the optics happen to describe well, which is a different and smaller claim. A rhyme, not a proof.
