Reading the world as felt knowledge

Inner compass Reading the world as felt knowledge Every migrating body is made of matter that has already migrated once — forged inside a star, scattered across unthinkable distance, and gathered again by gravity into a bird, a whale, a galaxy, you. Migration was never a metaphor borrowed from animals. It's the oldest fact about star stuff. Birds cross oceans using a compass sense we still don't fully understand — something in their eyes that responds to the Earth's magnetic field, tied to quantum effects still being worked out (Mouritsen, 2018). No map. Just the world, read directly, as something felt. Salmon return to their birth river through magnetic imprinting and the memory of water. Humpback whales cross hemispheres between calving and feeding grounds. Elephants walk the routes their grandparents walked. Even a seed migrates, carried on wind or fur, landing on new ground — every one of these bodies built, ultimately, from the same stellar matter, just arranged into a different way of moving through the world. It's easy to think of migration as a straight line — departure, journey, arrival. The workshop pushed against that. Migration is transformation across time as much as displacement across distance. Gilles Deleuze (1994) circled something close to this in his work on difference and repetition: no repeated pattern is ever a true copy — each turn carries its own small variation. Migration, read this way, is a spiral. With every movement, everything changes. the tug begins here not arrival — transformation a spiral, not a loop every turn carries its own variation Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

inside a bird's eye earth's faint field light cryptochrome two spins, still linked separated — not separate a compass made of relation warm, alive, and airborne A quantum compass Linked, even at a distance Here's the strange part of the bird's compass that's worth slowing down on. Inside a bird's eye, light striking a protein called cryptochrome creates a pair of electrons whose spins become linked in a way physicists call entanglement. Once two particles are entangled, what happens to one is tied to the other — even after they've separated. That linked pair turns out to be sensitive to the Earth's very faint magnetic field, and that sensitivity is thought to be part of how a bird reads direction (Hore & Mouritsen, 2016; Mouritsen, 2018). This is one of the only places we know of where this kind of quantum behaviour seems to do real, working, felt-in-the-body science — not sealed in a lab near absolute zero, but warm, alive, and airborne. A bird's felt sense of direction may be, quite literally, a small piece of quantum physics happening inside a living eye. Entanglement means: once two things have been in relation, they stay in relation. Distance doesn't undo it. Separateness was always the less accurate story. Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

Relationship first Not fixed-thing-first, relationship-second There's a related idea in physics called relational quantum mechanics (Rovelli, 1996). In this view, a tiny particle doesn't quietly hold fixed properties of its own, waiting to be measured. What it is only becomes definite in relation to whatever it's interacting with — another particle, an instrument, an observer. Writing on Rovelli's work, philosopher George Webster (2026) draws out the wider stakes: objects don't come first and then differ from each other — they emerge out of something more fundamental, a process of difference and relation that was already under way. Not fixed-thing-first, relationship-second. Relationship first, all the way down. I'm not a physicist, and this is one interpretation among several that physicists still argue about. But as a multiply neurodivergent person, it's closer to how I actually experience being myself — not a fixed, separate thing moving through the world on its own, but something that shows up through relationship and encounter (Edgar, 2026a). A bird doesn't carry its compass in isolation from the field around it. Maybe none of us carry ourselves in isolation from the fields around us either. the tidy story a thing, then its relations the closer story definite only in relation difference and relation come first; the standalone object is what got built relation, then thing one reading — physicists still argue Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

in motion · not yet decided Milky Way Andromeda ~50/50, not fated Sagittarius dwarf — still arriving trajectories, revised as the data arrives a tug, not a destination an itinerary that keeps being rewritten The same tug, at galactic scale Galaxies migrate too Zoom out far enough and the same pattern is still running. The stars in the Milky Way's halo aren't all original residents — many arrived. The Sagittarius dwarf galaxy has been streaming its stars into our halo for billions of years, a slow-motion migration first identified by Ibata, Gilmore, and Irwin (1994) that is, in a very real sense, still arriving. For decades it was treated as settled science that the Milky Way and Andromeda are on a fixed collision course, due to merge in roughly four to five billion years. The most recent modelling, using the latest Hubble and Gaia data, found something more honest: closer to a fifty-fifty chance of that merger happening at all within the next ten billion years, once the pull of smaller nearby galaxies is properly accounted for (Sawala et al., 2025). What looked like an inevitable itinerary turns out to be trajectories, still being revised as better data arrives. In the meantime, the Milky Way is far more likely to slowly absorb one of its own smaller satellites, the Large Magellanic Cloud, over roughly the next two billion years. Nothing here is a fixed itinerary. It's motion under gravity — a tug, not a destination — the same shape as a bird's restlessness before flight, revised at every scale as new pulls make themselves felt. Always Migrating · Helen Edgar
The restlessness that arrives before thought

The tug The restlessness that arrives before thought Brigit Anna McNeill writes of the tug of migration — a bodily restlessness that builds before anything is consciously decided. The pull comes from within, shaped by season and sea, and the sense of direction follows from inside it. I recognise that tug. Monotropism (Murray, Lesser, & Lawson, 2005) describes the way Autistic and ADHD attention gathers intensely around a small number of interests rather than spreading evenly across many. I've written elsewhere about picturing my own attention as a galaxy rather than a chart — energy gathered gravitationally into a few bright points, rather than spread out in an even, undifferentiated glow (Edgar, 2026b). The tug is that gravity. It pulls the same way a star's gravity gathers the matter that will become its next generation of planets: not evenly, not by choice exactly, but by an attraction real enough to bend everything nearby around it. Many of us are taught early to override this. Autistic masking research describes suppressing natural responses in favour of alternatives judged safer in non-Autistic spaces (Pearson & Rose, 2021). The tug gets read as too much, too narrow — and over the years we learn to quieten it, moving further from our own inner compass, until we may not recognise our true self at all. Csikszentmihalyi (1990) described flow as the state where attention and challenge align closely enough that the sense of separate effort disappears. Monotropic hyperfocus may be one of that state's clearest expressions — often carrying an undercurrent of wonder, where the world briefly widens around whatever has caught you, the way a night sky widens once your eyes adjust to it. the even glow spread evenly, nothing gathered the galaxy a few bright points, gathered by gravity the tug is that gravity attention as a galaxy not evenly — not by choice exactly Always Migrating · Helen Edgar
Learning to trust the pull again

the needle was never broken N your own north the "correct" default pulled off, not demagnetised trust returns unevenly deflection, not defect the pull was outside you Letting go of neuronormativity Learning to trust the pull again Trusting our inner compass again isn't easy, and there's real privilege in being able to unmask and be your Autistic self among others. Neuronormativity — the assumption that evenly distributed, easily legible attention is the "correct" default — doesn't just ask us to behave differently. It makes us distrust ourselves. Neuroqueering (Walker, 2021) is an ongoing practice of subverting and resisting that assumption. Not a destination to arrive at — no more than a galaxy's merger is a fixed destination — but an ongoing refusal to be ashamed of who you are. Pernille Fraser's poem "Can We Trust?" names this same rupture from the other direction — not what we lose faith in within ourselves, but what has to be earned from everyone around us before that trust can return. Shared through Stimpunks Foundation, it repeats its question across sensory load, pacing, correction, and whether we'll be believed: "Can we trust the space you offer?" (Fraser, 2019/2024). It never resolves into an answer. It stays in the asking — the way migration stays in the tug, before any destination has been decided. Nota flaw to be corrected, or a phase to be outgrown. Notsomething owed only once you've proven yourself safe to include. Nota straight line, or a fixed orbit — trust returns unevenly, and it can be withdrawn. Always Migrating · Helen Edgar
No single frame is the fixed one

Many ways of moving through No single frame is the fixed one Migration is only one expression of the many ways living things exist in and move through the world. Tarragnat (2025) names this range ethodiversity — the variability of behavioural and existential styles within and across species, opening neurodiversity out beyond a purely human-centred neurological framing. A bird's compass, a salmon's imprinting, a whale's crossing, a galaxy's slow absorption of its neighbour, a human's monotropic pull — not the same mechanism in different costumes. Genuinely different ways of being, each valid on its own terms rather than measured against one baseline. That sits alongside Milton's (2012) double empathy problem, which cautions against treating any one frame of reference as the fixed one against which others are read as deviant. Difference here is already a form of connection. A migrating salmon doesn't just pass through a river — its body becomes part of it. When Pacific salmon return to their home streams to spawn and die, they carry marine-derived nutrients into freshwater and the ecosystems around it: something taken from one world into another. Whales do something similar at ocean scale, helping move nutrients such as nitrogen and iron back into sunlit waters and redistributing them across great distances. Neither salmon nor whale sets out to feed a forest or an ocean. But each unique way of moving through the world is, at the same time, an act of shaping it — and of being reshaped by it in turn. Barad's (2007) intra-action: a self, a species, a migrating body, a galaxy doesn't exist as a separate thing that then relates to its surroundings — it comes into being through the relating itself. The liminal space a migrating creature passes through isn't empty transit between two solid states. It's where the shaping actually happens, at every scale there is. the crossing is not empty self field shaped in the relating not before it — intra-action no frame is the fixed one intra-action the self forms in relation, not before it Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

a profile still measures axes · edges · a baseline a constellation moves no baseline · no rank always connecting, always becoming from chart to constellation never fixed, never finished Nothing stands still A migrating galaxy of intensities The workshop's real gift was permission: to stop treating change as the exception that needs explaining, and start treating it as the base condition everything else moves through. I used to picture the shape of my own bodymind as a spiky profile — real peaks, real troughs, instead of one flat line of neuronormativity running across the whole of who I am. It's a truer picture than the flat line. But a profile still measures. It still needs axes, still has edges. What I actually recognise, when I try to map myself, isn't a chart at all — it's a constellation of intensities, an ever-shifting arrangement of sensory, cognitive, and relational ways of being, always connecting, always becoming, never fixed, never finished (Edgar, 2026c). This zine is what happens when you let that constellation move. We are made of matter that has already migrated across unthinkable distances — forged in stars that lived and died before Earth existed, scattered by their deaths, gathered by gravity into a solar system, a planet, a body, an interest, a self. Not a chart with a fixed baseline, and not even a fixed arrangement of points — a galaxy, always in relationship with itself, always in motion. Migration isn't a metaphor borrowed from birds, whales, and galaxies. It's one of the oldest facts about life on Earth. Every one of us is a small, temporary constellation inside a much larger migration that hasn't finished, and is always moving. Life doesn't hold still and occasionally migrate. It migrates, and it moves, it transforms everything and everyone around it, living and non-living. We were never a line. We are not a chart. We are migrating stardust — never fixed, never finished. Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms Stimming and Belonging with AURORA Twenty-eight performances, weighted toward live — because the argument is the body — and the physics of the light she shares a name with. The companion rack to Warriors and Weirdos, Zine No. 13. Playlist & essay · Sound
She watched herself back, and did not change a thing

One She watched herself back, and did not change a thing Asked about the way she moves on stage, AURORA gave one of the more useful answers anybody has given about a body in public. The first time I saw myself playing live… on a video was kind of a terrifying. I didn't know that I looked like I was doing an exorcism or having a heart attack while performing live… but I can't really do anything about it. I'm a very emotional person, and I guess when you have songs with lots of emotions… I have to use everything I got to sing those songs, and I have lots of things to work with. AURORA, in the Red Bull session for “Conqueror.” Lightly condensed from her spoken answer; ellipses mark cuts. Read that again for the order of events. She saw it. She was shocked by it. She kept it. Not because she reframed it into something admirable, and not because someone reassured her — she says plainly that she can't do anything about it, and then, in the same breath, that she needs it. The movement is not decoration laid over the singing. It is part of how the singing happens. I have to use everything I got. Anyone who has been told to keep their hands still knows how rare that sentence is. The usual sequence runs the other way: you catch sight of yourself, you feel the shock, and you spend the next twenty years editing. Whose word is which She calls it emotion. We are the ones calling it stimming, and that distinction belongs on the page rather than buried in it. AURORA has spoken publicly about being neurodivergent, using that word; she has not, as far as we can find, described her stage movement as stimming, and we are not going to put the term in her mouth. What we are saying is narrower and, we think, still worth saying: a great many of us watch her move and recognise something — the whole body recruited, the motion arriving with the feeling rather than after it, the flat refusal to hold still for the comfort of onlookers. The recognition is ours. The title of this page describes what her work does for us, not a claim about what is happening inside her.
What the light she is named after is actually doing

Two What the light she is named after is actually doing The aurora takes its name from the Roman goddess of the dawn. So does she. That is a coincidence and we are going to make nothing of it — but the coincidence points at a piece of physics that turns out to be about exactly this. Here is the part everyone knows: charged particles from the Sun spiral down the magnetic field into the upper atmosphere and the sky lights up. Here is the part that matters. The colour is not the Sun's. The solar wind delivers energy and nothing else; what you actually see is an oxygen atom, having been knocked into an excited state, dropping back down and releasing a photon at the one wavelength its own structure permits. The famous green is 557.7 nm, and that number is not a property of the Sun or of the wind or of the weather. It is atomic oxygen's own line. Energy came from outside. The colour is the atom's. Now the part that stopped us. That green line is a forbidden transition. Atomic oxygen's auroral transitions, and the altitudes at which each is seen On the left, three energy levels of atomic oxygen: the 1S state at the top, the 1D state below it, and the 3P ground state at the bottom. A green arrow from 1S to 1D is labelled 557.7 nanometres with a lifetime of about 0.7 seconds; a red arrow from 1D to 3P is labelled 630.0 nanometres with a lifetime of about 110 seconds. Both are marked forbidden. On the right, an altitude scale showing red emission above roughly 150 kilometres, green emission between roughly 100 and 150 kilometres, and below that a crowded region labelled collisionally quenched where neither completes. Atomic oxygen ¹S ¹D ³P ground state 557.7 nm · green forbidden · waits ~0.7 s 630.0 nm · red forbidden · waits ~110 s Where it completes red above ~150 km — thin enough to wait out 110 seconds green ~100–150 km below that: nothing too crowded — a collision takes the energy before it can emit Altitudes approximate. “Forbidden” is a term of art. It does not mean impossible — it means the transition breaks the electric-dipole selection rules, so it happens slowly. An allowed transition is over in nanoseconds. The oxygen ¹S state sits for about 0.7 seconds before it releases the green photon, and the ¹D state waits about 110 seconds for the red. And that waiting is why altitude decides the colour. Low down, the air is crowded: long before the atom can complete its slow release, something collides with it and takes the energy away instead. Physicists call it collisional quenching, which is as bleak a phrase as it sounds. The green shows between roughly 100 and 150 km. The red needs to be higher still, because 110 seconds of undisturbed waiting is not available anywhere denser. The most famous light in the sky is a slow release that the rules call forbidden, and it only completes where nothing crowds it. Both halves matter. The label was never a verdict on whether it could happen. And the room is what decides whether it does. We are not going to spell out the analogy. You can see it. What we will say is what the physics licenses and what it doesn't: “forbidden” is a description of a ruleset, not of a possibility — the sky does it constantly — and whether a slow thing gets to finish depends on the density of what surrounds it, which is an argument about rooms rather than about atoms. A rhyme, not a proof Oxygen has no stake in any of this. Selection rules are not social rules, and quenching is not a metaphor for a classroom — the word is doing a specific job about collision cross-sections and it does not transfer. Nothing about the 557.7 nm line obliges anyone to make room for anyone. We are noticing that the sky's best-known trick has the same shape as the thing we keep asking for, and noticing is the whole of the claim.
The same song, again, and again

Three The same song, again, and again There is a word for the other half of this, and it is ours rather than the industry's. Stim listening — listening repetitively to a single song, album or playlist — was coined by Jim Irion, who describes using it to start work and to hold focus. It is the listening practice almost nobody designs for. Streaming services are built to move you along: the next track, the fresh recommendation, the endless lateral drift. Plenty of us want the opposite, and want it for good reasons — the same song forty times because the fortieth is doing something the first could not, because repetition is regulation, because you have found an auditory samefood and samefoods are not a phase. AURORA's catalogue takes this unusually well, and the rack below is arranged for it rather than against it: the same song appears more than once in different rooms, because Conqueror at a Red Bull session and Conqueror on late-night American television are not the same event, and running them back to back is a legitimate way to listen. Ryan keeps a YouTube playlist called Stimming with Aurora, and it is worth noticing what is in it: almost nothing but live performances. Not the studio versions, not the official videos — the sessions, the radio spots, the concerts. That is not an accident of collecting. When the body is the argument, you need the footage where the body is.
Queendom, and a people that names itself

Four Queendom, and a people that names itself The belonging half of this page is argued at length in Warriors and Weirdos, so we will not repeat it here. One thing is worth restating, because it is the mechanism. Queendom (2018) does not describe a place that exists. It describes one being declared — a country announced for everybody the existing countries had no room for, which is a different act from asking to be let into somewhere already standing. And her audience did the corresponding thing from the other direction: they took a name. Weird stops working as an insult at the exact moment a people picks it up and uses it as an address. That is the same move the word stimpunk makes, and crip, and mad, and neuroqueer. It is also why the reclamation is never available to bystanders: the word only turns when the people it was used against are the ones turning it.
No cure, and the wounds nobody can see

Five No cure, and the wounds nobody can see Two of her songs do work this collection keeps needing, and they do it from opposite ends. Cure for Me (2021) takes the brightest, most danceable arrangement on the record and puts it underneath a refusal — which is the correct setting for that refusal, because the demand for a cure is usually delivered warmly, by people who are sure they are helping. Invisible Wounds (2024) goes the other way and stays with the part that does not photograph: the injury nobody can see is still an injury, and the absence of a visible mark has never been evidence of anything except the limits of looking. Between them sits the practical fact that every access conversation eventually runs into. What can't be seen still has to be believed.

Six What this page refuses A page about a beloved performer's body carries specific risks, and it is better to name them than to hope nobody notices. Not a diagnosis. AURORA has said she is neurodivergent and we use her word, exactly as Zine No. 13 does. Aggregator and SEO pages have begun attaching specific conditions to her name; we are not repeating them, and neither should anyone citing this page. Not her art explained by her brain. “She makes music like that because she is neurodivergent” sounds like appreciation and works like a reduction — it turns a body of deliberate craft into a symptom with a soundtrack. Not stimming attributed to her. She describes emotion. We describe recognition. Those are different sentences and this page keeps them apart. Not inspiration. She is not evidence that being different works out fine if you have enough talent. Most of us are not going to be given a stage, and the argument for making room cannot depend on the person in the room turning out to be extraordinary. Not stimming as acceptable only when it is beautiful. This is the one that matters most here. Her movement is celebrated because it is on a stage, set to music, and lovely to watch. The same body doing the same thing in a classroom gets a behaviour plan, and a child who flaps in a supermarket gets stared at by people who would applaud this. If the movement is only permitted once it has been made into art, nothing has actually been conceded. Not physics as permission. The aurora does not authorise anything. It is a rhyme, and it is fenced as one above.
One — Watch the body Live, because that is where the argument is. Most of these come straight from Ryan's own Stimming with Aurora playlist.

born herefounds onenot cast out — in transit L★S · 001 The Wolf Between Packs Grey wolf · Canis lupus aged 1–3 · roughly 15–20% of a population A lone wolf is almost never a wolf that was cast out. It is a disperser — young, in transit, crossing the neutral ground between territories to find a mate and found a pack of its own. a life stagecalled a floatercrosses buffer zonesmay join another pack ▸ Field notes Field notes · Grey wolf · Canis lupus The phrase has been borrowed so thoroughly that it now means a dangerous man acting without a group. In wolves it means something close to the opposite. Wolves disperse from their natal pack between roughly nine and thirty-six months of age. A dispersing wolf — biologists often call it a floater — moves through the buffer zones between established territories, the neutral strips no pack claims. It is looking for unoccupied ground, or a mate, or an existing pack with room in it. Some disperse a second time, having not found a breeding opportunity the first time. Wolves can move between resident and dispersing states across a life. At any moment, something on the order of 15 to 20 per cent of a wolf population is doing this. It is not the exception. It is how the population reaches new ground at all. So the lone wolf is not the one the story failed. It is the one carrying the next pack in it, walking through empty country to get somewhere the species has not been. Every pack was founded by two animals who were, for a while, alone. We keep the borrowed phrase in the community — lone wolfing, as Betsy Selvam uses it in the essay this guide grew from — and it is worth knowing that the animal it came from was never the loner we meant. She was already right about the practice. The wolf just turns out to agree. Everything else is solitary: mason bees, leafcutters, mining bees, carpenter bees. A female builds a nest, stocks each cell with pollen and nectar, lays an egg on it, seals it, and moves on. She will not be alive to meet the adult that comes out. This matters because of what we did with the other ten per cent. The hive is one of the most heavily worked metaphors in the language — busy as a bee, worker bees, the hive mind, the queen. An entire vocabulary of virtuous collective industry, built on the rare case. The typical bee works alone and the whole world eats because of it. Solitary bees are, per individual, often far better pollinators than honey bees; they carry pollen loosely, visit more flowers, and fly in colder weather. Nobody has ever suggested that a mason bee is under-socialised. It simply has a different way of being a bee — and there are eighteen thousand more like her, which is what a norm actually looks like. solitaryeusocialsame species L★S · 003 One Species, Two Answers Sweat bee · Lasioglossum albipes solitary or eusocial · and it is heritable The same species nests alone in some populations and in cooperative colonies in others — and reared side by side in a lab, each population keeps doing what it did at home. social polymorphismboth forms are typicalcommon-garden testedno correct version ▸ Field notes Field notes · Sweat bee · Lasioglossum albipes Lasioglossum albipes is a halictid — a sweat bee — and it does something that should be more famous than it is. In some populations, females nest solitarily: one bee, one nest, no helpers. In others, they nest eusocially, with a foundress and a worker brood. Same species. Reared in a common garden — both forms in the laboratory under identical conditions, and again under swapped photoperiods — each population kept the behaviour it had in the field. That points at a genetic component rather than a purely environmental switch, and resequencing has since identified variants that differ between the social forms. What we want from this entry is only the shape of it: a single species in which "how much do you nest with others" has two answers, both normal, both heritable, neither pathological. Nobody has proposed a treatment for the solitary populations. There is a further finding here that we are deliberately not building on. It is named in the refusals below, and the reason it is refused is the more useful lesson. left to be foundthe trail others walk L★S · 004 The One Who Writes Ahead Giant panda · Ailuropoda melanoleuca over 80% of marks aimed at the trail A solitary animal that maintains a whole community by chemistry — leaving scent messages on trees, deliberately positioned where others will pass, for animals it may never meet face to face. asynchronous contactaimed to be foundidentity, age, statusa network without meetings ▸ Field notes Field notes · Giant panda · Ailuropoda melanoleuca Giant pandas are solitary, and they are not out of touch. They deposit urine and anogenital gland secretions on trees, and those marks carry individual identity, sex, age, reproductive status and social standing. Other pandas read them. The result is a maintained community structure among animals who have very little direct contact. Two details lift this out of the ordinary. Over ninety per cent of the marks used are the longest-surviving kind — the message is matched to how long it needs to last. And over eighty per cent of marks are oriented toward animal trails, on ridges, on locally dominant trees. Pandas go out of their way to put their marks where someone will come past. That is not withdrawal. That is effortful, deliberate, asynchronous outreach — composing something, placing it carefully where it will be found, and walking away before anyone reads it. We have a whole argument about this already, in Shared Signal (No. 21): a message that arrives later is not a downgraded version of a conversation. Most of the animal kingdom is doing it this way. Asynchronous is not the fallback channel. It is the majority channel. known · calmstranger L★S · 005 Dear Enemies Territorial neighbours · across many taxa Fisher, 1954 · and the inverse, 1994 Once two territorial animals have settled a border, they stop fighting over it — and respond far more strongly to a stranger than to the neighbour they have known for years. familiarity lowers aggressionbirds to crustaceansthe nasty neighbour inversea relationship at distance ▸ Field notes Field notes · Territorial neighbours · across many taxa Fisher named it in 1954, watching territorial birds: two neighbours, once their boundary is established, become dear enemies. They stop spending energy on each other. Present the same animal with a stranger and the response is immediate and much stronger. It has since been documented across birds, mammals, amphibians, reptiles, fish, insects and crustaceans. The logic is plain enough — a neighbour who already holds ground is not trying to take yours, and repeated non-aggressive encounters make them cheap to predict. The energy saved goes into foraging and breeding. Then the honest part. It does not always run that way. Temeles reviewed the cases in 1994 and named the inverse: nasty neighbours, where residents respond more strongly to the animals next door than to strangers — typically where the neighbour is the one actually competing for what matters. Both patterns are real and which one appears depends on where the threat is. We are keeping both, because the interesting claim survives either way: a solitary animal is not an unattached one. It holds specific, individually recognised, long-running relationships with animals it hardly ever meets. Some of them are peace treaties. Some of them are feuds. All of them are relationships. They range widely and alone. Males are either solitary or in stable coalitions of two or three — and a coalition, once formed, generally lasts the rest of their lives. The territorial geometry is genuinely strange. Male coalitions hold small territories covering less than ten per cent of a solitary female's home range, an arrangement described as unique among mammals. The female moves through many male territories; the males hold ground and wait. Two details are worth keeping. A single male, without a coalition, is usually a non-territorial floater — the same word the wolf entry needed, and the same disadvantage. And while coalitions are typically brothers who never separated, in the Serengeti roughly thirty per cent of coalition members are unrelated males who joined. So: within one species, at the same time, in the same grass — an animal who lives alone by default, an animal who lives in a permanent small group, and an animal who joined a group of people it was not born to. Nobody is doing cheetah wrong. same group, all dayhour by hour L★S · 007 The Party That Changes Hourly Fission-fusion species · Kummer 1971 chimpanzees · spider monkeys · elephants · dolphins Some of the most social animals alive do not stay in one group. Their parties split and re-form through the day, changing size and membership hour by hour — and nobody calls it instability. leave and rejoin freelysize and composition varynamed 1971, framed 2008a whole social system ▸ Field notes Field notes · Fission-fusion species · Kummer 1971 Hans Kummer used the term in 1971 for primates whose groups change size by splitting and merging according to what they are doing and what food is available. Aureli and colleagues formalised the framework in Current Anthropology in 2008, defining it along three axes that vary independently: spatial cohesion, subgroup size, and subgroup composition. Species are not in or out of this category — they are described by their degree of fission-fusion dynamics. Chimpanzees and spider monkeys are the classic cases. Elephants, hyenas and dolphins are in it too. Here is the part worth sitting with. These are not marginal or antisocial animals. Chimpanzees and elephants are among the most socially sophisticated species on the planet, and the way they do sociality is by constantly leaving and coming back. An individual peeling off to forage alone for six hours is not a warning sign. It is the mechanism. What makes it work is that the bond survives the absence, and the return is unremarkable. Which is precisely what a fission-fusion social life asks of a group: that leaving costs nothing, so that coming back costs nothing either. one fortnightseventeen years under L★S · 008 Seventeen Years, One Fortnight Periodical cicadas · Magicicada 13 or 17 years under · then all at once Nearly the entire life is spent alone underground drinking from a root. Then, on a schedule kept to the year, millions surface at once and the whole thing is loud, brief, and over. five instars undergroundsynchronised to the yearpredator satiationlongest-lived insects ▸ Field notes Field notes · Periodical cicadas · Magicicada Seven species of Magicicada live in eastern North America — twelve broods on a seventeen-year cycle, three on a thirteen-year cycle. A nymph spends those years underground through five instars, feeding on xylem from tree roots. Alone, in the dark, for longer than most vertebrates live. Then the brood comes up together, all of it, within days. They are among the longest-lived insects on Earth and they spend the visible part of it in a matter of weeks: moult, sing, mate, lay, die. The synchrony is doing real work. It is understood as predator satiation — arrive in numbers so overwhelming that predators are simply full, and enough survive to lay. Any cicada that emerged early, on its own initiative, would be eaten. Nobody can do this alone, and the only way to do it together is to spend seventeen years apart, counting. What we want from it is the shape: a life that is almost entirely solitary, punctuated by one enormous, non-negotiable, gloriously loud social event — and the long quiet is not a failure to socialise. It is the preparation. the runsame spots, each year L★S · 009 The Same Stretch of River Brown bear · Ursus arctos solitary all year · then the salmon run Solitary animals that gather in numbers when the salmon arrive, sort themselves out without much fighting, and return to the same fishing neighbourhood year after year. temporary aggregationa dominance hierarchyneighbourhood fidelitythen apart again ▸ Field notes Field notes · Brown bear · Ursus arctos Brown bears are solitary. Then, for a few weeks, they are not. Where salmon are forced to concentrate — a waterfall, a shallow stretch — bears assemble. At Brooks Falls in Katmai, as many as fifteen at once. What makes it possible is that the food is abundant enough that tolerating each other is cheaper than fighting. What makes it orderly is a dominance hierarchy: a dominant bear arrives, subordinates step aside, and often there is no growl exchanged at all. Work on Alaskan brown bears at small salmon streams has found something further — fidelity to particular foraging neighbourhoods. Bears return not just to the river but to their stretch of it, alongside a recurring cast. So it is not a random pile-up. It is closer to an annual gathering: same place, roughly the same people, understood rules, and everyone goes home afterwards. Set this beside the octopus entry at the bottom of the page, which is the same situation with one variable changed. Here, the resource is abundant and the gathering works. There, the resource is scarce, and it does not. Whether proximity becomes company depends almost entirely on whether there is enough to go around. 7.7× backnot kin L★S · 010 The Ledger of Who Shared Puma · Puma concolor 7.7× more likely to share back The textbook solitary carnivore turns out to share kills with animals it is not related to — and to be markedly more generous toward the individuals who once shared with it. reciprocity, on a slow clocknot predicted by kinship1,000+ carcassesa social network after all ▸ Field notes Field notes · Puma · Puma concolor Elbroch and colleagues put GPS collars and motion-triggered cameras on pumas in northwest Wyoming and watched what happened at more than a thousand prey carcasses. Pumas are the standard example of a solitary carnivore. The results, published in Science Advances in 2017, did not behave like it. Every puma in the study shared food with another puma at least once. Many did it repeatedly. Crucially, who they shared with was not predicted by kinship and was not random. Individuals were 7.7 times more likely to share with a puma that had previously shared with them — direct reciprocity, of a kind usually documented only in animals we already call social. The authors' framing is the useful one: the same social strategies as group-living species, over longer time scales. A puma's social life is not absent. It is slow. Encounters are rare, so each one carries more, and the accounting runs across months. This is the entry that keeps the guide honest about Symbioses. Mutual aid is not confined to animals who live in groups. It is here too, in the most solitary carnivore we could name, kept as a running tab between animals who mostly avoid each other. party sizemore fruit → L★S · 011 A Function of Fruit Orangutans · Pongo party size 1.05 → 1.9, by forest How sociable an orangutan is turns out to depend less on which species it is than on how much fruit the forest is producing. Change the food supply and the sociability changes with it. semi-solitaryparties above chancesociality tracks fruitthe old contrast revised ▸ Field notes Field notes · Orangutans · Pongo Orangutans are described as semi-solitary: usually alone, but forming temporary parties more often than chance would predict. Those parties appear to be for social reasons — mating, play, company, protection from harassment — rather than being accidents of two apes reaching the same tree. The textbook line used to be that Sumatran orangutans are the gregarious ones and Bornean orangutans the solitary ones, and that this was a species difference. Field data has been revising it. Average daily party size runs about 1.6 to 1.9 in West Sumatra against about 1.05 to 1.3 in East Sumatra and Borneo — but the between-site differences track fruit availability, not taxonomy. A forest with more fruit produces more sociable orangutans, whichever species is in it. Read that again slowly, because it is the whole collection's argument arriving through an ape. Sociability here is not a fixed trait of the animal. It is a property of the animal and its forest together. An orangutan in a poor-fruit forest is not a less social orangutan. It is an orangutan in a forest that cannot currently afford company. We say this constantly about ourselves and it is usually taken as special pleading: that whether we can manage company depends on the sensory and social conditions we are asked to manage it in. Here it is in a great ape, measured, in party sizes to two decimal places. You change the field, not the animal. one nest, one birda year out L★S · 012 A Sabbatical Year at Sea Wandering albatross · Diomedea exulans divorce rate ~0.3% Months alone over open ocean, a year off between breeding attempts, and one partner for life — a bond that survives more absence than almost any other on Earth. biennial breederchick-rearing to ~280 daysbonds take years to formuntil one of them dies ▸ Field notes Field notes · Wandering albatross · Diomedea exulans A wandering albatross rears a chick for up to about 280 days. Because that consumes most of a year, they are generally biennial breeders, and most individuals take what the literature cheerfully calls a sabbatical year at sea after each attempt — alone, over open ocean, for months at a stretch. And the pair bond holds. Divorce runs at about 0.3 per cent; pairs usually stay together until one of them dies, which for a bird that can live forty years and possibly longer means decades. Forming the bond in the first place is slow — an average of 3.2 years for males and 2.3 for females. Put those two facts against each other. This animal spends the overwhelming majority of its life physically alone, further from another member of its species than almost anything else alive. It is also about as pair-bonded as vertebrates get. Proximity and attachment are not the same measurement. We treat them as one all the time — assuming the person who is often alone must be less attached, and the person constantly surrounded must be well connected. The albatross takes a year off and comes back to the same bird. Slow to bond, then bonded for life, with long stretches of necessary solitude in between and no damage done. Many of us would recognise the pattern. the only hard groundevictions at the edge L★S · 013 Octopolis and Octlantis Gloomy octopus · Octopus tetricus Jervis Bay · ~23 dens · 10–15 animals Two dense octopus settlements on the sea floor off New South Wales, widely reported as proof that octopuses are secretly social. What the surveys describe is closer to a housing shortage. scarce hard substratedens on shell middenevictions and chasingno reframe table ▸ Field notes Field notes · Gloomy octopus · Octopus tetricus Octopolis was found in 2009: a bed of scallop shells two to three metres across, with a piece of scrap metal at the centre, and up to fourteen Octopus tetricus seen there at once. Octlantis, surveyed from December 2016, has no human debris at all — about eighteen metres by four, roughly twenty-three dens in three clusters built on rock outcrop and shell midden, with ten to fifteen animals present. The reporting was jubilant. Octopuses are the standard-issue solitary invertebrate, and here were octopus cities. Read the surveys and a plainer account appears. Both sites sit in soft sediment, where hard substrate to den in is scarce. Where a rock outcrop exists, octopuses accumulate on it, and the shell middens they generate by eating create more denning surface, which draws more octopuses. The interactions observed at these densities are largely den evictions, chasing, posturing and colour change — animals in each other's way. That is not a society. It is what happens when the only affordable housing is one small patch, and it produces exactly what forced proximity produces. We have not given this entry a reframe table because there is no misreading here to correct. The popular verdict is not wrong about the octopuses; it is a wish about us — that closeness follows from being put close together. Compare the brown bear nine entries up: same crowding, abundant food, and it works. Proximity is not company. Proximity plus scarcity is a fight. Anyone who has been put in an open-plan office, or mainstreamed into a classroom with no accommodations and told that the proximity itself would socialise them, already knows the finding. “Better Get Used To It” Ask for a slower pace and you will meet one answer so often that it has an acronym. Homework young because there's homework later. Grades young because there are grades eventually. No accommodation at school because the real world won't accommodate you. The logic never changes: life will be hard later, so hardship now is preparation. Hardship now is not preparation. BGUTI · named by Alfie Kohn, 2005 · early adversity is not a vaccine It has to ignore them The argument treats the timetable as the fixed thing and the child as the adjustable one. But children arrive at things at genuinely different rates — so “everyone gets this at this age” guarantees some are handed what they cannot yet use. BGUTI doesn't overlook developmental difference by accident. It cannot survive noticing it. And it isn't true Kohn again, and it is exact: people don't really get better at coping with unhappiness because they were deliberately made unhappy when they were young. Early adversity is not a vaccine. It mostly teaches you that adults will do this to you. Where it does its worst Behaviorism watches compliance and reaches for consequences, so it has no way to represent a child who needs longer. Needing longer shows up as refusing; refusing gets a consequence. The consequence never changes the pace. It only adds fear to it. “Almost by definition, the BGUTI defense ignores developmental differences.” Alfie Kohn · “Getting Hit on the Head Lessons” · Education Week · 7 September 2005 the full argument and every source: starstuff.earth/two-hundred-years-zine · Zine No. 34 print freely · share freely · CC BY-SA 4.0 See reverse Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms look at the water, not the creature Broadside · Open edition Side B of B The animal, and its bill 272 years, and 156 to grow up. The Greenland shark lives in water near freezing and grows less than a centimetre a year. Nielsen and colleagues dated 28 of them in Science in 2016: a life span of at least 272 years, the largest animal at 392 ± 120, and age at maturity of at least 156 ± 22 — inferred from body length, not observed. And that is not a superpower. A species that takes 156 years to reproduce even once has almost no capacity to replace losses. They were hunted in very large numbers and still turn up in trawls. The IUCN lists them as Vulnerable . Slowness is a strategy with a bill attached — superbly fitted to an ocean that held still, nearly defenceless against one that changes in decades. So look at the water. A ruined cornea is a disaster in bright water and nothing at 400 metres. A 156-year childhood works in an ocean that holds still and is fatal in one full of trawlers. None of those outcomes is a fact about the shark. You cannot tell whether a pace is a problem by looking at the creature — you have to look at the water. What to ask instead Not “how do we get this child up to speed?” But: what is this environment demanding, who chose that, and what would it cost to stop? Name the model. The social model of disability distinguishes a body's condition from the disabling produced by environments built as though that condition didn't exist. Stairs disable a wheelchair user. The pace of a school day disables a kid who needs longer. Ask for the design change, not the indulgence. Slow pedagogy — unhurried time, room to revisit, the present treated as though it counted. Not a kindness extended to slow children; a change that stops manufacturing failure. Change the water and hold the person. Naming the environment is not a reason to leave anyone without help while the world gets redesigned. Not: Not slow is better. See the bill, above. It's a set of trade-offs, and some are brutal. Not everyone just needs more time. Sometimes it's a different route, a support, a tool, or dropping the demand. “Go slower” is one accommodation, not the answer. Not “but the real world won't wait.” Sometimes true, and still no licence for BGUTI — and the real world is also built, also by someone, also changeable. Not a reason to skip support. Naming the environment must never leave anyone without help while we wait for it to change. Not biology proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof — a person's pace would deserve respect in an ocean where everything moved at one speed. We don’t prepare students for a world of potential oppression by oppressing them. She named it first, and that order matters

Dark Matter Field She named it first, and that order matters In My Monotropic Galaxy (More Realms, June 2026), Helen Edgar maps twenty constellations of her own Autistic self. The first of the twenty is the Dark Matter Field. Much of the lived experience of being Autistic for many people is weighed down by what I have called the Dark Matter Field in my galaxy. This is the heavy darkness of neuronormativity, reflected in the accumulated weight we carry around of a world that does not meet our needs, and does not love us down to our star stuff. Helen Edgar · My Monotropic Galaxy · More Realms, 2026 She reached for the cosmic vocabulary on her own, for her own reasons, before anybody asked what the physics of it was. We have left this constellation alone twice — No. 45 and No. 46 both took other namings from her map and said in their colophons that Dark Matter Field was being deliberately kept back. This is the piece that spends it. The direction of travel is the whole discipline of the thing. Her naming came first; the astronomy is set beside it afterward, to see what the careful version of that inference actually looks like. The reverse move — physics first, then a claim about people because the physics said so — is the one this whole collection exists to refuse. It has a name, and it has a body count. So: nothing on the next eleven spreads is evidence about a nervous system. What follows is a method, worked all the way through by people who were very good at it, and then the same method held up against how the question got answered about us. Which way the borrowing runs An arrow from her naming to the physics is marked allowed. He counted the light and weighed the cluster

Coma, 1933 He counted the light and weighed the cluster Fritz Zwicky did something very simple, with seven galaxies. He measured how fast they were moving relative to each other, and asked how much mass it would take to keep them from flying apart. Then he counted the light and asked how much mass that implied, assuming the stars were like our Sun. The two numbers did not agree. They did not nearly agree. the average density in the Coma system would have to be at least 400 times greater than that derived on the basis of observations of luminous matter Zwicky 1933 · Helvetica Physica Acta 6 · English translation Four hundred times. Not a rounding error, not a calibration problem, not something you argue away over lunch. The discrepancy was the finding — a gap between what a model predicted and what the bodies were actually doing. And he did name it. The translation has him writing that this “would lead to the surprising result that dark matter exists in much greater density than luminous matter.” So the word was there from the start. What he did with it next is the part nobody quotes. The two masses of the Coma cluster A short bar for the mass implied by the cluster's light sits beside a bar roughly four hundred times taller for the mass implied by the galaxies' motions. And then he called it an unsolved problem

What he declined to do And then he called it an unsolved problem Zwicky had a factor of four hundred and a name for it. He could have announced a discovery. Here is how the section actually ends: These considerations indicate that the large velocity dispersion in the Coma system (and other dense clusters of nebulae) holds an unsolved problem. Zwicky 1933 · closing the argument Read that again with the four hundred still in mind. He had the measurement. He had the word. He filed it as unsolved. That is not modesty and it is not hedging. It is a precise report of what he was entitled to say: a discrepancy of this size exists, and I do not know where it lives. He lists three candidate accounts in the paper and settles on none of them. The first thing a careful person does with a discrepancy is decline to place it. Hold onto that sentence. In ninety-three years it does not get improved on, and on spread ten we are going to want it badly. Zwicky's ledger Two columns. Under claimed: a discrepancy of at least four hundred, and the word dark matter as one possibility. Under not claimed: which account is correct, that the matter had been found, and that the problem was solved. The paper everyone cites never says dark

ApJ 238, 471 · 1980 The paper everyone cites never says dark Vera C. Rubin, W. Kent Ford, Jr. and Norbert Thonnard took spectra of twenty-one Sc galaxies out into their faint outer regions and published the rotation curves. It is the paper the whole story hangs on. Almost everything said about it is slightly wrong. the retelling · and the abstract You have heard The paper says flat rotation curves “Most rotation curves are rising slowly even at the farthest measured point” Rubin discovered dark matter “must have significant mass located beyond the optical image” a paper about dark matter subject heading: galaxies : internal motions The curves are not flat; they are still climbing where the light gives out. The negative claim in the abstract is narrower still and more careful than either version: “Neither high nor low luminosity Sc galaxies have falling rotation curves.” Not they are flat — they do not fall. That is what the data could carry. And then the conclusion, which is the sentence this zine is named after: Sc galaxies of all luminosities must have significant mass located beyond the optical image. Look at what that sentence does. It says where. It refuses to say what. The word “dark” does not appear in the abstract at all. Forty-seven years after Zwicky, with better instruments and twenty-one galaxies instead of seven, the claim is still only about the location of mass — and the paper is filed under internal motions, because that is what was measured. Twenty years on, she still would not place it

PASP 112, 747 · 2000 Twenty years on, she still would not place it In 2000, Rubin wrote a retrospective called One Hundred Years of Rotating Galaxies. By then she was the most cited person alive on this question. Here is what she was willing to say. Surprisingly, we cannot yet rule out a modified gravitational potential, rather than dark matter, as the explanation of our observations. Vera Rubin · PASP 112, 747 · 2000 Twenty years after the famous paper, the woman the discovery is named for is still holding two rival accounts open: maybe there is unseen mass, or maybe our law of gravity is wrong at these distances. She does not pick. She reports that the observations cannot yet decide. And then this, which is the reason this zine exists: It is folly to believe that we know what a galaxy is, while the extent, the density distribution, and the composition of ≥90% of its mass are still a dark mystery. Vera Rubin · the same essay Folly. Her word, about her own field, about the object she spent a career measuring. Not we are nearly there. Not the details remain. It is folly to believe that we know what a galaxy is. Then they placed it — and this is where we were wrong

ApJ 648, L109 · 2006 Then they placed it — and this is where we were wrong Two galaxy clusters collided. The hot gas — which is most of the ordinary matter — got slowed by the collision and left behind. The galaxies sailed on through. So for once, the ordinary matter and everything else were in different places. Clowe and colleagues mapped the gravity by how the cluster bent the light of things behind it, and found that the gravity was not where the gas was. It was out with the galaxies. Their title is not shy: “A direct empirical proof of the existence of dark matter.” An 8-sigma significance spatial offset of the center of the total mass from the center of the baryonic mass peaks cannot be explained with an alteration of the gravitational force law, and thus proves that the majority of the matter in the system is unseen. Clowe et al. · ApJ 648, L109 · 2006 This zine was proposed on a sentence that is wrong, and we are leaving the correction on the page. The pitch said the field is “never directly observed, only detected by its distorting effect” — and offered gravitational lensing as evidence of that. But lensing is the instrument that made the direct detection, and this paper explicitly rules out the modified-gravity account Rubin was still holding open six years earlier. The premise had to go. We publish our own errors; that is the house. Gravity where the gas is not Two lobes of hot gas sit near the centre of a collision. Unseen is not the same as unfindable

Two claims, held apart Unseen is not the same as unfindable Here is the thing the smoothed retelling flattens in both directions at once. The mass is established. The identity of that mass is not. Those are different claims and the field keeps them scrupulously apart. Deep underground, in tanks of liquid xenon, people have spent decades waiting for one of these particles to bump into something. LZ has now reported hundreds of live days of exposure and found nothing. XENONnT, tonne-years of exposure, nothing. The searches are widening to lighter and stranger candidates — axion-like particles, dark photons — because the obvious ones keep not being there. Ninety-three years after Zwicky, the ledger reads: we know it is there, we know roughly how much, we know where it sits, and we do not know what it is. Both halves of that get abused. Say only the first half and you have a settled science that brooks no questions. Say only the second and you have “scientists don't even know what dark matter is” deployed as if it discredited the measurement. The honest version is harder to shout and it is the only one that is true. Settled and open Two columns. Settled: a discrepancy exists, its size, where the mass sits, and that the force law cannot explain it away. Open: what the particle is, its mass, whether it interacts at all beyond gravity. Three places a discrepancy can live

The structural question Three places a discrepancy can live Strip away the galaxies and this is the shape of the whole thing. A model predicts what a body will do. The body does something else. The gap has to go somewhere. There are exactly three places to put it. In the mass: something is there that we are not seeing. In the law: our model of how things work is wrong at this scale. In the measurement: we are reading the instrument badly. Astronomy has spent ninety-three years arguing all three, out loud, in journals, with the rival accounts named and the failures published. Zwicky listed candidates and picked none. Rubin held mass and law open for twenty years past her own famous result. Clowe closed one of them and said precisely how — 8-sigma, and here is the configuration that made it possible. The null results from the xenon tanks are published, which is why anyone knows the particle is missing. None of that is a courtesy. It is the machinery that makes the eventual answer worth anything. A verdict is only as good as the alternatives that were allowed to compete with it. Three doors, all opened A measured gap leads to three labelled doors: the mass, the law, the measurement. This is not evidence about you

Where it breaks This is not evidence about you The proposal for this zine called the parallel “an exact structural match.” It is not, and here is the failure at full strength rather than tucked in a hedge. Dark matter is hidden by nature. Neuronormativity is hidden by convention. That is a different kind of hiding, and it changes everything about what follows. The field warping us is not undetected. It is written down. It is in the diagnostic criteria, the intervention targets, the compliance goal on an education plan, the phrase “culture fit” in a hiring rubric, the seating chart, the lighting spec. You do not need a tonne of liquid xenon a mile underground. You need to read the paperwork. The right word is not invisible — it is unmarked. It goes unnamed because it is the baseline, and the baseline is the one thing a measurement never lists among its objects. And that difference is good news. A particle that has evaded ninety-three years of the best instruments ever built may simply be beyond us for another century. A convention is a decision, written by people, and it can be read, quoted, contested and changed this year. Two kinds of hiding Hidden by nature requires new instruments and may take another century. Hidden by convention requires reading the existing paperwork and can be changed this year. The physics chooses neither, and that is the tell

One field, two readings The physics chooses neither, and that is the tell Helen's Dark Matter Field is the accumulated weight — the heavy darkness, the thing pressing down. That reading is hers and it is true to her life. Now take the identical fact. Unseen mass is most of what holds a galaxy together. Without it the thing flies apart. Read that way, the very same physics is the perfect emblem of something else entirely: the co-regulation nobody logs, the care work nobody bills, the friend who answers at 2am, the accommodations that never made it into a report. The unmeasured is not the unreal, and it is often the unmeasured that is holding everything in place. Same field. Same evidence. Same ninety-three years of measurement. Crushing weight and the only reason anything is still standing — and the physics does not adjudicate between them, because it was never asked about you. If one fact can carry two opposite morals, the moral was never in the fact. the whole reason we mark it This is the cleanest demonstration we have of why this collection keeps saying a rhyme, not a proof. Someone has to choose which reading to make, and then own the choosing rather than hiding behind the galaxy. Helen chose weight, in her own galaxy, about her own life, and said so in the first person. That is what an honest use of a metaphor looks like. Not:dark matter proving the field is real. Ninety-three years of rotation curves say nothing whatsoever about a nervous system. If you needed astrophysics to believe us, the problem was never the evidence. Not:an argument against evidence. The opposite. Careful public attribution is the thing we are asking for. Nulls published, rivals named, verdicts withheld — give us that and we will take our chances. Not:modified-gravity advocacy. Rubin's 2000 sentence was true in 2000. Clowe answered it in 2006 and we quote the answer, at 8-sigma, on spread seven. Not:“you are mysterious.” Rubin's folly line is about a galaxy. Turning it into mystique about Autistic people is the move we are refusing — being unexplained is not the same as being unknowable, and we are neither. Not:the inspiration story about Vera Rubin. She was shut out of observatories and she was scrupulously careful. Only the second one is our argument here, and borrowing the first would be doing to her what gets done to us. Not:a claim that bodies never contribute. A gap can have more than one source. The objection is to the question being closed, not to any particular answer. Not:Helen's reading corrected. Her galaxy is hers. Spread twelve adds a second reading to the same physics; it does not take hers away. The sentence this zine is named for is the one to keep. Rubin, Ford and Thonnard had twenty-one galaxies and every reason to reach, and they wrote: mass located beyond the optical image. Exactly what was measured. Nothing about what it was made of, or what it meant, or what anybody deserved. Ask for claims about us that narrow, and that honest. There is a great deal of you beyond the optical image — and the loving does not wait on the inventory. One fact, two morals A single central fact, unseen mass dominates a galaxy, branches to two readings: the weight that presses down, and the mass that holds it together. You are a body of water

Mostly water You are a body of water Roughly sixty percent of you is water. Your blood runs close to the salt of an old sea; each of your cells is a droplet that learned to hold a shape. Before it was ever "you," this water was rain, river, cloud, glacier, and the warm inside of other creatures. Astrida Neimanis puts it plainly: we are, each of us, a body of water — not a sealed vessel with water stored inside, but water itself, gathered for a while into the shape we answer to. And it doesn't stop at your skin. You drink the sky and breathe out the sea; you pass your water on. You are less a thing than a place — somewhere the planet's water is briefly passing through. You are not a container of water. You are water, briefly holding a shape. ≈60% drink · breathe in breath · sweat · give on a place water passes through ≈60% water · always in transit a place, not a container Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

the membrane is permeable born of another's water water moves across the line permeable · borrowed · shared we are all downstream Transcorporeality Nothing here is only yours Every one of us began inside another body of water. Neimanis calls this gestationality: your first world was someone else's inner sea. We are each born of a body of water — and built from water that others, human and not, once carried. Stacy Alaimo's word is transcorporeality — matter moving across the line we like to draw around a self. What is "environment" one minute is "you" the next: the river becomes your blood, your breath becomes the weather, the fish carry traces of us and we of them. So there is no clean edge. We are all downstream of one another — of every creature and cloud that held this water first, and every one who'll hold it next. The membrane is real, but it leaks. Belonging isn't a bond we add on afterward; it's the water already moving through. We are all downstream of one another. Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

Differentiation The confluence keeps the difference Here's the trap to refuse. If we all flow together, doesn't difference dissolve — everyone melting into one? Neimanis is careful: watery belonging is not a blur into sameness. Water is the great archive. It carries what passed through it; it stays particular; it remembers. You can watch this where two rivers meet. A confluence runs braided for miles downstream — one channel, two waters, still visibly distinct. Joined and different at the same time. That is the neurodiversity paradigm in a single image. Belonging as flow doesn't sand us down to a common shape. The spiky profile survives the merge. We are in it together and each unmistakably ourselves — no baseline to dissolve toward, no norm the water is trying to reach. Belonging doesn't ask you to lose your shape. you us one channel · two waters · still distinct joined and different at once interbeing without erasure Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

deep channels, turned the same way shared flow · the watering hole channels aligned · flow shared deep, together Collective flow Where the currents pool Attention flows too. Monotropism (Murray, Lesser & Lawson) describes minds that pour attention into a few deep channels at a time — a strong current, not a thin spread. In flow, the channel becomes the whole world. And currents can meet. When our attention tunnels line up — same interest, same rhythm, working side by side — they join into collective flow: parallel play, shared hyperfocus, the easy company of people deep in the same thing. Autistic Realms (Helen Edgar) names it shared flow — attention turned toward one another's, holding a channel open together. A watering hole is where flows gather — the literal one, where creatures meet to drink, and the kind Stimpunks builds into Cavendish Space: a place made for attention to pool without anyone being pushed out of their own channel. Belonging, here, is a confluence of attention. Flow isn't only solitary. Currents find each other. Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

Belonging as flow Build the watering hole If belonging is a flow, the work isn't to make people fit. It's to keep the water moving. You don't answer a drought by lecturing the fish about resilience — you restore the flow. So we build watering holes: places where currents of attention and care can gather; where you can drink without being drained; where no one has to leave their channel to be let in. More-than-human kin included — every body that shares this water has standing at the pool. Belonging isn't earned by sameness or paid for in masking. It runs upstream and downstream of you already. Much of Earth's water is older than the Sun — formed in cold interstellar clouds and carried in on ice and comets before there was an ocean to hold it. The sea in your cells is partly starlight's leftover frost. It has been vapour, rain, river, glacier, whale, fern, and stranger — and it will be again, long after us. You are one shape it is taking, on loan, for a little while. So when you feel the pull toward others — toward shared water, shared attention, shared air — that isn't neediness to apologise for. 1 Bone Song Bone Song on piezoelectric matter, star-forged calcium, and the universe that doesn't pathologize its own variation L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Yasuda, 1954 — 1957 Your bones are electric Dr. Iwao Yasuda discovered something extraordinary in the mid-twentieth century: human bone is piezoelectric. Press on it, bend it, move through the world, and it generates voltage. The word comes from the Greek piezein — to squeeze, to press. Squeeze the crystal and it sparks. The crystal, in this case, is you. Collagen and hydroxyapatite — the structural proteins and minerals that make up your skeleton — are arranged in a lattice so precise that mechanical stress becomes electrical signal. Every step you take is a small current. +V −V stress piezoelectric bone under compression hydroxyapatite lattice · collagen fibres · voltage potential Bone Song · Stimpunks

Ca Fe C Mg P N O Si forge stellar nucleosynthesis elements forged in dying stars · Ca, P, C, N, O Stellar nucleosynthesis Forged in a dying star The calcium in your bones was not born here. It was forged — fused in the nuclear furnace of a star that lived and died billions of years before our sun ignited. When that star collapsed and exploded, it scattered its elements across the galaxy. Over eons, gravity pulled the debris into new configurations. Eventually: a solar system. A planet. An ocean. A cell. A bone. You are the universe's way of turning its own ash into something that can walk and feel and think about where it came from. The nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, the carbon in our apple pies were made in the interiors of collapsing stars. — Carl Sagan, Cosmos Bone Song · Stimpunks

The poem Your bones are electric. Not metaphorically. Not as a figure of speech borrowed from the poets who came before. Literally. Measurably. Piezoelectric. Press on them and they spark. Move through the world and they sing voltage. Dr. Yasuda knew this. He pressed on the crystal and it answered. The crystal was bone. The bone was yours. The calcium that carries that current was forged in a star that died before our sun was born. You are walking around with stellar ash in your skeleton. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Storms are not disorders. Variation is not deficit. The electric bone that bends differently is still making the signal. We love you down to your star stuff. To the calcium. To the charge. To the exact configuration of atoms that has never existed before and will never exist again. L★S. Bone Song · Stimpunks
The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation

The paradigm The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation The neurodiversity paradigm says: difference is variation, not deficit. It names a lens — one that the DSM cannot offer — in which the full range of human neurological experience is part of the natural distribution, not a deviation from it. A star doesn't diagnose its own magnetosphere. A fault line doesn't pathologize its seismic activity. Turbulence is how the universe moves energy from one place to another. You were told your signal was noise. You were told your frequency was wrong. But the bone still made its electricity. The calcium still remembered the star. Reclamation The punk in Stimpunks is this: we take the diagnostic language back into the lab and ask a different question. Not what is wrong with this person but what did the instrument fail to measure? Not why can't they be like everyone else but what is the universe trying to do through this particular configuration of matter? Every kind of mind lights up the sky differently. That is not a problem to solve. Bone Song · Stimpunks
