We began meaning to sort by material, and the material sort kept failing, because a hermit crab supplies none and a gall wasp supplies none either. What varies is who does the work. The companion to What Looks Like Chaos (Zine No. 55), which asks how a nest gets built; this one asks what gets to count as one, and the answer is much wider. Built: a ten-centimetre pufferfish making a two-metre geometric court on the seabed that divers photographed for years before anyone believed the builder was that small (Kawase, Okata & Ito, Scientific Reports , 2013) — the pattern is not decorative, it sorts fine sand into the centre, which is the part the female inspects. Then the correction that reorganised the whole guide: a termite mound is uninhabited. That is the paper's own word. Fungus-farming termites build massive empty towers above their subterranean nests, and the daily swing of solar heating drives convection through the tunnel network (Ocko, King, Andreen, Bardunias, Turner, Soar & Mahadevan, Journal of Experimental Biology , 2017). The most-photographed animal architecture on Earth is routinely called the wrong kind of thing: it is not shelter, it is infrastructure — closer to a lung than a house. Borrowed: a hermit crab contributes no material to any home it will ever occupy, and when a single shell arrives the crabs gather and queue beside it in descending size order , so that when the largest moves in the whole line moves up at once. Lewis and Rotjan tested the prediction that matters and found it held — vacancy chains distribute benefits across many participants rather than to the first taker. The crab that waits is not being passive; it is standing in the only position from which the chain works. The largest bird nest on record, 2.9 m wide, 6 m deep and over two tonnes, was accumulated across decades until it was more than the tree could hold, which is inheritance and its cost in one object. And a woodpecker's ecological job is not its own nest but the vacancies it leaves behind for everything that cannot excavate. Induced: a gall is oak tissue that the insect made the oak build — the inducer injects effectors including phytohormones that redirect the plant's development, and different wasp species induce distinctively different galls on the same host, which is why the literature calls a gall an extended phenotype of the insect. And not building at all evolved independently at least seven separate times in birds: three times in the cuckoos, once in honeyguides, once in a duck, twice in songbirds (Sorenson & Payne, 2002). A thing discovered seven times over is not a mistake , and that is the sentence the guide would most like a reader to carry. Secreted, or worn: a swiftlet builds from nothing but its own hardened saliva, and the entry states plainly that this is why the species is farmed and harvested at industrial scale rather than leaving it as a footnote. An emperor penguin has no structure at all — an egg on two feet under a fold of belly skin, with the shelter being the huddle, whose walls are other penguins and which moves. If somewhere-to-be requires a structure, the emperor has nowhere and manifestly succeeds, so the definition has to give: some of us have been housed by other people rather than by rooms, and it counted. And a trapdoor spider known as Number 16 held one silk-lined burrow for 43 years , the longest life recorded for any spider — a record that is really about Barbara York Main , who began following that population in 1974 and kept returning for four decades. A long quiet life in one small place is invisible unless somebody decides it is worth watching. Not a nest: the bower, which every list of animal architecture files as the finest nest alive. No egg is ever laid in it and nothing lives there; the female builds the actual nest elsewhere, alone. It is a theatre with deliberate forced perspective — objects graded outward so they subtend a more even visual angle from where she stands (Endler, Endler & Doerr, Current Biology , 2010). We have spent a century calling a stage set a house. And the fourteenth card gets no reframe table, which is a fourth distinct reason for withholding the apparatus. The rooms people build are not graded here. Running a sounds-like/actually over somebody's own room would make us the observer in the doorway with the clipboard — the exact figure No. 55 spends ten spreads indicting — and No. 55 is also explicit that not every mess is a nest , since burnout collapses the architecture and from the doorway the ruins look identical to the curated version. Nobody can sort those two on sight, and the people most certain they can are the reason the guide has a refusals list. The weaver appears in one card that hands off to No. 55 rather than re-running it; the beaver is deliberately absent, already spent in Minor Worlds . Thirteen lineages, thirteen incompatible methods, none ranked, several of them the ones a tidy observer would call failures. The ninth guide to arrive independently at the same sentence: there is no standard nest. Field Guide No. 16 A Field Guide to Eggs Field Guide · 15 + 1 · companion to No. 57 The murre's pointed egg does not roll in a safe arc. That is the textbook explanation, and it is wrong. The egg you are imagining occupies one band out of five. Fifteen beginnings among our Terran kin, sorted by how far the egg gets from the body — because a material sort was tried first and collapsed. 15 ways of beginning → Details Fifteen beginnings among our Terran kin, sorted by how far the egg gets from the body — and the catalogue disagrees with the picture in your head. The egg you are imagining occupies one band out of five. A material sort was tried first and collapsed, because a hen's egg and a common murre's are the same object by every material measure. So: eggs that never leave, eggs grown over by skin, eggs carried, eggs set down and guarded, eggs left. In the first band, live birth turns out to have evolved at least 115 separate times in lizards and snakes alone — against roughly 140 origins in all vertebrates — and about a fifth of squamate species lay no egg at all; whether the transition ever runs backwards is genuinely contested and is left open here. A sand tiger shark shows an egg working as food : the mother goes on ovulating after mating, up to ten embryos begin, and two are born. Syngnathid fishes are the only vertebrates with male pregnancy , and it is literal — a placenta-like pouch, embryos joined to the father's circulation, a measured patrotrophy index of 1, and immune suppression to tolerate them. A Surinam toad's eggs are pressed into her back and her own skin grows over each one and builds it a lid ; there is no tadpole stage, and the toadlets push the lids off after three to five months. Giant water bug eggs are cemented to the male's dorsum, and the carrying is plumbing rather than devotion: unattended eggs die every time , in air or underwater. A Banggai cardinalfish father holds the clutch in his mouth for a month and eats nothing, because a mouth cannot be a foregut and a nursery at once. Then the band everybody pictures, where four of five are strange: a kiwi egg is 15 to 22 per cent of the female (an ostrich's is 2 to 3); a monotreme egg is leathery and porous enough to be fed through its own shell , with ten days of egg followed by four to seven months of milk; and a deep-sea octopus in Monterey Canyon was revisited eighteen times over fifty-three months , guarding one clutch, never seen to feed. The murre is the entry that indicts us rather than an animal: the pointed egg was explained for decades by rolling in a tight arc, Ingold found little support in 1980, and Birkhead's objection is embarrassingly simple — the arc is wider than the ledge. Stability on a slope and shell strength do the work instead. In the last band, walking away turns out not to be the failure state: a megapode chick hatches under 40 to 150 cm of compost, digs out unaided in a median forty hours, and can fly the same day; a brine shrimp cyst waits up to eighteen dry years and resumes where it stopped; and a cuckoo's shell has a second job no other egg here has, since it must survive being looked at — matched to host retinal function rather than to our eyes, by host-specific female lineages, with the arms-race framing now under live challenge. Then the sixteenth card, dashed, with no reframe table : the egg-crack accounts, borrowed from trans communities and credited as unowned, because there is no mistaken verdict about the morning your own life rearranged itself behind you. One thing the biology does supply is a limit rather than a licence — across birds, squamates, turtles, crocodilians and the echidna, the tool that opens an egg is on the inside . You cannot do it for anyone. You can only be audible. The tenth guide to arrive independently at the same sentence: there is no standard egg. Field Guide No. 17 A Field Guide to Resting Field Guide · 15 + 2 · companion to No. 59 there is no standard way to rest — not an amount, not a posture, not an organ Fifteen ways of resting among our Terran kin, sorted by what is doing the resting . An animal with no brain and no clock. A bird ten months airborne. A squirrel below freezing. And the famous twenty-hour bat, which is one measurement at one temperature. 15 entries → Details Companion to No. 59 , and it asks the question the zine assumes an answer to: what does resting actually look like, across kin who share almost no anatomy? The bands sort by what carries the rest rather than by taxon or by amount. Hydra and Cassiopea have a nerve net and no brain and meet every behavioural criterion for sleep, and Hydra has no circadian clock either — a roughly four-hour cycle instead (Kanaya et al. 2020). C. elegans rests for two to three hours before each of its four moults (Raizen et al. 2008). Great frigatebirds sleep 42 minutes a day aloft, in the soar and never while flapping; common swifts spend over 99 per cent of a ten-month phase airborne, and the record is not uniform — some individuals roosted in midwinter, others never landed (Hedenström et al. 2016). Sperm whales hang vertically and go silent, unresponsive to a boat until it touched them (Miller et al. 2008). Bears keep their skeleton through six months of disuse; arctic ground squirrels hold a core temperature of −2.9 °C by supercooling, with no antifreeze in the plasma (Barnes 1989); lungfish seal themselves in a cocoon of living cells for years. Emperor penguins reach 37.5 °C inside a huddle while it is −19 °C outside, and two thirds of the saving is geometry rather than warmth (Gilbert et al. 2008). Parrotfish build a mucus tent for 2.5 per cent of a day's energy and cut parasite attacks from nearly all to about one in ten (Grutter et al. 2011). Northern fur seals suppress REM for weeks and never pay it back . And the card the guide would keep if it could keep one: the sleepiest-mammal figure of 19.9 hours is a single 1960s measurement at 33 °C on an unknown number of animals, which becomes 11.0 hours at 26 °C — and about one per cent of mammal species have had their sleep measured at all (Harding et al. 2022). Two cards carry no reframe table : sponges, because nobody knows yet and writing actually over an open question is bluff; and plants, because nyctinasty was named by Linnaeus and Darwin himself called the daytime version “improperly” sleep, read here from the 1880 primary. Seventeen cards, fifteen entries. Field Guide No. 18 A Field Guide to Unfinished Animals Field Guide · 16 + 2 · companion to No. 61 there is no final draft — and what varies here is not the animals, it is us Sixteen animals we reconstructed wrong, sorted by the kind of mistake and tagged for whether the argument is over. Drawn upside down, then back-to-front. Three animals in three groups. A skull on a tail. Two arms for forty-four years. 16 entries → Details Companion to No. 61 , and it asks the question that zine assumes an answer to: how often does the record actually move? Sixteen animals we reconstructed wrong, sorted by the kind of mistake, and — this guide’s one addition to the house form, borrowed from How We Got Here — every card carries a status : revised (ten cards), contested (four), or name stuck (two). A catalogue of corrections that will not say which corrections are finished would read as a list of settled triumphs, which is the smoothing it is complaining about. Assembled wrong: Hallucigenia was published in 1977 walking on its spines, inverted by Ramsköld and Hou in 1991, and turned end-for-end by Smith and Caron in 2015 when they found the eyes, mouth ring and tooth-lined throat at the other end — wrong on one axis for fourteen years and on the other for twenty-four more . Anomalocaris spent most of a century as three animals in three groups: a shrimp-like appendage, the “jellyfish” Peytoia , and the “sponge” Laggania , united by Whittington and Briggs in 1985 — and then the correction was itself corrected , when Daley and Bergström found a three-plate oral cone in 2012 and Peytoia became valid again. Cope put the skull of Elasmosaurus on the end of its neck in 1868, reading a neck as a tail; and the famous story about who caught him is wrong — it was Joseph Leidy , on 8 March 1870, with Marsh in the room, and Marsh’s claim survives only in a newspaper piece two decades later. Mantell put the Iguanodon thumb spike on its nose; it took thirty-odd whole skeletons at Bernissart for Dollo to move it to the hand. Known from almost nothing: Deinocheirus was two arms found on 9 July 1965 and named in 1970 by Halszka Osmólska and Ewa Roniewicz , and it stayed honestly unplaced for forty-four years until two near-complete skeletons showed a humpbacked, duck-billed omnivore. The Spinosaurus holotype burned in the Munich bombing of 24–25 April 1944 , after Stromer’s requests to move the collection were refused — so every reconstruction since argues from photographs, and the aquatic reading is contested. Helicoprion ’s tooth whorl was placed on the snout, the upper jaw, the back and the tail before a 2013 CT scan put it in the lower jaw — of a specimen that had been in a drawer since 1950 . The line moved: Brontosaurus (the short form of the zine). Torosaurus , proposed as merely a mature Triceratops in 2010 and rejected in 2012, still unresolved — the mirror image of the Brontosaurus case, a merge rather than a split, with the opposite fate. Nanotyrannus , dismissed for forty years as a juvenile T. rex and reinstated in 2025 by Zanno and Napoli on a near-adult skeleton from the Duelling Dinosaurs block, with a second species nobody had separated out. And Tanystropheus , one species until a CT scan made it two, both size classes fully grown. Three of those four errors were the same error: explaining a difference by age. The name outlived it: Oviraptor means egg seizer and it was brooding its own clutch — and the card is careful that the 1995 brooding specimen is an oviraptorid later named Citipati , not Osborn’s animal , because the tidy version of that story is the one that travels. Basilosaurus means king lizard and Owen showed it was a mammal within five years; he proposed Zeuglodon and priority refused it. Both names are permanent , which is the band the zine cares about: a label outlives its refutation by rule or by repetition , and only one of those admits what it is doing. Tidier than the evidence: the fish-crawls-out story has a date problem — Devonian trackways about eighteen million years older than the earliest tetrapod bodies — and the retelling of that correction is smoothed too , because those trackways are themselves disputed. The film raptor is not the fossil one. And the tail-dragging dinosaur was corrected by a whole field changing its mind, from one 1969 monograph. Two cards are dashed and carry no reframe table. Mary Anning found, prepared and drew the first complete plesiosaur in 1823 and Conybeare presented it without naming her; women could not join the Geological Society until 1904, and on her only London trip no label carried her name. She is not a specimen , and running sounds like / actually down the side of a person would file her with the misreconstructed animals, which is the injury. And the last card has nothing to correct yet : on the guide’s own argument some entries above are currently wrong, and it says where to expect it — the age explanation, the fragment that fits every reading, and the instrument that arrives before the answer. Arrival line: there is no final draft , and the guide says plainly why it departs from the house formula: what varies here is not the animals but us. Eighteen cards, sixteen entries.
The limit the form found on itself

The limit the form found on itself The best thing this collection has produced is a place where the format stops , and it was the tenth guide that found it. Being a Turtle holds twelve animals and then, in a separate section behind a different card, five turtles that people made: Turtle Island, ao , Kurma, Great A'Tuin, and a Larrakia Star Dreaming it cites rather than retells. They are not entries. They have a dashed border instead of a solid one, and they do not get a reframe table — because the reframe table is a machine for correcting a mistaken verdict, and running “sounds like / actually” over somebody's cosmology would be obscene. The guide says so on its own face, and then makes the point structurally rather than only in prose: the format difference is the argument. A catalogue that had quietly filed five cosmologies as specimens would have been a tidier page and a much worse one. This is the sharpest thing the form has learned about itself, and it is now the standing rule — if a subject cannot take the apparatus, it gets a different card, not a smaller one. The drift Four of the first five guides were cosmological. Guides six through eleven are all biological. Constellations, elements, worlds and stars gave way to symbioses, nervous systems, migration, sharks, turtles and tortoises — and nobody decided that. It is easy to see why it happened: animals come with better-documented individual cases, and the deficit vocabulary this form exists to dismantle is thicker in biology than in astronomy. It is also worth naming, because a collection that drifts without noticing has stopped choosing. The sky has not run out of catalogues. Naming it worked, which is the only reason this paragraph is worth keeping. This section previously ended by saying the honest lead was “a guide that goes back to the sky, or to something that is neither animal nor star.” My Monotropic Galaxy is both at once — cosmic vocabulary throughout, and a subject that is neither animal nor star but a person's inner life. The drift is broken at twelve. Writing the gap down on a public page is what made it get filled. And then the thirteenth went straight back to animals, which is worth admitting in the same breath. The Ways of Being Alone is wolves, bees, pandas, pumas and apes — the drift's exact shape again, one guide after it was named as broken. It arrived that way because it came from Betsy Selvam's essay on Autistic solitude and went looking for what our kin do about company, and biology is where that question is answered. That is a reason, not an excuse. One guide out of the pattern does not make a habit; the sky still has not run out of catalogues. Not Not a cabinet of curiosities. These are not weird creatures assembled to be marvelled at. Every entry is an ordinary member of its group doing an ordinary thing, and the surprise is only ever about how narrowly we had drawn the category. Not diagnosis by analogy. The octopus is not autistic. The slime mold is not a metaphor for anybody's cognition. Where a guide reaches for a human parallel it marks it as a reach, and the entries themselves stay about the animals. Not proof. Biology does not settle questions about human belonging, and the naturalistic fallacy is a trap this form walks straight past if nobody holds it. A rhyme, not a proof is in these guides because it has to be. Not settled where it isn't. The symbioses guide keeps root-to-fungus mycorrhizal trade, which is settled, and hedges the forest-wide “wood wide web” story, which Karst, Jones & Hoeksema found insufficiently supported — “Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests,” Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023. It rhymes beautifully with mutual aid, which is exactly why it slipped past us in three pieces before anyone checked. Not a ranking, however it is read. Numbered guides and numbered entries are an index, not a league table. The number says when a guide was made; nothing in it says which entry won.

What is not here yet Nothing is scoped and waiting, which matches Sound and differs from Print , where a sheet sits deliberately unbuilt. The lead this section used to carry has been taken up. It read: a guide that goes back to the sky, or to something that is neither animal nor star. My Monotropic Galaxy answered it on both counts, and it is left recorded here rather than quietly deleted, because a gap that gets filled is the evidence that naming gaps in public does something. What is open now is narrower and comes from the twelfth guide rather than from the drift. It ends by asking readers to draw their own constellations, and the site gave them nothing to draw on — so The Constellation Sheet was built next and sits in Print : eighty stars, nothing joined, and a blank index on the reverse. It was held back one pass on purpose, so the guest guide could ship as Helen wrote it before we started adding things around it. Naming it here rather than keeping it on a private list is the same practice as everywhere else on this site — the list of what we have not done is part of the record. What the Rest Stands On A Star Stuff collection · eight pieces Every other page here argues about the world. These eight argue about us — what we think belonging is, how we intend to be right, what happens when we aren't, and how the work gets made.

What counts as a foundation A simple test, and it is narrower than it sounds: a foundation is a piece the other pieces presuppose. When a Kin zine says a shark's cartilage is a secondary loss rather than a primitive state, it is leaning on a paradigm it does not stop to restate, an ethic about checking the claim, and a position on why difference is not deficit. Those commitments had to be written down somewhere, once, or every zine would have to relitigate them and none of them would have room left for its actual subject. Which means Foundations is not the important collection and not the hard one . It is the collection whose contents are load-bearing for everything else — and load-bearing is a structural fact, not a compliment.

The one that makes the rest checkable

The one that makes the rest checkable If Foundations has a keystone it is Too Good to Check , because it is the only piece here that can be used against the others. A manifesto cannot be falsified. A creed cannot be falsified. But a claim about piezoelectric bone or a quotation attributed to a named thinker absolutely can, and this site makes several hundred of them. So the essay names the six failure modes, works seventeen real corrections through them, and points at the public record: the changelog in Notes & Rationale , where every error we have caught in our own work is published with what was wrong, what is right, and who caught it. An ethic about facts that produced no visible corrections would be a decoration. Its companion, Who Is Holding the Candle , argues the half underneath it. Checking is one of two modes and fails on its own; and the checker is always a particular person standing somewhere, so “verified” with no verifier named is the same deletion this site spends its time undoing. Read together, one says go back to the primary source and the other says somebody has to go, and it matters who . Not Not required reading. Foundations is what the site leans on, not what you have to read first. Most people should start somewhere else and arrive here later, if at all, when they want to know why a zine was so confident about something. Not scripture. These are positions we hold and argue for, and the manifesto in particular is written to be disagreed with in public. Nothing here is settled by having been declared. Not a code of conduct. The creed is about what belonging is , not a policy document with an enforcement procedure. It names harm as the disqualifier and stops there, because a creed that pretended to be a process would be worse at both jobs. Not a claim to have got it right. The presence of Too Good to Check in this collection is an admission, not a boast — it exists because we shipped a Martin Luther King Jr. line credited to Baldwin, a paraphrase dressed as a Sagan quote, and a forest-wide fungal network asserted as settled fact because it rhymed so well. How We Got Here A Star Stuff collection · 9 pieces One link per spread, from a settled fact in physical science to something that is happening to us now — and the strength of every link printed on its face.

Why we make these To take science back from the things that wear its clothes. Eugenics and behaviourism did not fail because they were too scientific. They took real mathematics — a curve built for observational error, a law of effect measured honestly in cats — and applied it to human beings without the discipline that made it work in the first place . That is what every chain in this collection turns out to be about. Three things get mistaken for science and are its opposite. Pseudo-science , which has none of the method. Scientism , which keeps the authority and drops the practice — the p-value and the phrase evidence-based without the pre-registration, the blinding, the reported harms, the published null. And the smoothed popular retelling , which files off every hedge until a contested finding arrives as a fact, because the tidy version travels further. When those tools get pointed at people, they flatten exactly the variation the science elsewhere insists is real — and they measure the surface, badly . The result is epistemic injustice with a citation attached, which is far harder to answer than a plain insult. So these chains are not arguments against evidence. They are arguments for the parts that got left behind on the way here.

What holds these together This collection sorts by form , not by register — the same odd axis Field Guides sorts on, and we say so here rather than let it read as an oversight. Everywhere else on this site a piece follows one fact down. A chain follows many facts sideways, across a century or two, and what carries the argument is not any single fact but the handoffs between them . The shape comes from James Burke's Connections (BBC, 1978), which Cosmic Connections already names as one of the two lineages inside this site's tagline — the other being Carl Sagan's The Cosmic Connection (1973). Burke's argument is that nothing in the modern world can be understood in isolation, because it was assembled out of centuries of unrelated people solving unrelated problems for reasons of their own, none of them aiming at what they produced. The name is borrowed twice over, and honestly. How did we get here is the title of the paper underneath No. 39 — Randall, Ewing, Marr, Jimenez and Bourouiba's reconstruction of the five-micron myth. We noticed the phrase fit the whole form only after two of these existed.

Why the joints are marked Here is the problem with the form, stated plainly: a chain is built to feel inevitable. Each link arrives just as the last one lands, the story accelerates, and by the end a reader has been persuaded by momentum rather than by evidence. Burke's chains are wonderful and some of his links are frankly loose. This site's standard is to verify everything and to say what we could not verify. Those two things are in direct tension. So the form carries the epistemics instead of a footnote doing it. Every link is claimed at one of three strengths, said in the prose and drawn into the running spine at the foot of each spread: documented There is a source for the causal link itself , not merely for the two things it joins. A supervision, a citation, a person acknowledging the debt in print. contested The connection is argued, inferred, or actively disputed in current scholarship — including by the historians we are relying on. Where they hedge, we hedge. leap We are rhyming, and we say so. A resonance worth drawing that licenses nothing . The star-stuff bridge in No. 39 is tagged this way on purpose. This is not decoration, and the test is whether the mix is real. In No. 38 : six documented, three contested, one leap — and the chain's own founding anecdote is among the contested ones , placed first so the notation is taught on the weakest link rather than the strongest. In No. 39 the load-bearing joint is marked contested because the paper reconstructing it will only call the connection likely , having found no explicit statement of it anywhere in the literature they reviewed.
What every chain here ends up saying

What every chain here ends up saying Nobody authored the road. Not one of the people in these chains was aiming at where it arrived. An astronomer wanted accurate transit times; a bacteriologist wanted to know how far a sneeze goes; an educator wanted children protected from arbitrary marking; an epidemiologist was preparing students for a real threat. Each solved their own problem competently, and could not have seen what it would join up with a century downstream. That is not an excuse — the harm is not smaller for being unintended. It is a route . A thing that was accumulated can be dis-accumulated , one competent adjustment at a time, in the other direction. You do not have to defeat a conspiracy. You have to go back and read the citation.
This page was made at two

This page was made at two Collections here are observed, not planned — the argument Cosmic Connections makes about the whole site. Thirteen collections were noticed only after thirty-five zines had accumulated in no folders at all, and Field Guides waited until there were eleven of them. So this one was deliberately deferred when the first chain shipped, and made when the second arrived with the same shape, the same notation and the same ending — Stars We Grew Up On having carried two numbered zines for months already. Two is the floor here, not a shortcut. The form was found in the work; the folder came after. Three more followed within the day, which is the part worth recording rather than quietly absorbing. The page did not cause them — but it is fair to note that naming a form makes the next instance easier to see, and that is exactly the risk the deferral was guarding against. Nine is not proof the category was real; it is what the category has attracted so far.

The tally, so far Across the nine chains: 84 documented joints, 21 contested, 8 leaps. Nos. 38 and 39 carried one leap and two; Nos. 40 and 41 carried none, and said so in their colophons as something to be suspicious of rather than pleased about; No. 42 restored one. No. 56 runs documented for ten rungs and then spends both of its weak joints in a row, at the end, on the same handoff — which is what an airtight rail and a genuinely uncertain transfer look like when neither is disguised as the other. A notation whose weakest tag never fires is measuring the choice of subject, not the care of the argument. These numbers are counted from the pages rather than remembered — an earlier version of this collection got them wrong, and the correction is in the changelog . The mix is not evenly spread, and the two ends of it are the argument for watching that. No. 52 runs twelve documented, four contested, one leap and carries the most contested joints of any chain here — not because its sourcing is worse but because its subject includes a smoothed retelling, a quarter-century disagreement about what counts as evidence, two elements that turned out not to exist, and an accusation of data selection that took sixty years to answer. A chain with no contested joints is usually a chain that did not look. No. 50 runs eleven documented, one contested, one leap — the highest documented share of any chain here, level with No. 40 , and that is a fact about its subject, not a boast. Its rail is a sequence of published resolutions, a maintained table of leap seconds and a paper in Nature ; a chain built out of minutes and votes is supposed to run documented. The honesty is in where the weak tag lands. The single leap is the step from how a standards body handles its own mismatch to how institutions handle ours, it is the joint the whole zine exists for, and putting the entire weight of the argument on one link that is openly marked as the weakest is the shape this notation was invented to make possible. Not Not a conspiracy genre. The chains here are about accumulation, not design. If a piece in this collection ever reads as though somebody planned the outcome, it has gone wrong — that reading makes the history smaller, and it lets the accumulation off. Not a licence to leap. The tags exist to make weak links visible, not permissible. A chain that needed three leap joints to reach its conclusion would not be publishable here; it would be a different, shorter piece. Not history as inevitability. Every one of these chains contains a moment where somebody could plainly have done otherwise, and often somebody said so at the time and was ignored. Naming those moments is the point. Not finished. Where a source could not be read at the primary, the piece says so on the page and the open item is logged. See the changelog for what we have got wrong and corrected.

The pieces In the order they were made. The number records when ; the collection records what . Zine No. 38 Eight Tenths of a Second Stimpunks Zines on a fired astronomer, a cat in a box, and the road to the dashboard In February 1796 the Astronomer Royal dismissed his assistant for marking star transits eight tenths of a second late. Bessel later showed observers differ irreducibly. 14 spreads → Details In February 1796 the Astronomer Royal dismissed his assistant David Kinnebrook for marking star transits eight tenths of a second late. Bessel later established that observers differ from one another systematically and irreducibly — and astronomy's answer was the personal equation: publish a constant for each observer, build the variation into the model, keep the observer. This zine follows the measuring apparatus out of the observatory: Wundt's laboratory, Cattell's “mental tests,” Thorndike's puzzle boxes and his 1918 credo that whatever exists at all exists in some amount, Kelly's Kansas Silent Reading Test, Pressey's machine built from typewriter parts, Skinner's teaching machines, and Lovaas at UCLA in 1987 — while a second rail runs alongside from Galton through Kraepelin to the DSM. The two meet at a table with a child at it. The first zine built as a Burke-style chain, and every joint is marked documented , contested or leap — six solid, three dashed, one dotted — because two of them are weaker than the story wants. The turn: school found the same human variation astronomy found, and made it the thing to remove. Accommodation is the older answer. Fourteen spreads, twelve diagrams, a running chain spine, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 39 Five Microns Stimpunks Zines on a number that answered a different question, and the room it left you in In March 2020 the WHO posted “FACT: COVID-19 is NOT airborne.” Not a lie — doctrine, faithfully applied, resting on a number that had quietly changed questions. 15 spreads → Details In March 2020 the WHO posted “FACT: COVID-19 is NOT airborne” and called the alternative misinformation. Not a lie — doctrine, faithfully applied, resting on a number that had quietly changed questions. William Wells put the boundary between droplets that fall and droplets that evaporate into lingering nuclei at 100 micrometres , and never wrote 5; his own table gives a 1 µm particle sixteen hours to fall two metres. The 5 µm figure came from industrial hygiene asking which particles reach the deepest lung — deposition, not suspension — and Alexander Langmuir fused the two in 1951, in a lecture preparing public-health students for biological warfare months after Korea began. Randall, Ewing, Marr, Jimenez and Bourouiba reconstructed it in Interface Focus under the title “How did we get here,” and refuse to solder the load-bearing joint, writing only that the deposition focus “likely” popularised the cut-off — so this zine marks it contested too. Meanwhile Flügge's team in Breslau had grown colonies nine metres from a sneeze in the 1890s, meant “droplets” to cover what we now call aerosols, waited five hours before reading their plates, and recommended ventilation. The 1–2 metre rule has its own separate lineage and turns out to match the width of a 1940s camera's field of view. The second chain zine, every joint marked documented , contested or leap . Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a running two-rail spine, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 40 Five Sigma Stimpunks Zines how much evidence is enough before you do something to a child Particle physics will not permit the word “discovery” below five sigma — one chance in three and a half million — and wrote down why. 16 spreads → Details How much evidence is enough before you do something to a child? Particle physics answered that question carefully and wrote it down. It will not permit the word “discovery” below five sigma — a p -value of 3 × 10⁻⁷, one chance in three and a half million — and the reason is empirical rather than principled: too many 3σ and 4σ results kept evaporating. Louis Lyons, whose paper is the spine of this zine, goes further and argues the bar should not be uniform at all, grading it by degree of surprise, impact, look-elsewhere effect and systematics : single top production 3σ, the Higgs 5σ, supersymmetry 7σ, faster-than-light neutrinos above 8σ. He also prints the statisticians' objection that his own gold standard is unsound. Against all that stands p = 0.05 — about 2σ — chosen by Fisher in 1925 with the word convenient , and unexamined since. The gap is roughly 170,000× , and the asymmetry runs backwards: if physics is wrong it retracts a paper and the particle is unharmed; if we are wrong a childhood already happened and there is no more data to collect. Run Lyons' four dials on an intervention and every one reads high — then the systematics column turns out to be empty, because 150 intervention studies for young Autistic children produced 11 that mentioned adverse events at all. Not an argument against science. An argument against scientism, which keeps the authority and drops the practice. The first chain here with no leap joints . Sixteen spreads, fourteen diagrams, two rails that never meet, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 41 A Conquering Gaze from Nowhere Stimpunks Zines parallax, positionality, and the research done on us For roughly two centuries the strongest objection to a moving Earth was that the stars showed no parallax. The reasoning was valid, and the conclusion wrong. 15 spreads → Details For roughly two centuries the strongest objection to a moving Earth was that the stars showed no parallax. The reasoning was valid, the observations careful, and the conclusion wrong — partly because the distances required seemed absurd, and partly because telescopic star discs are an artefact of the aperture rather than a property of stars. Then in 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured 61 Cygni at 0.3136 arcseconds from Königsberg — a two-centimetre coin seen from thirteen kilometres. The method carries the whole argument: the baseline is the observer's own displacement across Earth's orbit, so a viewpoint with no location has no baseline, no angle and no depth. A view from nowhere cannot measure distance even in principle ; it is the blindest available position. And it is the same Bessel, at the same observatory, who gave us the personal equation in No. 38 — twice showing that knowledge requires a located, particular observer. Every rung of the cosmic distance ladder above parallax is calibrated by the one beneath, and rung two — the period–luminosity relation — was built by Henrietta Swan Leavitt , employed as a Harvard “computer,” paid by the hour, not permitted to observe, and published under her director's name: “has been prepared by Miss Leavitt.” That is the third woman in three chains to do the work and lose the byline, and the zine stops to name all three. Donna Haraway gave the fantasy its name in 1988 — the god trick, the unmarked category claiming the power to see and not be seen — and her positive claim is the one usually dropped: only partial perspective promises objective vision . She refuses relativism just as flatly, calling it “a way of being nowhere while claiming to be everywhere equally.” Then the numbers: 96% of behavioural-science samples from Western industrialised nations, 68% from the US, reported as facts about humans. Then research done on Autistic people rather than with them, and double empathy as a finding that only exists because somebody stood at the other end of the baseline. The correction is neither removing the observer nor declaring all views equal: publish your coordinates. Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a single rail with a marked baseline, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 42 Look for the Air Stimpunks Zines two thousand years spent deleting character from the explanation, and the industry that put it back Aristotle explained motion by what a thing is . It is not a foolish theory — go outside and test it and every prediction checks out. 14 spreads → Details Aristotle's physics explained motion by what a thing is : heavy bodies fall because it is in their nature to seek the centre, faster in proportion to weight, slower in a denser medium. It is not a foolish theory — go outside and test it and every prediction checks out, because everyday observation happens in air. The error is where the explanation was put . Galileo showed the rule contradicts itself (tie a heavy body to a light one and it predicts both faster and slower), rolled balls down inclined planes, and made the strange move of reasoning about a fall with no medium at all — while the famous Leaning Tower demonstration turns out to come from a biography written decades later and is marked contested here. Newton finished it: acceleration is set by the forces acting plus one scalar property, and disposition disappears. Then, on 2 August 1971, David Scott released a geology hammer and a falcon feather together in the lunar vacuum and they landed together, on film. The difference was never in the feather. It was in the air. This chain argues that mindset marketing runs that two-thousand-year move backwards on children. Behaviourism looks like it made the same move but stopped one ring short — it deleted the interior and still left the child as the only adjustable thing. California's task force commissioned its own research, was told the associations between self-esteem and its expected consequences were “mixed, insignificant, or absent,” and shipped in 1990 regardless. Growth mindset fails the same way across 63 studies and 97,672 participants, with higher-quality studies less likely to show benefit — and Dweck and Duckworth both objected to the deployment while it kept growing. The dashboard completes it: a schema with fields for effort, focus and behaviour points, and no field for the room. Along the way the zine corrects its own source — the famous Eric Hoffer line about a movement becoming a business and degenerating into a racket is a misquotation that invents a moral arc he never wrote. It closes on scarcity and slack, on equity literacy, and on the first leap joint since No. 39, marked because it is the sentence a reader most wants to be true. Fourteen spreads, twelve diagrams, two rails running in opposite directions, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 43 The Elimination of Waste Stimpunks Zines on a word that meant one thing in a steam engine and another in a school In 1824 Sadi Carnot proved a heat engine has a hard, provable ceiling on its efficiency — and that waste heat is not sloppiness, it is the fee. 15 spreads → Details In 1824 Sadi Carnot proved something strange: that a heat engine has a hard, provable ceiling on its efficiency, set only by the two temperatures available and beatable by no engineer who ever lives. And with it came the result that matters here — waste heat is not sloppiness, it is the fee. An engine with nowhere to dump it does not run at all. So “eliminate all waste” isn't an ambitious goal not yet reached; in thermodynamics it names the one outcome that is ruled out. (He reached this from caloric theory, which was wrong — Clausius and Kelvin supplied the formula later, so “Carnot derived the efficiency equation” is itself a smoothed retelling, and the joint is marked contested.) Then the word left the engine room, and what it shed in transit was the ceiling. Frederick Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management appeared in 1911, and Raymond Callahan's Education and the Cult of Efficiency (1962) dates what followed to the month: in July 1911, one month after Taylor's American Magazine series concluded, a school board member told the NEA that “scientific management” held a message for every teacher — and that if teachers did not voluntarily increase their efficiency, the business world would force them to. By 1916 Cubberley's textbook was listing what schools must take from the factory: good tools, specialized machinery, continuous measurement of production, and “the elimination of waste in manufacture.” Ninety-two years after Carnot, the phrase arrives in a book about children as a specification. By 1912 an educator was already complaining that teachers were “curiously protected in inefficiency.” And the question nobody asked sits in Callahan's own parenthesis: would Schmidt, the pig-iron handler, have agreed that science had reduced his fatigue? It ends at spoon theory — and then spends an entire spread arguing that this argument should not need physics at all , because you are not a heat engine and deriving rest from thermodynamics is precisely the move the collection condemns. Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a spine that crosses its own ceiling, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 50 The Sky Was Not Regular Enough Stimpunks Zines on cutting a standard loose from the thing it measured, and whether you say so out loud Until 1960 a second was one 86,400th of a day, and the definition pointed at the sky. Then the instrument became steadier than the thing it measured. 16 spreads → Details Until 1960 a second was a piece of a day — one 86,400th of it — and the definition pointed at something . Not a prototype in a vault, but the sky: you could check it against a star. Then quartz clocks arrived and, for the first time in the history of measurement, the instrument was steadier than the Earth. Scheibe and Adelsberger reported the seasonal wobble in 1936; Stoyko put it at about two milliseconds in 1937. The Earth was never irregular to itself — it became irregular the moment we had something steadier to compare it to. So the tie was cut, twice. In 1956 the second became a fraction of the tropical year 1900 , a year that had already ended and could never be re-measured; in 1967 it became 9,192,631,770 caesium transitions, and after that the definition points at no day, no year, no sky at all. Every one of those moves was an improvement, and this zine says so — the collection exists to reclaim science, not to indict it. Since 1972 the gap between the atomic standard and the turning planet has been closed in public by leap seconds: 27 of them, first on 30 June 1972, last on 31 December 2016, and none since, because the Earth started spinning faster and the correction now due is a negative leap second that has never been tested. Duncan Agnew showed in Nature in 2024 that melting Greenland and Antarctic ice slowed the spin enough to postpone it from 2026 to 2029 — climate change bought the world's timekeepers three years, and he refuses to call that good news. Resolution 4 of the 27th CGPM decided in 2022 to widen the tolerance by 2035, and the implementing vote is at the 28th CGPM this October ; the proposal is a leap hour. The argument: a leap second is not a bug but an honesty mechanism — a standards body saying in public, on a named date, with a number attached, that its standard and the world disagree by exactly this much. Abolishing it is defensible engineering. What it costs is the announcement. And that is the one thing carried across to us, marked leap because caesium licenses nothing about a person: an accommodation is a leap second, and the objections to it arrive in the same order — it's irregular, it breaks the system, everybody handles it differently — with the same proposed remedy, widen the tolerance and stop announcing. Ends at processing speed and crip time: the Earth is not slow, the second left. Eleven documented joints, one contested, one leap. Sixteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a running spine that is a plot of its own data, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 52 We Learned to Build the Eclipse Stimpunks Zines on an element nobody would accept because it could not be put on a bench, and on the day we stopped travelling to the Moon's shadow A chain about how a whole branch of physics stopped waiting for the Moon — the corona, for most of astronomy's history available only during totality. 21 spreads → Details A chain about how a whole branch of physics stopped waiting for the Moon. The Sun’s outer atmosphere is always there and almost never available: the photosphere drowns it, so for most of astronomy’s history the corona and the prominences could only be studied during totality — a few minutes, roughly every eighteen months, along a track a few hundred kilometres wide, usually somewhere difficult, and one cloud ended the expedition. It begins in 1604, where pinhole solar diameters came out systematically too large and nobody could say why until Kepler supplied the theory of how an image forms behind a small hole: the method came first and worked badly; the understanding came second and fixed it. Then Guntur, 18 August 1868, where several observers caught a yellow line near sodium’s — and where what Janssen actually took away was not the line but its brightness . The next morning he observed the prominences again with no eclipse at all , spreading the sky’s glare thin with dispersion while the emission line stayed put. Lockyer, who had wanted this since 1866 and was blocked by glass rather than by ideas, got there on 20 October; both reports reached the Académie within days and it struck a medal for the pair — for the method . Neither report flagged the yellow line, which is the first of four contested joints: the famous sentence “helium was discovered during an eclipse in 1868” is wrong in almost every part, and what the compression deletes is years of argument. Lockyer alone later called it D3 and proposed an element; for a quarter century chemists refused it, not because the spectroscopy was faulty but because nobody could put the gas on a bench — and a thing visible only in light from 150 million kilometres away did not, to them, count as a thing. They were rigorous and they were wrong, and the zine insists on both, because the same method also produced two elements that were never there : coronium and nebulium, dissolved by Bowen in 1927 and Grotrian and Edlén in 1939 and 1942 as forbidden lines of ordinary oxygen and iron — which is also how we learned the corona is millions of degrees hotter than the surface. Ramsay got helium out of cleveite on 26 March 1895, twenty-seven years late, and it had been underfoot the whole time. Then the chain runs downhill , because capability is specific: in 1919 the Moon was needed again to see whether starlight bends, the Sobral astrograph plates were set aside, Earman and Glymour charged Eddington with seeing what he wanted, and Kennefick later established that the call was Dyson’s and that the plates could only agree with Newton if the instrument had also changed magnification — a reason to distrust them other than what they said , which is the whole difference between rejecting bad data and rejecting inconvenient data. Finally Bernard Lyot, chasing stray light up a mountain, photographed the corona with no eclipse on 12 July 1931: an eclipse at a time and place of human choosing, turning minutes per expedition into hours per clear day. We now fly manufactured occulters at other stars. The transfer, marked leap because it is one , refuses the obvious framing first: eclipses were computed years ahead, so the difficulty was never luck but a structural condition — the observation existing only there, only then, with the ocean, the freight, the years and the weather all charged to whoever needed it. An expedition demonstrates what is required and is a catastrophe as a delivery mechanism. So there are three states, not two: reach it, ask for it, or have it — and the middle one is what we named accommodation , which is the word Stimpunks' own page exists to criticise, since the problem is structural and the response is individual. Lyot did not apply for access to the corona; he built an instrument in which it is simply there, and the occulting disc is not a concession but where the precision comes from . Which is a curb cut: Michael Pachovas and friends poured cement into a crude ramp one Berkeley evening and rolled off into the night, and Berkeley cut its first official kerb on Telegraph Avenue in 1972 — while the sledgehammer version of that story is disability lore, not history , which a chain that spends a spread on smoothed retellings could not close on. Angela Glover Blackwell named the curb-cut effect in 2017, and the zine states plainly that it is an observation about what built-in conditions do and never the justification . Twenty-one spreads, twelve documented joints, four contested, one leap, a generated spine, and a “Not:” set that refuses the reading that barriers are valuable for what they reveal. A rhyme, not a proof. Zine No. 56 The Noise Floor Stimpunks Zines every receiver has one, no design removes it, and the biggest discovery in modern cosmology arrived as noise two engineers spent ten months trying to get rid of A chain about a limit nobody beats, and the rooms we build as though it were free. Johnson and Nyquist, printed on facing pages in 1928. 15 spreads → Details A chain about a limit nobody beats, and the rooms we build as though it were free. In July 1928 one volume of Physical Review printed the measurement and its explanation on facing pages — J. B. Johnson at 97–109, H. Nyquist at 110–113, whose first footnote is three words long: “See preceding paper.” Every conductor above absolute zero hisses, and Nyquist’s conclusion is that the effect is “a universal function of frequency, resistance and temperature and of these variables only” — not the metal, not the workmanship, since “one may be made of silver and the other of lead.” The available power in a band is kTB , and that is in the primary rather than a modern gloss on it. The part that usually goes missing is why it cannot be engineered away. Nyquist did not measure the floor, he deduced it — from the second law. Two resistors at one temperature must pass equal power both ways in every band, or a resonant circuit between them would move heat between equal-temperature bodies for free. The hiss is not permitted, it is required : a silent resistor would be a perpetual-motion machine , which is the same law that says you cannot un-stir the milk from the tea — and nobody files that under insufficient effort. Twenty years on, Shannon’s Theorem 17 turns the floor into a limit on meaning , with the sentence that closes the door: “It is not possible to transmit at a higher rate by any encoding system without a definite positive frequency of errors.” You cannot filter your way to clarity , and that is a theorem rather than a complaint. So engineering stopped hunting for a quieter resistor and changed the question: cool it, shield it, narrow the band — three moves, none of which asks the receiver to beat physics, all of which change the conditions the listening happens in. Which is exactly the instrument at Holmdel, where a maser and a reference load both sat in liquid helium at 4.2 K — a floor lowered deliberately so a remainder would mean something. A remainder was left: 3.5 ± 1.0 K, and the paper is mostly a list of what it was not, down to taping the seams with aluminium and walking a transmitter to ten positions on the ground. The pigeon story is corrected against its primary, and the correction is better than the version that travels: Wilson wrote that evicting them “obtained only a small reduction in antenna temperature” — the floor survived them, and that clause is the one that gets cut. The famous phrase “white dielectric material” is not in his Nobel lecture, and the birds are not in the 1965 paper at all. What could not be removed was “isotropic, unpolarized, and free from seasonal variations (July, 1964-April, 1965)” , and every property that made it impossible to eliminate is a property that made it the universe. Then the 1928 shape repeats mirrored — theory at 414–419, measurement at 419–421, thirty-seven years on. The most consequential discovery in modern cosmology arrived as noise two engineers spent ten months trying to get rid of. Meanwhile the transfer to rooms turns out not to be ours to make: ANSI/ASA S12.60 caps classroom background at 35 dBA because the profession already calls the quantity signal to noise ratio and wants about 15 dB of it — and its instruction is to lower the floor rather than amplify the teacher. Wilkins halved headaches by removing 100 Hz fluorescent flicker, with his own caveat that the harm fell on “a minority that is particularly affected” ; Kim and de Dear found sound privacy the largest source of dissatisfaction in any building, and found open plan bought no more ease of interaction than a private office. The last two joints refuse to overclaim, on the page rather than in a footnote: the step to Autistic auditory experience is contested — there is no k for a nervous system — carried by Remington and Fairnie’s finding of increased auditory capacity, one mechanism producing both the distress and the ability, and by Rosas-Pérez’s 2026 acoustics thesis, in which no Autistic respondent among 311 noise-sensitive people found filtering easy — printed with her caveat that the whole sample was already sensitive. Her other finding is where the zine says the analogy breaks, and the break is worth more than the resemblance: no habituation, but an accumulation effect. Thermal noise is stationary; kTB is the same in the tenth hour as the first. The human pattern is cumulative. A resistor never gets tired of being warm — so the floor in a room is crueller than the floor in a circuit, not merely like it. Which also means “you’ll get used to it” is testable, and the exposure hypothesis under it rests on five participants, none noise-sensitive, and two pure tones. The closing analogy is leap , because physics entails nothing about who deserves a quiet room. What it does is remove an excuse. Fifteen spreads, ten documented joints, one contested, one leap, a spine the page calls schematic rather than letting it pass for a plot, and a coda pointing at the practice already written down. Kin A Star Stuff collection · 6 pieces Our relatives, read against the primary literature — and the reflexes that make us disown them.

What holds these together These are natural-history essays, read against the primary literature and written slowly. A crab-like body plan that really did evolve at least five separate times — and was lost at least seven. A shark skeleton that is cartilage not because it never got to bone but because its lineage secondarily lost it, which makes the textbook reading of “primitive” not merely loaded but false. A vertebrate that does not reach maturity until it is about 156 years old. Turtles, everywhere that turtles go. A pilot whale carrying roughly twice our count of neocortical neurons, under a ranking that outlived its evidence. Every one of them ends somewhere about us, and none of them starts there. The creature is not a metaphor waiting to be cashed in; it is an animal with a literature, and the moral has to survive the reading.

Why disgust belongs here The Ick Is a Border is the odd one, and it is the hinge. The other five are about relatives. This one is about the reflex that makes us disown them — disgust, which feels like a fact about the animal and is a fact about the frame. Rozin & Fallon (1987) treat it as a food emotion at root, whose objects are largely learned. A collection of kin needs the piece about how kinship gets refused. Its siblings elsewhere on the site are the Field Guides to Being a Shark , a Turtle and a Tortoise — same register, different form. Not Not the animal as mascot. No creature here is a costume for a human point, and none of them is inspirational. Not “nature says so.” That a body plan recurs, or that a shark lives four centuries, licenses no conclusion about how anyone ought to be treated. The argument for belonging is an ethical one; the animals are why we noticed.

The pieces In the order they were made. The number records when ; the collection records what . Zine No. 31 Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not Stimpunks Zines convergence, attractors, and the ones who crawled back out of the valley The crab-like body plan really did evolve at least five times, which is the part everyone quotes. Written after Brett D. Wick's When Everything Becomes a Crab . 12 spreads → Details Convergent evolution and “attractors,” read against the primary literature — written after Brett D. Wick's essay When Everything Becomes a Crab . The crab-like body plan really did evolve at least five times in decapod crustaceans, which is the part everyone quotes. It was also lost at least seven times — decarcinization, the commoner event — and Wolfe, Luque & Bracken-Grissom ( BioEssays , 2021) report that the reasons for the recurrence remain a mystery , with carcinized lineages running from millimetres to metres across nearly every habitat on Earth. So convergence produced no sameness, and the basin is not a destiny. Our eye and the octopus's converged on the same camera and were built backwards from each other, which is why a system that grades the route instead of the outcome will fail an eye. Waddington's canalized landscape gives the picture; “attractor” is named as a metaphor borrowed from dynamical systems. Then the turn: nature's basin permits the millions who never roll in, while engineered systems write the attractor into the rules — engagement chosen as the objective and everything downhill of it becoming vertical video, one route to the answer and a diagnosis for the others. Cavendish monoculture against Cavendish Space, on the ARLES Environment and Systems rungs. Ideas ripen the same way: Ogburn & Thomas's 148 multiples, Merton's singletons-are-the-exception, Tao's “maths at internet speed,” and Brian Eno's scenius quoted from the 1996 primary rather than the altered version in circulation. Closes on our own history — neurodiversity was itself developed collectively. Gould and Conway Morris are left unresolved on purpose. A rhyme, not a proof. Zine No. 32 The Skeleton That Skipped Bone Stimpunks Zines sharks, tesserae, and what happens to a body once somebody decides it's a cure Sharks, rays and chimaeras are vertebrates with no true bone at all. A companion and a counter-song to Bone Song . 12 spreads → Details A companion and a counter-song to Bone Song , written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. This collection opens on a skeleton that is piezoelectric — press it and it makes voltage. Sharks, rays and chimaeras are vertebrates with no true bone at all : a cartilage skeleton stiffened by thousands of mineral tiles called tesserae, which Dean & Summers ( Zoology , 2006) describe as tuned species by species and even to how the animal feeds. Then the finding that changes the story. Sharks were taught for a century as the before picture — cartilage first, bone later, primitive, not there yet. But Brazeau and colleagues ( Nature Ecology & Evolution , 2020) describe endochondral bone in Minjinia turgenensis , an Early Devonian fish near the common ancestry of jawed vertebrates. If the shared ancestor had bone, the shark's bonelessness is not a failure to arrive — it is a loss , derived rather than primitive, and the same shape of fact as the crab body plan being lost more often than gained. Which exposes the verdict buried in the word primitive , the same one hiding in low-functioning and delayed . Then the other half: because sharks were said not to get cancer, their cartilage was ground into pills. Ostrander et al. ( Cancer Research , 2004) documented 42 chondrichthyan tumours across at least 21 species, at least 15 malignant; Loprinzi et al. ( Cancer , 2005) ran the trial and found no benefit to survival or quality of life. A body read as a cure gets harvested — and extraction always starts as appreciation. The skeleton is for the animal. A rhyme, not a proof. Zine No. 33 The Ick Is a Border Stimpunks Zines bone-eating worms, fused fish, a whale that becomes a town — and the reflex that rules bodies out Disgust feels like a fact about the animal. It is a fact about the frame — Rozin & Fallon (1987) treat its objects as largely learned. 13 spreads → Details Disgust feels like a fact about the animal. It is a fact about the frame. Rozin & Fallon ( Psychological Review , 1987) treat disgust as a food emotion at root, whose objects are largely learned — arriving across a child's first eight years and running on the magical law of contagion, where one touch renders a whole plate inedible forever. A reaction that far out of proportion to any physical fact is a rule about categories, and rules about categories are taught. Then three arrangements that read as gross and are, in frame, simply competent. Osedax , the bone-eating worm (Rouse, Goffredi & Vrijenhoek, Science , 2004): no mouth, no gut, a vascularised root system dissolving whale bone, dozens of dwarf males inside the female's tube. The deep-sea anglerfishes, whose fused males cost them their immunity — Swann, Holland, Petersen, Pietsch & Boehm ( Science , 2020) found loss of functional aicda , and in permanent attachment loss of rag , abolishing the hallmark of adaptive immunity. To stay joined to another body they gave up the machinery that tells self from not-self. And the whale fall (Smith & Baco, 2003): a pulse of food worth roughly 2,000 years of background supply, a sulphophilic stage lasting decades, a mean of 185 macrofaunal species — richer than any other hard surface down there. Then the turn. The same reflex fires at feeding tubes, drooling, stimming, incontinence and AAC; Nussbaum calls it projective disgust , where a group of people becomes a buffer against the animal nature we would rather deny. Two frames to widen past — the neuronormative and the anthronormative. A house companion to Helen Edgar's Wyrd & Weird : weird was reclaimed, gross gets disarmed. Nobody is guilty of a flinch; everyone is answerable for the two seconds after. Zine No. 34 Two Hundred Years Before You're Grown Stimpunks Zines the oldest vertebrate we know of, and the question of who is holding the calendar The Greenland shark does not reach maturity until it is about 156 years old. Nielsen et al. ( Science , 2016) radiocarbon-dated the eye lenses of 28 females. 13 spreads → Details The Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate known, and it does not reach maturity until it is about 156 years old . Nielsen et al. ( Science , 2016) radiocarbon-dated the eye lenses of 28 females — the lens core is laid down before birth and never replaced, so they read each animal's age against the atmospheric bomb pulse from 1950s nuclear testing — and found a life span of at least 272 years, the largest animal at 392 ± 120. It is also the slowest fish for its size: 0.34 m/s, one tail-beat every seven seconds (Watanabe et al., 2012), and it eats seals anyway, apparently by arriving quietly while they sleep — the strategy needs the trait . Nearly all of them carry a copepod clamped to the cornea, and it costs them almost nothing, because vision is not what the Arctic deep asks for. So late turns out to be a comparison, not a measurement; the ruler was always the variable. But this is not a zine about slow being beautiful: Nielsen's own paper raises the conservation alarm, because an animal needing a century and a half to reproduce cannot recover from pressure arriving in decades, and the species is IUCN Vulnerable. Slow is survivable or it isn't, and the environment decides — which is the social model of disability, stated in fish. Names the standard defence of the clock too: Alfie Kohn's BGUTI , "Better Get Used To It," which almost by definition ignores developmental differences — and cannot survive noticing them. A rhyme, not a proof. Zine No. 35 Everywhere That Turtles Go Stimpunks Zines range, kinship, and the animal every people had to think with A Star Dreaming that “goes everywhere that turtles go — and there are turtles all over the world.” That reads like a figure of speech and is not. 13 spreads → Details Tyson Yunkaporta writes in Sand Talk that a Star Dreaming Oldman Juma Fejo of the Larrakia People wants to share with all peoples "goes everywhere that turtles go — and there are turtles all over the world, even in desert country, so it connects everybody." That reads like a figure of speech and is actually a range map, so we checked it: roughly 357 species on every continent but Antarctica, in every warm ocean, and in the arid interior, where Chelodina steindachneri buries itself in a dry Pilbara riverbed and waits out a year without water. The primary literature then reverses the obvious reading twice. Lyson et al. ( Current Biology , 2016) find the shell began as an adaptation for burrowing, not armour — broadened ribs "provide little protection" and cost you speed and breath; protection is a later exaptation. And Lyson et al. ( Nature Communications , 2014) find the price: lock your ribs into a shell and you lose the ordinary way of breathing, so turtles run their lungs off a sling of abdominal muscle instead. Side-necks and hidden-necks answered one problem two ways. Sex is set by the temperature of the sand, not by chromosomes — which makes the Discworld philosophers' failed expedition to determine Great A'Tuin's sex a better joke than they knew. A hatchling learns the magnetic field of one beach and finds it again decades later. And every people had to think with this animal: Turtle Island, ao in the Huainanzi , Kurma — who is a pivot for churning and not a world-bearer — and Great A'Tuin. They are not the same turtle, and that is the connection. Carries the Fibonacci passage and says plainly where it stops being biology. ~48% of turtle species are threatened. A rhyme, not a proof. Zine No. 36 The Layer We Call Essential Stimpunks Zines cetacean brains, the missing layer IV, and a ranking that outlived its evidence The long-finned pilot whale's neocortex holds roughly 37.2 billion neurons — the first animal ever counted above us. Then, in the same paper, the conclusion turns. 13 spreads → Details Mortensen et al. ( Frontiers in Neuroanatomy , 2014) counted the long-finned pilot whale's neocortex and found roughly 37.2 billion neurons — "almost twice as many neocortical neurons as humans," the first animal ever counted above us. Then, in the same paper, they conclude that absolute neuron number is "not correlated with the superior cognitive abilities of humans." The yardstick came back against us and the ranking survived, because it was never resting on the count . Underneath sits the architecture: the cetacean neocortex is agranular, with layer IV — the input layer our textbooks call canonical — absent or underdeveloped , and layer I apparently taking the job instead, giving "a very different connectivity scheme compared to more commonly studied species, like rats and macaque monkeys." Manger (2006) read that missing layer as evidence there is no neural basis for complex cognition in cetaceans ; sixteen authors replied in Biological Reviews that these features are "a non-primate route to neuroanatomical (and cognitive) complexity." Difference read as deficit, conducted by neuroscientists, about whales. Held with care: thermogenesis is a serious hypothesis and a brain can do heat work and thought work at once — the claim here is only about which reading you get for free. On neurodiversity, the honest answer: there is no cetacean diagnostic literature and this zine does not invent one. What exists is variation inside single populations — sponging in 15 of 141 known Shark Bay mothers, down one matriline (Krützen et al., 2005), spongers more solitary and foraging longer (Mann et al., 2008) — read through ethodiversity (Ombre Tarragnat), which needs no clinic. Plus 8,719 sperm whale codas resolving into ~143 combinations where 21 had been described, because someone borrowed rubato from music. And eight days off Pico with an S-spined bottlenose dolphin among sperm whales, the rubs returned — a paper titled "Repeated Non-Agonistic Interactions," because "adopted" was the press's word. Douglas Adams got the joke in 1979, ranking us third behind the mice. Then he went to see the baiji. A rhyme, not a proof.
