More Than Human A Star Stuff collection · 7 pieces Neurodiversity, de-anthropocentrized. Biodiversity contains ethodiversity contains neurodiversity.

What holds these together Neurodiversity is usually argued at human scale. These pieces refuse that ceiling. Following Ombre Tarragnat's ethodiversity — the variety of ways of being and behaving across all beings with a nervous system — the nesting runs biodiversity ⊃ ethodiversity ⊃ neurodiversity . Not a rainforest but a chorus: ways of being, all of them whole. So: the tick's three signals and the mantis shrimp's light, each a complete world rather than a partial version of ours. A council where soil, river, beaver and meadow all get a chair. Organisms that don't merely adapt to a fixed environment but build the environment that then shapes them. The octopus's mind distributed down its arms, the jellyfish's centreless net — no standard nervous system, not across species and not within one. And one population of sea otters that, put under pressure, fans out into individual specialists rather than converging on an average otter — with the ones who carry a stone keeping their teeth for it. And a freshwater polyp with no brain at all that sleeps anyway, and needs to, which is where any account of rest as something earned runs out of ledger.

A declared trilogy The Council of All Beings , Every Creature's Own Sky and Minor Worlds are a loose trilogy, and Minor Worlds says so itself: how we treat other worlds, how we sense them, and then how we build them. They are kept together and in that order here. Not Not the wood-wide-web overreach. Mycorrhizal symbiosis — fungus and root trading minerals for sugar — is settled and ours to use. The forest-wide story is not: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema ( Nature Ecology & Evolution , 2023) find the prevalence of common mycorrhizal networks and their benefit to seedlings insufficiently supported, and find no published evidence that elder trees preferentially feed their own offspring. We keep the kinship and name the contested part. It rhymes beautifully with mutual aid, which is exactly why it slipped past us in three pieces before we caught it. Not speaking for other beings. Giving a creature a chair is not the same as claiming to know what it would say.

The pieces In the order they were made. The number records when ; the collection records what . Zine No. 5 Underground Stimpunks Zines on mycelial networks, decomposition, and the quiet dark where we do our realest work — the below to Bone Song's above The mycelial worldview as an act of love. Six spreads with a prose poem, diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and reflection questions. 6 spreads → Details Six spreads, and the below to Bone Song 's above. The mycelial network and the oldest anarchist in the room; decomposition as bricolage, where nothing is wasted, only waiting; the prose poem; the quiet and the dark; and the line the zine turns on — the work that changes everything is the work no one is watching. It ends on mischief and punk. Diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and reflection questions. On the science, it keeps the kinship and drops the overclaim: mycorrhizal symbiosis is well established, and the popular wood-wide-web picture of forests wired together is named as contested, citing Karst, Jones & Hoeksema ( Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023). Zine No. 14 The Council of All Beings Stimpunks Zines on multispecies justice, more-than-human governance, and the star stuff that convenes Every being at the table is forged from the same stellar matter, so the Council is the universe convening with itself — and you cannot rank what you are made of. 9 spreads → Details Multispecies justice and more-than-human governance, read as star stuff. Every being at the table — soil, river, beaver, cuckoo, meadow — is forged from the same stellar matter, so the Council of All Beings is the universe convening with itself, and you cannot rank what you are made of. Carries the ethodiversity thread from No. 8 outward: the cosmos varies not only in what it makes but in how its creatures live. Six spreads of argument, then a hydrofeminist coda — the “service provider” critique and the four dimensions of justice, ethodiversity and ethonormativity after Tarragnat, the role-play method (speaking as the soil and the river), the proxy problem and the Umwelt, and Rights of Nature meeting hydrofeminism at Te Awa Tupua, closing on a coda where the council dissolves into flow. Nine spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 15 Every Creature's Own Sky Stimpunks Zines on umwelt, attention-worlds, and why there was never a neutral way to sense Every creature is sealed in its own complete perceptual world — the tick's three signals, the bat's echo, the dog's scent-time — and each world is whole. 8 spreads → Details Umwelt as star stuff. Every creature is sealed in its own complete perceptual world — the tick's three signals, the bat's echo, the mantis shrimp's light, the dog's scent-time — and each world is whole, not a partial view of one real world underneath. There is no neutral, default way to sense. The animals do the arguing, so that when minds enter, the point lands as recognition: monotropism is an attention-world, Autistic perception a different and complete sky, not a broken copy of a standard one. And when two worlds meet — human and bat, one mind and another — the gap is mutual: the double empathy problem, arrived at without lecturing. Not one correct channel, but mutual translation. Carries the Umwelt thread from No. 14 inward, from von Uexküll through Tarragnat, Manning, Milton, and Despret. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 16 Minor Worlds Stimpunks Zines on niche construction, stimming, and how difference doesn't just see a world — it builds one Organisms don't just adapt to a fixed environment; they remake it — the beaver's dam, the spider's web — and pass the built world on. 8 spreads → Details Niche construction as star stuff, and the third of a loose trilogy — how we treat other worlds (No. 14), how we sense them (No. 15), and here, how we build them. Organisms don't just adapt to a fixed environment; they remake it — the beaver's dam, the spider's web — and pass the built world on as ecological inheritance. So the neurodiversity turn is plain: don't fix the mind, change the environment (positive niche construction — there is no “normal” brain in a vat). Stimming is worldmaking; minor worlds and niche communities are real, not lesser; and no niche is neutral — the “default” room was built for one kind of mind, so the fix is reconstruction, not accommodation. Grounded in Odling-Smee & Laland, Armstrong, Tarragnat, Manning, Kadodia & Krueger, and Haraway, and rooted in Stimpunks' own glossary. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 27 Every Nervous System Stimpunks Zines on more-than-human neurodiversity, and the animality we reclaim There is no standard nervous system — not across species, and not within one. Read neurodiversity literally and it never stopped at us. 8 spreads → Details More-than-human neurodiversity, read through star stuff. There is no standard nervous system — not across species, and not within one: the octopus's mind distributed down its arms, the jellyfish's centreless nerve net, the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons. Read neurodiversity literally and it never stopped at the human. Following Ombre Tarragnat's antispeciesist–posthumanist philosophy: there's “no valid reason to be anthropocentric when you talk about neurodiversity,” and ethodiversity — behaviour reclaimed as “a subjective response to a bodymind's situation” — is a fundamentally animal phenomenon. Ethonormativity punishes the ethodivergent (the horse who refuses the rider, the cat who resists petting — abandoned or euthanised). And the core move: neurodivergent people are pathologised by being animalised, so the liberation is to reclaim animality — not bestialisation (the speciesist, neuronormative “less-than-human” split, after Butler 2020) but (hum)animality, kin. Distance is not disconnection: shutting down can be how we keep relation. Every nervous system is the universe wired up to feel itself, no two ever the same. “I would rather be a divergent animal than a typical human.” Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 58 The Stone You Keep Guest zine · after Helen Edgar on otters, monotropism, and the measurable advantage of being specifically yourself One otter population under pressure fans out into individual specialists, each measurably better at its own prey. Some carry a stone and some never do — and the ones with the stone keep their teeth. 10 spreads → Details Developed after Helen Edgar's essay on the otter cam that runs every Saturday at Solidarity Sesh, where nobody has to watch and that is the part that makes it work. Then past the essay to the papers. Tinker, Bentall & Estes (2008) followed one sea otter population closely enough to tell the individuals apart: where food was scarce it did not converge on one best way to be an otter but fanned out into distinct specialists — snails, clams, urchins, crabs — each with a matched suite of diving behaviours, and each measurably better at its own prey than a generalist. The averaged otter forages nowhere. Hall & Schaller (1964) counted the blows: a mussel took a mean of 35.5, and a range of 6 to 88, so there is no correct number of blows, only yours. Law et al. (2024), across 196 tagged otters, found tool use varies enormously between individuals and that non-users are not behind — they specialise on prey a stone would not help with — while the tool users showed less tooth damage. The accommodation is legible in the skeleton. Also: no blubber, the densest coat measured on any mammal and varying sixfold across one body, a resting metabolism three times what its size predicts from heat leaking out of its own muscle since birth — the calm surface is not the whole cost. They rest in rafts wrapped in kelp, so the holding is done by the forest rather than by anyone's effort; and the kelp is there because the otters are (Estes & Palmisano 1974). Held by what it sustains. Then the fur trade took ninety-nine per cent of them, because they were remarkable, not because they were deficient. Ten spreads, eight diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set of seven that declines cute, inspiring, superpower, rest-to-produce, and the smoothed retellings. Zine No. 59 The Rest You Keep With Helen Edgar · companion to No. 58 on Autistic rest, monotropism, burnout — and the ledger that was never there Hydra has no brain and it sleeps — and deprive it of sleep and its cells stop dividing properly. Rest is not a reward released after enough work. It is older than the machinery of earning. 11 spreads → Details Built with Helen Edgar from her essay Reclaiming Rest: Autistic Burnout, Monotropism, and Resistance , whose inversion is the centre of the zine: rest that fights your attention is not rest, and recovery for monotropic people often means going deeper rather than switching off. Then past the essays to the papers. Kanaya et al. (2020) showed that Hydra vulgaris — a nerve net, no brain, nothing gathering it into a decision-maker — meets the behavioural criteria for sleep: it goes quiescent, it is harder to rouse, and after deprivation it rebounds. Deprive it further and the number of dividing cells drops, so rest is when the building happens rather than a pause in it. It also has no circadian clock: under constant conditions the daily rhythm vanishes and a roughly four-hour cycle remains, returning and returning. Great frigatebirds sleep a mean of 42 minutes a day on the wing against twelve hours ashore (Rattenborg et al. 2016), mostly one hemisphere at a time and while soaring rather than flapping — and a separate study found them aloft up to two months without landing (Weimerskirch et al. 2016), so rest is not the opposite of motion. Hibernating grizzlies and black bears go six months without weight-bearing movement and lose no bone at all, because formation and resorption fall together and stay balanced (McGee-Lawrence et al. 2009) — the bear does not out-work the problem, it turns remodelling down at both ends. Meanwhile the den lowers the energy bill: metabolism to about a quarter of basal with core temperature down only five or six degrees (Tøien et al. 2011). Rest as a property of an arrangement, not a feat of will. Closes on Tricia Hersey and the ledger: a debt that was issued can be refused. Eleven spreads, eight diagrams, and a “Not:” refusals set of seven that declines rest-to-produce, “just relax”, rest-as-project, meltdown-as-rest, and natural-therefore-allowed. Interoception gets its own spread, and this zine explicitly does not call meltdown or shutdown a form of rest. We Left the Workings In A Star Stuff collection · five working papers The apparatus, published on purpose: what changed and when, every error we caught in our own work, how the pages are built for screen and for paper, and what the measuring tools still cannot see.
Why publish the apparatus at all

Why publish the apparatus at all Most projects keep this material in a drawer. Ours is in the open for one reason, and it is a consistency argument rather than a virtue: a site that spends this much time telling you to check the primary source cannot then ask you to take its own work on trust. Too Good to Check , over in Foundations , names six ways a fact goes wrong here. That essay is only worth anything if there is visible evidence of the checking actually happening — a dated record of what we got wrong, what is right, and who caught it. Otherwise it is a page about rigour, which is the cheapest kind of page there is. So this collection is the receipts. It is also, frankly, the part most likely to be useful to someone building something of their own: the design system and the print rules are the accumulated results of getting it wrong first, and they are CC BY-SA like everything else.

Published, and not There is a gradient here rather than a wall, and it is worth naming since this page is where a reader would wonder: On the site. The five pages below. The changelog also answers at /changelog , because it is the one people link to. In the repository, public but not a page. FACTCHECK.md — the full per-piece ledger, keyed by number, with every status and open item. Linked from the changelog for anyone who wants the long version. In the repository, deliberately a working doc. DECISIONS.md says on its own face that it is not published — it's for us. It tracks choices made and choices still open, in a register that would be misleading as a public statement. Nothing here is hidden; some of it is simply not a page. The line is about what has been written for a reader versus what is still shop talk, not about what we are willing to show. Changelog What Changed, and When Notes · the public error log Publishing our own errors is the method, not an embarrassment. These are living documents, and a living document should show its work. Every piece as it arrived, every substantial revision, and every fact-check — including the errors we found in our own work and how we fixed them. Dated, newest first → Details The public half of the fact-check ledger, backfilled from the collection's full commit history and kept up from there. It records three kinds of change and no others: a piece added, a piece substantially revised, and a fact-check or attribution audit — typo and styling passes do not earn an entry. The corrections are the point of the page rather than something buried in it : a paraphrase we had dressed as a Sagan quote, a line credited to Baldwin that is Dr. King's, a forest-wide fungal network asserted where the literature is contested, a coinage returned to its author. Each names what we got wrong, what is right, and who caught it. Newest date first, every entry tagged New , Revised , Fact-check or Site . Design The Design System Notes · how the screen works Accessibility-first, printable, and credited. The visual language of this collection is itself an argument about access. One typeface chosen for legibility, five accents held at near-uniform lightness, and body text that never fades — with its numbers and its receipts. Tokens & rationale → Details Six sections: Typeface , Palette , Palette lineage , Principles , Print and Shared assets . Atkinson Hyperlegible, chosen because it was drawn for readers the standard face failed. Five accents held within sixteen points of each other in lightness, so no one collection outshouts another. Body text at 18.84:1 , because full opacity is the house rule and a faded grey is a hierarchy decision made at the reader's expense. The lineage section is the honest one: the palette began as a Solarized variant and no Solarized value remains , so Solarized is cited for the method and never for the colours. Every artifact here is a single self-contained HTML file with no dependency beyond a web font. Design Designing for Paper Notes · how the paper works Every number on the page, and why it is that number. Every number here was arrived at by printing something and finding out it was wrong. The working behind the print rack — the spec, the inks, the gates, and the faults that no gate can see. Measured, not assumed → Details The working behind the print rack, where every number was arrived at by printing something and finding out it was wrong: 190 × 259 mm as the intersection of A4 and US Letter, 9 mm margins rather than 10 because 0.4 mm of slack tipped a sheet onto a third page, ink on white in both media because browsers omit background graphics, borders instead of backgrounds, and five house hues darkened until they clear AA on white. Plus the three gates that measure it — and a standing list of the faults none of them can see. Backing Material The Difference-First Frame Notes · the frame behind the frame A resonant frame, not a proof — and it says so. Reference notes behind Love You Down To Your Star Stuff . Backing material for anyone who asks why difference gets to be the starting point — a summary of Helen Edgar's essay “Why Difference Comes First.” After Helen Edgar → Details A summary of Helen Edgar's essay Why Difference Comes First , held here for anyone who asks why difference gets to be the starting point rather than a deviation from a norm: the cosmic microwave background needing tiny perturbations to make any structure at all, Deleuze on difference before identity, relational quantum mechanics, and ethodiversity. Kept as backing material rather than promoted to a zine, precisely because it is a resonance across four fields and not an argument any one of them makes. Why this whole section is off the reading chain Nearly every page in the collection is linked into a single prev/next reading order — a hundred and nine of them, running from Start Here through to the last broadside. All five pages above sit outside it, and so does this one — the only collection page that does. That is deliberate and it follows from what these are. A changelog is something you consult when you want to know whether a claim moved; a design system is something you open when you are building. These pages exist because they get used: the print rules came out of forty-four pages that printed blank, and the design system out of a contrast audit that found real failures. A document that recorded no failures would not be worth the file. Not the interesting part. If you have limited attention today, spend it on a zine . Why paper at all The rest of this collection is light on dark, and the shared stylesheet inverts it for print so that a zine handed to a printer comes back readable. That is a rescue operation, and it works — but it means every other page here was designed for a screen and then made to survive paper. The broadsides run the other way. Each one is drawn as ink on white in both media, so what you see on this site is not the artifact — it is a preview of the artifact. The sheet is the thing. The web page is how you get one. That inversion follows from what a broadside is for . A zine is read; a broadside is carried, handed over, and pinned up . It goes into a room where nobody is going to open a laptop — a kitchen table, a clinic waiting area, a staff room, a door. It gets photocopied badly and folded into a pocket. The historical form is the same one, and we are not being clever by borrowing it: a single cheap sheet, posted where people would see it. Proclamations, ballads, manifestos.

What earns a sheet Those nine are the whole rack, and it stays small on purpose. Four rules decide what joins it, applied in order — they exist because “this would make a good broadside” is an easy thing to say about almost anything, and most of the time it is wrong. A proposal that fails rule three is not a weaker broadside; it is a zine , and should be built as one. It compresses something already argued at length on the site, and links back. A broadside invents no new claim. Every line on it is a compression of text that exists in full somewhere else, with its sources attached, so the sheet inherits that piece's fact-checking rather than needing its own. If a draft starts making an argument its parent never made, it has stopped being a compression and become a new piece — which needs its own primary sources and its own ledger row. Side A is a face you'd pin up; side B does the work. The face carries one thing, large enough to read from across a room. The reverse is where the habits, the receipts, the full text and the sources go. This division is what separates a broadside from a poster: a poster is finished when you have looked at it, and a broadside has a second half that expects to be read . You can name the moment someone reaches for it, away from a screen. This is the rule that does the actual filtering. Six Ways is consulted when a claim arrives and something about it feels too neat. L★S is handed to someone you love. The Same Water is for the day you cannot do what you did last week. If you cannot finish the sentence “someone picks this up when…”, you do not have a broadside — you have a summary, and summaries belong on the page they summarise. Ink on white in both media, 190 × 259 mm, two sides, no third page, two spot inks that clear AA. The physical specification. It is not negotiable per-sheet, because the point of a fixed format is that nine different arguments come off the printer as the same object — a rack, not a pile. The fourth rule is the physical one, and every number in it was arrived at by printing something and finding out it was wrong — the paper size, the margin that tipped a sheet onto a third page, the inks, and the three gates that measure it. That working lives on its own page: Designing for Paper → Not Not a poster. A poster is finished when you have looked at it. Every sheet here has a reverse, and the reverse is where the sources are. Not merch. Open edition, CC BY-SA 4.0 . No numbered prints, no scarcity, nothing to buy — print as many as you want and give them away. If a sheet works, we would rather it circulate without us. Not a summary standing in for the argument. A broadside compresses a piece that exists in full, and points at it. It is not the short version for people who won't read the long one. Not screen-first with a print stylesheet bolted on. That approach is exactly how 44 pages came to print blank. Paper is the target, not the fallback.
The one that was held, and why that is worth recording

The one that was held, and why that is worth recording Until 15 August 2026 this section read What is not here yet , and the thing it named was the functioning-labels field card — the sheet you hand across the table when someone is about to say “mild,” “high-functioning,” or “low support needs.” It had the clearest moment of anything on the list, which by rule three should have made it the strongest candidate in the rack. It was held anyway, and not for want of an argument to compress. It was held because Zine No. 21 is after Helen Edgar , and constellation of intensities is her phrase. A broadside circulates harder than a zine — it goes on walls, into meetings, into photocopiers — so who gets to move a phrase into that kind of circulation is a decision to ask about rather than assume. The sheet now exists , and it exists in the order the hold was for: built first, then shown to Helen as a PDF of the actual artifact rather than described, then shipped on her word. She reviewed it and approved it on 15 August 2026. Describing a sheet is not the same as showing someone the thing that will end up on the wall, which is why the asking came after the building rather than instead of it. The note stays rather than being quietly deleted, because a hold that vanishes on the day it lifts teaches nobody anything. What it records is that the delay was the correct cost, and that the same question gets asked again next time. The odd axis, again Five of the collections on this site sort zines by register — what kind of argument a piece is making. Print broke that pattern by sorting on medium instead, and said so on its face rather than letting it read as an oversight. Sound is the second one on that axis, so the same disclosure applies: this is a shelf, not a claim about kinds of argument. What the four racks have in common is that you listen to them. But there is a sharper difference, and it is the thing worth saying here. Everything else on this site is ours — we wrote the zines, drew the diagrams, checked the claims, and if a page is wrong it is wrong in our voice. A rack is not ours. The songs belong to the people who made them; what we contribute is selection, arrangement, and a reason per track. That is a real contribution and also a modest one, and it changes what the work has to be careful about. Mostly it changes this: the recording is the destination and the writing is the doorway. A card that is more interesting than its song has failed. If you read a note and do not press play, we have wasted both our time.

In July 1977 Bob Marley recorded Punky Reggae Party with Lee Perry after hearing The Clash cover a Jamaican record — a guest list for an alliance that did not exist until it was read out, and the following April roughly 100,000 people marched six miles through National Front territory to hear The Clash, Steel Pulse and X-Ray Spex on one Rock Against Racism bill. Naming a thing helped it happen, which is what neurodiversity did too. Then the physics, because the physics is unreasonably good: sound needs matter — in a vacuum there is none at all — so every note anyone has heard was carried by nitrogen and oxygen forged in stars. A pure sine wave has a pitch and almost no identity; Helmholtz worked out in 1863 that what tells you who is playing lives entirely in the overtones above the note. And distortion, the sound the genre is named by, is a nonlinearity adding harmonics that were never sent in — difference, deliberately added . It reaches you at the skeleton, too: you hear your own voice partly through skull bone, which is why recordings sound wrong. It opens on AURORA's own account of seeing herself on video for the first time — she was shocked, said she couldn't do anything about it, and kept it: I have to use everything I got. Then the physics of the light she shares a name with, which turns out to be about exactly this. The solar wind delivers energy and nothing else; the colour is the atom's own — that famous green is oxygen's 557.7 nm line. And that line is a forbidden transition : it breaks the electric-dipole selection rules, so instead of the nanoseconds an allowed transition takes, the atom waits about 0.7 seconds before letting go, and the red line waits 110 . Which is why altitude decides the colour — lower down the air is crowded and a collision takes the energy first. The most famous light in the sky is a slow release the rules call forbidden, and it only completes where nothing crowds it. Twenty-eight performances across six movements, plus stim-listening (Jim Irion's coinage) and the reason Ryan's own playlist is nearly all live footage. The page is careful about whose word is whose: she calls it emotion; we are the ones calling it stimming , and it says so rather than putting the term in her mouth. The sharpest refusal is saved for last — her movement is celebrated because it is on a stage and lovely, while the same body doing the same thing in a classroom gets a behaviour plan . Rack · One artist Nobody Got His Eyes Right Sound · 31 tracks + essay The shape: one career, chronologically, and two corrections. The most-looked-at face in pop, and the one fact everybody repeats about it. Thirty-one songs from Space Oddity to I Can't Give Everything Away — the listening companion to Turn and Face the Strange (No. 12). 31 + essay → Details The long version of the five Bowie cards that open the L★S Playlist, and the listening companion to Turn and Face the Strange (No. 12) — thirty-one songs from Space Oddity to I Can't Give Everything Away . It starts from the most-looked-at face in pop and the one fact everybody repeats about it, which is wrong. He did not have different-coloured eyes. Both irises were the same colour; in February 1962 a schoolfriend punched him and a fingernail paralysed the muscles that contract the left iris, so that pupil could never close again — anisocoria, not heterochromia . A pupil stuck wide is a hole full of shadow, which is why the eye reads darker in exactly the bright light where a working pupil contracts, which is to say under every stage light and camera flash he ever stood in. That changes what kind of thing the famous feature was : heterochromia is a variation you're born with; this was an injury, reportedly with lasting effects on his depth perception. Glamour is not an accommodation. Then the second thing everyone knows — the constellation named for him in 2016 is not a constellation ; there are 88, the list was fixed in the 1920s, and the observatory that made it said plainly it was an invented asterism. Both errors lean the same way: they round a damaged iris and a small tribute up into something more elegant, and the tidier version travels further. Which is Too Good to Check with a soundtrack — and it has a cost, because while the myth is that beautiful nobody asks what a fixed pupil is like under a follow spot.

What earns a rack Three is few enough that the rules could be tacit, which is exactly when they should be written down instead. These are applied in order, and the first one does most of the filtering. The music has to be doing the arguing. Not illustrating an argument the prose already finished. If the songs could be swapped for different songs without changing what the page says, this is a zine with a soundtrack and should be built as a zine. The test is whether removing the audio removes the point. Every track carries a written reason. No vibes-only entries, no filler to reach a round number. Each card says why this recording is on this rack — which is also the honest limit on how long a rack can get, because a hundred and twenty-one reasons is already a lot of reasons and twice that would be padding. Every embed is resolved before it ships. A card whose embed quietly points at a different recording is invisible to every gate we run: the markup is valid, the contrast is fine, the words are all there. So each video ID goes through the oEmbed endpoint and comes back with its real title and channel before the page is published. 95 of them so far , and that pass has already produced two corrections — an unattributed song turning out to be Le Butcherettes, and a release year that would have shipped wrong from memory. Describe the song; don't reproduce it. The words belong to the people who wrote them, and a lyric sheet is not what a rack is for. Cards describe, characterise and argue; the recording is where you meet the song. This also keeps the writing honest — it is much harder to fake a reason than to quote a good line. Rule four arrived with the second rack, and the first one predates it: seven cards on the L★S Playlist quote short lyric fragments. They are brief, attributed and long-standing, and we are naming the inconsistency here rather than quietly conforming the older page or pretending the rule was always in force. If it changes, it will change in the changelog .
Two pages, one piece of physics

Two pages, one piece of physics This was not planned and is the best thing about the shelf, so it gets its own heading. The punk rack went looking for what makes an amplifier sound like punk and arrived at overtones : a pure sine wave has a pitch and almost no identity, and what tells you who is playing lives entirely in the harmonics above the note. Distortion is a nonlinearity that adds harmonics which were never in the signal — character as surplus. The AURORA rack went looking for the physics of the northern lights and arrived at emission lines : the solar wind delivers energy and nothing else, and the famous green is atomic oxygen's own 557.7 nm line. Energy from outside; colour from within. Those are the same fact wearing different clothes. What comes out is characteristic of the material, whatever put the energy in. Neither page set out to say that, and neither knew the other was going to; the convergence was noticed afterward, reading them side by side — which is the whole method described on Cosmic Connections , arriving without being asked. It is also, as both pages say at length, a rhyme rather than a proof . Spectroscopy has no opinion about anybody's belonging. Worth adding that the third essay did not join in. The Bowie rack went looking for its own fact and came back with optics and an anatomy correction instead — a paralysed iris, and a constellation that is not one. Three essays, two convergences, one page that went somewhere else entirely. We are recording that rather than stretching the pattern to fit it, because a pattern you have to push into shape is not one you observed. The gap A collection built out of audio and video has an access problem, and we have not solved it. Everything else on this site is text: it reflows, it takes a screen reader, it prints, it can be read at whatever pace you need. The shelf is 121 embedded videos. What exists: every card carries a written note that stands on its own, so the argument of each rack survives without playing anything, and the essays are text. What does not exist: transcripts, and any guarantee of caption quality. Captions on the embeds are whatever the uploader provided or whatever the platform generated, and auto-generated captions on sung material are frequently poor. We do not control them and we have not audited them. Naming it is not fixing it. It is here because a site that argues for access every week should say plainly where its own work falls short, and because the next person to build a rack should know this is the outstanding job. Not Not a mood board. A rack is an argument you can play. If the only thing holding a set of songs together is that they feel similar, that is a playlist and it belongs on a streaming service, where it will be better recommended than we could manage. Not ours to own. We select and we write; the music is the artists' work, and we link back to it rather than hosting it. The CC BY-SA on this site covers our writing, not their recordings. Not a lyric sheet. See rule four. Cards describe songs; they do not reprint them. Not artists diagnosed from a distance. Where a musician has spoken about being neurodivergent we use their word and no other, and where we recognise something they have not named, we say the recognition is ours. This is stated in full on the AURORA rack , which is where the temptation is strongest. Not a soundtrack for the reader's suffering. These racks are not sad-playlist infrastructure. Several of the songs are about being unwell and several are about joy, and neither kind is here to be a mood you are supposed to arrive in.

What is not here yet This section named two candidates when the shelf held three racks, and one of them has since been built — the Bowie rack above was on this list as not started before it existed. We are leaving the trace rather than editing it out, because a to-do list you quietly rewrite once it is done stops being evidence of anything. What remains: a rack for the happy-flappy and stim-dancing material, which is currently distributed across stimpunks.org rather than collected. It would need to clear rule one on its own terms — the argument there is about bodies moving for pleasure, and it is not obvious yet whether the music carries that or merely accompanies it. Not started. Named here rather than kept on a private list, same as everywhere else on this site. The list of things we have not done is part of the record. Star Gazing A Star Stuff collection · 6 pieces Awe-inspiring and not definite. Possibilities of thought, possibilities of connecting things and ideas.

What holds these together This collection is named and described by Helen Edgar, who wanted somewhere for the more experimental thinking to live: “i kind of like star gazing though — it is awe inspiring and not definite — it is possibilities of thought, possibilities of connecting things and ideas.” That is the register exactly. In Star Stuff the settled fact carries the claim. Here the work is done by philosophy of difference, relation and becoming — Deleuze on identity produced out of a prior field of difference, Rovelli on properties that only become determinate in relation, the rhizome with no trunk and no chain of command, wyrd as the old word for becoming rather than fate.

The hinge Why Difference Comes First is where the collection turned. It is still cosmic — the cosmic microwave background, relational quantum mechanics — but it is the first piece to move from settled physics as a direct claim about matter into philosophy of difference as the organizing frame . Everything else here follows through that door. Four of these six are Helen's own, in her own voice or developed after her essays. The masthead is shared; authorship is not — each piece says whose it is. Not Not a looser standard of sourcing. Experimental register, same ledger. Speculation is labelled speculation, contested interpretations are named as contested — relational quantum mechanics is one interpretation among several, not consensus, and we say so on the page rather than in a footnote. Every quotation still traces to a primary source. See the changelog for what we have got wrong and corrected. Not poetry standing in for an argument. Being evocative is not a licence to be unfalsifiable about the physics we invoke.

The pieces In the order they were made. The number records when ; the collection records what . Zine No. 11 · Guest Why Difference Comes First Guest zine · Helen Edgar I've been thinking about the connections in-between — physics, philosophy, my own life as an Autistic person. This is me following that thread. A guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), in her own voice — one thread followed down three scales to the same shape: difference comes first. 10 spreads · guest → Details A guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), in her own voice, and the site does not translate it into house voice. Ten spreads following one thread down three scales — relational quantum mechanics, the cosmic microwave background, and Deleuze — arriving at the same shape each time: difference comes first, and the baseline is the thing that got built. It opens on I'm not a fixed thing , picking up her earlier writing on relational quantum mechanics, and ends where the flat line gives out. Filed in Star Gazing rather than Star Stuff because it is possibility-forward rather than one settled fact followed honestly — the physics is real, and it is being thought with rather than argued from. The backing notes are The Difference-First Frame , in Notes & Rationale . Zine No. 22 No One Is the Leader Stimpunks Zines on murmurations, emergence, and the whole that exceeds its parts — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self Each starling tracks only its six or seven nearest neighbours, and the whole emerges from that. After Ballerini & the STARFLAG project. 8 spreads → Details Emergence and the murmuration — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self. Hundreds of thousands of starlings make vast rolling shapes with no leader and no plan: each bird tracks only its six or seven nearest neighbours (Ballerini & the STARFLAG project), and the whole emerges from that one local rule. Philip Anderson's “More Is Different” (1972) is the spine — the founding statement of anti-reductionism: at each level of scale new laws appear that the parts don't contain, so knowing the parts never rebuilds the whole. The early universe did the same, self-organising faint density ripples into the cosmic web with no architect. Two payoffs land it home: the whole person is realer than any diagnostic checklist of parts (you are not a list of deficits — you are the murmuration), and our best neurodivergent collectives — NeurodiVentures — are leaderless murmurations, not org charts (competency networks and catalysts rather than leaders; decisions where the knowledge lives). A “the whole exceeds the parts” zine. Held with care: leaderless is not structureless. Eight spreads, flock-and-web diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 26 A Mycelium and a Rhizome Stimpunks Zines how neurodivergent knowledge grows: no trunk, no center, many doors A tree has one trunk and a chain of command; you climb it or you're lost. A rhizome has no root to ask permission of, so you can enter anywhere. 8 spreads → Details How neurodivergent knowledge and community grow, read through star stuff — no trunk, no center, many doors. A tree has one trunk and a chain of command; you climb it or you're lost. A rhizome (Deleuze & Guattari) has no root to ask permission of, so you can enter anywhere — Spiky Profiles → Monotropism → Deep Attention, or in from burnout, or a word that finally fit. No prerequisite, no gatekeeper. And a mycelium is the life in that shape: fungal threads carry nutrients and signals between trees that never touch (the “wood wide web,” Simard), thickening the paths that help and letting the rest fade; a brainless slime mold rebuilds the Tokyo rail network (Tero et al.). Zoom all the way out and the shape returns — the cosmic web of dark-matter filaments, the universe's largest structure, looks like a mycelium, like a neuron: not a pyramid, a web. We're already building it. Gray-Hammond and Munday name it neuro-anarchy; the Autistic Rhizome is “a network with no single point of origin,” members as equals held by a do-no-harm ethic, resilient because nothing depends on a center (with Helen Edgar's watering holes). Where the map meets soil is Cavendish Space. Decentralization isn't disorder — it's the oldest structure there is. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 28 · Guest Wyrd & Weird Stimpunks Zines · Helen Edgar on the old word for fate, and the newer word we made of it Old English wyrd comes from weorþan , “to become,” and is twined with the root of “worth.” A guest zine by Helen Edgar. 9 spreads → Details On the old word for fate, and the newer word we made of it — a guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), rehoused in the Star Stuff style. Long before “weird” meant strange, wyrd meant becoming: Old English wyrd comes from weorþan, “to become,” and is twined with the root of “worth.” Fate was never drawn as a straight line from birth to death but as cloth — the Norns' weaving at the well beneath Yggdrasill, the “web of man” — many threads crossing, none load-bearing alone. The Weird Sisters carried the word down through Holinshed to Shakespeare's Macbeth; over centuries “weird” drifted into an insult, and Autistic and disabled communities have run that drift backward, taking it up again as a name, not a verdict — which is etymologically honest, not just cheek. Held with care: wyrd is not a script, not doom, not a synonym for wrong, not something done to you alone. Under the root, weorþan meant “to become,” never “to be”: nobody is finished, and becoming was never the flaw — it was the design. You were never written; you are still being woven. Nine spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, a “threads already running” map of its kin in the collection, and Helen's own sources & notes. Zine No. 29 · Guest Only in Relation Stimpunks Zines · after Helen Edgar relational quantum physics, and what it means to be Autistic In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics a particle has no standalone properties. Developed after Helen Edgar's essay “We Are Made of Relations.” 9 spreads → Details Relational quantum physics, and what it means to be Autistic — a guest zine developed after Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms) from her essay “We Are Made of Relations.” In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics a particle has no standalone properties; what it is becomes definite only in relation to another system (Rovelli, 1996). The count gives it away: two distinct coins make four outcomes, but two identical bosons make only three — what's fundamental isn't the standalone particle but the symmetry, the relation (Webster, 2026). Karen Barad calls the relation-before-parts intra-action; the human version, intradependence — made of each other, deeper than interdependence — Helen draws from Barad too. Read through Deleuze, “objects emerge out of more fundamental processes of differentiation”: difference first, then relation, and the tidy standalone object is the thing that got built. The payoff lands on our own work — the double empathy problem (Milton, 2012) lives in the relation, not one mind, and Helen widens it into DEEP; and in the ARLES ladder Relational sits near the base with Regulation inside it, because regulation is relational, so you change the field, not the person. Held with care: not quantum mysticism, not “everything is connected” as a vibe, not dissolution into sameness — the spiky profile survives the merge. A rhyme, not a proof. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. Zine No. 30 · Guest Always Migrating Stimpunks Zines · Helen Edgar migration, monotropism, and the galaxy you're already made of A guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), written after Brigit Anna McNeill's The Living Page workshop and rehoused here in the Star Stuff style. 11 spreads · guest → Details Migration, monotropism, and the galaxy you're already made of — a guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), written after Brigit Anna McNeill's The Living Page migration workshop and rehoused here in the Star Stuff style. Every migrating body is made of matter that already migrated once, so migration was never a metaphor borrowed from animals: it's one of the oldest facts about star stuff. A bird crosses an ocean on a compass sense we still can't fully explain — light striking cryptochrome in the eye makes a pair of electrons whose spins stay linked, and that linked pair is thought to be part of how it reads the Earth's faint field (Hore & Mouritsen; Mouritsen). Entanglement's lesson: once two things have been in relation, they stay in relation — separateness was always the less accurate story, which is Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics in a wingbeat. Zoom out and the pattern holds: the Sagittarius dwarf is still arriving in our halo, and the Milky Way–Andromeda collision everyone called settled is now closer to a coin-flip (Sawala et al., 2025) — a tug, not a destination. Then the turn inward: the bodily restlessness that builds before anything is decided is monotropism's gravity, attention gathered into a few bright points rather than spread as an even glow — and masking teaches us to quieten it until we lose our own north. Neuroqueering is the refusal; Pernille Fraser's “Can we trust the space you offer?” asks it from the other side. Widened by ethodiversity and the double empathy problem, and by Barad's intra-action — the liminal crossing isn't empty transit, it's where the shaping happens. Closes past the spiky profile: not a chart, a constellation of intensities. Eleven spreads, eight diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and a threads-already-running map of its kin.
