Close enough and you deform each other

Distance is doing work Close enough and you deform each other Here is where a warmer piece would say and neither star has to change shape to stay in relation. That is not true, and the way it fails is the most useful thing in this zine. Bring two stars close and they stop being spheres. Tidal forces stretch each one along the line joining them — the same effect that raises Earth's ocean tides, scaled up until it is the shape of the star itself. Astronomers see it directly: the brightness of a close pair rises and falls as those stretched shapes turn, which is why the effect has its own name, ellipsoidal variability. Push closer still and the deformation runs to its conclusion: what proximity does to a star's shape separation shape wide both stay round; each evolves as if alone close stretched into ellipsoids, brightness varying as they turn closer drawn to a teardrop, its point aimed at the other star touching a shared envelope, dumbbell-shaped — matter crossing between them At the last stage the star can no longer hold its own outer material: it spills across to its companion, and what each one becomes is rewritten by the transfer. Proximity is not automatically good for a star. Being bound does not deform you. Being bound too closely deforms you — and the star cannot choose its separation. We can. the only part of this we get a say in And the far end of the range is enormous. Gaia has resolved over a million bound pairs out to separations of a parsec, with orbital periods running to a hundred million years. Those stars are genuinely companions — held by mutual gravity, one orbit longer than the entire history of flowering plants — and each of them keeps its own shape completely. Distance does not weaken the binding. It only stops the binding from being the thing that reshapes you. Separation and shape Three pairs of stars. No path can be solved alone

At three, the mathematics changes No path can be solved alone This is the argumentative centre, and it is not an interpretation. It is a set of theorems. With two gravitating bodies you can write the solution down. Newton did. Give the positions and velocities now, and there is a formula that returns them for any time you like, exactly, forever. Add a third body and that stops being available. Not because it is hard — because it was proved not to be there: what was actually shown who result Bruns, 1887 beyond the ten classical conserved quantities, the three-body equations admit no further integrals that are algebraic in the coordinates and their derivatives Poincaré, 1890 and none that are single-valued analytic functions either — the stronger closure, and the one that ended the search Sundman, 1912 a convergent series solution does exist (non-zero angular momentum, no triple collision) — and converges so slowly it is useless for computation or for understanding So astronomers integrate these systems numerically: step the whole configuration forward a little, recompute every force, step again. There is no shortcut, and there is no way to do one body at a time. You cannot solve for one body's path on its own and add the others afterward. The paths exist only as a solution to the whole system, together, at once. the sentence the zine turns on The same work is where chaos was found. Poincaré discovered that arbitrarily small differences in the starting conditions can lead to completely different outcomes later — and the crucial part, the part the popular word destroys: nothing is random. Every rule is exact and fully known. The system is deterministic and still unpredictable far out. Those are compatible, and holding them together is the whole idea. What this does not say. It does not say the bodies stop being distinct — each keeps its own mass and its own light. It says their trajectories are not separable. That is a claim about dynamics and prediction, not about what a thing fundamentally is; the ontological version belongs to No. 29 and is not being re-argued here. The objection that was perfectly good

1543–1838 · the long objection The objection that was perfectly good If the Earth really moves around the Sun, then over six months your viewpoint shifts by the whole width of that orbit — and nearby stars should visibly slide against the distant ones. They don't. Not to the naked eye, not to Tycho Brahe's superb instruments, not to anyone for nearly three hundred years after Copernicus. So the Earth does not move. That was not stupidity. It was valid reasoning from careful data, and it is the strongest empirical objection the heliocentric model ever faced. The answer — the stars are simply much, much further away than that — sounded like special pleading, because the distances required were, by the standards of the time, absurd. And there was a second trap underneath, which is the part that should make anyone nervous. Through a telescope, stars show small discs. Take those discs as real and you can compute a physical size — and at the distances parallax would require, stars come out grotesquely, impossibly enormous. Tycho ran that calculation and rejected the conclusion. The discs were not there. They are an artefact of light passing through a finite aperture — the instrument drawing its own signature on the sky and handing it back as data. the trap under the trap So the chain opens on a failure with three parts, all of them still with us: absence of evidence read as evidence of absence; a conclusion rejected because its implications felt too large; and an instrument's own artefact mistaken for a property of the thing observed. What eventually broke it was not a better argument. It was somebody measuring the shift. documented the missing parallax → Bessel The shift nobody could see Two observing positions at either end of Earth's orbit, with sight lines to a near star that barely changes its apparent place against the background stars. The angle is marked as too small to detect. Königsberg · 1838 Somebody measured the shift Friedrich Bessel picked 61 Cygni because it moved. Not much — but its motion across the sky was unusually fast, and fast usually means near. With a Fraunhofer heliometer, on every clear night he could get, he tracked it against two neighbouring stars. In 1838 he published the result: a parallax of 0.3136 arcseconds. That is an angle it is worth trying to feel. A two-centimetre coin, seen from thirteen kilometres away. That is the entire wobble on which the first known distance to a star was built. It gave about 10.4 light years; the modern figure is near 11.4. He was narrowly first. Thomas Henderson had Alpha Centauri and Friedrich Struve had Vega at almost the same moment. Three people, three stars, one method, within months. Three hundred years of "we looked and saw nothing" ended the moment the instrument got good enough to see a coin at thirteen kilometres. The stars had been moving the whole time. what actually settles an argument And here is the detail this collection has to stop and mark. Bessel did this at Königsberg — the same man, at the same observatory, who established the personal equation: the finding that observers differ from one another systematically, and that the right response is to publish a constant for each of them and correct the data rather than correct the observer. Twice, from opposite directions, the same person demonstrated that knowledge requires a located, particular observer. Once by needing their displacement. The geometry · and what it forbids No baseline, no depth Strip parallax down to what it actually is, because the whole zine is in the geometry. You look at a star. You wait six months, which carries you to the far side of Earth's orbit. You look again. The star appears to have moved a little against the far background, and from that angle and the width of your orbit you get the distance. The width of your orbit is called the baseline. It is not a nuisance in the measurement, not a source of error to be minimised, not contamination from the observer's situation. The observer's displacement is the instrument. Take it away and you have not made the measurement purer. You have made it impossible. the sentence this zine turns on Consider what a genuine view from nowhere would be. No location, therefore no second location, therefore no baseline, no angle, no distance. An observer at no position sees a flat sky and cannot tell a nearby star from a far one. Not "with difficulty." At all. The god's-eye view is, in the one domain where we can check it exactly, the blindest possible position. And the reverse holds too, which is the constructive half. The more your positions differ, the better your measurement gets. That is why space astrometry beats ground-based: a wider, better-known baseline. Difference between viewpoints is not noise to be averaged out. It is signal, and it is the only signal there is. documented parallax → the whole distance ladder Two positions, and none On the left, two observing positions with a baseline between them yield an angle and a distance. Everything rests on the bottom rung

Everything above it Everything rests on the bottom rung Parallax only reaches so far. Past that, astronomy does something audacious: it builds a ladder, and calibrates each rung against the one below. Rung one is geometry — parallax, an observer moving, no assumptions required. Rung two is the period–luminosity relation. Certain variable stars pulse at a rate that tracks their true brightness, so if you can read the period you know the intrinsic luminosity, and comparing that to how bright it looks gives distance. Calibrated by rung one. Rung three reaches further still with exploding stars of standardisable brightness. Calibrated by rung two. And so on out to the expansion of the universe itself. Every distance in cosmology — every one — is ultimately anchored to somebody standing in a particular place and moving to another. what the ladder is bolted to Which means the ladder inherits the bottom rung's fate. Move the calibration and every rung above it moves. This is not hypothetical: recalibrations of the variable-star rung have historically resedimented the entire extragalactic distance scale, and disagreements about that calibration sit near the centre of live arguments about the expansion rate today. Hold that structure, because the rest of the zine is about a different ladder with the same property. When the bottom rung is a person in a position, and you have pretended there is no person and no position, everything built on top inherits the error and none of it knows. documented rung two → who built it The distance ladder Four stacked rungs — parallax, period-luminosity, standard candles, and cosmic expansion — each labelled as calibrated by the rung below, with the bottom rung marked geometry, an observer moving. cosmic expansion exploding stars period–luminosity parallax · geometry an observer, moving each rung calibrated by the one below move the bottom and everything moves Figure 4 · anchored to a located observer baselinethe chain 4 · the ladder Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks
The woman not permitted to observe

Harvard College Observatory · 1895–1912 The woman not permitted to observe Rung two of the ladder — the one everything above it stands on — was built by a person who was not allowed to use the telescope. Henrietta Swan Leavitt joined Harvard College Observatory in 1895 as one of the women hired as computers: paid by the hour, assigned tasks rather than choosing them, employed to measure photographic plates that men had exposed. On those plates she found and measured the periods of roughly 1,700 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds. And she noticed the thing nobody had: because everything in the Small Magellanic Cloud sits at essentially the same distance from us, differences in apparent brightness there are differences in actual brightness. That single observation converts a pattern into a ruler. The result — the period–luminosity relation, the Leavitt Law — appeared in Harvard College Observatory Circular 173 in 1912, titled "Periods of 25 Variable Stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud." It was published under the name of the observatory's director, Edward Pickering. It opens by noting that the statement "has been prepared by Miss Leavitt." HCO Circular 173, 1912 Prepared by. The measurement of the universe rests on rung two, and rung two is credited in a subordinate clause. Now put that next to the argument of the last three spreads. Parallax says knowledge requires an observer in a position. Leavitt was denied the position of observer and made the discovery anyway — from a chair, with a magnifying glass, on somebody else's plates. She had a standpoint. The institution simply declined to record that it was hers. documented this erasure → the pattern Who is at the telescope and who is at the plates A telescope with a named observer beside it, and a desk of photographic plates where the discovery was actually made, with the credit line reading prepared by Miss Leavitt. the observer named on the paper the plates where the law was found “has been prepared by Miss Leavitt” Figure 5 · rung two, in a subordinate clause baselinethe chain 5 · Leavitt · rung two Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

1988 · the name for it The god trick In 1988 Donna Haraway gave the fantasy its name, in an essay about vision, and about who gets to be looked at. "I would like to insist on the embodied nature of all vision and so reclaim the sensory system that has been used to signify a leap out of the marked body and into a conquering gaze from nowhere. This is the gaze that mythically inscribes all the marked bodies, that makes the unmarked category claim the power to see and not be seen, to represent while escaping representation." Haraway, "Situated Knowledges," Feminist Studies 14(3), 1988, p. 581 Read the mechanism slowly, because it is precise. There are marked bodies — visible, particular, available for study. And there is an unmarked category, which is not neutral but simply unexamined: it holds the power to see and not be seen, to describe others while never appearing in the description. Haraway calls the whole manoeuvre a god trick — "the god trick of seeing everything from nowhere" — and is blunt about its status: "that view of infinite vision is an illusion, a god trick." She is not describing something exotic. She is describing the default voice of a methods section: subjects were observed. Observed by whom, from where, with what stake in the result? The sentence is constructed so the question cannot be asked. And note where the essay is set, because it is not incidental. Haraway's examples are satellites, space probes, planetary imaging, the “brilliant space platforms of the powerful.” She even quotes a magazine's epigraph on the infinitesimal: “The stuff of stars has come alive.” The critique of the view from nowhere was written, from the start, in the vocabulary of looking at the sky. documented the god trick → her positive claim Marked and unmarked An eye at the top, drawn without a body and without a position, looking down at three marked figures who are fully rendered and labelled as available for study. unmarked · no position marked bodies · fully visible to represent while escaping representation Figure 7 · the power to see and not be seen baselinethe chain 7 · the god trick Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

The line that usually gets dropped "Only partial perspective promises objective vision" Haraway is routinely read as an opponent of objectivity. She is the opposite, and she says so in a sentence she flags as the moral of the essay. "The moral is simple: only partial perspective promises objective vision. … Feminist objectivity is about limited location and situated knowledge, not about transcendence and splitting of subject and object. It allows us to become answerable for what we learn how to see." Haraway, 1988, p. 583 Not objectivity is impossible. Not all views are equal. Partiality is the precondition of objectivity — and what you gain by having a location is the ability to be answerable, which a view from nowhere structurally cannot be. You cannot check the work of an observer with no address. Now set that beside the geometry from spread four. parallax no position → no baseline → no depth situated no location → no accountability → no objectivity They are the same claim in two vocabularies. In astronomy it is a theorem you can check with trigonometry: the measurement is constituted by the observer's position, and pretending otherwise destroys the measurement. In epistemology it is an argument. The astronomy does not prove the epistemology — but it does demonstrate that the shape of the claim is not mystical, because there is at least one domain where it is exactly, boringly true. Marked contested, and here is what is contested. Haraway never mentions parallax, and we are not claiming she had it in mind. The parallel is ours. What makes it more than a pun is that both claims have the same structure — position is not a contaminant of the measurement, it is a component of it — and that Haraway independently reaches for astronomical imagery throughout. What it is not is a proof: a theorem in trigonometry cannot settle an argument in epistemology, and if this spread reads as though it does, it has overstepped. contested parallax → situated knowledges The same shape, twice Two parallel three-step arguments — one in geometry ending at distance, one in epistemology ending at objectivity — both beginning from having a position. geometry a position a baseline depth measurable epistemology a location answerable checkable objective same shape · one is a theorem, one an argument Figure 8 · a rhyme, and we mark it as one baselinethe chain 8 · partial perspective Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks
Relativism is also a god trick

The guard rail · in her own words Relativism is also a god trick The obvious misreading of everything so far is therefore all views are equally valid. Haraway blocks that exit herself, in the same essay, and more sharply than her critics do. "Relativism is a way of being nowhere while claiming to be everywhere equally. The 'equality' of positioning is a denial of responsibility and critical inquiry. Relativism is the perfect mirror twin of totalization in the ideologies of objectivity; both deny the stakes in location, embodiment, and partial perspective; both make it impossible to see well. Relativism and totalization are both 'god tricks' promising vision from everywhere and nowhere equally and fully." Haraway, 1988, p. 584 That is as complete a refusal of "it's all subjective" as anyone has written, and it comes from the person the phrase is most often blamed on. The geometry says the same thing, and it is worth spelling out because it is not obvious. Two well-known positions give you a distance. Infinitely many positions, none of them recorded, give you nothing at all — you cannot form a baseline out of viewpoints you refuse to specify. Relativism is not many baselines. It is the refusal to state one, which is the same epistemic position as the view from nowhere wearing different clothes. She is equally careful about the standpoints of the subjugated, which she says are preferred but explicitly not "innocent": they are preferred "because in principle they are least likely to allow denial of the critical and interpretive core of all knowledge," and they remain subject to critical re-examination like any other. And: "not just any partial perspective will do." documented the guard rail → what happens without it Two positions, no positions, all positions Three panels: two stated positions give a distance; no position gives nothing; and unlimited unstated positions also give nothing, labelled as the mirror twin. two, stated depth none nothing all, unstated nothing mirror twins relativism is not many baselines it is refusing to state one Figure 9 · the exit she closes herself baselinethe chain 9 · the guard rail Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

2010 · the unmarked sample The unmarked sample Here is the god trick with numbers on it. In 2010, Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan asked a question nobody had bothered to ask systematically: who are the people in the studies? The answer, across the top journals of the behavioural sciences: 96% of samples from Western industrialised nations 68% of subjects from the United States 12% share of world population those countries hold They named the sample WEIRD — Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic — and made the finding that turns it from awkward into serious: on many measures these subjects are not merely unrepresentative but frequent outliers compared with the rest of the species. Notice what the problem actually is, because "unrepresentative sample" undersells it. The results were not published as facts about American undergraduates. They were published as facts about human beings — the population went unstated because the researchers' own position was the unmarked category. A methods section that does not say where you are standing is not neutral. It is a claim to be standing nowhere, and it is always false. the god trick, operationalised And this is the ladder problem again, exactly. Rung one was a narrow, unstated sample. Everything built on top inherited it, and none of it knew. documented unstated samples → research done on us Who is in the studies A bar showing 96 percent of samples drawn from countries holding 12 percent of world population, with the claim generalised to all humans. where the subjects come from 96% Western industrialised share of world population 12% reported as “human behaviour” Figure 10 · rung one, unstated baselinethe chain 10 · WEIRD Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

Where it lands on us Research done on us Autism research is close to a controlled experiment in what the god trick costs, because for most of its history the observers and the observed were disjoint sets. Look at what that arrangement produced, using findings this collection has already walked. Outcome measures chosen from outside: the endpoint inherited from 1987 was indistinguishability — how much like everyone else the child seemed — a target nobody standing on the inside would have written down (No. 38). Harms not measured: 150 intervention studies, 11 mentioning adverse events (No. 40). You do not ask about harms you cannot imagine, and you cannot imagine harms you have never been on the receiving end of. And the finding that only exists because somebody moved. Damian Milton's double empathy problem (2012) reframes the communication breakdown between Autistic and non-Autistic people as mutual and relational — a mismatch between two positions rather than a deficit inside one of them. That is a parallax result. It is invisible from one position and obvious from two, and getting it required an Autistic researcher — an observer at the other end of the baseline. why the sample includes the analyst Decades of research described the deficit as a property of the Autistic person, the way Tycho described stellar discs as a property of the stars. In both cases the finding was partly an artefact of the apparatus — and in both cases you could only see that by observing from somewhere else. Which is what participatory research is for. Not courtesy, and not a legitimacy ritual. A second position on the baseline, which is the only way anyone has ever measured depth. documented the failures → what the correction actually is One position and two From one position the gap between two people is read as a deficit located in one of them; from two positions the same gap is visible as mutual, sitting between them. one position “the deficit” located in one two positions the gap is mutual it sits between same people · same gap only the number of observers changed Figure 11 · double empathy as a parallax result baselinethe chain 11 · research done on us Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

The correction Publish your coordinates Two exits are closed. You cannot remove the observer — that destroys the measurement. You cannot declare all views equal — Haraway refuses it, and so does the geometry. What is left is the answer Bessel gave twice, and it is embarrassingly practical: state where you are standing, and publish the constant. In 1838 that meant recording the baseline: which two points the observation was made from, how far apart, how accurately known. In the personal equation it meant recording the observer: this one runs 0.2 seconds late, here is the number, correct the data and keep the person. The research equivalents are unglamorous and already invented: Say who the sample was, in the claim and not only in the appendix. Say who the researchers were and what they had at stake. Put people with the experience in the design, not the debrief. Choose outcome measures with the people who will be measured. Report harms. Name the coordinates the work was done from. the baseline, in a methods section Every one of those is usually filed under ethics or inclusion. They belong under method. A positionality statement is not a confession or a disclaimer — it is a published baseline, and it does the same job Bessel's constants did: it makes the reading correctable by somebody who was not there. And it is the reason "nothing about us without us" is an epistemic claim before it is a political one. A study of us that contains none of us has one position. Whatever else is wrong with it, it cannot measure depth. Marked contested. The synthesis is ours: Bessel did not think of the personal equation as a template for research ethics, and Haraway does not cite him. What we are claiming is a shared form — make the observer's position explicit and correctable rather than invisible or irrelevant — not a historical descent. And the practical claim underneath, that participatory methods produce better findings rather than only fairer process, is an empirical question that deserves its own evidence and does not get to lean on the analogy. contested the personal equation → research practice Two answers from one man Bessel's two results side by side: parallax, where the observer's displacement is published as a baseline, and the personal equation, where the observer's difference is published as a constant. The turn The sky is not flat There is a real answer to how far away 61 Cygni is. It is about 11.4 light years, and nothing in this zine softens that. We got it by knowing exactly where somebody was standing, twice, six months apart, and by publishing both positions so anyone could check. The precision came from the situatedness. It did not survive despite it. So this is not an argument that science is only perspective, and it cannot be turned into one without contradicting both halves of its evidence — the geometry says a position is required, and Haraway says relativism is a god trick. The view from nowhere is not too rigorous. It is not rigorous enough, because it has thrown away the one thing that makes a measurement checkable: a stated place to have made it from. Objectivity is not the absence of a position. It is a position you have written down, so that someone standing elsewhere can correct you. what the chain arrives at And nobody built this road on purpose. Tycho was doing his best with an instrument that lied to him. Pickering ran an observatory whose employment practices he had not invented. The researchers in the WEIRD survey were using the subjects who were available. Each did competent work from an unexamined position — which is exactly the failure the whole chain describes, performed by the people describing it. Which is the hopeful part, and the reason this collection keeps writing chains instead of villains. An unexamined position is not a moral defect. It is a missing line in the methods section. Those can be written. Not:that all perspectives are equal. Haraway calls that a god trick in the same essay, and the geometry agrees: unstated positions give you nothing. Two known baselines beat infinite unrecorded ones. Not:that lived experience is automatically right. Haraway is explicit that subjugated standpoints are "not 'innocent' positions" and stay open to critical examination. Preferred is not the same as unquestionable. Not:that parallax proves any of this. A theorem in trigonometry cannot settle epistemology. It shows the shape of the claim is real in at least one place. We marked that joint contested. Not:an attack on measurement. The zine's hero is a man who measured a coin at thirteen kilometres and published his baseline. What in your field is treated as a property of the thing observed, and is actually a signature of the instrument? Whose second position would change what your work can see — and what would it take to have them on the baseline rather than in the sample? What are your coordinates? Could someone standing elsewhere correct you with them? Sources Haraway, read at the primary. Donna Haraway, "Situated Knowledges: The Science Question in Feminism and the Privilege of Partial Perspective," Feminist Studies 14(3), Autumn 1988, 575–599. Every quotation here is verbatim from pages 581–585 of the article itself: the conquering gaze and the unmarked category claiming "the power to see and not be seen, to represent while escaping representation" (581); "the god trick of seeing everything from nowhere" (581) and "that view of infinite vision is an illusion, a god trick" (582); "The moral is simple: only partial perspective promises objective vision" and "Feminist objectivity is about limited location and situated knowledge … It allows us to become answerable for what we learn how to see" (583); "Relativism is a way of being nowhere while claiming to be everywhere equally," "Relativism is the perfect mirror twin of totalization," "Relativism and totalization are both 'god tricks'," and the standpoints of the subjugated as "not 'innocent' positions" (584); "not just any partial perspective will do" (585). Her astronomical imagery — the "brilliant space platforms of the powerful" (583) and the epigraph "The stuff of stars has come alive" (582) — is quoted from that text and is not our embellishment. Parallax. Friedrich Bessel's 1838 parallax for 61 Cygni of 0.3136″, measured at Königsberg with a Fraunhofer heliometer and giving roughly 10.4 light years against a modern value near 11.4; Thomas Henderson (Alpha Centauri) and Friedrich Struve (Vega) reached comparable results within months. The "two-centimetre coin at thirteen kilometres" is our own arithmetic from that angle, and is approximate. The pre-Bessel objection from absent parallax, and the star-size problem arising from spurious telescopic discs, are given qualitatively; the discs are a diffraction artefact of a finite aperture. The ladder and Leavitt. Henrietta Swan Leavitt joined Harvard College Observatory in 1895 as one of its women "computers," measuring plates; she found and measured periods for roughly 1,700 variables in the Magellanic Clouds. The period–luminosity relation appeared as "Periods of 25 Variable Stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud," Harvard College Observatory Circular 173 (1912), issued under director Edward Pickering's name and opening with the statement that it "has been prepared by Miss Leavitt." The distance-ladder description is given structurally rather than with figures; the remark that recalibrating the variable-star rung has historically moved the whole extragalactic scale is stated qualitatively and is not primary-sourced here. WEIRD. Joseph Henrich, Steven J. Heine & Ara Norenzayan, "The weirdest people in the world?", Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33(2–3), 2010, 61–83 — 96% of samples from Western industrialised nations, 68% of subjects from the United States, from countries holding about 12% of the world's population, and the finding that such subjects are frequent outliers on many measures. Double empathy is Damian Milton, "On the ontological status of autism: the 'double empathy problem'," Disability & Society 27(6), 2012, 883–887, already carried elsewhere in this collection. The framing of this zine comes from Conquering Gaze from Nowhere at Stimpunks; Haraway and the physics were traced to their own primaries here rather than carried across. Cretyl Mills and Mildred Wells are as recorded in No. 39. Held honestly. Two joints are marked contested and argued in place rather than hedged: the parallax-to-situated-knowledges parallel on spread 9 (Haraway never mentions parallax; the analogy is ours, and a theorem cannot settle an epistemology), and the personal-equation-to-research-practice synthesis on spread 13. The three-erasures reading on spread 7 documents each case individually; treating them as a pattern is our interpretation, and we have not searched for counter-examples — the spread says so on its face. This chain again contains no leap joints — 10 documented, 2 contested — which is now two chains running. Worth watching rather than celebrating: if the weakest tag never fires, that may say more about which subjects we choose than about how carefully we argue them. L★S · 001 The Stimmer formerly · Gemini · The Twins 07h 45m · +22° · mag 1.9 Seen for centuries as two identical figures standing side by side. The old charts missed what was actually there: two bodies in constant, purposeful, self-regulating motion. Not mirror images. Not twins. Each one moving exactly as they need to move. self-regulationmovementembodimentrhythm ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Stimmer Stimming is not a symptom. It is a technology — one of the oldest human technologies, and one of the most sophisticated. The body knows things the diagnostic manual doesn't. The Stimmer is one of the brightest constellations in the winter sky and one of the most misread. The old charts saw identical twins. The reclaimed chart sees what's actually happening: two bodies in dialogue with themselves and with each other, each one moving in the precise way that keeps the nervous system regulated, present, and intact. Every culture that has ever watched the sky has found patterns here. Every nervous system that has ever inhabited a body has found its own version of this too. The motion that looks like repetition from the outside is, from the inside, a conversation between the body and the world — one that the body is very good at having, if it's allowed to. The Stimmer rises in the northeast in late autumn and is best observed in winter. At its culmination it stands almost directly overhead for observers in mid-northern latitudes. In clear conditions you can resolve Castor into its six component stars — three binary pairs orbiting one another in a gravitational conversation that has been going on for billions of years. L★S · 002 The Deep Diver formerly · Cetus · The Sea Monster 01h 44m · -11° · mag 2.0 The old charts called it a monster and placed it in the outer dark, at the edge of the maps where the ocean poured off the world. The monotropic mind goes all the way in. It doesn't skim surfaces; it finds the bottom of things. The old charts made Cetus a monster because the deep sea was where monsters lived. That logic has always been about the map-maker, not the territory. The deep is not monstrous. It is where the interesting things are. L★S · 003 The Pattern Seeker formerly · Virgo · The Maiden 13h 25m · -11° · mag 0.97 The largest constellation in the zodiac, and for good reason: pattern recognition at this scale takes up a lot of sky. The old charts saw a figure holding a sheaf of wheat. The reclaimed chart sees what that figure was doing — finding the signal in the noise, which is what wheat is. Grain selected from grass by someone who noticed. pattern recognitionsystemizingsignal detectionclassification ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Pattern Seeker Pattern seeking is not obsession. It is one of the foundational cognitive capacities of the human species — the one that produced agriculture, mathematics, music theory, taxonomy, and astronomy itself. Every person who has ever looked at the sky and found a pattern in the stars was doing exactly what The Pattern Seeker does, all the time, about everything. The pathologizing of pattern-seeking is one of the stranger moves of the diagnostic tradition. The same capacity that lets a person memorize every train schedule in the metropolitan area, map the complete ecosystem of a backyard, or hear the harmonic structure in a piece of music is described, in the diagnostic literature, as a "restricted and repetitive" behavior. The frame is the problem, not the capacity. Spica, this constellation's brightest star, is a binary system — two stars so close together and moving so fast that they've distorted each other into egg shapes. The Pattern Seeker's brightest point is a system that has been deeply, structurally changed by its relationship with another pattern. Porrima is also a binary, famous among double-star observers for its beauty and its long orbital period. Two stars, each completing the other's picture of the sky. L★S · 004 The Flood formerly · Aquarius · The Water Bearer 22h 05m · -13° · mag 2.9 The old charts saw a figure pouring water from a jar — an image of controlled, measured, deliberate giving. The reclaimed chart sees what actually happens when a mind holds too much and the vessel finally tips: not a failure of containment, but a return to equilibrium. The flood is not the disaster. The flood is the water going where it needs to go. emotional intensityoverwhelmequilibriumrelease ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Flood The diagnostic tradition describes emotional intensity as dysregulation. The word "dysregulation" assumes a correct regulation — a factory setting from which the neurodivergent nervous system has deviated. But a nervous system that feels things deeply is not a miscalibrated nervous system. It is a nervous system doing exactly what nervous systems do, at a higher amplitude. The Flood is one of the oldest constellations in the sky. In Babylonian astronomy it was associated with the god Ea, who was, among other things, the god of wisdom — a figure who held all the water of the deep and who poured it out when it was needed. The pouring was not a loss of control. It was the wisdom itself. Sadalsuud — "the luckiest of the lucky" — was the star that rose with the first rains of spring. In cultures that depended on rain, this was not merely a meteorological event. It was the world coming back to life. What looks from the outside like the system being overwhelmed is often, from the inside, the system working — bringing the water where it needs to go, at last. L★S · 005 The Navigator formerly · Ursa Minor · The Little Bear 15h 44m · +77° · mag 2.02 The old charts saw a small bear — a diminutive, lesser version of the great bear nearby. The reclaimed chart sees what this constellation actually does: it contains Polaris, the pole star, the fixed point around which the entire sky appears to rotate. The smallest-seeming pattern holds the center. navigationorientationfixed pointsthe unseen anchor ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Navigator The Navigator doesn't move the way the other constellations move. While everything else in the sky wheels overhead in great arcs through the night, The Navigator holds still — or appears to. Polaris sits less than one degree from the celestial north pole and has been used for navigation for at least three thousand years. There are minds that work like this: that provide a fixed reference, a stable orientation point, for everyone around them. They may not be the most dramatic presence in the room. They may not move in the ways the culture expects. But when you need to know which way is north, you look for them. Kochab was the pole star before Polaris. Due to the slow precession of Earth's axis — a wobble that takes about 26,000 years to complete one cycle — the position of true north moves gradually through the sky. In 3000 BCE, Kochab was the star the navigators used. In 14,000 CE, Vega will take the role. The Navigator is a reminder that fixed points are real but not permanent. They hold for as long as they need to hold, and then something else steps in. L★S · 008 The Forge formerly · Orion · The Hunter 05h 35m · +5° · mag 0.12 The most recognized constellation in the sky. The old charts saw a hunter with a raised club and a belt of three perfect stars. The reclaimed chart sees what is actually at its center: the Great Nebula, a stellar nursery where new stars are being forged right now, out of gas and gravity and the remains of everything that came before. creationmakingthe processwhat gets made from wreckage ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Forge The Orion Nebula — M42, the middle "star" in Orion's sword — is a stellar nursery 1,344 light-years away and 24 light-years across. Within it, new stars are being born from collapsing clouds of gas and dust. Some of those stars will have planets. Some of those planets may eventually have bones. Those bones will be piezoelectric. The Forge makes star stuff, right now, while you look at it. Betelgeuse is a red supergiant — a star so large that if it replaced our sun, it would extend past Jupiter. It is also dying. At some point in the next hundred thousand years (possibly much sooner; possibly last Tuesday, the light just hasn't arrived yet) it will explode in a supernova visible in daylight and scattered its own star stuff across the surrounding parsecs. The Forge contains a star that is, right now, in the process of becoming the raw material for everything that comes next. The three belt stars — Alnitak, Alnilam, Mintaka — are nearly perfectly aligned, which is why they're so striking. The odds of three unrelated stars lining up like that by chance are low; these are all part of the same young star-forming region, born in the same cloud of gas, traveling together through the galaxy. They are not a coincidence. They are a cohort. This is the constellation to watch when you want to remember that the universe is still making things out of its own wreckage. Cosmic Connections Three sites, one web. Nothing here was arrived at in a straight line, and none of it is anybody's alone. This is the page about the links — what travels between Stimpunks, More Realms, and Star Stuff, and why the connections are the content rather than the packaging. Cosmic Connections is Helen Edgar 's phrase for what this collection is doing, and it landed because it was already carrying two histories. The first is Connections , James Burke's BBC series, first broadcast in 1978. Ryan Boren grew up on it, and a good deal of how this collection thinks came from watching it young. Its method is the opposite of the tidy march of great men and eureka moments: Burke's argument is that you cannot understand any piece of the modern world in isolation, because the thing you are holding was assembled out of centuries of unrelated people solving unrelated problems for reasons of their own — profit, boredom, war, faith — none of them aiming at the outcome they produced. An episode starts somewhere medieval and arrives, by way of eight things that have no obvious business with each other, at the object on your desk. Burke went on making the argument across three more series, in 1994, 1997, and 2023. The second is The Cosmic Connection: An Extraterrestrial Perspective , Carl Sagan's 1973 book — the one where he first put the line in print that this whole collection runs on: we are made of star-stuff. Sagan's connection was between our bodies and the interiors of dead stars. Burke's was between a stirrup and a computer. They turn out to be the same move made at different scales: follow the thread, and the thing that looked separate turns out to be continuous with everything around it. Connection isn't a metaphor we apply to the material. It is how the material got made — and how we make it.

Three sites, one web There are three places, and they do different work. Calling them a collaboration is accurate but too flat; what actually happens is traffic. The three sites and what travels between them Stimpunks, More Realms, and Star Stuff drawn as three nodes of one web. Stimpunks sends glossary, patterns, and design method; More Realms sends essays, coinages, and speculative framing; Star Stuff sends both of them back finished, printable, citable artifacts. Every arrow runs in both directions. coinages · citations · corrections glossary patterns design method essays speculative framing felt time · relations STIMPUNKS the garden MORE REALMS the wandering STAR STUFF the flowering no source, no downstream — every edge runs both ways Figure 1 · Not a pipeline with an origin and an output. A web, where each site is upstream of the other two. Helen wrote about Monotropa uniflora — the ghost pipe, which grows no chlorophyll and takes all its carbon second-hand from fungi — as a botanical expression of being monotropic. Monotropa means one turn : the same root as monotropism , the Autistic attention style named by Murray, Lesser and Lawson in 2005. A plant name from Linnaean botany, an attention theory from Autistic researchers, and a mutual-aid ethic about receiving without shame, all sitting on one etymology. Nobody planned that. It was found by following a link.

Why links, and not folders Stimpunks has kept its knowledge as a web of small linked pieces rather than a hierarchy of folders, on the argument that a web of notes with links between them is far more useful than a fixed hierarchical system — the design principle underneath both Tim Berners-Lee's original proposal for the web and Niklas Luhmann's card-index practice. The payoff is not tidiness. It's that connecting notes makes higher-level concepts appear that nobody wrote down , and connecting those makes larger categories appear in turn. The categories are outputs, not inputs. That is emergence , which Stimpunks glosses as the way complex systems and patterns arise out of a multiplicity of relatively simple interactions. It is the same principle physics states as more is different — that a large enough collection of parts obeys laws you cannot read off the parts themselves — and the same one adrienne maree brown builds organizing practice from in Emergent Strategy : small actions and connections create complex systems. Link density and emergence Three panels. In the first, eight notes sit unconnected in a grid — a filing system. In the second, a few links appear between them. In the third, the links are dense enough that a higher-level concept, drawn as a ring around a cluster, has formed without anyone writing it. FILED eight notes, no edges LINKED edges start doing the work EMERGENT a concept nobody wrote Figure 2 · The dashed ring is the point. It is not a folder somebody made; it is a pattern that appeared once the links got dense enough, and it can be named afterward. This is why the collection is built the way it is — every zine cross-linking its siblings, every term linking back out to the glossary, search that indexes down to the individual spread rather than the page. The link density is the argument. A collection where each piece sat in its own folder would make all the same claims and none of the same connections.

Accumulated, not authored The part of Burke that stuck hardest is the timescale. His chains run for centuries, and no single link in them is a breakthrough. Each is a small competent adjustment by someone who could not have known what it would join up with. Progress in Connections is not a person; it's an accumulation. Stimpunks calls this iteration and treats it as the working method rather than a phase: as Cornelius Minor puts it, learning is a series of iterations — not linear, and needing deliberate room made for revision and failure. Which is also why this site publishes its own errors. The changelog and the fact-check ledger are the iteration made visible: what we got wrong, what's right, who caught it. A living document that never shows a correction is just a document making a claim about itself. Everything is a remix The phrase is Kirby Ferguson 's, from his video series Everything Is a Remix (2010–2012, with a fifth part in 2023) — the argument that copying, transforming and combining is not a failure of originality but the mechanism of creativity itself. Stimpunks' license page puts the same thing in the house register: “Nothing comes from nowhere. Punk understood this. So did bricoleurs, rhizome thinkers, and every neurodivergent kid who built something strange and new out of whatever was at hand.” That is why everything here is CC BY-SA 4.0 and made to be printed, forked and passed on. A collection that argued for interdependence and then locked its own doors would be arguing against itself.

The refusals Not: Not a genealogy of geniuses. Burke's whole point is that nobody in the chain saw the end of it, and we are not adding ourselves to a lineage of great minds. Not “everything is connected” as mysticism. Specific links, named and checkable, or it doesn't go on the page. Not interdisciplinary as tourism — borrowing a physics word for its glamour and leaving the physics behind. Not connection as extraction. Crediting the source is the connection; taking the idea and dropping the name is the opposite of one. Not a shared masthead standing in for a shared byline. Where a piece is Helen's, it is hers and says so. Held honestly Emergence is a real property of complex systems, and the physics of more is different is well established. It does not follow that any particular web of notes will produce insight, that our three sites are a complex adaptive system in the technical sense, or that link-density guarantees anything. Burke's chains are also a storyteller's selection: he picks the path that arrives somewhere, and the unchosen paths that went nowhere don't get an episode. We are noticing a rhyme between how knowledge accumulates and how we work, and using it as a method. That's a good reason to link generously. It isn't a proof. So: follow the links. Read a zine, hit a term you don't know, land in the glossary, come back by a different door than you left. That route through the material is not a failure to organize it. The Design System One typeface chosen for legibility, five accents held at near-uniform lightness, and body text that never fades. The visual language of this collection is itself an argument about access — so here it is, with its numbers and its receipts. Every artifact here is a single self-contained HTML file with no dependencies beyond Google web fonts — no build step, no framework, no JavaScript required to read a word. That constraint is the first design decision, and most of the others follow from it. A zine should be one file you can save, print, fork, or hand to someone. Accessibility isn't a layer applied at the end. It is the thing that decides the palette.

Typeface The collection sets its prose in Atkinson Hyperlegible , released free by the Braille Institute in 2019 and named for its founder, J. Robert Atkinson. It was drawn for readers with low vision, and its whole argument is letterform distinction — making characters that are commonly confused resolve differently from each other rather than merely look handsome together. The disambiguation problem I l 1 | 0 O o r n m a e s Look at the tail on the lowercase l , the slashless but narrowed 0 , the distinct apertures on a , e , and s . In a face built for elegance these converge; here they are deliberately pulled apart. For a collection about not being sorted into a norm, a typeface designed by and for people the standard face failed is not a neutral choice. Display · Atkinson Hyperlegible Next Bold The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Body · Atkinson Hyperlegible, 1.02rem / 1.75 Almost every atom heavier than helium was forged in stars and their deaths. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood came from stars that died before the Earth existed. Labels & counters · Space Mono STIMPUNKS FOUNDATION · ZINE NO. 1 · SPREAD 3 / 7 Two other faces earn their place. Space Mono carries every eyebrow, label, page counter, and colophon — a monospace voice for the machinery around the text, deliberately unlike the prose so it never competes with it. Fraunces appears where a piece needs an editorial register rather than a documentary one; Bone Song , Underground , and You Were Never One Thing are set in it with Space Mono, and use no Atkinson at all. The migration, and the bug it uncovered The collection ran on two versions of the face for a while: 18 pages on Atkinson Hyperlegible Next (the 2025 release, which adds five weights, a variable format, and support for over 150 languages), 26 still on the original, and 3 — the Fraunces-set trio above — on neither. All 44 Atkinson pages now load Next. Switching cost nothing in layout: the same measuring string set at 16px came out 286.97px before and 286.78px after, and across 126 measured text blocks not one changed height, width, or line count. The sweep turned up something worse than a split. Every page requesting Next asked Google Fonts for a 200..900 weight range — but Next only publishes 200–800 , so the request returned HTTP 400 and no @font-face rule at all. Those pages had been quietly falling back to system-ui for every visitor who didn't happen to have the font installed locally, which is to say almost all of them. A typeface picked specifically because it was drawn for readers the standard face fails was not reaching those readers. Corrected to 200..800 ; the woff2 now actually downloads.

Palette The canonical tokens live in starstuff.css as :root { --sp-* } — one source of truth for every recurring color. Each page aliases them inline ( --purple: var(--sp-purple) ), so a palette change happens in one place instead of forty-seven. A new shared color means a new --sp- token, never a hex pasted across pages.

Grounds --sp-void-deep #07070f L* 2.1 --sp-void #0a0a14 L* 3.0 --sp-deep #0d0d1a L* 4.0 --sp-page #0f0f1c L* 4.8 --sp-card #0f0f2a L* 5.5 None of them is black. Each carries a violet cast — #0a0a14 sits at hue 290° in CIELAB — so the ground reads as night rather than as absence. --sp-card is the most saturated of the five, which is what makes a card lift off the page without a border or a shadow doing the work.

Accents --sp-purple #a78bfa L* 64.6 · 7.24:1 --sp-pink #f472b6 L* 65.5 · 7.44:1 --sp-gold #fbbf24 L* 80.7 · 11.80:1 --sp-cyan #22d3ee L* 77.9 · 10.90:1 --sp-green #4ade80 L* 79.2 · 11.30:1 Five accents, all of them clustered between L* 64.6 and 80.7 — a spread of 16 points across the whole set. That tight band is the discipline: any accent can replace any other on a given page without changing how heavy the page feels. It's why each zine can be tinted differently (cyan for water, green for aurora, gold for bone) and still be recognizably the same collection. The lowest-contrast accent on the darkest ground still clears 7.2:1 .

Text & neutrals --sp-white #f9fafb L* 98.2 · 18.84:1 --sp-white-soft #f4f2fb L* 95.9 · 17.76:1 --sp-secondary-soft #d4d0e4 L* 84.3 · 13.07:1 --sp-muted #c4b5d4 L* 75.8 · 10.23:1 --sp-secondary #b8aed0 L* 72.9 · 9.38:1 --sp-dim #8a86a0 L* 57.1 · 5.62:1 --sp-dim-soft #807d98 L* 53.5 · 4.97:1 Note what the ladder does not do: it never dips below full opacity to make text quieter. "Muted" here means a different hue at high contrast, not the same hue at 60% alpha. Every value above clears WCAG AA for body text against --sp-void — the dimmest by the smallest margin, and only after being lifted for exactly that reason. The one that failed, and what it cost to fix --sp-dim-soft used to be #63607a — 3.27:1 , under the 4.5:1 AA floor. It styles page counters, series numbers, colophons and refs at 0.5–0.55rem, so it is small text and gets no large-text exemption; publishing a contrast table with that in it was the thing that made it obvious. Raised to #807d98 : same CIELAB hue and chroma, L* 41.9 → 53.5, now 4.97:1 on the void and 4.73:1 on the lightest ground, still visibly softer than --sp-dim . Auditing every text element against its own composited background then turned up four more: an accent pink on a tinted card that came to 4.43:1, three runs of alpha-faded cream on the broadside — the exact "faded gray" this system claims to refuse — and two links left unstyled, falling back to the browser's default blue at 2.11:1 on near-black. All fixed. All 47 pages now pass AA on screen.

Palette lineage The palette began as a Solarized dark variant. That happened before this repository existed, so there's no commit to point at — and it matters less than it sounds, because none of Solarized's sixteen values survive anywhere in the collection. The accents are Tailwind CSS v3's 400-weight ramp, exactly: --sp-purple is violet-400, --sp-pink is pink-400, --sp-gold is amber-400, --sp-cyan is cyan-400, --sp-green is green-400, --sp-white is gray-50. The grounds are ours; no Tailwind gray is that violet. What we kept from Ethan Schoonover is the method , and it's worth naming precisely because the method is the valuable part: A small, fixed, named accent set used as semantic tokens rather than color picked per occasion. --sp-* is that idea. Accents pinned to a narrow lightness band, so substitution doesn't disturb the page. Ours sit at L* 64.6–80.7; Solarized's at L* 49.1–60.1. A ground that refuses pure black and commits to a hue. Solarized's #002b36 leans cyan at hue 230°; our #0a0a14 leans violet at 290°. Warm cream instead of white for paper — --paper: #f5f0e8 in the broadside, --bone: #e8dfc8 in Bone Song , both close cousins of Solarized's base3 #fdf6e3 . And then we threw out its central move. Solarized's stated goal is to reduce brightness contrast while keeping hue separation. We push contrast as high as it goes: Body text against its own ground Scheme Text Ground Contrast Star Stuff #f9fafb #0a0a14 18.84:1 Solarized dark #839496 #002b36 4.75:1 Solarized dark (emphasis) #93a1a1 #073642 4.86:1 "Full-opacity body text, no faded grays" is a direct repudiation of the scheme this palette started from. A low-contrast colorscheme is a lovely thing in a code editor at 2am and the wrong thing entirely for a document meant to be readable by people with low vision, printed on a cheap printer, and handed across a table. Accessibility-first won the argument. Credit Solarized for the discipline, not for the colors.

Principles Full opacity Text is never dimmed with alpha to signal hierarchy. Hierarchy comes from size, weight, and hue at full strength. Generous leading Body copy runs 1.75 line-height. Long measure is capped around 36–38rem so lines stay trackable. 8px radius Cards round at 8px — soft enough to read as an object, tight enough to stay documentary. 3px left border A colored left rule marks anything set apart: claims, callouts, specimens, cards. The system's most reused gesture. Pure-CSS starfield Stars are layered radial-gradient stops on body::before , plus a few absolutely-positioned twinkling dots. No images, no canvas. Spectrum rule A 2px gradient through all five accents, used once per page as a signature — the palette introducing itself.
Motion, and the option to refuse it

Motion, and the option to refuse it The starfield twinkles from one shared @keyframes twinkle-anim in starstuff.css — it used to be copy-pasted into some twenty-five pages. Anyone whose system asks for less motion gets none: a global prefers-reduced-motion block collapses every animation and transition to 0.001ms and disables smooth scrolling, across every page at once. Motion here is decoration, and decoration must be declinable.

The refusals Not: Not low-contrast because low-contrast looks sophisticated. Not gray text on gray backgrounds to signal "secondary." Not a framework, a build step, or a bundle to read one page of prose. Not a design system that can't survive being printed in black and white. Not accessibility as a compliance checkbox added after the visual design was settled.

Print These are meant to be printed and handed to people, so paper is a first-class target rather than an afterthought. starstuff.css strips the site navigation and paging chrome from every printed page — that chrome is never content. On paper the whole collection inverts: white sheet, near-black type, decoration dropped. Because every page aliases the --sp-* tokens, the shared stylesheet inverts them once inside @media print and all forty-seven pages follow. Accents become ink there too — gold #fbbf24 on white is 1.6:1, so an accent that carries meaning as text has to give up its color to stay readable. The one exception is the spectrum rule, a 2px sliver kept in full color with print-color-adjust: exact , which survives the browser's background-graphics setting. Diagrams inherit the same treatment: SVG paints with fill and stroke rather than color , so labels and line art are inverted separately — the diagrams are content here, not ornament. Paged zines also turn inside out for paper. On screen a zine shows one .spread at a time; a single Cmd/Ctrl+P reveals every spread and starts each on its own sheet, so you get the whole zine rather than the visible page. This was broken until it wasn't Worth recording plainly, because the failure is more instructive than the fix. Browsers leave "Background graphics" off by default. For most of this collection's life, no page inverted its colors for print — so a light-on-dark zine sent near-white type to a white sheet and printed blank . Measured with print media emulated, 44 of 46 pages printed illegibly . On one, no pixel anywhere on the sheet was darker than mid-gray. The Bone Song poem — a piece built to be printed and handed to someone — came out as an empty page. Only the changelog was correct. The L★S broadside was half-right: its recto prints as designed, but its verso carried the poem in cream on near-black and vanished too. All forty-seven pages now print legibly, verified two ways — computed text contrast against white for every text element, and pixel sampling of the rendered sheet. A stated principle nobody measures is a wish.

Shared assets What every page pulls in File Carries starstuff.css The --sp-* palette tokens, the .ss-nav site navigation, the shared twinkle keyframe, the reduced-motion block, the print rules, and the injected spread-footer nav styles. starstuff.js Per-spread prev/next controls and #spread-N deep linking for paged zines. A safe no-op on any page that isn't one. favicon.svg The L★S mark. og-card.jpg The 1200×630 link-unfurl card shared by every page. Everything is linked by relative URL, which is what lets any page be saved, moved, or served from a subdirectory without breaking. Each page tints the shared nav by setting one custom property — --nav-accent — on the nav element, which is the whole theming API. Reuse it This system is CC BY-SA 4.0 , like everything else here. Take the tokens, take the contrast floor, take the refusals. If you build something with it, the only ask is that you keep it free and pass it on. Solidarity, not charity. Every correction to this page, and to every piece in the collection, gets published in the changelog — our own errors included. The Difference-First Frame A summary of Helen Edgar's essay Why Difference Comes First (Autistic Realms · More Realms), shared with Stimpunks and used with her blessing. Reference notes behind Love You Down To Your Star Stuff — for a funder, researcher, or skeptical parent who asks why difference gets to be the starting point. A resonant frame, not a proof. What this is, and isn't This is not physics or philosophy proving that our ethic is true. Experts disagree about much of what follows, and relational quantum mechanics in particular is one interpretation among several, not settled consensus. What this is: a resonance — three fields, working independently at wildly different scales, keep arriving at the same shape of idea. That convergence is worth having in our back pocket. It is not evidence, and we will not present it as evidence. Zine No. 9, The Lines We Drew , warns against precisely the move we must avoid here: dressing a human value up as a law of nature, the way the bell curve was recruited to make "normal" look like physics and eugenics followed. So we say it plainly, up front. The atoms do not owe us this conclusion. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof.

The claim, in one line Sameness is the fragile or fabricated thing. Difference isn't a deviation from a baseline — it's the condition anything real, including a self, gets made from. One clarification keeps that line honest, because it braids together two different mechanisms that happen to teach the same lesson. At the cosmic scale, sameness is fragile : near-uniformity was simply the early universe's default, and it was unstable — the smallest unevenness grew into everything. At the social scale, sameness is fabricated : the "typical profile," the flat baseline, is manufactured and then treated as ground truth. Two mechanisms. One moral. We should never blur them into a single tidy slogan, because the precision is where the argument holds.

Three scales, one shape Cosmology · the strongest leg The early universe was almost perfectly uniform: the cosmic microwave background — the oldest light we can see, the Big Bang's afterglow — varies in temperature by only about one part in 100,000 across the whole sky. A truly uniform cosmos would have stayed a dead, featureless fog forever: nothing dense enough for gravity to gather, no stars, no us. Everything that exists, exists because that near-sameness broke. The tiny perturbations are not noise on top of the story; they are the story. This part is well established (Penzias & Wilson 1965; mapped by COBE, WMAP, and Planck). Philosophy · the core Gilles Deleuze argued that Western thought habitually treats difference as secondary — judged by a thing's identity to a concept, its opposition to a contrast, its analogy to a standard, its resemblance to an ideal. All four smuggle in the same assumption: that a fixed baseline exists first, and difference is only the distance from it. Deleuze reverses it — identity is produced out of a prior field of difference, not the ground difference strays from (Deleuze 1994). That is exactly what a diagnostic model does to Autistic people: it measures us against identity, opposition, analogy, and resemblance to a "typical" profile that was never the ground truth to begin with. The flat line is the construct. Difference is what's actually there. Damian Milton's work on the ontological status of autism (Milton 2012) makes a kindred point from inside autism studies — the neurodivergent "spiky profile" gets read as deviation from a flat, typical baseline that was never the ground truth. Quantum physics · the most speculative, most hedged At the opposite end of every scale, Carlo Rovelli's Relational Quantum Mechanics proposes that particles don't carry fixed, standalone properties — what a thing is only becomes determinate in relation to another system (Rovelli 1996). Reading Rovelli from the inside, Helen describes not being a fixed, bounded thing moving through the world but something that emerges in and through its relations and encounters (Edgar 2026). We flag this leg as the shakiest: it is interpretation, offered as rhyme, not as physics settling a question about people. (A related move we add here, not in Helen's essay: Karen Barad's agential realism holds that it is relationships, not pre-given separate objects, that come first — Barad 2007.)
One term we have to handle carefully

One term we have to handle carefully Deleuze's "smooth space" (Deleuze & Guattari 1987) does not mean uniform. It means a field of ungridded, intensive variation — the opposite of striated space, which is fixed, measured, gridded. So the CMB's uniform fog is not "smooth" in Deleuze's sense; it's a pre-individual field, prior to both. The useful move is not "the universe was smooth and that's good." It's that diagnostic categories are the striation — the grid laid over a field that was full of ungridded variation before the grid arrived — and what LYDTYSS protects (the spiky profile, ★stuff, no-wrong-configuration) is the ungridded variation the grid keeps trying, and failing, to fully capture.

The bridge: ethodiversity Between the cosmic argument and the single nervous system sits a middle layer, and it keeps the whole thing from being merely personal or merely abstract. Ombre Tarragnat's ethodiversity — the variety of ways of being and behaving across humans and other animals — makes the same claim at the scale of behaviour, and locates it precisely: not inside one organism, but as a property of a relational field , the way biodiversity belongs to an ecosystem rather than any single species in it (Tarragnat 2025). Its opposite, ethonormativity — the unspoken grid of which ways of being are allowed to count — is functionally striation applied to behaviour: a grid laid over a field that was varied before the grid arrived. Stimpunks keeps this in the ethodiversity glossary ; the term also has earlier roots in conservation biology (Cordero-Rivera 2017), which we note as a Stimpunks aside rather than part of Helen's essay. So the chain runs: CMB perturbations, quantum relation, Deleuzian difference-before-identity (why difference is fundamental) → ethodiversity (the same claim, scaled to behaviour and species) → the spiky profile and LYDTYSS (the same claim again, scaled to one bodymind). Ethodiversity is what lets the cosmic-scale idea land as something ecological and communal, not only intimate. Zine No. 8, The Universe Runs on Difference, already carries this layer.
What it gives LYDTYSS — and how to use it

What it gives LYDTYSS — and how to use it It doesn't make the phrase heavier. LYDTYSS should stay exactly as unadorned as it is; the page works because it stays intimate, not academic, and this material must never be folded into it. What it gives us is an answer , ready when someone asks why difference gets to be the starting point rather than a thing to explain or excuse: because that's the shape reality takes wherever we've actually looked, from the CMB to a nervous system. Not despite the mess — because of it. Hold this as backing material: something to draw on if a funder, researcher, or skeptical parent asks us to justify the framing. Physics and philosophy have been implicit in the zines already; if this becomes a future zine, its distinct claim must stay clear of No. 8. No. 8's point is one of breadth — variety beats monoculture. This page's point is deeper and different: difference is ontologically prior — identity is produced out of a field of difference, not the baseline it deviates from. "Difference comes first," not merely "difference is good." Framed that way, it's a genuine addition, and the ontological floor under both No. 8 and No. 9. If it becomes a zine, it should keep Helen's first-person voice and byline — the essay's intimacy is the point, and flattening it into institutional "we" would lose exactly what makes it land.

On the CMB, for the curious The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light we can observe — the Big Bang's afterglow. For about 380,000 years the universe was too hot and dense for light to travel freely; once it cooled enough for atoms to form, light was released to travel in straight lines, and it has been arriving ever since as faint microwave radiation from every direction. Two things matter here: it is extremely uniform (about one part in 100,000), and the tiny variations that do exist are everything — gravity grew them into galaxies, stars, and us.
