A story that travels with an animal

The claim A story that travels with an animal Most claims about connection are wishes. This one is a range map. In Sand Talk, Tyson Yunkaporta — Apalech clan, Wik — sets out to tell part of a big story, and marks plainly whose it is and that it was given to be given away: "I will tell parts of a big story, a metastory that connects and extends all over Australia through massive songlines in the earth and sky, a Star Dreaming that Juma Fejo from the Larrakia People wants to share with all peoples. It goes everywhere that turtles go—and there are turtles all over the world, even in desert country, so it connects everybody." Tyson Yunkaporta, Sand Talk (2019), p. 15 Read quickly, that last sentence sounds like a lovely figure of speech. It isn't one. It is a testable statement about where an animal lives, and the reach of the story is pinned to the reach of the turtle. So we did the obvious thing and checked. The sentence holds. What follows is what we found on the way — including two places where the turtle's own biology turns out to say the opposite of what everybody assumes. A path that meanders is not a path that failed. It is just how a path is. the story's reach is the animal's reach sea river swamp claypan desert no word for nonlinear — the winding path is just how a path is so it connects everybody yunkaporta · sand talk · p. 15 a claim you can go and check Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks

The range Every continent but one Roughly 357 living species of turtle, and they are almost everywhere you are. Sea turtles in every warm ocean. Freshwater turtles in rivers, lakes, billabongs, ditches, drainage canals and city ponds on six continents. Tortoises on land from the Mojave to Madagascar to the Aldabra atoll. Softshells buried in river mud. The only continent without them is Antarctica — and the only reason is the cold. They are also old. The turtle body plan has been recognisably itself for more than 200 million years. It has crossed oceans, watched continents split, and outlasted the animals that were supposed to be the story. Yunkaporta's sentence works because of a fact about the world, not a fact about language. If you want one animal that nearly every human community on Earth has had to live alongside, look at your options. There are not many. The turtle is one of them. Which means every people had to think about it — and, as we'll see, they did not all think the same thing. where turtles are every warm ocean rivers · lakes · swamps · city ponds grassland · scrub · forest floor desert — and under it antarctica — the one exception ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✕ ≈357 species · turtle taxonomy working group six continents out of seven Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks

Even in desert country The ones who wait underneath "Even in desert country" is the part of the sentence that sounds like a stretch. It is the part that is most literally true. In the Pilbara and Gascoyne of Western Australia, Chelodina steindachneri lives in pools that can dry up and stay dry for a year or more. It does not leave and it does not die. It digs into the riverbed or bank and waits, and comes back to the surface after heavy rain. Across the world in the Mojave, the desert tortoise Gopherus agassizii spends up to 95% of its life underground, in burrows, out of a heat that would kill it in the open. And here is the part that makes it more than trivia: those burrows are not only the tortoise's. Other animals shelter in them. The desert tortoise is a keystone species — the one who dug itself a survivable place made a survivable place for everybody else. Which is, more or less, the whole argument for building rooms that fit the people who need them most. a survivable place, dug dry claypan · no water for a year or more and the lodgers buried, and waiting keystone species · the burrow shelters more than its digger c. steindachneri, pilbara · g. agassizii, mojave up to 95% of a life, underground Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks

The reversal The shell was a shovel Everyone knows what a turtle shell is for. Everyone is wrong about how it started. It did not begin as armour. In Eunotosaurus africanus, an early relative on the turtle stem line from the South African Karoo, the ribs broaden long before there is anything shell-like to hide inside. Lyson and colleagues (Current Biology, 2016) put the case plainly: broadened ribs on their own provide little protection, and they cost you — a stiffened trunk shortens your stride and slows you down, and it gets in the way of breathing. What broad ribs are good for is digging. A rigid trunk is a stable base to swing a powerful forelimb against. The shell starts as the anchor for a shovel. Protection is an exaptation — a use the structure was not built for, discovered later, and now the only use anyone remembers. Read it back onto spread 4 and the sentence closes: the animal that got everywhere, including desert country, got there by first learning to go down. The thing you are told is a hiding place is the thing that let somebody survive. what broad ribs are actually for ordinary ribs narrow · they move you breathe with them broadened ribs wide · they lock a stable base to dig from a shovel's anchor, not a shield protection came later — an exaptation · lyson et al. 2016 eunotosaurus africanus · karoo basin it began as a way to go down Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks
They had to invent a new way to breathe

The cost They had to invent a new way to breathe Every adaptation is a bargain, and in turtles you can read the receipt. Almost every land vertebrate breathes with its ribs. The ribcage expands, the lungs fill. Mammals, birds, crocodilians, lizards — all of us, all the time, without thinking about it. Lock your ribs into a shell and that door closes. It is not a small inconvenience; it is the removal of the standard mechanism for staying alive. And Lyson and colleagues (Nature Communications, 2014) found the stem-line evidence for exactly this trade already in place: a rigid ribcage, the inferred loss of the muscles between the ribs, and the bony signatures of a different system taking over. What took over is a sling of abdominal muscle wrapped around the lungs and organs — a division of labour in which the ribs gave up ventilation and the belly muscles picked it up. No other animal breathes this way. So: they lost the ordinary way, and they are not diminished. They are a turtle. They went everywhere. the door that closed, and the one that opened rib ventilation unavailable — the ribs are now the shell abdominal sling lungs belly muscle takes the job a division of labour, not a deficiency lyson et al., nature communications, 2014 no other animal breathes like this the receipt for the shell Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks
Two ways to put a neck away

Two answers Two ways to put a neck away Once you have a shell, you have a head problem. There are two solutions alive today, and neither is the right one. The hidden-necked turtles — Cryptodira — fold the neck vertically, in an S, and pull the head straight back under the front of the shell. Sea turtles, tortoises, snappers, sliders, softshells. They are the ones most people picture. The side-necked turtles — Pleurodira — do not pull back at all. They lay the neck sideways along the shell's edge, tucking the head in under the rim. Every living one lives in fresh water in the southern hemisphere: South America, Africa and Madagascar, and Australia. Their map is a map of Gondwana, the supercontinent that broke apart beneath them. These are not a good version and a poor version. They are two lineages that met the same constraint and answered it differently, and both are still here, hundreds of millions of years on. The turtle a reader in Sydney pictures and the turtle a reader in Ohio pictures fold their heads away by different means. Neither of them is doing it wrong. one problem, two solutions, both alive cryptodira hidden-necked · side view the S folds up and down head pulls straight back pleurodira side-necked · top view folds left or right, flat head tucks under the rim every living side-neck is southern: s. america · africa · australia their range is the shape of gondwana two suborders, two folds no universal solution Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks
Sex is not in the genes

The sand decides Sex is not in the genes In most turtles, nothing in the egg says what sex the hatchling will be. The nest says. It is called temperature-dependent sex determination. Cooler sand, one outcome; warmer sand, the other; and a narrow pivotal temperature between them where a fraction of a degree decides. The machinery is now partly known: the enzyme KDM6B strips a silencing mark from the male-determining gene Dmrt1 and switches the male path on, and at warmer, female-producing temperatures a signalling protein binds the Kdm6b locus and shuts it down. And it is not even tidy across the group. In the Asian yellow pond turtle, researchers found XY chromosomes and temperature sensitivity in the same animal, working together. The neat binary of "genetic or environmental" was ours, not the turtles'. Which brings us to the philosophers of the Discworld. In Terry Pratchett's novels, the great turtle Great A'Tuin carries the world, and the learned spend enormous effort trying to determine A'Tuin's sex. They never manage it. The joke is better than they knew. They were looking in the wrong place. In a real turtle the answer is not written in the animal at all. It is in the temperature of the sand where somebody laid it. what the nest decides cooler warmer pivotal temperature a fraction of a degree KDM6B on Dmrt1 switched on pSTAT3 represses Kdm6b · male path off and in some species, XY chromosomes as well — both at once temperature-dependent sex determination the binary was ours, not theirs Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks
A map made of the planet

Finding the way back A map made of the planet A sea turtle hatchling crosses the beach once, in the dark, weighing less than a bar of soap. Decades later it comes back to lay its own eggs on the same stretch of coast. How? Earth's magnetic field varies from place to place, and every stretch of coastline carries a slightly different signature. The evidence is that a hatchling learns the field of its natal beach and holds onto it — geomagnetic imprinting — then uses it to navigate home across an ocean. Brothers and Lohmann (Current Biology, 2015) tested this against nineteen years of nesting records along 600 km of Florida coast. As the field drifted, the nesting drifted with it. Where two stretches of coast came to share a signature, turtles crowded in; where the signatures pulled apart, nesting thinned. They are carrying a route in the body, learned once, held for a lifetime, and read against a planet that keeps quietly moving underneath it. A route held as knowledge, carried across a life, tying a people to a country. That is a rhyme with what a songline does — and a rhyme is all it is. The Larrakia story is not turtle magnetoreception, and turtle magnetoreception is not a songline. Two true things, next to each other. one beach, learned once, found again the field — different at every stretch of coast natal beach out, as a hatchling back, decades later, to the same coast 19 years of nesting records shifted as the field drifted brothers & lohmann, current biology, 2015 geomagnetic imprinting · natal homing a rhyme, not a proof Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks

The pattern in the shell One, two, three, five, eight Yunkaporta records Oldman Juma Fejo giving the sequence in the shell, and then records their own reaction to it: "I couldn't believe it when Oldman Juma told me the sequence—one became two, then three, then five in a row along the center of the shell. Then, at the eight points where each part met, eight new parts formed. The sequence goes: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and so on." Tyson Yunkaporta, Sand Talk (2019), pp. 225–226 Here is what is on an actual carapace. The keratin plates — scutes — are laid out to a plan: a small one at the neck, then five down the midline, flanked by four pairs at the sides and about twelve pairs around the rim. Five in a row along the centre of the shell is not a poetic flourish. It is what you count when you look. And we will say plainly where the passage stops being biology. Yunkaporta goes on to call this the golden ratio "that all nature is built upon, from flowers and trees to your body and even DNA." That last step is not supported. The golden ratio is not a general law of living form, and it is not in the structure of DNA. Both things are true at once, and we are not going to collapse them. A knowledge system that counts a real pattern in a real animal is not made better by a modern number, and not made worse by that number turning out to be over-claimed. The count in the shell is right. The cosmology is Larrakia. The maths claim is a maths claim, and it doesn't stand. a carapace, counted 123 45 1 nuchal 4 pairs pleural 5 vertebral down the midline ≈12 pairs marginal five in a row along the centre — that part you can count the scute plan of a typical carapace true count · over-claimed maths Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks

The thesis Not the same turtle Because turtles are almost everywhere, almost everybody had to think with one. What they thought is not the same thought. In Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe accounts, Sky Woman falls, animals dive for earth, the muskrat surfaces with mud in its claws, and the land is spread on a great turtle's back. This is why Turtle Island is a name for the continent — not a metaphor for it, a name. In the Chinese Huainanzi, the four poles of the world collapse, and Nüwa cuts the legs from the great sea turtle ao to prop the sky back up. The turtle is not a foundation; it is a repair. In the Hindu texts, Kurma is Vishnu's tortoise form, a pivot on the seabed so a mountain can be used to churn the ocean. Kurma is not carrying the world. The world-on-a-turtle's-back story is not this story, and the conflation is a Western habit. And in Terry Pratchett's Discworld, Great A'Tuin — Chelys galactica — swims through space with the world on its back, and nobody knows where or why. Here is the connection, and it is not that these are one story. They are five peoples who met the same animal and each made something different of it. The turtle didn't unify anybody. It gave everybody something to think with, and then let them think. A note we owe you: "turtles all the way down" is not William James and not Bertrand Russell. James wrote it with rocks, in 1882. The turtle version was hung on him in a 1967 thesis and has been repeated ever since. Its earliest printed appearance is from 1854. four turtles, drawn four ways, on purpose turtle island the land itself ao · huainanzi legs as pillars — a repair kurma a pivot for churning not a world-bearer great a'tuin chelys galactica and the star dreaming larrakia · told by its own people the connection is the meeting, not the matching five peoples, one animal, five thoughts not versions of each other Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks

What it costs to say this The shell is bone One last fact, and then the thing we actually came to say. A turtle shell is not a house it climbed into. The carapace is the animal's ribs and vertebrae, grown wide and fused. It is bone. And bone, as Iwao Yasuda found in the 1950s, is piezoelectric: press it and it answers with a small electrical charge. That is where this whole collection started, on page one of Bone Song. So the shell is not inert cover. It is a living structure that turns pressure into signal — the part of the animal that responds when the world leans on it. Which is why the phrase grates. "Come out of your shell" is said to quiet kids, to Autistic kids, to anyone whose way of being in a room is read as absence. It assumes the shell is a hiding place, and that the real person is elsewhere. In the animal that gave us the phrase, the shell is the skeleton. There is no coming out. There is no one in there behind it. The shell was never armour. It was how somebody got underground, and stayed alive, and then went everywhere. And the ones who did all that are in trouble. Around 75% of the testudine species studied show slow or negligible senescence — most of them age more slowly than we do, and some barely age at all. A lineage that largely does not die of being old is being killed anyway: roughly half of all turtle species are threatened. Deep time is no protection from a net, a road, or a bought beach. ~75% of studied testudines age slowly or not at all ~48% of all turtle species are threatened NotNot "come out of your shell." The shell is the skeleton. There is nobody hiding behind it. NotNot one world turtle. Five traditions are not five drafts of one story, and treating them that way is how a knowledge system gets flattened into a motif. NotNot a proof. Turtles rhyme with what we want to say about difference. The ethics do not rest on the rhyme; difference would deserve welcome in a universe that made only one shape. NotNot a mascot. Borrowing the animal for a metaphor is not the same as leaving it a beach to come back to. NotNot deep time as comfort. Surviving the Permian does not survive us. "Mountains rise and fall, and under them the Turtle swims onward. Men live and die, and the Turtle Moves. Empires grow and crumble, and the Turtle Moves. Gods come and go, and still the Turtle Moves. The Turtle Moves." Didactylos, in Terry Pratchett's Small Gods (1992) Asked whether that is really true, Didactylos shrugs and says the Turtle exists, that this will go on happening whether or not you believe it, and — the three words the whole zine has been walking toward — "It is real." the shell, from the inside vertebrae ribs, grown wide and fused pressure pressure charge bone is piezoelectric · yasuda, 1950s the carapace is ribs and vertebrae there is no coming out of it Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks

Three things we are flagging rather than smoothing. One: Yunkaporta's Fibonacci passage extends to the claim that the golden ratio is what "all nature is built upon, from flowers and trees to your body and even DNA." The five vertebral scutes down the midline of a carapace are real and countable; the general golden-ratio-in-nature claim, and specifically the golden ratio in DNA, are not supported, and we say so on spread 10 rather than quietly omitting it. Carrying a knowledge system faithfully includes not laundering an empirical claim through it. Two: the resemblance between natal homing and songlines is a rhyme. A route held in the body across a lifetime is not the same kind of thing as a route held in law, song and country by a people, and we are not claiming it explains anything about the other. Three: the Didactylos passage shipped as unconfirmed — attribution to Small Gods was solid but the wording had come from quote aggregators, which this house treats as leads and not as citations. Ryan then checked it against the book. It is verbatim, including the italic on the final Moves, so the zine now quotes the whole run rather than a fragment. We are leaving this note in rather than deleting it: the point is not that we were right, it is that we did not know we were until somebody opened the page. See the changelog, where corrections and closures are published rather than buried. And the standing one: as about.html puts it, we are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. That variation persists in nature is not why difference deserves welcome. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. It just keeps making animals that go everywhere, and letting them go. March 2020 · the sentence "FACT: COVID-19 is NOT airborne" The World Health Organization posted that on social media, and added that saying otherwise was misinformation. The same month the US CDC said the virus spreads "through respiratory droplets produced when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks that can land in the mouths or noses of people who are nearby or possibly be inhaled into the lungs." The CDC did not begin using the words "airborne" or "aerosol" to describe transmission until October 2020. In July of that year, 239 scientists wrote to the public health agencies asking them to recognise the airborne route. This zine is not about who lied. Nobody lied. It was doctrine, faithfully applied — and the doctrine rested on a number that had quietly changed jobs. Current recommendations, as the historians of this put it, rest on four tenets: that transmission is basically droplets versus aerosols; that the difference is droplet size alone; that the cut-off is 5 µm; and that each route matters at a different distance. "Yet, a relationship between these assertions is not supported by current scientific knowledge." Randall, Ewing, Marr, Jimenez & Bourouiba, Interface Focus 11(6), 20210049, 2021 Their paper is called "How did we get here." So is this collection. What follows is their reconstruction, walked one link at a time, with the strength of every link said out loud. documented the guidance, and its four tenets The four tenets Four stacked statements — a droplet/aerosol binary, size alone decides it, the cut-off is five micrometres, and each route matters at a different distance — with a single line beneath noting that the relationship between them is unsupported. i · droplets vs aerosols ii · size alone decides which iii · the cut-off is 5 µm iv · each route has its distance no relationship between them is supported Figure 1 · four claims, one missing link suspensiondeposition the guidance · 2020 Five Microns · Stimpunks

Breslau · the late 1800s The careful version came first Carl Flügge and his assistants set agar plates around rooms — at different distances, at different heights — and had people talk, cough, sing and sneeze. Then they waited. Up to five hours before collecting the plates, because they already understood that it takes time for respiratory emissions to settle, and that collecting early would only show you what fell fast. Three things about their work matter enormously, and all three were lost: One. They applied the word droplets to all respiratory emissions — regardless of initial size, regardless of whether they were still wet. Their "droplets" encompass both what we now call droplets and what we now call aerosols or droplet nuclei. The category that later split the field did not exist for them. Two. They found air currents significantly affect the range, and so recommended ventilation and avoiding crowding — not distance alone. Three. They understood infectious dose as pathogen-specific, and framed their distance recommendations for tuberculosis in those terms, not as a universal law. A hundred and twenty years before the argument of 2020, the answer was already on the table, with the measurements attached. what makes this a chain and not a mystery documented Flügge → Chapin What Flügge's word covered A single bracket labelled droplets spanning the whole size range, above a later diagram splitting the same range into droplets and aerosols at five micrometres. The same lab · the distances they actually got Twenty-one metres, reciting Shakespeare Flügge's people had a method that is hard to improve on for sheer nerve: rinse your mouth with a culture of something harmless and brightly coloured, then talk. Von Weismayr and Laschtschenko had subjects rinse with a saline suspension of Serratia marcescens and then speak, sing, cough and sneeze at plates set around the room. Colonies grew as far as 2 m from speakers, 4 m from coughers, and 9 m from sneezers — and that was without notable background airflows. Koeniger allowed ordinary indoor air currents to keep moving, which is what rooms actually do, and found that in speaking, droplets reached the extreme corners of a very large room, up to 12.5 m. And then the one that ought to be famous. At the dispatch box of the UK House of Commons, a speaker gargled a broth culture of Bacillus prodigiosus and recited Shakespeare in a loud voice to the empty chamber. Colonies were denser near the speaker, as you'd expect. They were also on plates more than 21 metres away. The evidence that breath travels the length of a room is older than the aeroplane. It was collected by people declaiming Shakespeare into the dark. and it stayed collected, and unread, for a century Why did later researchers keep finding nothing past 1–2 m? Partly because they collected their plates quickly. The Flügge team waited five hours. The first move is a loss

Providence, Rhode Island · 1910 The first move is a loss Most chains start with a discovery. This one starts with a deletion. Charles Chapin was Health Officer of Providence and later president of the American Public Health Association — by every account a formidable and effective public health official, credited as the foremost teacher of the paramount role of contact infection. In 1910 he published The Sources and Modes of Infection. In it he took a disdainful line on airborne transmission: the evidence did not support it, and worse, attending to it would divert effort from contact prevention — which was working, and which he had built a hospital around. He was not being unreasonable. Germ theory had just won. Handwashing, disinfection, water purification and sanitation were producing real, countable victories over the miasma theory of bad air. And to a field that had just buried miasma, airborne sounded like exhuming it. The Wellses would later note that some rejected airborne transmission precisely because the term seemed to revive the ancient and exploded theory of miasmas. Airborne transmission did not lose an argument. It lost a resemblance — to a theory that had just been beaten. why the deletion held Chapin's book became a seminal text for decades, and his doctrine held the field's focus on short-range contact for the next twenty years. Flügge's nuance — the ventilation, the nine metres, the word that covered everything — went with it. The early 1930s · the physics Wells said one hundred William and Mildred Wells, working on tuberculosis, put a real physical mechanism under the whole question — a race between two clocks. A droplet leaves a mouth and two things start at once. It falls, and it evaporates. If it is large, it hits the floor before it has dried, and lands as a visible stain near the person. If it is small, it dries first, and what is left — a droplet nucleus, the residue of everything that was dissolved in it — is light enough to stay up for a very long time. Wells worked out where the race turns over. The threshold he published was 100 micrometres. Not five. Wells' 1934 papers do not mention a 5 µm threshold at all. His own settling table is the part worth carrying around: 10 min 10 µm particle falling 2 m 30 min 5 µm particle falling 1.5 m 16 h 1 µm particle falling 2 m Sixteen hours. That is not a cloud that dissipates when someone leaves the room. That is the room. The idealization, and why it is load-bearing. To get 100 µm, Wells used a diffusion-based evaporation model in idealized quiescent conditions, applied to isolated droplets, with settling from Stokes' speed. Both assumptions are false in a real room: indoor air is never quiescent — temperature and pressure gradients alone drive flows of centimetres per second — and exhalations are not isolated droplets but a continuum of sizes carried inside a warm turbulent cloud. This is No. 38's lesson again from the other side. There, the observer's difference was idealized away and the correction was to put them back. Here, the room's motion was idealized away, and the number that came out was then used as if the room were still. A leap, declared. Stokes' settling law is not a medical equation; it is what any small thing does in any fluid. The same regime governs why dust grains stay suspended in an interstellar cloud for millions of years while larger grains settle to the midplane. The physics genuinely is continuous. But nothing about a nebula tells you anything about a classroom, and we are not going to pretend otherwise — so this bridge is tagged, and the tag is honest. leap Stokes here → Stokes in a molecular cloud documented Wells' physics → the 5 µm cut-off The race Wells described Two droplets leaving a mouth. The large one falls to the floor before it evaporates. The small one evaporates first, leaving a nucleus that stays suspended. Elsewhere · the 1930s and 40s A different question entirely While Wells was asking what stays in the air, another field was asking what gets into a lung. These are not the same question, and the answers are not interchangeable. Biologists and agricultural researchers were taking up new tools for studying microorganisms in air — the beginning of aerobiology — and industrial hygienists were studying what workers breathed. Their attention sat at the receiving end of the system: inhalation, penetration, and deposition in the different regions of the respiratory tract. As the historians put it, their interest was in where particles land, "and not on how the particles move through the air." Their finding, from industrial hygiene in the 1930s and 40s: only the smallest particles — 1–5 µm — reach the deepest part of the lungs. That is a good number. It is correct. It is about deposition. Then in 1951, Alexander Langmuir — first Chief of Epidemiologic Services at the CDC's predecessor, and one of the most forceful sceptics of natural airborne transmission — gave a presentation preparing public health students for airborne infection delivered as a weapon. It came months after the start of the Korean War. His words: "[P]articles larger than 5 µm in diameter are almost completely removed in the nose and upper respiratory passages," while "progressively increasing proportions of inhaled particles reach the terminal bronchioles and alveoli" below 5 µm. Langmuir, 1951 — a correct statement about deposition Note the shape of his position, because it is remarkable: airborne infection was not considered to occur naturally, but was understood to occur under artificial circumstances. The route he denied to tuberculosis he granted to biological warfare. The centre of this zine The joint nobody will solder Here is where the two numbers become one number, and here is where the people who reconstructed it stop and refuse to say it plainly — which is the most honest thing in the whole paper. In 1955 Wells published a book expanding his airborne theory, and in it he too now referred to the research showing that 1–5 µm particles reach deep into the lungs. His focus had shifted: not only what stays suspended, but what is truly infectious by reaching the deep lung. In 1964, in public remarks, Langmuir used the 5 µm figure as the distinction between large droplets and aerosols outright — stating that droplet size is relevant because of where the aerosols deposit in the lungs. So how did a deposition number become a suspension boundary? The historians looked, and wrote this: "Though no association is made explicit in any of the literature we reviewed, this focus on particle deposition in the lungs likely popularized the 5 µm diameter cut-off." Randall, Ewing, Marr, Jimenez & Bourouiba, 2021 Likely. No association made explicit in any of the literature they reviewed. The single most consequential link in a chain that shaped global infection control for seventy years is one that careful historians, having read the sources, will only call probable. The load-bearing joint is inferred. Its receptors sit throughout the respiratory tract, and initiation in the nose and upper airway matters. The literature · citing itself A number with no parent Once the number existed, it stopped needing a source. It had guidelines. The historians traced how the word airborne travels through the citation record, from WHO and CDC infection-control guidance backwards. What they found is that three incompatible definitions are in circulation under one word: particles that remain suspended, particles that can be inhaled, and particles that are infectious. Guidelines cite guidelines. And sometimes they cite sources that disagree with them — in one traced case, a CDC document cites Duguid to support an airborne definition about infectiousness, when Duguid used "airborne" to mean only what remains suspended. "Despite the prominence of this size threshold in the literature, a 5 µm threshold to distinguish between 'droplets' and 'aerosols' is not scientifically grounded." Where citations are given, they frequently trace back to William Wells. Who said one hundred. This is the mechanism, and it is not exotic. It is the same thing that happens to a misattributed quotation — the sort this collection keeps catching in itself. One to two metres · a separate lineage The other broken number The distance rule and the size rule arrived from different places, at different times, for different reasons — and were then bolted together as though one implied the other. The distance has its own long history. During the Crimean War, the Royal Commission recommended keeping beds in soldiers' barracks at least three feet apart. Biernacki advocated spacing beds to create an "invisible barrier" limiting a pathogen's excursion. These were sound empirical observations — more space, less transmission — but the mechanism attached to them later, that liquid droplets fall out within a metre or two, is not what the observations showed. The only explicit mechanistic link the historians find is narrow: Ziesché and Flügge, specifically for tuberculosis, referencing about 1 m tied to a particular exposure time and an extrapolated infectious dose of 400 bacilli. One pathogen, one dose model, one distance. Look at what descended from that: 1 m WHO · parts of Europe 1.5 m Australia 2 m USA · Canada UK Same virus. Same physics. Three different safe distances, which is the signature of a number that is conventional rather than derived. There is one more reason the zone felt real, and it is almost funny. When photography made it possible in the 1940s to actually see emissions from a cough or a sneeze, the observation window was 1–2 m wide — and the smallest particles could not be imaged at all. Consequence · one What the wrong number buys A number is not an opinion. It is a purchase order. Believe transmission is ballistic droplets falling out within a metre or two, and a whole shopping list follows automatically. Surfaces, because that is where ballistic droplets land. Barriers, because a sheet of plexiglass stops a ballistic thing. Distance, because the arc is short. Hand hygiene, because the route runs through touch. Each of these is a rational response to the model. And one more, which is the sharpest edge in this whole chain. If the danger is droplets at close range during specific procedures, then respirators are protective equipment for those procedures. So early guidance recommended N95 respirators for healthcare workers only during aerosol-generating procedures — and not while otherwise caring for the same patients, in the same rooms, for whole shifts. The number decided who got a respirator. Who paid · and who is missing from the paper The people nearest the risk Two groups have been on the wrong end of this number, and they are the same group in different decades: the people closest to the danger, telling everyone what they could see. The turn The swinging pendulum of history Langmuir lived long enough to say so himself. Decades after insisting that measles travelled by large droplets and close contact only, and having spent years disparaging Wells, he wrote a retrospective of his time at the CDC and admitted Wells had been right all along. He also wrote, in 1980, about the burden that doctrinal teaching places on public health decision-making, and about the difficulty of maintaining what he called the "eternal skepticism of the true scientist." In 2024 the WHO published a report that finally removes the droplet/aerosol dichotomy. And the commentary that greeted it said, in its own title, that it "does not move us forward in infection control strategies." The definition changed. The buildings did not. Fundamental insights are lost in history, and then cyclically re-discovered. That is not a metaphor here. It is the paper's finding. Randall et al., 2021 So: nobody authored this road either. Flügge did careful work and recommended ventilation. Chapin was defending a public health practice that was saving lives. Wells did real physics and published an honest number. Langmuir was preparing students for a threat that was, in 1951, entirely real. Every step was competent, and a number walked out of one question and into another without changing its name. The word they would not say

CERN · 4 July 2012 The word they would not say For years, physicists at the LHC had a bump in their data where the Higgs boson should be. They would not call it a discovery, and the reason was a number. The convention is exact, and Louis Lyons — who wrote the paper on where it came from — states it plainly: "It has become the convention in Particle Physics that in order to claim a discovery of some form of New Physics, the chance of just the background having a statistical fluctuation at least as large as the observed effect is equivalent to the area beyond 5σ in one tail of a normalised Gaussian distribution, or smaller; i.e. the p-value is no larger than 3 × 10⁻⁷." Louis Lyons, "Discovering the Significance of 5σ," arXiv:1310.1284, October 2013 Three in ten million. About one chance in three and a half million that the background alone could have thrown up something this big. And the discipline is enforced socially, not just statistically. Lyons notes that journals are very reluctant to allow the word 'discovery' to appear in the title, abstract or conclusions of a paper, unless the p-value is that small. Hold that beside a fact about what was at stake. If the physicists had been wrong, the universe would have been unaffected. No particle would have suffered. The cost of a false claim was a retraction and some embarrassment. They set the bar at one in three and a half million anyway. documented the convention → why 5 and not 3 Where five sigma sits A normal distribution with the region beyond two sigma shaded and labelled p equals 0.05, and the region beyond five sigma marked far out in the tail and labelled three times ten to the minus seven. 2σ p = 0.05 5σ 3 × 10⁻⁷ one in 3,500,000 before you may say “discovery” Figure 1 · the tail, and the far tail physicshuman sci 1 · the Higgs · 5σ Five Sigma · Stimpunks
A field that kept being wrong

The reason · empirical, not principled A field that kept being wrong The 5σ bar was not derived from theory. It was set because the field kept announcing things that turned out not to exist. "In the past there have been many 'phenomena' that corresponded to 3 or 4σ effects that have gone away when more data were collected. The 5σ criterion is designed to reduce the number of such false claims." Lyons, 2013 — the first argument he lists Read that as an institutional confession. Three sigma is already odds of about one in a thousand. Four sigma is about one in sixteen thousand. Physics found that even those were producing claims that evaporated, and so raised its own bar against its own enthusiasm. That is the move worth stealing. Not the specific number — the willingness to notice your field's error rate and respond by making your own life harder. And it went further. Lyons prints, in his own paper, the objection that the whole thing is unsound: "Statisticians who hear about the 5σ criterion are very skeptical about it being sensible." Lyons, 2013 — quoted by the man defending the criterion He does not bury that. He states it, gives the statisticians' reasoning — that probability distributions rarely describe reality accurately that far out in the tails — and then concedes: "Thus the Statisticians' criticism may well be valid." A field that publishes the case against its own gold standard is doing science. Keep hold of that sentence; the last third of this zine is about what it looks like when a field does not. documented false claims → the look-elsewhere effect Claims that evaporated A row of signals at three and four sigma, most of them fading to nothing as more data arrives, with the threshold moved rightward to five sigma in response. announced at 3–4σ after more data so the field raised its own bar against its own enthusiasm Figure 2 · an institutional confession physicshuman sci 2 · why 5, not 3 Five Sigma · Stimpunks

Dial one · multiplicity The look-elsewhere effect Search a wide enough space and something improbable will turn up somewhere. That is not a discovery. That is arithmetic. Physics has a name and a correction for this. The local p-value asks how unlikely a fluctuation this big is at the mass where you found it. The global p-value asks how unlikely it is anywhere you were looking — and it is always larger, sometimes enormously so. The correction depends on how honestly you define "anywhere," and Lyons enumerates the choices: any reasonable mass, anywhere in the current analysis, or anywhere in analyses by anyone in the whole collaboration. Then this: "It is clearly important to decide in advance of the analysis what procedure will be used; and to specify in any publication exactly how the global p-values are defined." Lyons, 2013 That is pre-registration, argued as ordinary practice, in a physics note, in 2013 — while psychology was still discovering it needed the idea. Now count the search space on the other side. Thousands of researchers, hundreds of candidate interventions, dozens of outcome measures each, decades of trials, and a publication system that prints the positives. The look-elsewhere effect there is not a correction term. It is the dominant feature of the landscape. And almost nobody applies it. documented multiplicity → extraordinary claims Local versus global A wide noisy spectrum with one tall peak. Dial two · degree of surprise Extraordinary claims How much evidence you need depends on what you are claiming. Physics builds this in deliberately, and calls it the subconscious Bayes' factor. The reasoning is straightforward once stated. The evidence in front of you multiplies your prior belief; it does not replace it. So a result that would be convincing for an expected effect is not convincing for an impossible one. "even if the likelihood ratio favours H₁, we would still prefer H₀ if our prior belief in H₁ was very low. An example would be that, in order to claim that we had discovered energy non-conservation in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, we would require extremely strong evidence from the data because our prior belief in energy non-conservation is very low." Lyons, 2013 He is explicit that this is a Bayesian argument sitting inside a frequentist practice, and defends it anyway: "this type of reasoning does and should play a role in requiring a high standard of evidence before we reject well-established theories. There is sense to the oft-quoted maxim 'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence'." Lyons, 2013 So hold the question open, because the whole zine turns on it. Is it an ordinary claim or an extraordinary one to say that a standardised intervention, delivered to wildly heterogeneous children, produces a durable improvement in their lives? Dial three · the errors you cannot count The errors you cannot count Statistical error is the part you can compute from your sample. Systematic error is everything else — the miscalibrated instrument, the selection you did not notice, the assumption baked into the model. It is much harder to estimate, and physics treats that difficulty as a first-class problem rather than a footnote. Lyons puts a number on the exposure: "a 5σ claim should be reduced to merely 2.5σ if the systematic uncertainties had been underestimated by a factor of 2; this corresponds to the p-value increasing from 3 × 10⁻⁷ by a dramatic factor of 2 × 10⁴." The entire distance between "discovery" and "shrug" is inside a factor of two on the thing you did not measure. And Lyons is clear that the honest response is to model the uncertainty, not to paper over it with a bigger number: "It is far better to have a procedure which allows in some way for uncertain systematics than to raise the significance level for all experiments as a way of coping with this." The other rail · 1925 Convenient There is a second number in the world, and almost every claim ever made about a child rests on it. In Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925), Ronald Fisher wrote the sentence that set it: "The value for which P=0.05, or 1 in 20 is 1.96 or nearly 2; it is convenient to take this point as a limit in judging whether a deviation is to be considered significant or not." R. A. Fisher, Statistical Methods for Research Workers, 1925 Two things in that sentence deserve a much longer look than they get. First: "convenient." Not derived, not calibrated, not justified by an error-rate analysis. A working statistician picking a round number because the arithmetic was tidy and the tables were printable. He said so. Second: "1.96, or nearly 2." The most consequential threshold in the human sciences is, in the units this zine has been using all along, two sigma. Physics looked at 3σ and 4σ results, watched them evaporate, and moved up. The human sciences settled at 2σ and stayed for a hundred years. One field treated its threshold as a hypothesis about its own reliability and kept testing it. The other treated a convenience as a law. the two rails, and they never meet It is worth saying that Fisher himself did not intend a bright line — he treated significance as one input to judgement, and elsewhere used other levels. The objection · at full strength Where this analogy breaks The previous spread is the most persuasive thing in this zine, which is exactly why it gets a spread arguing against it. Here is the case we would have to answer. One: physics is asking a different kind of question. A 5σ threshold is for an existence claim — is the particle there at all? Scientism is not too much science

The name for it Scientism is not too much science There is a word for using the authority of science without the discipline of science, and it is not science. Scientism is the aesthetics: the p-value, the effect size, the phrase evidence-based, the citation, the graph. What it leaves behind is the practice — pre-registration, blinding, adverse-event reporting, replication, publishing your nulls, printing the case against your own standard, and calibrating your threshold to what you are claiming and what being wrong would cost. Every device in the first half of this zine is science protecting itself from its own enthusiasm. Scientism keeps the enthusiasm and discards the protection. the distinction the whole collection runs on And it has a characteristic victim, which is why this argument belongs to us and not only to methodologists. When a field claims scientific authority while ignoring inconvenient findings and lived experience, the people who have the inconvenient experience are not merely disbelieved — they are disbelieved on scientific grounds, which is a much harder thing to answer. That is epistemic injustice (Fricker), and Robert Chapman has traced how it operates specifically against neurodivergent people: our testimony about our own lives arrives already discounted, because the apparatus has spoken. We have watched this happen twice already in this collection. In No. 9 the border between disorder and difference is redrawn by committee while the people either side of it stay the same. In No. 39 people asking about the air are told they are catastrophising, by institutions resting on a number nobody had checked. Same shape every time. We are asking for more science, not less

The turn We are asking for more science, not less Everything in this zine is borrowed from physicists. That is the point, and it is worth being unmistakable about it. We did not arrive with a philosophical objection to measurement. We arrived with a physicist's own paper, and asked why the standard it describes — calibrate your threshold to how surprising the claim is, how much impact it carries, how wide you searched, and how badly you understand your own errors — stops at the laboratory door. Eugenics and behaviourism did not fail because they were too scientific. They failed because they took real mathematics — a curve for observational error, a law of effect measured honestly in cats — and applied it to human beings without the discipline that made it work in the first place. That is the whole subject of this collection. Reclaiming science from scientism is not a retreat from evidence. It is a demand for the parts that got left behind: the harms column, the pre-registration, the null result, the published objection to your own gold standard. what How We Got Here is for And there is a version of this that is not a complaint but a design. Set the bar by what it costs to be wrong. Where an intervention is reversible, low-stakes and chosen, a modest evidence base is fine. Where it is compulsory, intensive, delivered during childhood and impossible to undo, ask for something closer to what you would want before announcing a particle — and until you have it, change the conditions rather than the child, which is the option that has been scored as "no intervention" this whole time. That is not anti-scientific. A field that raised its own bar because its own results kept evaporating would recognise it immediately. Not:that statistics are the enemy. The best material in this zine is a statistics paper. The enemy is a threshold nobody has examined since 1925 doing work nobody chose it for. Not:that 5σ should govern education. We ran physics' dials on a human question and marked that transfer contested, then spent a spread arguing against ourselves. The claim is that the dials exist and nobody turns them. Not:that doing nothing is safe. Withholding real support is a harm too. That is an argument for measuring both columns, not for leaving one blank. Not:a proof. The pattern Everything keeps becoming a crab Give the ocean enough time and it keeps arriving at the same animal. A wide flattened shell, a tail tucked under, legs out to the sides. Crustaceans have found that body over and over, from ancestors that looked nothing like each other and were never trying to match. The zoologist L. A. Borradaile named it in 1916 — carcinization, which he called one of the many attempts of Nature to evolve a crab. It happened at least five times: once or twice among the true crabs, and at least three times among the false ones — porcelain crabs, hairy stone crabs, king crabs. King crabs are not crabs. They came up out of hermit crabs and arrived at the shape anyway. And it isn't only crabs. Camera eyes evolved separately in us and in octopuses. Echolocation in bats and in whales. Flight in insects, pterosaurs, birds, bats. Convergence is real. We're not here to debunk it — it's one of the most striking things biology has found. We're here for what happens next, when a real pattern gets read as a verdict. five separate arrivals, one silhouette spongecrabs eubrachy-urans porcelaincrabs hairy stonecrabs kingcrabs nobody was copying anybody carcinization · borradaile 1916 at least five times over Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

Inside the basin Convergence is not sameness Here is the thing the word "converge" hides. They did not end up alike. Crab-shaped lineages live in nearly every habitat on Earth — bright coral reefs, sealed marine caves, abyssal plain, mountain streams, dry land. Their bodies run from millimetres to metres. Reviewing that range, Wolfe and colleagues reach for Darwin's last line in the Origin and call it endless forms most beautiful. So five lineages converged on a description — wide, flat, tucked — and then diversified wildly inside it. The attractor isn't a point. It's a neighbourhood, roomy enough to hold a pea-sized cave dweller and a metre-wide giant and count both as the same solution. We already know this shape of argument. Sharing a category never made anyone identical, and the spiky profile survives the merge. Two rivers meeting run braided for miles. The route Same window, different wiring Our eye and the octopus's eye are the showpiece of convergence: lens, iris, retina, a chamber that throws an image. Built independently. Built backwards from each other. In our retina the light-sensing cells face away from the light, and their nerve fibres run back across the retina's inner surface and bundle out through it — which punches a hole in our field of view. You have a blind spot because of how yours is wired. The octopus's photoreceptors face the light, and the nerves leave from behind. No hole. Same outcome. Opposite construction. The function converged; the machinery never did. Now say it about people. The terrain The valley, not the virtue Why does anything converge? Because the ground slopes. The embryologist C. H. Waddington drew the picture in 1957: development as a ball rolling down a landscape of branching valleys, its path canalized — a word he'd coined in 1942 — by the shape of the terrain rather than aimed at a target. Deep valley, reliable outcome. Same ball, different landscape, different animal. "Attractor" is a real term, borrowed here. It comes from dynamical systems — Lorenz found his in 1963 — where it means a state a system settles toward. Applied to evolution or to culture it is a metaphor, a good one, doing analogical work. We should say that out loud, because the metaphor is what makes the overreach feel rigorous. And the honest state of the flagship case: reviewing all of it, Wolfe and colleagues report that the reasons for the repeated evolution of the crab-like body plan remain a mystery. They add that nobody yet knows whether it's true convergence or a shared inheritance being switched back on. So the crab is not a proven optimum. It's a place the ground happens to slope toward, for reasons still being worked out. Convergence is evidence about terrain — the constraints, the pressures, the materials at hand — and not about the merit of whatever lands in the bottom. waddington's landscape the slope decides, not the destination canalization · waddington 1942, 1957 a valley is not a verdict Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

Ripeness Ideas ripen too Discovery converges the same way bodies do, and for the same reason. Newton had calculus by about 1666; Leibniz built it independently in the 1670s, and they spent years fighting about it. That story gets told as an anomaly. It isn't one. In 1922 Ogburn and Thomas assembled a list of 148 inventions and discoveries made independently by two or more people — sunspots four times over in 1611, conservation of energy four times in 1847, the telescope claimed by nine. Reviewing the same phenomenon decades later, Robert K. Merton concluded that these "multiples" are the dominant pattern in science, and the lone singleton the exception. It's faster now. In November 2022 Terence Tao logged what he called maths at internet speed: Justin Gilmer posted a breakthrough on the union-closed sets conjecture on the 16th, Gil Kalai blogged it the next day, and four days after that three independent groups had sharpened the same argument to the same constant. Ripeness is not inevitability, though. In 2025 Hannah Cairo, then 17, disproved the Mizohata–Takeuchi conjecture — roughly four decades of people trying to prove it, undone by one person going a different way. The field was ready. It still took her. There is a name for what ripens, and it isn't the individual. In the mid-1990s Brian Eno — fed up with the art-history idea of genius, where gifted individuals turn up out of nowhere to light the way for the rest of us — coined scenius. In his own words it "means ‘the intelligence and intuition of a whole cultural scene’. It is the communal form of the concept of genius." He set it against the "Big Man" theory of history, and preferred a world constantly remade by all its inhabitants — a cooperative enterprise. His own list of scenius moments runs through Dada, the American experimental music scene, and punk, 1975–8. Eno then guards the flank we would guard. He says plainly that it would be foolish to pretend everyone's contribution is therefore equal, and he would never claim it. Scenius doesn't dissolve the person who did the work — it moves the unit, from the lone mind to the scene that made the answer findable. An attractor is not a mandate

The turn An attractor is not a mandate In the ocean, the crab basin permits everyone who never rolls into it. Most decapods are not crab-shaped. Shrimp, prawns, lobsters, crayfish — millions of individuals living entire successful lives outside the famous attractor, and nothing in the water enforces anything. The slope is just a slope. Non-crabs are not failed crabs; the category doesn't exist. Engineered systems are different, and this is where the metaphor stops being charming. In a designed system, somebody picks the slope. Every platform converged on short vertical video. Not because that is the optimum of human expression — because engagement was chosen as the objective, and everything downhill of that objective rolled to the same place. The convergence is real, and it is also somebody's decision, and the two facts are usually presented as one. School does it more bluntly: one route to the answer, one pace, one accepted way of showing your work. Then the other routes — the ones that arrive by a different wiring and get there fine — collect a diagnosis. That isn't the terrain sloping. That's a wall, and someone poured it. This is the Cavendish banana: uniform, efficient, one blight from collapse. The answer is Cavendish Space — environments built for caves and campfires and watering holes, for dandelions and tulips and orchids. Deliberately re-graded ground. In Stimpunks' ARLES terms, this zine lives at the top two rungs — Environment and Systems. Change the terrain and the attractors move. They always did. If it's not working, it's not the person. It's the environment, the relationships, or the system. — Stimpunks · ARLES a slope, and a wall found terrain the ones who never rolled in are fine poured terrain the ones who don't get a diagnosis nature permits · institutions require someone chose the second slope · it can be re-poured arles · environment & systems change the terrain, not the person Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

The live argument Gould's tape, Conway Morris's constraint Biologists have not settled this, and we should not pretend otherwise. Stephen Jay Gould, in Wonderful Life (1989), argued that history is contingent: rewind the tape of life, play it again, and you get something else. We are here by accident, not by arrival. Simon Conway Morris, in Life's Solution (2003), argued the opposite from the same evidence: convergence is everywhere, the channels are narrow, and outcomes — up to and including intelligence — are close to inevitable. It's a genuine disagreement between serious people, and this zine does not resolve it. Both readings are compatible with five crabs and seven un-crabbings. What we refuse is the thing that gets smuggled in when the second is read loosely: that because a form recurs, it is the form things ought to take. Convergence is a description of what happened. It licenses nothing about who belongs. replay the tape Gould 1989 different every time Conway Morris 2003 the same, near enough unresolved — and either way, recurrence is not permission a rhyme, not a proof we are not settling this here Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

Held with care What we are not saying Convergence is a beautiful finding sitting one inch from an ugly argument. Here is the inch. Notconverge or lose. Most decapods aren't crabs and are doing fine. A shape that recurs is not a shape that's required. Notoptimality. The reasons for the crab's recurrence remain a mystery in the literature, and it's been abandoned more often than adopted. "Recurring" and "best" are different words. Notone right shape. The basin holds millimetres to metres, reef to abyss. Convergence never produced sameness, and belonging doesn't either. Notbiology proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. That a pattern recurs in nature says nothing about what we owe each other — deriving an ought from an is is a fallacy we'd rather name than commit. Not"you're a crab too." Belonging that requires you to have arrived at the same form isn't belonging. It's a membership test with better manners. Nota counsel of despair about design. Attractors move when terrain changes. That's the whole reason to bother building anything. the same forms, arranged two ways not a ladder one level different sizes, same standing no ticks · no crosses · no rungs variation is a spread, not an order a spread, not an order the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

Closer to home Ours was a multiple too The word you are reading this collection through is itself a case of ripeness. "Neurodiversity" is not one person's coinage. Following Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley and Walker (Autism, 2024), "neurological diversity" and "neurodiversity" reached print in 1997 and 1998 through the journalist Harvey Blume — who attributed them to the online Autistic community — and the concept and its theory were developed collectively by neurodivergent people. The terrain was ready. Jim Sinclair's "Don't Mourn For Us" (1993) and Autism Network International had done the ground work. Martijn Dekker's InLv list opened in 1996 and gave a scattered community one room. Kassiane Asasumasu coined neurodivergent in 2000. Nick Walker named the paradigm and the pathology paradigm it replaces. Several people, arriving at the same words at nearly the same time, under a shared pressure none of them chose — and the pressure was the thing worth naming. That is a multiple, in our own history, about our own lives. So both facts sit together, and neither cancels the other. Convergence happens. And nobody has to be a crab. Five times into the valley. Seven times back out. Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not is Zine No. 31 in the Stimpunks Star Stuff series. It was written after Brett D. Wick's essay When Everything Becomes a Crab: The Strange Phenomenon of Convergent Evolution in Nature, Mathematics, and Human Systems (Washington University in St. Louis, 2026), which supplied the frame — convergence as attractors in possibility space, across biology, mathematics and technology — and the mathematical cases. Wick is not part of this collaboration and this reading is not his; the turn the zine makes, and the three findings it turns on, come from the primary crab literature rather than from the essay. A companion to The Universe Runs on Difference (8), The Lines We Drew (9), Every Nervous System (27) and Only in Relation (29). Sources & notes. Wolfe, J. M., Luque, J. & Bracken-Grissom, H. D. (2021). How to become a crab: Phenotypic constraints on a recurring body plan. BioEssays, 43(5), 2100020 — read in the primary; source of the counts (carcinization "has evolved at least five times, and has been lost at least seven times," with likely further losses), of the statement that the reasons "remain a mystery," of the unresolved parallelism-versus-convergence question, and of the habitat and millimetre-to-metre range. "Endless forms most beautiful" is Darwin's closing line in On the Origin of Species (1859), which Wolfe and colleagues borrow. Borradaile, L. A. (1916) coined carcinization. Waddington, C. H. (1942). Canalization of development and the inheritance of acquired characters. Nature, 150, 563–565; and The Strategy of the Genes (1957), where the epigenetic landscape appears. Lorenz, E. N. (1963). Deterministic nonperiodic flow. Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences, 20, 130–141 — the attractor as a term of art. Ogburn, W. F. & Thomas, D. (1922). Are inventions inevitable? A note on social evolution. Political Science Quarterly, 37(1), 83–98 — the 148 multiples. Merton, R. K. (1961). Singletons and multiples in scientific discovery. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society, 105(5), 470–486. Scenius is Brian Eno's, coined in the mid-1990s and set down in A Year with Swollen Appendices (Faber, 1996) in a letter to Dave Stewart among the appendices — quoted here from that primary, along with the “Big Man” theory of history, the cooperative-enterprise passage, his list of scenius moments (Russia 1905–15, Dada, the American experimental music scene, the Anglo-American psychedelic sixties, punk 1975–8), and his own caveat that it would be stupid to pretend everyone's contribution is therefore equal. A note on the wording: the version of the definition in wide circulation — “Scenius stands for the intelligence and the intuition of a whole cultural scene. It is the communal form of the concept of the genius” — is not what the book says. It entered circulation through Kevin Kelly's “Scenius, or Communal Genius” (The Technium, 10 June 2008), which presents it as Eno's exact words; Eno's actual text reads “it means ‘the intelligence and intuition of a whole cultural scene’. It is the communal form of the concept of genius.” We follow the book. Kelly's four conditions for a ripe scene — mutual appreciation, rapid exchange of tools and techniques, network effects of success, local tolerance for novelties — are Kelly's own, from the same post, and are the reason he is credited on the figure.
