The Hatchery Twelve cosmic eggs · a specimen sheet · an easter egg Twelve eggs drawn for this site. One of them is the small door at the foot of every page; the other eleven are the ones we drew on the way, kept because each carries something we can check. The cosmic egg — the universe as something that was closed and then opened — is one of the most widely repeated images people have. It is in the Rigveda as Hiraṇyagarbha, the golden womb; in the Ogdoad's egg at Hermopolis; in the Kalevala , where Ilmatar's eggs become the sky and the earth; in Pangu's shell, which takes eighteen thousand years to open; in Taʼaroa's, in the Society Islands; in the Dogon Amma; in Zoroastrian texts that use the egg as an analogy for the shape of the cosmos. None of those is drawn on this page, and that is deliberate. These twelve are ours. We name the motif and leave the cosmologies to the people who hold them — the same line Field Guide No. 10 drew when it put five turtles people made in their own section with no reframe table, because running sounds like / actually over somebody's cosmology would be obscene. A borrowed shape is not a borrowed belief. What every egg here has in common is the thing the whole site is about: something that looks like a single smooth object turns out, up close, to be made of variation — and the variation is not the flaw in it. Twelve drawings, twelve arguments, one of them load-bearing. Where this form stops A drawing is not evidence. Each egg below is a picture attached to a claim, and the picture proves nothing — the source line under each one is where the actual work is. Where a claim is contested or thin, the entry says so rather than letting a confident illustration carry it. That is the failure mode this collection was built against: a thing that rhymes too well gets believed on the strength of the rhyme. The first egg is the one with a live argument against it, and it is the one we shipped anyway. See The Spiky Shell , which explains what it had to change to be usable here.

The one on the door This is the mark at the bottom of the front page , and it replaced an egg emoji on 14 August 2026. A cracked egg, its jagged seam open and lifted, with stars inside where a yolk would be.
The Spiky Shell on every page

The Spiky Shell on every page A jagged line with nothing behind it to be measured against An egg cracked open and lifted ajar, with sky inside instead of yolk. It began as a straightforward idea — make the crack a spiky profile — and that idea is wrong here, which is worth saying out loud on the page rather than quietly fixing. We have already published the argument against it. No. 21, Not a Line grants that the spiky profile beat the single severity dial, then shows what it kept: it still plots peaks and troughs as distances from a flat expected baseline, frozen at one moment of assessment. A better chart is still a chart. Its spine runs line → spiky profile → constellation , and putting a celebratory spiky profile on the front page would have parked our door one step behind our own argument. So the drawing keeps the jag and throws away the apparatus. There is no baseline and no grid — the two things that made the profile a measurement. A crack in a shell is jagged because that is how shells break, not because it is scoring anything, and there is no line running through it from which its peaks could be deviations. What is inside is a constellation: stars in no order, with no rank. On the profile and its limits: No. 21 , built on Patrick Dwyer, “The Autism Constellation” ( Autistic Scholar , 2020) and Helen Edgar, “The Constellation of Intensities: Neuroqueering the Spiky Profile” ( Autistic Realms , 2026). The constellation metaphor belongs to the Autistic community and predates both essays — see No. 21's colophon, which names Caroline Hearst, Larry Arnold, Damian Milton and the late Dinah Murray.

And eleven more Four of these were the original proposals; seven were drawn afterwards to fill the sheet. None of them is on the door, and none of them is a lesser piece of work for it — an easter egg is a door that moved, not a standard that dropped. An unbroken egg with a five-pointed star where the yolk would be, and five coloured rays reaching out through the shell.

The Yolk Is a Star L★S, held whole Unbroken. The star sits where the yolk goes, and five rays reach out through the shell — one in each of the house accents, one for each of the five collections that sort by register. This is the most brand-like of the twelve and the least argumentative, which is why it is not the door. It says a star is inside this , and the whole site says that already. It survives shrinking better than anything else here, so if the mark ever needs to work at favicon size, this is the one that would. The accents are Tailwind CSS v3's 400 ramp, verified against v3.4.17 — see the design system . The five registers are Star Stuff, Star Gazing, More Than Human, Kin, and Stars We Grew Up On. An egg whose shell is twelve interlocking plates, no two the same size, shape or colour.

The Ossicle Egg No two plates alike, and that is the shell Twelve interlocking plates, no two the same size, shape or hue. The picture is borrowed from an animal already in the collection: the leatherback has no bony carapace at all — just hundreds of small interlocking ossicles set in oily skin — and it is the deepest-diving reptile alive, recorded to 1,280 m , holding its body up to 18 °C above the water around it. Every item on that list reads as a missing part, and together they are the animal's range. The shell holds because of the variation in it, not despite it. Field Guide No. 10 , the leatherback entry, where the primary citations sit. There is no standard turtle. Egg-shaped contours nested inside one another, narrowing to a single bright core.

The Monotropic Egg Attention as a tunnel, not a spotlight Contours nested down to a bright core. Monotropism describes attention pulled strongly into a few interests at a time, with a great deal of processing going into whatever is in the tunnel and correspondingly little to what is outside it — which reframes a long list of “deficits” as the predictable shape of that distribution rather than separate faults. Drawn this way the shell is not a barrier. It is the outermost ring of one interest. Murray, Lesser & Lawson, “Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism” ( Autism , 2005). Further reading at stimpunks.org/monotropism . An egg with sound waves leaving it and answering waves arriving from outside.

The Arrau Egg The silence was ours The giant South American river turtle, Podocnemis expansa , was filed for a very long time as a silent animal — until somebody brought a hydrophone. The recordings hold 2,122 sounds sorted into eleven types . Hatchlings vocalise from inside the egg , then in the open nest, then in the river; adult females vocalise while basking and nesting, and in the river the females were recorded coming and answering. It is the first evidence of post-hatching parental care in any turtle. The animal was never silent. The silence was in the equipment, and in the assumption that made nobody go looking. That is the entire reason this egg is drawn with the call going out and an answer coming back. Field Guide No. 10 , the Arrau entry, where the primary citations sit. An egg under pressure from above, its interior drawn as slanted fibres, with a charge spark at the base.

The Collagen Egg Press it and it answers in current The founding fact of this site, drawn as a shell: bone is piezoelectric . Load it and it produces charge. Fukada and Yasuda measured it in 1957, and the skeleton you are sitting on is doing it right now. And the part that is easy to get wrong, which we got wrong ourselves: the effect is collagen's , not the mineral's. Collagen fibres are arranged without a centre of symmetry and generate charge as they shear past one another — which is why the drawing is fibres, slanted, sliding. Hydroxyapatite is centrosymmetric , and that rules out classical piezoelectricity in the mineral. Our own Manifesto credited the mineral, twice, until a fact-check caught it. Fukada & Yasuda, “On the piezoelectric effect of bone” ( Journal of the Physical Society of Japan , 1957); later work by Bassett and colleagues. The correction is logged in the changelog and in FACTCHECK.md . A large egg containing a smaller, complete egg of its own, with a dotted path showing it arrived from outside.

The Egg Inside the Egg It arrived; it did not grow here A complete egg inside another egg, with a dotted line showing where it came in from. This is endosymbiosis : the mitochondria in your cells descend from free-living bacteria that took up residence rather than organs your lineage grew. You are not one thing that developed. You are a merger that held — which makes “self-contained individual” a claim your own cell biology declines to support. Lynn Margulis, publishing as Lynn Sagan, “On the Origin of Mitosing Cells” ( Journal of Theoretical Biology , 1967), reviving earlier proposals by Mereschkowsky and Wallin; phylogenomics has since confirmed the core. See You Were Never One Thing . An egg of smooth unfrozen liquid, with a single ice crystal starting at one point where something touches the shell.

The Supercooled Egg Not how tough it is — what touches it Painted turtle hatchlings spend their first winter in a shallow nest that goes below −10 °C , and they survive it by supercooling : staying liquid below the freezing point, because nothing has started the crystal. Which means what decides whether one lives is not how tough it is but what touches it . A single ice nucleus at the shell — one contact — and the whole thing goes at once. It is the least metaphorical access argument in the collection: the outcome is set by the surroundings, and calling the difference resilience would be a straightforward misreading of the physics. Field Guide No. 10 , the painted turtle entry, where the primary citations sit. The same mechanism — supercooling, and critical slowing down alongside it — is turned on human thresholds in The Same Water . An egg containing five nested shells around a small dense core, like the burning layers of a massive star.

The Onion Egg The shell that actually made us Late in the life of a massive star, fusion runs in nested shells around a dense core — lighter elements burning in the outer layers, heavier ones further in, iron accumulating at the centre where fusion stops paying. It is an onion, and it is also an egg: a closed thing that eventually opens, violently, and scatters what it made. The honest caveat, which this site has had to issue before: “every element heavier than hydrogen and helium was made in stars” is not true as usually told. Lithium, beryllium and boron are the exception — stars largely destroy them rather than build them, and they come mostly from cosmic-ray spallation. Six of our own pages were making the tidy version, three of them already marked verified. The correction, and every page it touched, is logged in the changelog . The smoothed retelling that files off the exception is exactly the failure How We Got Here exists to mark. An egg pierced with many small pores, with oxygen arrows passing inward through the shell and carbon dioxide and water vapour passing outward.

The Breathing Shell A boundary that works only because it leaks An eggshell looks like a sealed container and is nothing of the sort. It is drilled through with thousands of microscopic, trumpet-shaped pores , and those pores are the only channels by which anything moves between the embryo and the world: oxygen in, carbon dioxide and water vapour out. Seal it properly and you do not get a safer egg. You get a suffocated embryo inside a perfectly intact shell. Protection and permeability are not opposites here — they are the same piece of engineering , and the shell is tuned so precisely that its conductance has to match the embryo’s demand over the whole of incubation. That is the argument this site keeps making about the rooms we put people in. The ones that work are not the ones sealed hardest. S. G. Tullett, “Pores and gas exchange of avian eggs: a review” ( Journal of Experimental Zoology Supplement, 1987). Figures approximate and stated as a scaling relationship, not a measured count: pore number rises with egg mass from roughly 300 in a 1 g egg to about 30,000 in a 500 g egg, which puts a hen’s egg in the thousands. We have not seen a chicken-specific count we could check, so we do not give one. Two half-eggs facing each other, each with a jagged edge; the two edges do not interlock, leaving a gap between them.

The Double Seam The gap is between them, not inside either Two half-eggs, facing. Both are drawn at the same weight, in the same hand, and their jagged edges do not interlock — there is a gap, and neither edge is the broken one. This is the double empathy problem : the misunderstanding between Autistic and non-Autistic people runs both ways , as a mismatch between two differently-built minds rather than a deficit inside one of them. Look for the fault in either half and you will not find it, because it is not in a half. Damian Milton, “On the ontological status of autism: the ‘double empathy problem’” ( Disability & Society , 2012). Worked through in Only in Relation . An egg drawn only as a dotted outline, empty inside except for a single faint star.

The Egg Not Yet Laid Left open on purpose A dotted outline and one faint star. This is the twelfth so that the sheet does not close: the pieces not made yet, the corrections not sent yet, the eggs somebody else draws. It has a precedent here. The Print collection contains a sheet that is deliberately blank, and it earns its place the same way — the empty one is doing work the full ones cannot . If you want to fill this in, the call is open . Companion to No. 4, the call for contributors . Everything here is CC BY-SA 4.0 — take the shape and draw your own. Sources & honest limits The world-egg list is named, not retold. The traditions in the opening paragraph are named to credit a motif we are borrowing the shape of, and each is stated at the level of “this exists here” rather than summarised, retold or blended. We have not drawn any of them, and none of the twelve below is a version of anybody's cosmology. Where the popular framing of these motifs runs to every culture had the same idea , that is a smoothing we decline to make: the resemblance is real and the explanation for it is not settled. Every scientific claim here is one this site has already checked , and each entry links to the piece that holds the primary citation rather than restating one from memory. Three are worth repeating because they are the errors we personally made: bone's piezoelectricity is collagen's , not hydroxyapatite's; lithium, beryllium and boron break the “made in stars” line; and Lynn Margulis published the 1967 endosymbiosis paper as Lynn Sagan, reviving Mereschkowsky and Wallin rather than starting from nothing. The first egg argues with us, and we left the argument in. No. 21 is a case against the spiky profile, and the door mark started life as a celebration of exactly that. Rather than drop the drawing or quietly stop mentioning the profile, the entry states the collision and what changed because of it. A house style that only ever agreed with itself would be worth less than one that shows the seam. Why this page is an easter egg. It is a specimen sheet for one small mark — genuinely useful if you are working on the site or want to take the drawings, and not something the front page owes a section to. It is unnumbered on purpose: numbers here are chronological and load-bearing, and a sheet of drawings for existing arguments does not need a date stamped into the sequence. A star cannot stop telling you

Locution one · infodumping A star cannot stop telling you There are five neurodivergent love locutions, and the deficit story has a ranking ready for all of them. Infodumping goes near the bottom: too much, unprompted, not reciprocal, not really conversation. Here is what a star does. Every photon leaving its surface passes out through its own atmosphere, and on the way each element takes its specific bite out of the spectrum. The light arrives carrying a complete, unedited account of what the star is made of, whether or not anyone is reading. Joseph von Fraunhofer catalogued the dark lines in sunlight in 1814 without knowing what they were. Four decades later Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen established what they meant: each line is the fingerprint of an element, and a spectrum is therefore a composition read at a distance. In 1925 Cecilia Payne read that record properly and found the stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen — a conclusion she was pressured to soften, and which was right. The infodump is not a side effect of stellar physics. It is the entire evidentiary basis of this collection. We know we are star stuff because stars will not shut up about themselves. the fact this whole site rests on Nobody asked the Sun for its elemental abundances. It is telling us anyway, continuously, in full detail, at every wavelength at once — and every claim on this entire site is downstream of somebody finding that worth reading. An absorption spectrum is a composition A continuous band of light crossed by dark vertical absorption lines, each labelled with an element — hydrogen, sodium, iron — under a note that the star broadcasts this unprompted. H He Na Mg Fe Ca every element it holds, unprompted continuously · in full · to anyone Fraunhofer 1814 · Kirchhoff & Bunsen 1859–60 Payne 1925 · it is mostly hydrogen Figure 1 · the unasked-for account How Anything Gets Built · Stimpunks

Locution two · parallel play Bound without interacting Parallel play is doing separate things in shared space without either of you steering the other. Developmental psychology filed it, for decades, as a stage — something a child is supposed to pass through on the way to real play. The sky's version is the wide binary. Two stars, genuinely gravitationally bound, separated by so much distance that neither meaningfully perturbs the other's surface, atmosphere or evolution. They are not orbiting so much as accompanying. These are not rare or marginal. Working from Gaia eDR3, Kareem El-Badry, Hans-Walter Rix and Tyler Heintz catalogued 1.3 million pairs with better than 90 percent probability of being bound, at projected separations running from a few astronomical units out to a full parsec — 3.26 light years, roughly the distance from here to Proxima Centauri. At that separation an orbit can take millions of years. Neither star will complete one in the lifetime of anything watching. They are simply going the same way, together, indefinitely, and the binding is measurable in the proper motions. Nothing is being worked toward. There is no closer configuration this is a rehearsal for. Wide binaries are not failed close binaries — they are the most common outcome the galaxy produces, and they are stable. what the catalogue actually shows Zine No. 46, Companion Stars, took the close orbit — the barycentre, the tidal deformation, the three-body problem. This spread takes the other end of the same distribution, and deliberately does not re-argue any of it. Locution three · support swapping The shared envelope Support swapping is the reciprocal one — you remind me to drink water, I write the email you cannot start. Spoons pooled rather than counted. Christine Miserandino gave us the spoons in 2003; the swapping is what a community does with them. Some binary stars are close enough to touch. In a W Ursae Majoris contact binary the two stars overflow into a single shared convective envelope, joined by a neck, and energy moves freely through it from the more massive component to the less massive one. The consequence is measurable and strange. These pairs have genuinely unequal masses — mass ratios around 0.3, one star roughly three times the other — and yet their surface temperatures come out within about 200 K of each other. The smaller star runs far hotter and brighter than its own mass could ever sustain, because the larger one is feeding energy across the shared envelope. Two bodies of very different capacity, sharing one envelope, arriving at nearly the same temperature. The redistribution is not charity and not a deficit being covered — it is a property of the configuration they are in together. energy transfer in contact binaries And now the part that keeps this honest, because support swapping is not free. In an Algol-type binary, mass flows one way. The star that was originally more massive fills its Roche lobe first and transfers most of itself to its companion — ending up as the less massive, less luminous, apparently less-developed star of the pair. For years that looked like a contradiction, because more massive stars are supposed to evolve faster. Crawford resolved it in 1955: the one that looks behind is the one that gave. It was never lagging. It was donating, and the record of the donation is written as apparent deficiency. Locution four · deep pressure Nothing fuses unsqueezed The fourth locution has the bluntest name in the set: please crush my soul back into my body. Weighted blankets, firm hugs, being sat on by a large and willing dog. Temple Grandin built herself a squeeze machine for it and then published on what it did. A star is a thing being crushed. That is not a figure of speech — it is the definition. Hydrostatic equilibrium is the balance between gravity pulling every layer inward and pressure pushing back out, and a star simply is that balance, held for billions of years. At the Sun's centre the pressure is around 2.4 × 1016 pascals — over 200 billion times the atmosphere you are sitting in — at roughly 15 million kelvin and 150 grams per cubic centimetre. Take the crushing away and there is no fusion. No fusion, no carbon, no oxygen, no iron, no calcium in the bone that this collection keeps going on about. The pressure is not an unfortunate condition the star endures on the way to making elements. The pressure is the manufacturing process. Every atom heavier than helium in your body exists because something, somewhere, was squeezed hard enough for long enough. Deep pressure is the literal precondition of star stuff. stellar nucleosynthesis, stated plainly Which does not make a weighted blanket a fusion reactor, and we are not going to pretend it does. It makes the shape of the thing familiar: a body that regulates under compression is not behaving strangely for a thing made in a furnace. Locution five · penguin pebbling The only mechanism fast enough A rock. A button. A leaf. A screenshot of a bird. I found this and thought of you. Of all five locutions this is the one most readily filed as sweet-but-slight — a small thing offered in place of a real gesture. Planet formation had a serious problem for decades. The classical picture built worlds by planetesimal accretion: kilometre-scale bodies colliding and merging, gradually. Run the numbers for a giant planet's core and it does not work. The gas disk dissipates in a few million years, and the core has to be there before the gas goes, or there is nothing to capture an atmosphere from. The big collisions were too slow. In 2012 Michiel Lambrechts and Anders Johansen named the process that solves it. Millimetre- to centimetre-scale pebbles drift through the disk and are aerodynamically braked as they pass a growing body, so they are captured across a cross-section approaching the whole Hill sphere rather than the body's physical size. Cores reach several Earth masses in 104 to 106 years — fast enough, with room to spare. The small offerings did not supplement the big collisions. The big collisions could not do the job, and the small offerings could. Pebble accretion is not a lesser route to a planet. For the giant cores it is the route. Lambrechts & Johansen 2012 And it stops itself. Once a core reaches ten to twenty Earth masses it opens a pressure bump outside its own orbit, the drifting pebbles are halted before they arrive, and the accretion ends. Even the sky knows when someone has had enough pebbles. Adélie penguins do this with stones, which is where the name comes from — a name that reached us later than the other four, by way of Lindsey. The physics does not know about the penguins. It arrived at the same answer independently: this is how you build something large out of care you can actually carry. Two routes to a planetary core Two horizontal timelines. Planetesimal accretion runs past the point where the gas disk dissipates and fails. Pebble accretion completes far short of it and succeeds. planetesimals too slow pebbles done gas disk gone a core must exist before the gas leaves pebbles: 10⁴–10⁶ yr · in time the small offering is the mechanism Lambrechts & Johansen 2012 Figure 5 · what actually got there in time How Anything Gets Built · Stimpunks
Down to is not because of

The turn · what this is not Down to is not because of Five locutions, five mechanisms, each one landing. That tidiness is the most dangerous thing on these pages, and we would rather say so on the face of the zine than in a footnote nobody reads. We keep a whole page about claims that circulate because they are shaped well rather than because they are true. A five-for-five correspondence between a community's love languages and the assembly mechanisms of matter is exactly that shape. So here is the load-bearing sentence: The physics does not justify the love. The universe is not signing anything off, and if it were, its approval would be worth nothing — a universe that could approve could also decline. the refusal this zine is built on This is the same defect we caught in a sentence of our own. The universe loves you for it makes the star stuff into the reason — and a reason can be revoked. Love you down to your star stuff has no such flaw: the implied subject is we, and down to measures how far the loving reaches, not why it is given. Down to is not because of. So the claim here is narrower, and it survives contact with a skeptic. Not the cosmos endorses infodumping. Just this: the deficit story says these five are substitutes — thin stand-ins for reciprocal conversation, real play, real gifts. That story requires them to be structurally deficient forms of connection. And structurally, they are how things get built. Not: Not a proof. A rhyme. Five good analogies are still analogies, and analogy is not evidence about human beings. Not validation from the sky. You did not need the sky's permission, and it has not got any to give. Not a superpower. Pebble accretion is not special or heroic. It is ordinary, and it is load-bearing. So is this. Not a claim that these are easy. Support swapping costs the donor something real, and the Algol star wears the cost as apparent deficiency. Not a ranking with a new winner on top. Replacing one hierarchy of the five with another is not what any of this was for. What is left is small, and it is enough: there is no standard way to assemble a planet, a star, or a person — and the universe does not pathologize its own variation. TEMPERATURE150°−272°usthem L★S · 001 The One Who Waits Tardigrade · water bear −272°C to 150°C · vacuum · at rest Half a millimetre long, and able to outlast vacuum, radiation, and years without water — not by toughing it out, but by stopping. It dries into a suspended grain called a tun, near-zero metabolism, and waits for conditions to change. dormancyrest is a strategyvacuumthe tun ▸ Field notes Field notes · Tardigrade The tardigrade is famous for surviving things that would kill almost anything — the open vacuum of space (it was among the first animals shown to survive it, on an orbital experiment in 2007), radiation at a thousand times a lethal human dose, temperatures near absolute zero. It is usually filed under "toughest animal alive." But look at how, because the how is the whole point. It does none of this while active and striving. It survives by drying into a tun — expelling most of its water, folding down to almost no metabolism, and going still until the world becomes livable again. It doesn't power through. It pauses. That is worth sitting with. The most durable animal we know of endures by resting — by treating dormancy as a legitimate state of being, not a failure to keep going. Not every survival is a fight. Some is knowing when to stop the clock and wait for a better day. MOISTUREsoakedvacuumusthem L★S · 002 The Partnership Lichen · fungus + alga bare rock · desiccation · even open space Not one organism but at least two — a fungus housing an alga or cyanobacterium — living so closely they were mistaken for a single species for centuries. Together they colonize bare rock, and have survived unprotected exposure to space. symbiosisnever one thingbare rockinterdependence ▸ Field notes Field notes · Lichen A lichen is not a thing; it is a relationship. A fungus provides structure and water-holding; a photosynthesizing partner — a green alga, a cyanobacterium, sometimes more than one, and often a yeast nobody noticed until recently — provides food. Neither could live on bare rock alone. Together they are one of the toughest, most patient colonizers on Earth. They tolerate near-total desiccation by simply going dormant when dry, and reviving when wet. In European Space Agency experiments, lichens were bolted to the outside of a spacecraft and exposed to raw space — vacuum, radiation, the works — and came back alive. This is the point You Were Never One Thing keeps making, written across a rock face: the resilience isn't in any single organism. It's in the partnership. What looks like one hardy individual is a collaboration that decided not to face the impossible alone. SUNLIGHTfull sunno lightusthem L★S · 003 The Sunless Economy Riftia · vent tubeworm no light · crushing pressure · sulfide Two metres tall, rooted around deep-sea vents in total darkness, with no mouth and no gut. They farm bacteria inside their own bodies that turn the vent's toxic chemistry into food — an entire ecosystem that owes nothing to the sun. chemosynthesisthe unseen economydeep seasymbiosis ▸ Field notes Field notes · Vent tubeworms Until 1977, textbooks agreed that all life ultimately ran on sunlight. Then a submersible reached the Galápagos Rift and found dense gardens of giant tubeworms crowded around hydrothermal vents in total darkness, kilometres below any sunbeam. The rule was simply wrong. An adult tubeworm has no mouth and no digestive tract. Instead it houses billions of bacteria inside a special organ and feeds them the hydrogen sulfide venting from the seafloor — a compound that is lethal poison to us. The bacteria turn that chemistry into food; the worm's blood-red plume is packed with a special hemoglobin that carries both oxygen and sulfide at once. An entire thriving economy, running on an energy source and an infrastructure the surface has never seen and does not depend on. Not a lesser life for lacking the sun — a whole different, self-sufficient world, getting on fine in the dark. The One That Eats the Poison

RADIATIONreactorbackgroundusthem L★S · 004 The One That Eats the Poison Radiotrophic fungi · Chernobyl grows toward radiation · reactor walls Black, melanin-rich fungi found thriving on the walls of the Chernobyl reactor — and apparently growing toward the radiation. Evidence suggests they use melanin to turn ionizing radiation into usable energy, the way plants use chlorophyll for light. radiotropismone's poison, another's foodmelaninreclamation ▸ Field notes Field notes · Radiotrophic fungi Inside one of the most radioactive places humans have ever made, something was growing. Black fungi coat the walls of the Chernobyl reactor, and studies found some strains grow toward radiation sources — a behavior researchers named radiotropism. The leading hypothesis is radiosynthesis: that the fungi use melanin, the same pigment that darkens our skin, to capture ionizing radiation and convert it into chemical energy, roughly the way a leaf uses chlorophyll to capture light. The mechanism is still debated and being studied — but the fungi are unmistakably at home where we cannot go. The reframe writes itself: what is poison to one living thing can be food to another. "Harmful" is not a property of a place alone; it's a relationship between a place and a body. A ruin to us can be a habitat — even a feast — to someone built differently. SALINITYbrinefreshusthem L★S · 005 The Salt Dwellers Halophiles · Halobacterium saturated brine · 10× seawater Microbes that need brine so concentrated it would sterilize almost anything else — the Dead Sea, salt flats, the pink evaporation ponds. That vivid pink is not lifeless water. The pink is them, in the millions, exactly where they belong. salt-lovingthe word "should"brinethe pink lakes ▸ Field notes Field notes · Halophiles Extreme salt kills most life by pulling the water straight out of it. So high-salt places "should" be sterile. That word — should — is doing an enormous amount of quiet work, and halophiles spend their whole lives contradicting it. They thrive in brine up to ten times saltier than the sea, in the Dead Sea and the salt flats and the industrial evaporation ponds. They balance the osmotic pull by loading their own cells with salts to match, so nothing gets drawn out. The startling pink of those waters — the color that reads to us as chemical and dead — is the organisms themselves, pigment and all, packed in by the million. "Should" is a statement about a default, dressed up as a law of nature. The places we're sure are lifeless are, often, simply full of a life we weren't the measure for. The Gift from the Boiling Spring

TEMPERATURE100°Ccoolusthem L★S · 006 The Gift from the Boiling Spring Thermophiles · Thermus aquaticus thrives near boiling · ~70°C optimal Microbes at home in near-boiling hot springs — water we could not touch. One of them, pulled from a Yellowstone pool a scientist was told held nothing worth studying, gave molecular biology the enzyme that makes DNA testing possible. heat-lovingthe margin is foundationalhot springsPCR ▸ Field notes Field notes · Thermophiles Hot springs were long assumed too hostile to bother studying. Then, in the 1960s, Thomas Brock started looking closely at the boiling pools of Yellowstone and found them teeming — including a heat-loving microbe he named Thermus aquaticus, happiest around 70°C. Decades later, that organism's heat-stable enzyme — Taq polymerase — became the engine of PCR, the technique that copies DNA and underpins modern genetics, forensics, and the tests that tracked a global pandemic. A creature from a pool everyone had written off turned out to be foundational infrastructure for the whole field. There's a pattern here worth naming. The margins — the places and beings the mainstream dismisses as too fringe to matter — are, over and over, exactly where the essential things turn out to have been waiting. TEMPERATUREwarm−2°Custhem L★S · 007 The Clear-Blooded Psychrophiles · Antarctic icefish −1.9°C seawater · antifreeze · no hemoglobin Fish that live in water cold enough to freeze their blood — so they make their own antifreeze. The icefish among them went further and abandoned red blood cells entirely: clear-blooded, a body plan that would be fatal anywhere warmer, and works perfectly here. cold-lovinga different body planantifreezeclear blood ▸ Field notes Field notes · Icefish The water around Antarctica sits at about −1.9°C, below the point where ordinary blood would freeze solid. The fish that live there make antifreeze glycoproteins that bind to tiny ice crystals and stop them growing — a chemistry evolved precisely for a place we'd call unlivable. The icefish took it even further. They are the only vertebrates known to have no hemoglobin — no red blood cells at all. Their blood runs clear. By any warm-water standard this is a catastrophic defect; a body simply should not be able to do that. But in freezing, oxygen-rich water, with big hearts and oxygen absorbed straight through the skin, it works. Read cold, the icefish is broken: it's missing the thing every textbook says a vertebrate needs. Read in its own home, it is fitted — a different design for a different world. The deficit was never in the fish. It was in judging it by someone else's conditions. METABOLIC PACEfastmillenniausthem L★S · 008 The Slow Ones Endoliths · rock-dwellers inside solid rock · millennia per generation Microbes that live inside solid rock, deep underground, on almost no energy — some may take centuries or millennia between generations. Barely metabolizing, easy to mistake for non-living, they are among the best models for where life might hide on Mars. deep biospherea different tempoinside rockastrobiology ▸ Field notes Field notes · Endoliths Kilometres down, inside what looks like solid stone, life persists in the pore spaces of the rock. With almost no energy and almost no water, these microbes run their chemistry so slowly that some estimates put centuries or even millennia between one generation and the next. Barely ticking over, they can be hard to tell apart from the non-living rock around them. But slow is not the same as dead. They are metabolizing, repairing, persisting — living, just on a clock scaled to geology instead of to our days. Disability communities have a name for this idea: crip time — time that runs by the body's own pace rather than the factory's. The endoliths keep crip time at a planetary scale. And it matters far beyond Earth: this quiet, sheltered, ultra-slow way of living is one of the best templates we have for where life could be waiting under the surface of Mars. A pace we'd dismiss as barely alive may be exactly the pace that survives where nothing fast could. i · the whole of it Here is the whole of it, before anything else: your place among us is not a prize you win. It is yours because you are here. "Inclusion safety is not earned but owed. […] Giving inclusion safety is a moral imperative." Timothy R. Clark, The 4 Stages of Psychological Safety (2020), Stage 1

ii · worth before worthiness We will not audition you. Inclusion is a judgment about your worth — which you have, entire, already — not a verdict on your worthiness, which is no one's to weigh at the door. "Including another human being should be an act of prejudgment based on that person's worth, not an act of judgment based on that person's worthiness." Timothy R. Clark, The 4 Stages of Psychological Safety There is no litmus test at this threshold — not your diagnosis, your speech, your output, your history, or how easily others can make sense of you. Worth comes first. Worthiness, if it is ever anyone's business at all, comes long after, and not here.

iii · be human, be harmless What does it take to qualify? Two things. Be human. Be harmless. Meet both and you are in. There is exactly one disqualifier at this door, and it is not difference — it is harm. We say the second part out loud, because a welcome that tolerated harm would betray the very people it exists to keep safe. The one bar Acceptance is owed to everyone. Safety from harm is owed to everyone, too — and it is the single thing that can cost you your place here. Not your way of being. Only harm.

iv · the binding thing Frederick Douglass drew the line for good: "I know of no rights of race superior to the rights of humanity." Frederick Douglass, Our Composite Nationality — Boston, 7 December 1869 Read it for every characteristic, not race alone. When we include one another, we set our differences beneath a deeper, common thing — and agree that the common thing matters more.

v · older than humanity And here we go one floor deeper than the textbook. The common thing beneath our differences is older than humanity. You, and we, and everyone at this door were made in the same stars — the same hydrogen from the same beginning, the same calcium and iron from the same dying giants. Kinship is not a courtesy we extend to you. It is the material you are made of. You do not have to earn your way in. You were ★stuff all along. Belonging here is not conferred; it is constitutive — true of you before you arrived, true whether or not anyone ever tells you so. We are only saying out loud what the atoms settled long ago.

vi · come in So: if you have flesh and blood, we accept you. If you are made of stars — and you are — you are already one of us. Come in. Rest. You are owed this. Inclusion is the first of four doors — beyond it lie the freedom to learn, to contribute, and to challenge. But none of them open until this one does. So we hold this one open first, and for everyone.

Owed, not earned. Inclusion safety — the first stage of psychological safety — is not a reward for the worthy. It is the baseline we owe one another simply for being here. This is our creed for it. L★S A Star Stuff creed on inclusion safety — the first of Timothy R. Clark's four stages of psychological safety. The definitions and the quoted lines are Clark's, from The 4 Stages of Psychological Safety (Berrett-Koehler, 2020) — worth before worthiness; be human and be harmless; the only disqualifier is the threat of harm. The two sentences in the pull-quote above are both verbatim from Stage 1 but are not adjacent in the book, which is why an ellipsis sits between them. Frederick Douglass's line is his own, from Our Composite Nationality, delivered in Boston on 7 December 1869 (the Library of Congress catalogues its manuscript of the lecture as 1867). For the fuller treatment, and how it meets neurodiversity, see Stimpunks' Psychological Safety. The move past "common humanity" to common origin — that belonging is constitutive because we are made of the same star stuff — is ours. This page rests here. You made it to the bottom. You were ★stuff all along — and you were owed a place the whole time. We love you down to it. Where Timothy Clark grounds it in common humanity, Star Stuff goes one floor deeper: you were ★stuff all along, so belonging is constitutive, not conferred.

An Essay Too Good to Check Stimpunks × More Realms How a story gets smoother than the science, and what reading the primary source puts back. Six ways a fact goes wrong, and seventeen worked corrections — most of them ours, published, dated, and fixed in public. The method→ Details How a story gets smoother than the science, and what reading the primary source puts back. Six ways a fact goes wrong — the quote nobody said, the number that went stale, the story told backwards, the credit that drifted, the press release instead of the paper, and the finding that flatters you — with seventeen worked corrections, most of them errors we published and had to fix. Why “go to the primary” is the opposite move from “do your own research,” and why the primary source for an Autistic life is an Autistic person. Two diagrams, a table of receipts, a “Not:” refusals set.

An Essay Who Is Holding the Candle Stimpunks × More Realms Skepticism and wonder, learned at the same time and called uneasy neighbours. Two Sagans and one method — and the reason this site says we. The stance→ Details Two Sagans and one method. Carl learned skepticism and wonder together — from parents who knew almost nothing about science, and from no teacher at all — and called them two uneasily cohabiting modes of thought. His son Dorion argues that the passive voice, the “objective” stance and the anonymity of the scientist betray the fact that every observation is made from a distinct place and time by a particular individual. Why the two modes are held at full strength instead of averaged, why the funding decides which questions get asked, and why an accessibility-first collection writes in the first person plural, names whoever caught each error, and publishes its own corrections. One diagram, a table of deletions, a “Not:” refusals set.

An Essay A Promise, Not a Finding Stimpunks × More Realms For forty-nine issues we have signed off Love you down to your star stuff. The subject is us, not the cosmos — and “down to” measures how far the love reaches, not why it is given. What we may claim→ Details For forty-nine issues this project has signed off Love you down to your star stuff, and the grammar of that phrase has been doing the hardest work on the site. The subject is us, not the cosmos — and “down to” measures how far the love reaches, not why it is given. The star stuff is the extent of the claim, not its warrant. Which matters, because grinding the universe down and sieving it turns up no atom of justice in the powder: a belonging claim resting on “variation persists in nature” would be revoked by any paper finding that it doesn't, and the same move run backwards is how eugenics argued. Ours never rested there. Includes the sentence we did write once, in the colophon of Zine No. 1, and repaired in the same breath. Two rules follow. Every piece here is a lie-to-children in Jack Cohen and Ian Stewart's sense — honest only where it marks the rung it stops at, which is what “a rhyme, not a proof” has been doing unnamed — and the ladder has a moral limit as well as an epistemic one. And First Sight and Second Thoughts, from Pratchett's Wintersmith, names what the six gates and the public changelog implement, with the catch that only the second half can ever be automated. One diagram, two tables, a “Not:” refusals set. All three ideas are borrowed, and credited on the page's face.

An Essay Starlight Stimpunks × More Realms This repository is public — every page, every tool, every error. Making in the open, in the shine of the cosmic latte: a colour first published wrong, and corrected in public by the astronomers who got it wrong. The method→ Details Making in the open, in the shine of the cosmic latte. Average the light of 200,000 galaxies and you get a warm off-white someone named cosmic latte — and the first published answer was pale turquoise, wrong because the software assumed a reddish white point, corrected in public within weeks by the astronomers who got it wrong. The most-shared fact about the colour of the universe is an erratum, and that is the whole argument for an open repository. What is public here, in nouns: the pages, the ledger, the errors, the reasoning, the tools, the index — and the one thing deliberately kept private, your search query, which never leaves your browser. Then the machines in detail: six automated gates, what each one asks, and the fault that created it — 44 pages that printed blank, four links nested inside a link, three collisions every other gate passed, a live zine never listed in the sitemap, a page indexed at 12% that passed its own check. Plus the rules those failures produced: measure, don't count; wait on a condition, never a clock; a page nobody looked at reads UNREAD, never ok. And the division of labour underneath: machines hold ground, people take it — every gate here was written after a person found the fault. Ends with the first plain statement on this site of how generative AI is used, what it is never allowed to do, and why a smoothing machine is a strange thing to build a fact-checked site with. Two diagrams, four tables, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 3 Neurodiversity Field Guide Stimpunks Zines What the paradigm actually claims. What it means to say variation instead of disorder. The paradigm, plainly stated — two frameworks compared, three key definitions, five myth/fact pairs, five principles, and what it means in practice. 7 spreads→ Details Seven spreads, and the primer the rest of the collection leans on. Two frameworks set side by side, one of them a medical model. Neurodiversity as a paradigm rather than a buzzword. What the DSM actually is — a tool, with the emphasis on what a tool is for. The universe that doesn't pathologize its own variation. And what all of it changes in practice. Three key definitions, five myth/fact pairs and five principles, running from assessment through to self-understanding.

Zine No. 18 The Garden and the Stars Stimpunks Zines on knowledge gardens, the commons, and how star stuff comes to know itself A self-portrait of the whole project: if stimpunks.org is the knowledge garden, starstuff.earth is where it flowers, and these zines are the blooms. 8 spreads→ Details Knowledge gardening as star stuff — a self-portrait of the whole project. If stimpunks.org is the knowledge garden, starstuff.earth is where it flowers, and these zines are the blooms. A garden, not a stream: evergreen, cross-linked, walkable, grown from lived experience rather than handed down as hierarchy (a rhizome and a mycelial network, after Deleuze & Guattari). The cosmic turn: a knowledge garden is how star stuff comes to know itself — a supernova scatters its forged elements like a seed-head (SN 1006, liberating iron), and the universe knows itself not as a vault but as a garden, by growing and seeding. Held in common, not enclosed: CC BY-SA, print free, share freely — the licence line is the seed dispersal. Grounded in Caulfield, Appleton, Bush, Deleuze & Guattari, Ostrom, and Sagan, and rooted in Stimpunks' own garden and commons. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a cover bed of blooms keyed to the prior zines' colours, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 1 Bone Song Stimpunks Zines on piezoelectric matter, star-forged calcium, and the universe that doesn't pathologize its own variation Six spreads including the full prose poem, diagrams, and the neurodiversity reframe. 6 spreads→ Details Six spreads that run from a laboratory bench to a paradigm. Iwao Yasuda's finding, 1954–1957, that bone is piezoelectric — press it and it makes voltage — set against stellar nucleosynthesis, which forged the calcium doing the pressing inside a dying star. Then the full Bone Song prose poem; the neurodiversity paradigm; the line the whole collection is built on, that the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation; and a closing spread on reclamation. Zine No. 1, and the piece that set the house form — real sources, diagrams, a poem, and a colophon that shows its working.
Love You Down To Your Star Stuff

Zine No. 2 Love You Down To Your Star Stuff Stimpunks Zines on the full phrase as a zine — the cosmology of care What Sagan said, what the elements are, what “down to” means as a direction, and six affirmations across every register. 6 spreads→ Details The phrase itself, in four movements. What Carl Sagan actually said, checked against the source rather than the paraphrase everybody repeats. The six elements that make up almost all of you, and where each one was forged. Love read at every scale, from the atomic to the communal. And then the grammar that does the work: down to is a direction, measuring how far the loving reaches — not why it is given. Six affirmations across every register, from the tender LYSS to the loud LUSS to the mark itself.

Zine No. 6 Eternal Sunshine Stimpunks Zines on warmth, authenticity, and the counter-deficit turn The Sun is the nearest star, so every warm morning is starlight — the light was always yours, and the sky was in the way. 6 spreads→ Details The Sun is the nearest star, so every warm morning is starlight — and the light was always in you. A golden-hour zine on warmth, authenticity, and the counter-deficit turn: the light was always yours, the sky was in the way. Six spreads with diagrams, affirmations, and a "Not:" refusals set.

Zine No. 7 You Were Never One Thing Stimpunks Zines on endosymbiosis, the cell as a truce, and interdependence written into the body You are a collective. Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria that never left — every cell you have is a truce between former strangers. 6 spreads→ Details You are a collective. Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria that never left — every cell you have is a truce between former strangers. A companion to Bone Song, grounding interdependence over independence in verified cell biology, with diagrams, a prose poem, and a "Not:" refusals set.

Zine No. 8 The Universe Runs on Difference Stimpunks Zines on variety, monoculture, and why sameness is the fragile thing The Cavendish argument across scales: the near-uniform early universe that needed tiny differences to make any structure at all, the banana, the spiky profile, ethodiversity. 7 spreads→ Details Variety is resilience; monoculture is the fragile, engineered thing — one blight from collapse. The Cavendish argument across scales: the near-uniform early universe that needed tiny differences to make any structure at all, the Cavendish banana, neurodiversity via the spiky profile and the competency network, and ethodiversity — the more-than-human variety of ways of being. Sameness is a single point of failure; difference is the default state of matter. Seven spreads, five diagrams, a "Not:" refusals set.

Zine No. 9 The Lines We Drew Stimpunks Zines on constellations, the bell curve, and the border we mistook for the sky Orion's stars sit light-years apart at wildly different depths, and the belt only lines up from here. A figure imposed from one vantage point. 8 spreads→ Details Constellations are lines we impose from one vantage point — Orion's stars sit light-years apart at wildly different depths, and the belt only lines up from here. So is the bell curve; so is the border between "disorder" and "difference." The companion argument to the Constellation Field Guide: the error curve borrowed from astronomy and turned into "the average man," the DSM's moving border, epistemic injustice and the words to name ourselves, and why a human-made line is ours to redraw. Eight spreads, five diagrams, a "Not:" refusals set.
The Dead Stars Still Reach Us

Zine No. 10 The Dead Stars Still Reach Us Stimpunks Zines on starlight, inheritance, and the debt we owe the people who made the room We see stars as they were; some still shining have already gone dark — and their scattered elements become us. 8 spreads→ Details The time-delay of starlight as inheritance and accountability. We see stars as they were; some still shining have already gone dark — and their scattered elements become us. A memorial register read as ancestry: Highlander and our own elders, the ones the Cult of Compliance took, and why memory is labor owed forward. Carries Ira Socol and Page & Woodland in full, closing on “forgetting is a tool of white supremacy — memory is the work.” Eight spreads, five diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 17 The Nearest Body Stimpunks Zines on tides, co-regulation, and how the bodies closest to you pull your nervous system into rhythm The Sun out-masses the Moon 27 million times, yet the Moon runs the tide — because nearness beats mass. So co-regulation is gravity. 8 spreads→ Details Tides and co-regulation as star stuff. The Sun out-masses the Moon 27 million times, yet the Moon runs the tide — because tidal force falls off with the cube of distance, and nearness beats mass. So co-regulation is gravity: a safe-enough nervous system nearby pulls yours into rhythm, at a distance, without touching. Spring and neap tides as aligned or crossed pulls, parallel presence as tidal locking, meerkat mode as a sea that lost its moon, and the ecosystemic turn — the storm is in the weather, not the water. Grounded in the Stimpunks glossary (co-regulation, polyvagal theory, meerkat mode, ARLES, regulation-first), with a hydrofeminist thread carried inward from No. 14. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 19 No Universal Now Stimpunks Zines on relativity, crip time, and the clock that was never the universe's — with a coda by Helen Edgar Physics says there is no universal “now,” so the one true clock is a human invention — a convention we mistook for the world. 9 spreads→ Details Crip time, read through relativity — with a guest coda by Helen Edgar. Physics says there is no universal “now”: simultaneity is relative and clocks run at different rates by speed and gravity (your phone's GPS corrects for it). So the one true clock is a human invention — railway-and-factory standard time, a convention we mistook for a law and then began grading bodies and minds against. Crip time (Zola & Gill, Kafer, Samuels, Price) bends the clock back to fit us instead of bending us to it — the same move as Minor Worlds, now applied to time. Monotropic spiral time and felt time (Helen Edgar, Bergson, Deleuze) are their own real clock, measured in intensity, not minutes; Samuels' time travel, grief time, and broken time hold the hard edges too. The reading: no clock is master, and being “off the clock” is closer to the truth than fitting it. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and a closing coda by Helen Edgar on spiral time.

Zine No. 20 The Same Water Stimpunks Zines on phase transitions, fluctuating capacity, and why “you could do it yesterday” was never the point Water doesn't get gradually stiffer as it cools — it holds, then flips to ice all at once. Same substance; the conditions decide the state. 8 spreads→ Details Fluctuating capacity, read through the physics of phase transitions. Water doesn't get gradually stiffer as it cools — it holds, then flips to ice all at once at a threshold. Same H₂O, different state, and the conditions (not the substance) decide which. So the exhausting question — why could you do it yesterday and not today? — has a clean answer: capacity is a state, not a trait, and you were near a boundary. The hardest part is the crossing itself (threshold anxiety is sensitivity to a real edge — broken thresholds, not broken people); you can be supercooled, held past your limit until one small thing tips everything at once; and recovery slows near the edge, because that's how systems behave. Nothing is fixed or broken — fluid adaptation and weather-bodies, re-adapting to a changed climate. Extends Minor Worlds: change the conditions, not the substance. Grounded in phase-transition physics, Cynthia Kim, Helen Edgar, and Stimpunks' own threshold anxiety. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 21 Not a Line Stimpunks Zines on spectra, constellations, and why “mild to severe” was always the wrong picture — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer A real spectrum isn't a ladder — split a star's light and every element signs its own fingerprint. No rank, no norm, no line. 8 spreads→ Details The spectrum was never a severity scale — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer. “Spectrum” is the most misread word in our vocabulary: people hear a line from mild to severe. But a real spectrum isn't a ladder — split a star's light and every element signs its own pattern of lines, a fingerprint, which is the only way we know what stars are made of. And the sky's figure was never a line: it's a constellation. The zine follows the escalation from Helen Edgar's brand-new essay — the line of neuronormativity, to the spiky profile (better, but still a grid measured from a baseline), to a constellation of intensities: no rank, no norm, no line. Patrick Dwyer's autism constellation anchors it; the functioning-labels critique shows how the line gatekeeps support (“not disabled enough” vs “too disabled”). Held with care: refusing the line doesn't erase that some of us need far more support — need is not a rank; name it instead. Cashes in the rainbow motif on every page and hands off to the Constellation Field Guide. Eight spreads, spectrum-forward diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 23 Bodies of Water Stimpunks Zines on hydrofeminism, shared flow, and belonging that moves between us You are not a container of water; you are water, briefly gathered into a shape — and none of it was ever only yours. After Astrida Neimanis. 8 spreads→ Details Hydrofeminism as belonging, read through star stuff — after Astrida Neimanis. You are not a container of water; you are water, roughly 60% of you, briefly gathered into a shape. And none of it is only yours: it was rain, river, cloud, and the inside of other creatures first. Neimanis's gestationality (we each began inside another body's water) and Stacy Alaimo's transcorporeality dissolve the clean edge — we are all downstream of one another, permeable and borrowed. The crucial move, held with care: watery belonging is not dissolution into sameness. Where two rivers meet, the confluence runs braided for miles — one channel, two waters, still distinct. That's the neurodiversity paradigm in an image: the spiky profile survives the merge. A dedicated spread carries shared/collective flow — monotropism's deep channels can align into shared flow (Autistic Realms, Helen Edgar); a watering hole is where currents pool. So belonging is a current, not a border — build watering holes, keep the water moving. Much of Earth's water is older than the Sun. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 24 Shared Air Stimpunks Zines on breath, co-regulation, and the air we hold in common There is only one air, so thoroughly mixed that your next breath very likely holds atoms once breathed by strangers and by trees. 9 spreads→ Details The air we share, read through star stuff and solarpunk — a companion to Bodies of Water. There is only one air: a single, well-mixed body with no walls in it, so thoroughly circulated that your next breath very likely holds atoms once breathed by strangers and by trees across the world. It's a reciprocal breath — we exhale what plants inhale, and our oxygen is the exhaust of ancient cyanobacteria (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago), forged first in stars. Every room we share is a shared-air space (a term coined by Helen Edgar & Ryan Boren): in it we trade breath and co-regulate, nervous systems settling into a shared rhythm. The neurodiversity turn: many of us are the canaries of that room. Miners carried canaries because the birds felt the bad air first — not because they were weak, but because they were sensitive, and their alarm was information. Our sensitivity to fragrance, stale air, and fluorescent hum is an early-warning system, not a flaw: don't blame the bird, change the air — build it breathable for the canaries and it's breathable for all. Which raises the harder question: habitable, and for whom? The burden of shared air falls unevenly, so breathable air is a commons, not a private accommodation one person quietly manages. The response is solarpunk: clean air as infrastructure as resistance — open windows, plants, masks, DIY Corsi–Rosenthal boxes — mutual aid you can build in an afternoon. Move quietly and plant things. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 25 Shared Signal Stimpunks Zines on distance, the clearer channel, and the rhythm we carry when we can't share a room Radio waves and starlight are the same phenomenon at different wavelengths — and shared-signal space is Helen Edgar's coinage. 9 spreads→ Details Connection carried across distance, read through star stuff — a companion to Shared Air. The electromagnetic spectrum is one continuous field: radio waves and starlight are the same phenomenon at different wavelengths, and the same physics that carries a voice call carries a star's light. Shared-signal space — a term coined by Helen Edgar — is the counterpart to shared-air space: a call, a message, a voice note, a synthesised voice, carrying the rhythm on a signal instead of the air of a room. A voice note is breath, timestamped and sent; co-regulation crosses a screen too — thinner, but real (Porges; Streuber et al.). For many of us, text and AAC aren't a fallback from speech but the clearer channel — thinking time, structure, fewer sensory demands, a record to return to (Howard & Sedgewick) — and AAC is the real communication, not a workaround. Aversion to the phone is information, not fragility. Reachable, and for whom? Communication access is a commons; we build our own watering holes — the Autistic Rhizome (Edgar), Discords, AAC — sideways and underground, where lurking counts. The oldest signal of all is a dead star's light still reaching your eye: signal lets connection cross a gap touch can't, so no channel is the master channel (Milton). Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 44 You Cannot Flatten a Sphere Stimpunks Zines on curvature, map projections, and what a single number has to throw away Gauss proved in 1827 that no flat map can preserve everything. An IQ score is literally a projection — so it must destroy information. 12 spreads→ Details Try wrapping a sheet of paper smoothly around an orange. It creases, always, and that is not clumsiness — it is forbidden. Gauss proved it in 1827 and liked the result enough to call it the Theorema Egregium, the remarkable theorem: a surface’s curvature is intrinsic, so bending that doesn’t stretch can never change it. Paper rolls into a tube or a cone because those are still flat in the sense that matters; a sphere is not, and no care gets you there. You have used this today without noticing — fold a pizza slice and the tip stops drooping, because curving it one way forces it to stay straight the other. The consequence: no flat map of the world can preserve everything, and every projection must sacrifice area, angle, distance or direction. Mercator chose angle, in 1569, so a constant compass bearing would be a straight line — superb for sailors, and it swells Greenland to the apparent size of an Africa roughly fourteen times larger. The map never says what it chose, and that silence is the scandal rather than the distortion. Then Tissot’s answer from 1859, which is the honest one: you cannot remove the distortion, so draw it — a grid of ellipses showing exactly what this map did to this place. And then the turn. An IQ score, a DSM-5 support level, a functioning label: each takes a many-axis person and returns one value, which is not a metaphor but literally a projection — so it must destroy information, the choice of what to destroy is somebody’s, and the number never records it. Worse than a map, in fact: a Mercator keeps every place badly, while a single number doesn’t distort the other dimensions, it deletes them. Ask what a summary was optimised for and you learn whose journey it serves — Mercator for sailors, a support level for a budget, a functioning label for a gate. If you must summarise, publish the indicatrix: the axes it came from, the range it moves across, what it was built for, reviewed by the person measured. Closes on the gentlest thing the theorem gives — a globe has no edges and no corners, so being at the margin was never information about you, only about where somebody cut. Companion to No. 21 Not a Line, which asks what shape the thing is; this asks what a reduction costs. Twelve spreads, ten diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 45 The Cloud Phase Stimpunks Zines on the last stage of a supernova remnant, and how long the in-between actually lasts The story we get told about a dead star ends about one step past the explosion. The physics runs further than the sentence does. 11 spreads→ Details The story we get told about a dead star ends about one step past the explosion: the shell expands, thins, cools, and disperses into the interstellar medium. Fade out. But the physics runs further than the sentence does, and there is another word waiting at the end of it. Romano, Behrendt & Burkert (2024) followed remnants through their long cold decline and found the radiative phase divides into four stages — and the last one they call the cloud phase. Not the end phase. Not the dispersal phase. The cloud phase: once nothing is driving the shell and the pressure inside has fallen to match the pressure outside, nothing holds the cavity open, so the remnant falls back into itself and settles as a chemically enriched cloud. That is a 2024 simulation and it is held here as proposed, flagged in place — because the argument's weight sits somewhere firmer. Murray (2011) measured what clouds actually do: in the Milky Way's most luminous star-forming complexes, the star formation efficiency averages 0.08, so ninety-two percent of the cloud never becomes a star — and that is the flattering number, since the Galactic average of 0.005 puts it nearer ninety-nine and a half. A giant molecular cloud lasts 27 ± 12 million years, and the bright episode inside it is short, late, and the thing that tears the cloud apart. Which turns the story the other way round: the in-between is not the wait between the real states. It is the majority state, by mass and by duration — and that is a measurement, offered as fact rather than as comfort. Along the way, SN 1987A: at least 0.2 solar masses of dust condensed inside its own wreckage, grains that did not exist anywhere before the star died. The debris field is a foundry. Written after Helen Edgar, whose Supernova Remnant and Emergence Point map the same stage from the inside — burnout as “remnants of my old self entangled in new ways of being,” recovery as re-assembly rather than return, and deterritorialisation as “a soft loosening of pressure.” A cloud never decides to collapse; it is collapsed upon, by gravity and radiation and its neighbours, so the honest question when one of us reorganises is what the pressure is and where it comes from. Held with care throughout: gestation is not a promise of a star, most of the mass never lights, and the claim is only that the cloud is a real state, not a waiting room. Closes on aluminium-26 in the Allende meteorite — something nearby and freshly dead was in our own birth cloud, and which star is openly contested fifty years on, so we name the contest instead of picking a winner. Eleven spreads, nine diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 46 Companion Stars Stimpunks Zines on gravitational binding, the three-body problem, and why no one's path can be solved alone A star that shares a system with another star already has a name, and it is astronomy's own working word: a companion star. 9 spreads→ Details A star that shares a system with another star already has a name, and it is astronomy’s own working word: a companion star. Helen Edgar’s thirteenth constellation carries it — “the people who orbit close … who don’t need me to perform and who just ‘get it’.” But before any of that, a correction, because this collection exists partly to take science back from the version that travels furthest. You have met the line most stars are in binaries — the Sun is the odd one out. It isn’t so. Charles Lada put the binary statistics beside the stellar mass function in 2006 and published the answer as his title: most stars are single — two-thirds of main-sequence systems in the Galactic disk. Multiplicity climbs steeply with mass (~26% of M dwarfs, 44 ± 2% of Sun-like stars, near-total for the most massive), and the galaxy is overwhelmingly made of the small end. So this zine will not tell you that everybody has their people. The claim it makes instead is smaller and holds all the way down: where the binding is real, here is exactly what it is. Sirius A and its white-dwarf companion trace a 50.13-year orbit about a barycentre lying in neither star — and equal binding is not equal motion, since the heavier body is displaced less, which is worth saying out loud for anyone who has been told they’re imagining who does more of the moving. Then the hardest spread: bring two stars close and they do deform each other — stretched to ellipsoids, drawn to teardrops, finally sharing one dumbbell envelope with matter crossing between them. Proximity is not automatically good. It is the wide pairs — bound out to a parsec, one orbit longer than the whole history of flowering plants — where both keep their shape. And then the turn, which is theorems rather than reading: with two bodies you can write the solution down, but Bruns (1887) proved no further algebraic integrals exist, Poincaré (1890) closed off the single-valued analytic ones, and Sundman’s 1912 series converges far too slowly to use. So these systems are stepped forward numerically, together, and no one body’s path can be solved on its own and the others added afterward. That same work is where chaos was found — and the part the popular word destroys is that nothing is random: every rule is exact and known, and the system is still unpredictable far out. Read beside the language this community built first — David Gray-Hammond’s Chaotic Self (“you can’t unqueer a queer mind”) and Autistic Rhizome, with Helen’s Rhizome Array and Mycelial Stars — and holding the tension honestly rather than smoothing it: the rhizome describes resilience, no node depending on another to exist; the three-body physics describes non-separability while bodies are bound. Both true, neither cancelling. Closes on what actually holds a bound system: no agreement, no shared origin, no similarity, no upkeep, no performance — mutual gravity and nothing else, which means there is no version of a companion star that has to earn it. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. A rhyme, not a proof.
The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing

Zine No. 48 The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing Stimpunks Zines on the black hole nobody photographed, and what can only be known by its effect on everything else Nobody has photographed a black hole, and nobody will — the ordinary way of knowing a thing is simply unavailable, and no better lens fixes it. 12 spreads→ Details Nobody has photographed a black hole, and nobody will. A camera works by catching light that left the subject, and the event horizon is the surface where every outward direction has stopped existing — so the ordinary way of knowing a thing is simply unavailable, and no better lens fixes it. What the Event Horizon Telescope released in April 2019 and May 2022 is a shadow: the set of directions in which light that might have reached you went into the hole instead, ringed by the light that passed far enough out to be bent around and escape. Then the fact this zine is built on, which is exact geometry rather than an impression. For a non-spinning black hole the event horizon sits at 2 GM/c² and the edge of the shadow at 3√3 GM/c² — so the dark circle is about 2.6 times wider than the object casting it. Gravity does not merely hide the thing; it magnifies the hiding. And that magnification is nearly constant across spins and viewing angles (5 ± 0.2 GM/Dc², a spread of about four percent), which is the only reason anyone can work backwards from it. The instrument was the planet: eight radio telescopes at six sites from Spain to the South Pole, observing at 1.3 mm, writing ~3.5 petabytes to helium-filled hard drives that had to be flown to two correlators — the Antarctic share stranded until the winter ended. No site saw the ring; no site could have. Four imaging teams then worked blind to one another, on two different families of algorithm, because everyone involved knew what they hoped to find. M87*’s ring came out at 42 ± 3 microarcseconds — an orange, on the Moon. Sagittarius A* was harder despite being nearer, because its innermost orbit takes about thirty minutes against M87*’s thirty days: the subject rearranges itself while the shutter is open. Then the turn, in two halves. Some things are known only by their effect on everything around them — monotropism, pain, a sensory environment, an access need — and the absence of a photograph was never evidence of an absent thing. But the geometry has a second half, and this piece does not stop before it: what people see of an unmet need is the disruption, not the need, and the disruption is the larger object, inflated by every year of bending and masking and quiet accommodation that got folded into it. In physics you can divide the factor out. In a life there is none, which is exactly why you ask. Closes on the guardrail rather than the warm note: unseeable is not unreal, and it is not a blank cheque either — the collaboration pinned Sagittarius A* to 51.8 ± 2.3 microarcseconds without ever seeing it. Twelve spreads, ten diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set that turns down the obvious reading first. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 51 Almost Shadow Stimpunks Zines on the zone Kepler had to name, why partial is the enormous one, and the two fields that borrowed the word In 1604 Kepler was drawing the geometry of an eclipse and ran out of language — so in the middle of a diagram he made a word: penumbra. 13 spreads→ Details In 1604 Johannes Kepler was drawing the geometry of an eclipse and ran out of language. The Sun is not a point of light but a disc, so every part of it throws a shadow in a slightly different direction and the result comes out layered: a core where the whole disc is hidden, an outer region where some of it still shines through, and between them no edge at all — just a handover. He had umbra for the core. For the handover he had nothing. So in the middle of a diagram in Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena he made one: quod est inter KE, NM penumbra dicatur — let what lies between be called penumbra. The verb is dicatur, let it be called; that is not a man using a word, it is the word being made because a drawing demanded it. Paene plus umbra: almost-shadow, and what gets named is neither the dark nor the light but the thing between them. Astronomy keeps three zones now, and the third is the one nobody has heard of: the antumbra, past the shadow cone’s apex, where the Moon sits entirely in front of the Sun — nothing sticking out, nothing off to one side — and it is still not a total eclipse, because the Moon is simply too small in your sky to cover what is behind it. Complete obstruction, and the darkness never comes. Two words would have forced that case into one of the other two and both would have been wrong. Then the pair of facts this zine refuses to separate. First, the partial zone is the enormous one: the umbral track lands as a stripe a hundred-odd kilometres wide while the penumbra covers thousands, so the overwhelming majority of everyone who has ever seen a solar eclipse saw a partial one. The penumbra is where we live; totality is the exception. Second, and cutting the other way, 99 percent obscured is still daylight. The corona is only about as bright as a full Moon, and the surviving sliver of photosphere is hundreds to thousands of times brighter than that — so it obliterates the corona and keeps the sky blue. Illuminance falls roughly a hundred-fold in the last two minutes, another order of magnitude in the final half minute, more than four orders of magnitude in all. The last increment is not an increment; it is a change of state, and on the far side of it the birds go quiet. Gradient and threshold, and any account that can hold only one of them is describing something other than the world — all gradient gives you “everyone’s a bit like that” and owes nobody anything; all threshold gives you the eligibility form and makes the enormous middle vanish. Two other fields worked this out and reached for Kepler’s word, both times because a binary would cost lives. In 1981 Astrup, Siesjö and Symon found two thresholds in ischaemic brain — electrical failure, then ion-pump failure — and named the zone between them the ischaemic penumbra: functionally silent, structurally intact, salvageable on reperfusion. That word is the reason acute stroke has a treatment window at all; every intervention is aimed at the penumbra, because the core is past help and the healthy tissue does not need it. And in Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) Justice Douglas held that guarantees have “penumbras, formed by emanations” — a borrowing the zine presents alongside its critics rather than beneath them, since a shadow with no measurable edge can be stretched to cover whatever the reader wanted covered.
