Zine No. 38 Eight Tenths of a Second Stimpunks Zines on a fired astronomer, a cat in a box, and the road to the dashboard In February 1796 the Astronomer Royal dismissed his assistant for marking star transits eight tenths of a second late. Bessel later showed observers differ irreducibly. 14 spreads→ Details In February 1796 the Astronomer Royal dismissed his assistant David Kinnebrook for marking star transits eight tenths of a second late. Bessel later established that observers differ from one another systematically and irreducibly — and astronomy's answer was the personal equation: publish a constant for each observer, build the variation into the model, keep the observer. This zine follows the measuring apparatus out of the observatory: Wundt's laboratory, Cattell's “mental tests,” Thorndike's puzzle boxes and his 1918 credo that whatever exists at all exists in some amount, Kelly's Kansas Silent Reading Test, Pressey's machine built from typewriter parts, Skinner's teaching machines, and Lovaas at UCLA in 1987 — while a second rail runs alongside from Galton through Kraepelin to the DSM. The two meet at a table with a child at it. The first zine built as a Burke-style chain, and every joint is marked documented, contested or leap — six solid, three dashed, one dotted — because two of them are weaker than the story wants. The turn: school found the same human variation astronomy found, and made it the thing to remove. Accommodation is the older answer. Fourteen spreads, twelve diagrams, a running chain spine, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 39 Five Microns Stimpunks Zines on a number that answered a different question, and the room it left you in In March 2020 the WHO posted “FACT: COVID-19 is NOT airborne.” Not a lie — doctrine, faithfully applied, resting on a number that had quietly changed questions. 15 spreads→ Details In March 2020 the WHO posted “FACT: COVID-19 is NOT airborne” and called the alternative misinformation. Not a lie — doctrine, faithfully applied, resting on a number that had quietly changed questions. William Wells put the boundary between droplets that fall and droplets that evaporate into lingering nuclei at 100 micrometres, and never wrote 5; his own table gives a 1 µm particle sixteen hours to fall two metres. The 5 µm figure came from industrial hygiene asking which particles reach the deepest lung — deposition, not suspension — and Alexander Langmuir fused the two in 1951, in a lecture preparing public-health students for biological warfare months after Korea began. Randall, Ewing, Marr, Jimenez and Bourouiba reconstructed it in Interface Focus under the title “How did we get here,” and refuse to solder the load-bearing joint, writing only that the deposition focus “likely” popularised the cut-off — so this zine marks it contested too. Meanwhile Flügge's team in Breslau had grown colonies nine metres from a sneeze in the 1890s, meant “droplets” to cover what we now call aerosols, waited five hours before reading their plates, and recommended ventilation. The 1–2 metre rule has its own separate lineage and turns out to match the width of a 1940s camera's field of view. The second chain zine, every joint marked documented, contested or leap. Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a running two-rail spine, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 40 Five Sigma Stimpunks Zines how much evidence is enough before you do something to a child Particle physics will not permit the word “discovery” below five sigma — one chance in three and a half million — and wrote down why. 16 spreads→ Details How much evidence is enough before you do something to a child? Particle physics answered that question carefully and wrote it down. It will not permit the word “discovery” below five sigma — a p-value of 3 × 10⁻⁷, one chance in three and a half million — and the reason is empirical rather than principled: too many 3σ and 4σ results kept evaporating. Louis Lyons, whose paper is the spine of this zine, goes further and argues the bar should not be uniform at all, grading it by degree of surprise, impact, look-elsewhere effect and systematics: single top production 3σ, the Higgs 5σ, supersymmetry 7σ, faster-than-light neutrinos above 8σ. He also prints the statisticians' objection that his own gold standard is unsound. Against all that stands p = 0.05 — about 2σ — chosen by Fisher in 1925 with the word convenient, and unexamined since. The gap is roughly 170,000×, and the asymmetry runs backwards: if physics is wrong it retracts a paper and the particle is unharmed; if we are wrong a childhood already happened and there is no more data to collect. Run Lyons' four dials on an intervention and every one reads high — then the systematics column turns out to be empty, because 150 intervention studies for young Autistic children produced 11 that mentioned adverse events at all. Not an argument against science. An argument against scientism, which keeps the authority and drops the practice. The first chain here with no leap joints. Sixteen spreads, fourteen diagrams, two rails that never meet, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 41 A Conquering Gaze from Nowhere Stimpunks Zines parallax, positionality, and the research done on us For roughly two centuries the strongest objection to a moving Earth was that the stars showed no parallax. The reasoning was valid, and the conclusion wrong. 15 spreads→ Details For roughly two centuries the strongest objection to a moving Earth was that the stars showed no parallax. The reasoning was valid, the observations careful, and the conclusion wrong — partly because the distances required seemed absurd, and partly because telescopic star discs are an artefact of the aperture rather than a property of stars. Then in 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured 61 Cygni at 0.3136 arcseconds from Königsberg — a two-centimetre coin seen from thirteen kilometres. The method carries the whole argument: the baseline is the observer's own displacement across Earth's orbit, so a viewpoint with no location has no baseline, no angle and no depth. A view from nowhere cannot measure distance even in principle; it is the blindest available position. And it is the same Bessel, at the same observatory, who gave us the personal equation in No. 38 — twice showing that knowledge requires a located, particular observer. Every rung of the cosmic distance ladder above parallax is calibrated by the one beneath, and rung two — the period–luminosity relation — was built by Henrietta Swan Leavitt, employed as a Harvard “computer,” paid by the hour, not permitted to observe, and published under her director's name: “has been prepared by Miss Leavitt.” That is the third woman in three chains to do the work and lose the byline, and the zine stops to name all three. Donna Haraway gave the fantasy its name in 1988 — the god trick, the unmarked category claiming the power to see and not be seen — and her positive claim is the one usually dropped: only partial perspective promises objective vision. She refuses relativism just as flatly, calling it “a way of being nowhere while claiming to be everywhere equally.” Then the numbers: 96% of behavioural-science samples from Western industrialised nations, 68% from the US, reported as facts about humans. Then research done on Autistic people rather than with them, and double empathy as a finding that only exists because somebody stood at the other end of the baseline. The correction is neither removing the observer nor declaring all views equal: publish your coordinates. Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a single rail with a marked baseline, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 42 Look for the Air Stimpunks Zines two thousand years spent deleting character from the explanation, and the industry that put it back Aristotle explained motion by what a thing is. It is not a foolish theory — go outside and test it and every prediction checks out. 14 spreads→ Details Aristotle's physics explained motion by what a thing is: heavy bodies fall because it is in their nature to seek the centre, faster in proportion to weight, slower in a denser medium. It is not a foolish theory — go outside and test it and every prediction checks out, because everyday observation happens in air. The error is where the explanation was put. Galileo showed the rule contradicts itself (tie a heavy body to a light one and it predicts both faster and slower), rolled balls down inclined planes, and made the strange move of reasoning about a fall with no medium at all — while the famous Leaning Tower demonstration turns out to come from a biography written decades later and is marked contested here. Newton finished it: acceleration is set by the forces acting plus one scalar property, and disposition disappears. Then, on 2 August 1971, David Scott released a geology hammer and a falcon feather together in the lunar vacuum and they landed together, on film. The difference was never in the feather. It was in the air. This chain argues that mindset marketing runs that two-thousand-year move backwards on children. Behaviourism looks like it made the same move but stopped one ring short — it deleted the interior and still left the child as the only adjustable thing. California's task force commissioned its own research, was told the associations between self-esteem and its expected consequences were “mixed, insignificant, or absent,” and shipped in 1990 regardless. Growth mindset fails the same way across 63 studies and 97,672 participants, with higher-quality studies less likely to show benefit — and Dweck and Duckworth both objected to the deployment while it kept growing. The dashboard completes it: a schema with fields for effort, focus and behaviour points, and no field for the room. Along the way the zine corrects its own source — the famous Eric Hoffer line about a movement becoming a business and degenerating into a racket is a misquotation that invents a moral arc he never wrote. It closes on scarcity and slack, on equity literacy, and on the first leap joint since No. 39, marked because it is the sentence a reader most wants to be true. Fourteen spreads, twelve diagrams, two rails running in opposite directions, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 43 The Elimination of Waste Stimpunks Zines on a word that meant one thing in a steam engine and another in a school In 1824 Sadi Carnot proved a heat engine has a hard, provable ceiling on its efficiency — and that waste heat is not sloppiness, it is the fee. 15 spreads→ Details In 1824 Sadi Carnot proved something strange: that a heat engine has a hard, provable ceiling on its efficiency, set only by the two temperatures available and beatable by no engineer who ever lives. And with it came the result that matters here — waste heat is not sloppiness, it is the fee. An engine with nowhere to dump it does not run at all. So “eliminate all waste” isn't an ambitious goal not yet reached; in thermodynamics it names the one outcome that is ruled out. (He reached this from caloric theory, which was wrong — Clausius and Kelvin supplied the formula later, so “Carnot derived the efficiency equation” is itself a smoothed retelling, and the joint is marked contested.) Then the word left the engine room, and what it shed in transit was the ceiling. Frederick Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management appeared in 1911, and Raymond Callahan's Education and the Cult of Efficiency (1962) dates what followed to the month: in July 1911, one month after Taylor's American Magazine series concluded, a school board member told the NEA that “scientific management” held a message for every teacher — and that if teachers did not voluntarily increase their efficiency, the business world would force them to. By 1916 Cubberley's textbook was listing what schools must take from the factory: good tools, specialized machinery, continuous measurement of production, and “the elimination of waste in manufacture.” Ninety-two years after Carnot, the phrase arrives in a book about children as a specification. By 1912 an educator was already complaining that teachers were “curiously protected in inefficiency.” And the question nobody asked sits in Callahan's own parenthesis: would Schmidt, the pig-iron handler, have agreed that science had reduced his fatigue? It ends at spoon theory — and then spends an entire spread arguing that this argument should not need physics at all, because you are not a heat engine and deriving rest from thermodynamics is precisely the move the collection condemns. Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a spine that crosses its own ceiling, a “Not:” refusals set.
The Sky Was Not Regular Enough

Zine No. 50 The Sky Was Not Regular Enough Stimpunks Zines on cutting a standard loose from the thing it measured, and whether you say so out loud Until 1960 a second was one 86,400th of a day, and the definition pointed at the sky. Then the instrument became steadier than the thing it measured. 16 spreads→ Details Until 1960 a second was a piece of a day — one 86,400th of it — and the definition pointed at something. Not a prototype in a vault, but the sky: you could check it against a star. Then quartz clocks arrived and, for the first time in the history of measurement, the instrument was steadier than the Earth. Scheibe and Adelsberger reported the seasonal wobble in 1936; Stoyko put it at about two milliseconds in 1937. The Earth was never irregular to itself — it became irregular the moment we had something steadier to compare it to. So the tie was cut, twice. In 1956 the second became a fraction of the tropical year 1900, a year that had already ended and could never be re-measured; in 1967 it became 9,192,631,770 caesium transitions, and after that the definition points at no day, no year, no sky at all. Every one of those moves was an improvement, and this zine says so — the collection exists to reclaim science, not to indict it. Since 1972 the gap between the atomic standard and the turning planet has been closed in public by leap seconds: 27 of them, first on 30 June 1972, last on 31 December 2016, and none since, because the Earth started spinning faster and the correction now due is a negative leap second that has never been tested. Duncan Agnew showed in Nature in 2024 that melting Greenland and Antarctic ice slowed the spin enough to postpone it from 2026 to 2029 — climate change bought the world's timekeepers three years, and he refuses to call that good news. Resolution 4 of the 27th CGPM decided in 2022 to widen the tolerance by 2035, and the implementing vote is at the 28th CGPM this October; the proposal is a leap hour. The argument: a leap second is not a bug but an honesty mechanism — a standards body saying in public, on a named date, with a number attached, that its standard and the world disagree by exactly this much. Abolishing it is defensible engineering. What it costs is the announcement. And that is the one thing carried across to us, marked leap because caesium licenses nothing about a person: an accommodation is a leap second, and the objections to it arrive in the same order — it's irregular, it breaks the system, everybody handles it differently — with the same proposed remedy, widen the tolerance and stop announcing. Ends at processing speed and crip time: the Earth is not slow, the second left. Eleven documented joints, one contested, one leap. Sixteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a running spine that is a plot of its own data, a “Not:” refusals set.
We Learned to Build the Eclipse

Zine No. 52 We Learned to Build the Eclipse Stimpunks Zines on an element nobody would accept because it could not be put on a bench, and on the day we stopped travelling to the Moon's shadow A chain about how a whole branch of physics stopped waiting for the Moon — the corona, for most of astronomy's history available only during totality. 21 spreads→ Details A chain about how a whole branch of physics stopped waiting for the Moon. The Sun’s outer atmosphere is always there and almost never available: the photosphere drowns it, so for most of astronomy’s history the corona and the prominences could only be studied during totality — a few minutes, roughly every eighteen months, along a track a few hundred kilometres wide, usually somewhere difficult, and one cloud ended the expedition. It begins in 1604, where pinhole solar diameters came out systematically too large and nobody could say why until Kepler supplied the theory of how an image forms behind a small hole: the method came first and worked badly; the understanding came second and fixed it. Then Guntur, 18 August 1868, where several observers caught a yellow line near sodium’s — and where what Janssen actually took away was not the line but its brightness. The next morning he observed the prominences again with no eclipse at all, spreading the sky’s glare thin with dispersion while the emission line stayed put. Lockyer, who had wanted this since 1866 and was blocked by glass rather than by ideas, got there on 20 October; both reports reached the Académie within days and it struck a medal for the pair — for the method. Neither report flagged the yellow line, which is the first of four contested joints: the famous sentence “helium was discovered during an eclipse in 1868” is wrong in almost every part, and what the compression deletes is years of argument. Lockyer alone later called it D3 and proposed an element; for a quarter century chemists refused it, not because the spectroscopy was faulty but because nobody could put the gas on a bench — and a thing visible only in light from 150 million kilometres away did not, to them, count as a thing. They were rigorous and they were wrong, and the zine insists on both, because the same method also produced two elements that were never there: coronium and nebulium, dissolved by Bowen in 1927 and Grotrian and Edlén in 1939 and 1942 as forbidden lines of ordinary oxygen and iron — which is also how we learned the corona is millions of degrees hotter than the surface. Ramsay got helium out of cleveite on 26 March 1895, twenty-seven years late, and it had been underfoot the whole time. Then the chain runs downhill, because capability is specific: in 1919 the Moon was needed again to see whether starlight bends, the Sobral astrograph plates were set aside, Earman and Glymour charged Eddington with seeing what he wanted, and Kennefick later established that the call was Dyson’s and that the plates could only agree with Newton if the instrument had also changed magnification — a reason to distrust them other than what they said, which is the whole difference between rejecting bad data and rejecting inconvenient data. Finally Bernard Lyot, chasing stray light up a mountain, photographed the corona with no eclipse on 12 July 1931: an eclipse at a time and place of human choosing, turning minutes per expedition into hours per clear day. We now fly manufactured occulters at other stars. The transfer, marked leap because it is one, refuses the obvious framing first: eclipses were computed years ahead, so the difficulty was never luck but a structural condition — the observation existing only there, only then, with the ocean, the freight, the years and the weather all charged to whoever needed it. An expedition demonstrates what is required and is a catastrophe as a delivery mechanism. So there are three states, not two: reach it, ask for it, or have it — and the middle one is what we named accommodation, which is the word Stimpunks' own page exists to criticise, since the problem is structural and the response is individual. Lyot did not apply for access to the corona; he built an instrument in which it is simply there, and the occulting disc is not a concession but where the precision comes from. Which is a curb cut: Michael Pachovas and friends poured cement into a crude ramp one Berkeley evening and rolled off into the night, and Berkeley cut its first official kerb on Telegraph Avenue in 1972 — while the sledgehammer version of that story is disability lore, not history, which a chain that spends a spread on smoothed retellings could not close on. Angela Glover Blackwell named the curb-cut effect in 2017, and the zine states plainly that it is an observation about what built-in conditions do and never the justification. Twenty-one spreads, twelve documented joints, four contested, one leap, a generated spine, and a “Not:” set that refuses the reading that barriers are valuable for what they reveal. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 56 The Noise Floor Stimpunks Zines every receiver has one, no design removes it, and the biggest discovery in modern cosmology arrived as noise two engineers spent ten months trying to get rid of A chain about a limit nobody beats, and the rooms we build as though it were free. Johnson and Nyquist, printed on facing pages in 1928. 15 spreads→ Details A chain about a limit nobody beats, and the rooms we build as though it were free. In July 1928 one volume of Physical Review printed the measurement and its explanation on facing pages — J. B. Johnson at 97–109, H. Nyquist at 110–113, whose first footnote is three words long: “See preceding paper.” Every conductor above absolute zero hisses, and Nyquist’s conclusion is that the effect is “a universal function of frequency, resistance and temperature and of these variables only” — not the metal, not the workmanship, since “one may be made of silver and the other of lead.” The available power in a band is kTB, and that is in the primary rather than a modern gloss on it. The part that usually goes missing is why it cannot be engineered away. Nyquist did not measure the floor, he deduced it — from the second law. Two resistors at one temperature must pass equal power both ways in every band, or a resonant circuit between them would move heat between equal-temperature bodies for free. The hiss is not permitted, it is required: a silent resistor would be a perpetual-motion machine, which is the same law that says you cannot un-stir the milk from the tea — and nobody files that under insufficient effort. Twenty years on, Shannon’s Theorem 17 turns the floor into a limit on meaning, with the sentence that closes the door: “It is not possible to transmit at a higher rate by any encoding system without a definite positive frequency of errors.” You cannot filter your way to clarity, and that is a theorem rather than a complaint. So engineering stopped hunting for a quieter resistor and changed the question: cool it, shield it, narrow the band — three moves, none of which asks the receiver to beat physics, all of which change the conditions the listening happens in. Which is exactly the instrument at Holmdel, where a maser and a reference load both sat in liquid helium at 4.2 K — a floor lowered deliberately so a remainder would mean something. A remainder was left: 3.5 ± 1.0 K, and the paper is mostly a list of what it was not, down to taping the seams with aluminium and walking a transmitter to ten positions on the ground. The pigeon story is corrected against its primary, and the correction is better than the version that travels: Wilson wrote that evicting them “obtained only a small reduction in antenna temperature” — the floor survived them, and that clause is the one that gets cut. The famous phrase “white dielectric material” is not in his Nobel lecture, and the birds are not in the 1965 paper at all. What could not be removed was “isotropic, unpolarized, and free from seasonal variations (July, 1964-April, 1965)”, and every property that made it impossible to eliminate is a property that made it the universe. Then the 1928 shape repeats mirrored — theory at 414–419, measurement at 419–421, thirty-seven years on. The most consequential discovery in modern cosmology arrived as noise two engineers spent ten months trying to get rid of. Meanwhile the transfer to rooms turns out not to be ours to make: ANSI/ASA S12.60 caps classroom background at 35 dBA because the profession already calls the quantity signal to noise ratio and wants about 15 dB of it — and its instruction is to lower the floor rather than amplify the teacher. Wilkins halved headaches by removing 100 Hz fluorescent flicker, with his own caveat that the harm fell on “a minority that is particularly affected”; Kim and de Dear found sound privacy the largest source of dissatisfaction in any building, and found open plan bought no more ease of interaction than a private office. The last two joints refuse to overclaim, on the page rather than in a footnote: the step to Autistic auditory experience is contested — there is no k for a nervous system — carried by Remington and Fairnie’s finding of increased auditory capacity, one mechanism producing both the distress and the ability, and by Rosas-Pérez’s 2026 acoustics thesis, in which no Autistic respondent among 311 noise-sensitive people found filtering easy — printed with her caveat that the whole sample was already sensitive. Her other finding is where the zine says the analogy breaks, and the break is worth more than the resemblance: no habituation, but an accumulation effect. Thermal noise is stationary; kTB is the same in the tenth hour as the first. The human pattern is cumulative. A resistor never gets tired of being warm — so the floor in a room is crueller than the floor in a circuit, not merely like it. Which also means “you’ll get used to it” is testable, and the exposure hypothesis under it rests on five participants, none noise-sensitive, and two pure tones. The closing analogy is leap, because physics entails nothing about who deserves a quiet room. What it does is remove an excuse. Fifteen spreads, ten documented joints, one contested, one leap, a spine the page calls schematic rather than letting it pass for a plot, and a coda pointing at the practice already written down. A rhyme, not a proof.

Field Guide No. 5 A Field Guide to the Ways of Being a Star Star Stuff Field Guides There is no standard star. Field Guide No. 6 A Field Guide to Symbioses Star Stuff Field Guides Mutual aid, written into biology. Twelve partnerships across the tree of life — fungi and roots trading underground, a cleaner fish trusted by predators who could swallow it, the fig and its wasp. 12 symbioses→ Details Mutual aid, written into biology — twelve partnerships across the tree of life, read as mutual aid. Fungi and roots trading underground, bacteria making soil, a cleaner fish trusted by predators who could swallow it, algae building reefs that shelter a quarter of ocean life, the fig and its wasp that cannot live without each other. Interdependence is the rule, not the exception: Kropotkin showed mutual aid is a factor of evolution; Margulis, that life “took over the globe not by combat, but by networking.” This isn't “nature is nice” — parasites are real too, and the ghost pipe (Monotropa uniflora) is the honest one-way case, a myco-heterotroph that only takes, modelling receiving without reciprocating — and a bridge to monotropism (with Helen Edgar's tribute to Dinah Murray). It's that nothing living stands alone. What biology has always done, disability-justice communities name and practice: the human specimen is our own care webs and spoon shares (Spade, Mingus, Piepzna-Samarasinha, Kafai, Lewis), and a closing coda swaps the language of management for the language of living systems — symbiosis over competition, competency networks over leadership, coordination over management. Each entry maps who gives what and gets what, with full field notes. Solidarity, not charity; interdependence, not independence.
A Field Guide to Nervous Systems

Field Guide No. 7 A Field Guide to Nervous Systems Star Stuff Field Guides There is no standard nervous system. Eleven ways to have one — the jellyfish's centreless net, the octopus's mind spread through its arms, the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons. Companion to No. 27. 11 systems→ Details Eleven ways to have a nervous system — the companion catalogue to Every Nervous System (Zine No. 27). The jellyfish's centreless net, older than brains; the octopus's mind spread through its arms (two-thirds of its neurons outside the brain); the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons; the honeybee's million-neuron cognition and swarm mind; a jumping spider planning routes with a brain smaller than a pinhead; an electric fish reading a sense we lack; the star-nosed mole's 22-ray touch-world; the corvid's forebrain packed denser than a primate's (Olkowicz 2016); the elephant's 257 billion neurons, almost all cerebellar; a slime mold solving mazes with no neurons at all; and us — about 86 billion neurons, one arrangement among many, not the top of any ladder. Neuroscience hides verdicts in its words — “primitive,” “simple,” “lower” — but the animal kingdom keeps no standard nervous system. Each entry maps its architecture, reframes the deficit reading (“sounds like / actually”), and carries full field notes. There is no standard nervous system.
A Field Guide to the Ways of Migrating

Field Guide No. 8 A Field Guide to the Ways of Migrating Star Stuff Field Guides Say “migration” and most of us picture one shape. Almost nothing does that. Fifteen ways of migrating — the Arctic tern flies ~71,000 km a year and refuses the straight line. The companion catalogue to Always Migrating (No. 30). 15 ways→ Details Fifteen ways of migrating — the companion catalogue to Always Migrating (Zine No. 30). Say “migration” and most of us picture one shape: a long line, north in spring, back in autumn. Almost nothing does that. The Arctic tern flies ~71,000 km a year and refuses the straight line, riding wind in vast S-shaped detours because the long way is the cheap way. A juvenile godwit crossed 13,560 km in 11 days without landing — held with care, since it shrinks its own organs to do it and a migrant who rests is not a lesser migrant. No monarch finishes the round trip: several short-lived generations work north and one “super” generation, living 8–9 months instead of weeks, flies the whole way back. Salmon find one stream by the magnetic field they imprinted on, then die and carry the ocean up into the forest. The largest migration on Earth is a few hundred metres straight up, every night, in the dark — distance was never the measure. Spiderlings rig silk and let atmospheric electricity carry them; trees migrate at metres a year, seed by seed; the Sahara crosses an ocean as dust and fertilises the Amazon; a star gets handed to a wider orbit and the Sun is probably not from here. The centre of the guide is partial migration — populations holding both migrants and residents, described in the literature as the commonest form, the one all others derive from. Variation within a population isn't the anomaly; it's the mechanism. Closes on us: the crossing made in place, when the word arrives and every year behind you rearranges. Held with care throughout — this reads migration as a way of being, never as a frame for forced human displacement. Fifteen entries, route-shape diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.
A Field Guide to Being a Shark

Field Guide No. 9 A Field Guide to Being a Shark Star Stuff Field Guides One clade, one body plan, four hundred million years — and inside it, almost nothing holds. Twelve ways to be a shark, written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. Companion to Zines 32, 33 and 34. 12 ways→ Details Twelve ways to be a shark — the companion catalogue to the shark set (Zines 32, 33 and 34), written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. These are not distant relatives: one clade, one body plan, four hundred million years. And inside it, almost nothing holds still. The whale shark reaches ~18.8 m and lives on plankton; the dwarf lanternshark tops out near 20 cm and erases its own silhouette by lighting its belly to match the light coming down. The goblin shark cannot give chase in the dark, so it doesn't — the jaws fire forward at up to 3.1 m/s, the fastest protrusion known in any shark. The thresher hunts with the far end of itself, whipping its tail overhead to stun several fish at once. The epaulette shark walks between tide pools on its fins and rides out near-anoxia by suppressing its own metabolism. The cookiecutter, at fifty centimetres, takes a neat plug out of animals hundreds of times its size and everything swims off alive. The bonnethead eats seagrass and — tested in 2018 — digests it, which made "sharks are carnivores" a category nobody had checked rather than a finding. Two entries are here because of a phrase rather than an animal: the great hammerhead's head does not sharpen its electrosense (tested directly, it widens the search area instead), and the frilled shark is not a living fossil, because nothing alive is. One points up, one points down, and both skip what the animal is doing. Twelve entries, schematic diagrams, a "Not:" refusals set. There is no standard shark.
A Field Guide to Being a Turtle

Field Guide No. 10 A Field Guide to Being a Turtle Star Stuff Field Guides Almost every entry is a thing a turtle is supposed to have and doesn't. Twelve ways to be a turtle, and five turtles people made — the leatherback has no bony carapace at all. Companion to Everywhere That Turtles Go (No. 35). 12 + 5→ Details Twelve ways to be a turtle, and five turtles people made — the companion catalogue to Everywhere That Turtles Go (No. 35). Almost every entry is a thing a turtle is supposed to have and doesn't. The leatherback has no bony carapace at all, just hundreds of interlocking ossicles in oily skin — and it dives to 1,280 m and holds its body up to 18 °C above the sea around it, which gives it the largest range of any reptile alive. The mata mata has weak jaw muscles and almost no tongue and is a superb predator, because it never bites: the mouth is a pump, and every "weakness" on the list is a component of it. The Fitzroy River turtle takes about 70% of its oxygen in through two enlarged sacs at the far end of itself. The Chinese softshell excretes urea through the lining of its mouth rather than its kidneys — the head-dipping that looks like drinking is the opposite of drinking. Painted turtle hatchlings spend their first winter in a nest below −10 °C by supercooling, and what decides whether they live is not how tough they are but what touches them. And the Arrau was filed as a silent animal until somebody brought a hydrophone: 2,122 recorded sounds in eleven types, hatchlings calling from inside the egg, and females coming and answering — the first evidence of post-hatching parental care in any turtle. The silence was ours. The last entry is the bill: Rafetus swinhoei, two or three animals left, the last known female dead in April 2023. The five turtles people made — Turtle Island, ao, Kurma (a pivot for churning, not a world-bearer), Great A'Tuin, and a Larrakia Star Dreaming we cite rather than retell — get a separate section and a deliberately different card, because they are not five drafts of one story. There is no standard turtle.
A Field Guide to Being a Tortoise

Field Guide No. 11 A Field Guide to Being a Tortoise Star Stuff Field Guides An arc that runs from the Moon to a graveyard to a beginning. Twelve land tortoises. It opens on 15 September 1968, when Zond 5 carried two Soviet steppe tortoises around the far side of the Moon and brought them back alive. 12 tortoises→ Details Twelve land tortoises — Testudinidae — and an arc that runs from the Moon to a graveyard to a beginning. It opens where this collection has to open: on 15 September 1968, Zond 5 carried two Soviet steppe tortoises around the far side of the Moon and brought them back alive, two months before Apollo 8 carried any human. They lost about a tenth of their body weight and were otherwise fine. Then the ordinary astonishments of a slow land animal: the gopher tortoise digs burrows over fourteen metres long that more than 350 other species live in, which is the argument for building rooms that fit whoever needs them most, stated in reptile. The pancake tortoise has a shell whose bone is full of holes and is the fastest and best-climbing tortoise there is — and the beloved story that it inflates itself inside a rock crevice is now believed to be wrong, so the guide says so instead of repeating it. In July 2020 an Aldabra giant tortoise was filmed hunting and swallowing a tern chick, the first deliberate hunt ever recorded in a wild tortoise, which turned "tortoises are herbivores" from a law back into a summary of what we had happened to watch. Jonathan hatched around 1832 and is still on the lawn. The speckled padloper is six centimetres and complete. And then four entries marked as unfinished, because their endings are decisions rather than facts: the star tortoise, most trafficked tortoise on Earth and trafficked because it is beautiful; the ploughshare, whose shell conservationists engrave to spoil it for the market, and it may not be working; Lonesome George, who died in 2012 and took Pinta with him; and Fernanda, found alive in 2019 after 113 years of "extinct." It ends on Île aux Aigrettes, where an Aldabra tortoise is doing an extinct Mauritian tortoise's job — 529 hatchlings in eleven years. Not restoring what was lost. Finding another way for the function to happen.

Field Guide No. 12 My Monotropic Galaxy Star Stuff Field Guides A guest guide, and the first whose subject is a person. Helen Edgar's deep-field image overlaid with constellation lines and an index of twenty named features of her own Autistic life — rehoused as the field guide it already was. 20 constellations→ Details A guest guide, and the first whose subject is a person. Helen Edgar made a deep-field image of space overlaid with constellation lines and an index of twenty named features of her own Autistic life — and the form she reached for is already a field guide, so this rehouses it as one, in her words, at her numbers. Dark Matter Field is “the weight of neuronormativity before I had words for it.” Stellar Current is the heart of the galaxy, the deep monotropic flow where “my whole bodymind system exhales and time dissolves.” Pebbling Cluster is how she shows love, after the way penguins offer pebbles. Time Drift is lived time “closer to superposition than sequence.” Friction Field is the exhaustion of having needs the world was not designed to meet. Emergence Point is what surfaces when something is finally ready, “trusted rather than forced, arriving in its own time, on its own terms.” It carries no “sounds like / actually” table, and that is the argument rather than an omission. Every other guide here has one, because that table corrects a verdict somebody else handed down — and there is no verdict in these twenty to correct. They are one person's naming of her own life. Field Guide No. 10 found the limit first with its five turtles people made; this is that rule at full scale, and the first guide in the collection to carry it end to end. The astronomy is not gone, it is simply not on the face: open any card and the real object is waiting — galaxies rotating too fast for their visible mass, the quantum tunnelling without which the Sun could not shine, pebble accretion building planets out of small offerings, ram-pressure stripping taking a galaxy's gas because of the medium it is moving through rather than any fault in the galaxy. Five of the twenty have already grown into pieces of their own here, so the index doubles as the hub they hang off. Ends where Helen ends, with the thing she asks for twice: draw your own. Twenty constellations, an index map, a “Not:” refusals set. There is no standard galaxy.
A Field Guide to the Ways of Being Alone

Field Guide No. 14 A Field Guide to the Ways of Being Alone Star Stuff Field Guides A lone wolf is not an outcast. It is a disperser. Twelve ways of keeping your own company among our Terran kin, grown from Betsy Selvam's Stimpunks essay Lone Wolfing: The Joys of Autistic Solitude. 12 ways of being alone→ Details Twelve ways of keeping your own company among our Terran kin, grown from Betsy Selvam's Stimpunks essay Lone Wolfing: The Joys of Autistic Solitude. A lone wolf is not an outcast. It is a disperser — typically nine to thirty-six months old, one of the roughly 15–20% of any wolf population currently between territories, crossing the neutral buffer ground to find a mate and found a pack. The animal we named the loner after was always on its way somewhere. The guide is sorted by four conditions it did not invent: writing in The Atlantic in 2017, Brent Crane quotes the developmental psychologist Kenneth Rubin — solitude is productive only if it is voluntary, if emotion can be regulated within it, if one can rejoin when one wants to, and if relationships outside it are maintained. Crane's own gloss is the hinge: the difference between rejuvenation and suffering is the quality of reflection available, and the ability to come back. So: social bees are fewer than 10% of all bee species (Danforth, Minckley & Neff, 2019) — we built the entire hive metaphor on the outlier. One sweat bee nests solitary in some populations and eusocial in others, and reared side by side each keeps its own way. Giant pandas aim over 80% of their scent marks at animal trails, going out of their way to be found by animals they will never meet — asynchronous is not the fallback channel, it is the majority channel. Territorial neighbours become dear enemies (Fisher, 1954), and sometimes nasty ones (Temeles, 1994), which is kept because both are true. Fission–fusion parties change membership hourly and nobody calls it instability. Cicadas spend seventeen years alone underground to be loud together for a fortnight. Pumas share kills with non-kin and are 7.7 times more likely to share with someone who once shared with them (Elbroch et al., Science Advances, 2017). Orangutan party size tracks fruit availability rather than species — you change the field, not the animal. A wandering albatross takes a sabbatical year at sea and divorces at 0.3%. Then the thirteenth card, which gets no reframe table on purpose: the octopus settlements at Octopolis and Octlantis are not a secret society but dens crowded onto the only hard substrate for miles, with evictions at the edges. Proximity is not company; proximity plus scarcity is a fight. Four gates, a “Not:” refusals set that declines the syntaxin 1a bait outright. There is no standard amount of company.

Field Guide No. 15 A Field Guide to Nests Star Stuff Field Guides Sorted by where the labour actually goes — and the catalogue disagrees with the word. Thirteen homes among our Terran kin. We began meaning to sort by material, and the material sort kept failing: a hermit crab supplies none, and neither does a gall wasp. 13 ways of having a home→ Details Thirteen homes among our Terran kin, sorted by where the labour actually goes — and the catalogue disagrees with the word. We began meaning to sort by material, and the material sort kept failing, because a hermit crab supplies none and a gall wasp supplies none either. What varies is who does the work. The companion to What Looks Like Chaos (Zine No. 55), which asks how a nest gets built; this one asks what gets to count as one, and the answer is much wider. Built: a ten-centimetre pufferfish making a two-metre geometric court on the seabed that divers photographed for years before anyone believed the builder was that small (Kawase, Okata & Ito, Scientific Reports, 2013) — the pattern is not decorative, it sorts fine sand into the centre, which is the part the female inspects. Then the correction that reorganised the whole guide: a termite mound is uninhabited. That is the paper's own word. Fungus-farming termites build massive empty towers above their subterranean nests, and the daily swing of solar heating drives convection through the tunnel network (Ocko, King, Andreen, Bardunias, Turner, Soar & Mahadevan, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2017). The most-photographed animal architecture on Earth is routinely called the wrong kind of thing: it is not shelter, it is infrastructure — closer to a lung than a house. Borrowed: a hermit crab contributes no material to any home it will ever occupy, and when a single shell arrives the crabs gather and queue beside it in descending size order, so that when the largest moves in the whole line moves up at once. Lewis and Rotjan tested the prediction that matters and found it held — vacancy chains distribute benefits across many participants rather than to the first taker. The crab that waits is not being passive; it is standing in the only position from which the chain works. The largest bird nest on record, 2.9 m wide, 6 m deep and over two tonnes, was accumulated across decades until it was more than the tree could hold, which is inheritance and its cost in one object. And a woodpecker's ecological job is not its own nest but the vacancies it leaves behind for everything that cannot excavate. Induced: a gall is oak tissue that the insect made the oak build — the inducer injects effectors including phytohormones that redirect the plant's development, and different wasp species induce distinctively different galls on the same host, which is why the literature calls a gall an extended phenotype of the insect. And not building at all evolved independently at least seven separate times in birds: three times in the cuckoos, once in honeyguides, once in a duck, twice in songbirds (Sorenson & Payne, 2002). A thing discovered seven times over is not a mistake, and that is the sentence the guide would most like a reader to carry. Secreted, or worn: a swiftlet builds from nothing but its own hardened saliva, and the entry states plainly that this is why the species is farmed and harvested at industrial scale rather than leaving it as a footnote. An emperor penguin has no structure at all — an egg on two feet under a fold of belly skin, with the shelter being the huddle, whose walls are other penguins and which moves. If somewhere-to-be requires a structure, the emperor has nowhere and manifestly succeeds, so the definition has to give: some of us have been housed by other people rather than by rooms, and it counted. And a trapdoor spider known as Number 16 held one silk-lined burrow for 43 years, the longest life recorded for any spider — a record that is really about Barbara York Main, who began following that population in 1974 and kept returning for four decades. A long quiet life in one small place is invisible unless somebody decides it is worth watching. Not a nest: the bower, which every list of animal architecture files as the finest nest alive. No egg is ever laid in it and nothing lives there; the female builds the actual nest elsewhere, alone. It is a theatre with deliberate forced perspective — objects graded outward so they subtend a more even visual angle from where she stands (Endler, Endler & Doerr, Current Biology, 2010). We have spent a century calling a stage set a house. And the fourteenth card gets no reframe table, which is a fourth distinct reason for withholding the apparatus. The rooms people build are not graded here. Running a sounds-like/actually over somebody's own room would make us the observer in the doorway with the clipboard — the exact figure No. 55 spends ten spreads indicting — and No. 55 is also explicit that not every mess is a nest, since burnout collapses the architecture and from the doorway the ruins look identical to the curated version. Nobody can sort those two on sight, and the people most certain they can are the reason the guide has a refusals list. The weaver appears in one card that hands off to No. 55 rather than re-running it; the beaver is deliberately absent, already spent in Minor Worlds. Thirteen lineages, thirteen incompatible methods, none ranked, several of them the ones a tidy observer would call failures. The ninth guide to arrive independently at the same sentence: there is no standard nest.

Field Guide No. 16 A Field Guide to Eggs Field Guide · 15 + 1 · companion to No. 57 The murre's pointed egg does not roll in a safe arc. That is the textbook explanation, and it is wrong. The egg you are imagining occupies one band out of five. Fifteen beginnings among our Terran kin, sorted by how far the egg gets from the body — because a material sort was tried first and collapsed. 15 ways of beginning→ Details Fifteen beginnings among our Terran kin, sorted by how far the egg gets from the body — and the catalogue disagrees with the picture in your head. The egg you are imagining occupies one band out of five. A material sort was tried first and collapsed, because a hen's egg and a common murre's are the same object by every material measure. So: eggs that never leave, eggs grown over by skin, eggs carried, eggs set down and guarded, eggs left. In the first band, live birth turns out to have evolved at least 115 separate times in lizards and snakes alone — against roughly 140 origins in all vertebrates — and about a fifth of squamate species lay no egg at all; whether the transition ever runs backwards is genuinely contested and is left open here. A sand tiger shark shows an egg working as food: the mother goes on ovulating after mating, up to ten embryos begin, and two are born. Syngnathid fishes are the only vertebrates with male pregnancy, and it is literal — a placenta-like pouch, embryos joined to the father's circulation, a measured patrotrophy index of 1, and immune suppression to tolerate them. A Surinam toad's eggs are pressed into her back and her own skin grows over each one and builds it a lid; there is no tadpole stage, and the toadlets push the lids off after three to five months. Giant water bug eggs are cemented to the male's dorsum, and the carrying is plumbing rather than devotion: unattended eggs die every time, in air or underwater. A Banggai cardinalfish father holds the clutch in his mouth for a month and eats nothing, because a mouth cannot be a foregut and a nursery at once. Then the band everybody pictures, where four of five are strange: a kiwi egg is 15 to 22 per cent of the female (an ostrich's is 2 to 3); a monotreme egg is leathery and porous enough to be fed through its own shell, with ten days of egg followed by four to seven months of milk; and a deep-sea octopus in Monterey Canyon was revisited eighteen times over fifty-three months, guarding one clutch, never seen to feed. The murre is the entry that indicts us rather than an animal: the pointed egg was explained for decades by rolling in a tight arc, Ingold found little support in 1980, and Birkhead's objection is embarrassingly simple — the arc is wider than the ledge. Stability on a slope and shell strength do the work instead. In the last band, walking away turns out not to be the failure state: a megapode chick hatches under 40 to 150 cm of compost, digs out unaided in a median forty hours, and can fly the same day; a brine shrimp cyst waits up to eighteen dry years and resumes where it stopped; and a cuckoo's shell has a second job no other egg here has, since it must survive being looked at — matched to host retinal function rather than to our eyes, by host-specific female lineages, with the arms-race framing now under live challenge. Then the sixteenth card, dashed, with no reframe table: the egg-crack accounts, borrowed from trans communities and credited as unowned, because there is no mistaken verdict about the morning your own life rearranged itself behind you. One thing the biology does supply is a limit rather than a licence — across birds, squamates, turtles, crocodilians and the echidna, the tool that opens an egg is on the inside. You cannot do it for anyone. You can only be audible. The tenth guide to arrive independently at the same sentence: there is no standard egg.

Field Guide No. 17 A Field Guide to Resting Field Guide · 15 + 2 · companion to No. 59 there is no standard way to rest — not an amount, not a posture, not an organ Fifteen ways of resting among our Terran kin, sorted by what is doing the resting. An animal with no brain and no clock. A bird ten months airborne. A squirrel below freezing. And the famous twenty-hour bat, which is one measurement at one temperature. 15 entries→ Details Companion to No. 59, and it asks the question the zine assumes an answer to: what does resting actually look like, across kin who share almost no anatomy? The bands sort by what carries the rest rather than by taxon or by amount. Hydra and Cassiopea have a nerve net and no brain and meet every behavioural criterion for sleep, and Hydra has no circadian clock either — a roughly four-hour cycle instead (Kanaya et al. 2020). C. elegans rests for two to three hours before each of its four moults (Raizen et al. 2008). Great frigatebirds sleep 42 minutes a day aloft, in the soar and never while flapping; common swifts spend over 99 per cent of a ten-month phase airborne, and the record is not uniform — some individuals roosted in midwinter, others never landed (Hedenström et al. 2016). Sperm whales hang vertically and go silent, unresponsive to a boat until it touched them (Miller et al. 2008). Bears keep their skeleton through six months of disuse; arctic ground squirrels hold a core temperature of −2.9 °C by supercooling, with no antifreeze in the plasma (Barnes 1989); lungfish seal themselves in a cocoon of living cells for years. Emperor penguins reach 37.5 °C inside a huddle while it is −19 °C outside, and two thirds of the saving is geometry rather than warmth (Gilbert et al. 2008). Parrotfish build a mucus tent for 2.5 per cent of a day's energy and cut parasite attacks from nearly all to about one in ten (Grutter et al. 2011). Northern fur seals suppress REM for weeks and never pay it back. And the card the guide would keep if it could keep one: the sleepiest-mammal figure of 19.9 hours is a single 1960s measurement at 33 °C on an unknown number of animals, which becomes 11.0 hours at 26 °C — and about one per cent of mammal species have had their sleep measured at all (Harding et al. 2022). Two cards carry no reframe table: sponges, because nobody knows yet and writing actually over an open question is bluff; and plants, because nyctinasty was named by Linnaeus and Darwin himself called the daytime version “improperly” sleep, read here from the 1880 primary. Seventeen cards, fifteen entries.
A Field Guide to Unfinished Animals

Field Guide No. 18 A Field Guide to Unfinished Animals Field Guide · companion to No. 61 there is no final draft — and what varies here is not the animals, it is us Sixteen animals we reconstructed wrong, sorted by the kind of mistake and tagged for whether the argument is over. Drawn upside down, then back-to-front. Three animals in three groups. A skull on a tail. Two arms for forty-four years. 16 entries→ Details Companion to No. 61, and it asks the question that zine assumes an answer to: how often does the record actually move? Sixteen animals we reconstructed wrong, sorted by the kind of mistake, and — this guide’s one addition to the house form, borrowed from How We Got Here — every card carries a status: revised (ten cards), contested (four), or name stuck (two). A catalogue of corrections that will not say which corrections are finished would read as a list of settled triumphs, which is the smoothing it is complaining about. Assembled wrong: Hallucigenia was published in 1977 walking on its spines, inverted by Ramsköld and Hou in 1991, and turned end-for-end by Smith and Caron in 2015 when they found the eyes, mouth ring and tooth-lined throat at the other end — wrong on one axis for fourteen years and on the other for twenty-four more. Anomalocaris spent most of a century as three animals in three groups: a shrimp-like appendage, the “jellyfish” Peytoia, and the “sponge” Laggania, united by Whittington and Briggs in 1985 — and then the correction was itself corrected, when Daley and Bergström found a three-plate oral cone in 2012 and Peytoia became valid again. Cope put the skull of Elasmosaurus on the end of its neck in 1868, reading a neck as a tail; and the famous story about who caught him is wrong — it was Joseph Leidy, on 8 March 1870, with Marsh in the room, and Marsh’s claim survives only in a newspaper piece two decades later. Mantell put the Iguanodon thumb spike on its nose; it took thirty-odd whole skeletons at Bernissart for Dollo to move it to the hand. Known from almost nothing: Deinocheirus was two arms found on 9 July 1965 and named in 1970 by Halszka Osmólska and Ewa Roniewicz, and it stayed honestly unplaced for forty-four years until two near-complete skeletons showed a humpbacked, duck-billed omnivore. The Spinosaurus holotype burned in the Munich bombing of 24–25 April 1944, after Stromer’s requests to move the collection were refused — so every reconstruction since argues from photographs, and the aquatic reading is contested. Helicoprion’s tooth whorl was placed on the snout, the upper jaw, the back and the tail before a 2013 CT scan put it in the lower jaw — of a specimen that had been in a drawer since 1950. The line moved: Brontosaurus (the short form of the zine). Torosaurus, proposed as merely a mature Triceratops in 2010 and rejected in 2012, still unresolved — the mirror image of the Brontosaurus case, a merge rather than a split, with the opposite fate. Nanotyrannus, dismissed for forty years as a juvenile T. rex and reinstated in 2025 by Zanno and Napoli on a near-adult skeleton from the Duelling Dinosaurs block, with a second species nobody had separated out. And Tanystropheus, one species until a CT scan made it two, both size classes fully grown. Three of those four errors were the same error: explaining a difference by age. The name outlived it: Oviraptor means egg seizer and it was brooding its own clutch — and the card is careful that the 1995 brooding specimen is an oviraptorid later named Citipati, not Osborn’s animal, because the tidy version of that story is the one that travels. Basilosaurus means king lizard and Owen showed it was a mammal within five years; he proposed Zeuglodon and priority refused it. Both names are permanent, which is the band the zine cares about: a label outlives its refutation by rule or by repetition, and only one of those admits what it is doing. Tidier than the evidence: the fish-crawls-out story has a date problem — Devonian trackways about eighteen million years older than the earliest tetrapod bodies — and the retelling of that correction is smoothed too, because those trackways are themselves disputed. The film raptor is not the fossil one. And the tail-dragging dinosaur was corrected by a whole field changing its mind, from one 1969 monograph. Two cards are dashed and carry no reframe table. Mary Anning found, prepared and drew the first complete plesiosaur in 1823 and Conybeare presented it without naming her; women could not join the Geological Society until 1904, and on her only London trip no label carried her name. She is not a specimen, and running sounds like / actually down the side of a person would file her with the misreconstructed animals, which is the injury. And the last card has nothing to correct yet: on the guide’s own argument some entries above are currently wrong, and it says where to expect it — the age explanation, the fragment that fits every reading, and the instrument that arrives before the answer. Arrival line: there is no final draft, and the guide says plainly why it departs from the house formula: what varies here is not the animals but us. Eighteen cards, sixteen entries.

It opens on AURORA's own account of seeing herself on video for the first time — she was shocked, said she couldn't do anything about it, and kept it: I have to use everything I got. Then the physics of the light she shares a name with, which turns out to be about exactly this. The solar wind delivers energy and nothing else; the colour is the atom's own — that famous green is oxygen's 557.7 nm line. And that line is a forbidden transition: it breaks the electric-dipole selection rules, so instead of the nanoseconds an allowed transition takes, the atom waits about 0.7 seconds before letting go, and the red line waits 110. Which is why altitude decides the colour — lower down the air is crowded and a collision takes the energy first. The most famous light in the sky is a slow release the rules call forbidden, and it only completes where nothing crowds it. Twenty-eight performances across six movements, plus stim-listening (Jim Irion's coinage) and the reason Ryan's own playlist is nearly all live footage. The page is careful about whose word is whose: she calls it emotion; we are the ones calling it stimming, and it says so rather than putting the term in her mouth. The sharpest refusal is saved for last — her movement is celebrated because it is on a stage and lovely, while the same body doing the same thing in a classroom gets a behaviour plan.

Playlist & essay Nobody Got His Eyes Right Stimpunks × More Realms The most-looked-at face in pop, and the one fact everybody repeats about it. Thirty-one songs from Space Oddity to I Can't Give Everything Away — the listening companion to Turn and Face the Strange (No. 12). 31 tracks + essay→ Details The long version of the five Bowie cards that open the L★S Playlist, and the listening companion to Turn and Face the Strange (No. 12) — thirty-one songs from Space Oddity to I Can't Give Everything Away. It starts from the most-looked-at face in pop and the one fact everybody repeats about it, which is wrong. He did not have different-coloured eyes. Both irises were the same colour; in February 1962 a schoolfriend punched him and a fingernail paralysed the muscles that contract the left iris, so that pupil could never close again — anisocoria, not heterochromia. A pupil stuck wide is a hole full of shadow, which is why the eye reads darker in exactly the bright light where a working pupil contracts, which is to say under every stage light and camera flash he ever stood in. That changes what kind of thing the famous feature was: heterochromia is a variation you're born with; this was an injury, reportedly with lasting effects on his depth perception. Glamour is not an accommodation. Then the second thing everyone knows — the constellation named for him in 2016 is not a constellation; there are 88, the list was fixed in the 1920s, and the observatory that made it said plainly it was an invented asterism. Both errors lean the same way: they round a damaged iris and a small tribute up into something more elegant, and the tidier version travels further. Which is Too Good to Check with a soundtrack — and it has a cost, because while the myth is that beautiful nobody asks what a fixed pupil is like under a follow spot.

Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms It Take a Joyful Sound New wave, new phrase, neurodiversity. Thirty-six songs from the Stimpunks public service announcement — and the argument underneath them, which is about physics before it is about music. Playlist & essay · Sound
Somebody had to name the party

One Somebody had to name the party In July 1977, in London, Bob Marley recorded a song with Lee “Scratch” Perry about a party that did not exist yet. He wrote it after hearing what The Clash had done to Junior Murvin's Police and Thieves — a Jamaican record, played back at him by white kids in torn clothes — and rather than take offence he took the hint. Punky Reggae Party is a guest list. It names The Wailers, The Damned, The Jam, The Clash, Toots & the Maytals and Dr. Feelgood, and by naming them it made a thing out of a coincidence. Two groups of outsiders, sharing a city and a set of enemies, were told they were at the same party. Then they behaved as if they were. They were not imagining the alliance. On 30 April 1978, roughly 100,000 people walked six miles from Trafalgar Square through Cable Street to Victoria Park in Hackney — deliberately, through National Front territory — for the Rock Against Racism carnival. The Clash, Steel Pulse, X-Ray Spex and the Tom Robinson Band played the same bill, and Misty in Roots led the march from the back of a lorry. Rock Against Racism had been founded in 1976, after Eric Clapton used a stage in Birmingham to endorse Enoch Powell. The mixed bill was the entire point: reggae and punk on one stage was the argument, and the music was how you made it in public. That is the move this whole page is about. An underground phenomenon gets named, and the naming helps it happen. Which is the same thing neurodiversity did, and roughly as recently. And the guest list had a hole in it We are not going to tell this as a fable. The Slits were reportedly in the namecheck and were cut — the reason given, in the accounts that record it at all, was that they were women. The song that named the alliance shipped with a woman-shaped gap where a band should have been, on a bill everyone remembers as the moment punk got principled. We flag it as reported rather than settled, because we could not trace it past secondary sources. But it points at something that is not in dispute at all, and that runs through the rest of this page: punk's inclusiveness was never automatic. It was fought for from inside, repeatedly, by the people it kept leaving out.
A joyful sound needs something to happen in

Two A joyful sound needs something to happen in Sound is not a thing that travels through the world. Sound is the world, briefly pushed. A mechanical wave is a pattern of compression and rarefaction passing through matter, which means it requires matter — a medium — and gets no exemption. In a vacuum there is no sound at all. Not a quiet sound. None. So every note anyone has ever heard was carried by atoms. Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, and neither of those was made here: nitrogen comes out of the CNO cycle running in stellar interiors, oxygen out of the fusion shells of massive stars and the supernovae that scatter them. The room is star stuff. The air between the amp and your ear is star stuff. So is the amp, and the ear, and the floor. A gig is star stuff, arranged into a body, pushing on star stuff, arranged into air, until it reaches star stuff, arranged into someone else. The whole mechanism. There isn't a step where it stops being true. This is not a metaphor we are stretching. It is the plain physical description, and it happens to be unreasonably moving: the universe cannot make a sound without lending you its own material to make it out of.
A pure tone has almost no identity

Three A pure tone has almost no identity Play a sine wave at 220 Hz. It has a pitch, and beyond the pitch it has nearly nothing. You cannot say what it is. You cannot say who it is. Now play the same note on a guitar, a cello and a human throat. Same fundamental, three unmistakable things. Hermann von Helmholtz worked out why in 1863, in On the Sensations of Tone: alongside the fundamental frequency, a real sound carries upper partials — harmonics sitting above it at multiples of the base frequency — and the particular recipe of those extras is what your ear reads as identity. The fundamental tells you the note. The overtones tell you who is playing it. Character is the surplus. It lives in everything above the note you asked for. A pure sine wave beside a clipped wave, with the harmonic content of each On the left, a smooth sine wave and a single tall bar marking one frequency component. On the right, the same wave with its peaks flattened by clipping, and a series of bars showing additional harmonic components above the fundamental that were not present in the input. Pure tone one frequency, almost no identity fundamental only Clipped same note, plus what wasn't sent in fundamental + added harmonics Overdrive a valve or a transistor and it stops responding proportionally: the peaks flatten because there is no more headroom. That flattening is a nonlinearity, and a nonlinearity generates frequency components that were not in the signal you fed it. The distorted guitar is not the clean guitar turned up. It is the clean guitar plus a stack of harmonics the amp invented on the way through. Bar heights here are indicative, not measured. The sound punk is named by is difference, deliberately added. That is not a poetic reading of distortion; it is what distortion is. A scene built an entire aesthetic on running the signal past the point where the system could keep it clean, and what came out the other side had more in it than what went in. A rhyme, not a proof Physics does not have opinions about people, and an amplifier is not an argument for anybody's belonging. Nothing about harmonic distortion obliges a scene to let you in. We are noting that the sound and the politics happen to be the same shape — surplus is where the character is — and that noticing it is worth something, while proving anything from it is not available.
It reaches you at the skeleton

Four It reaches you at the skeleton You already hear through bone. It is why your recorded voice sounds wrong to you and normal to everyone else. When you speak, part of the sound reaches your inner ear the ordinary way, through the air, and part of it arrives through the bones of your skull. Skull bone passes low frequencies far more efficiently than high ones — work by Tobias Reichenbach's group at Imperial College has mapped the mechanics in detail — so the voice in your head is bassier and fuller than the one anyone else has ever heard. A recording captures only the airborne half. The stranger on the tape is the version everybody else has always known. In a loud room the same channel opens outward. Low frequencies arrive as pressure on the chest and through the soles of your feet; you are not only listening, you are being pushed on, at a scale your body registers as an event. This is the ordinary, unmysterious reason a gig feels like something happening to you. And this collection has a standing interest in what bone does under pressure. Iwao Yasuda showed in the 1950s that bone is piezoelectric — put mechanical stress on it and it produces a small electrical charge. That is the founding fact of Bone Song and it is why the phrase is down to your star stuff rather than down to your feelings. What we are not claiming Nobody has shown that the sound pressure at a gig produces a piezoelectric signal in your skeleton that matters to you in any way. Yasuda's finding is about stress on bone; a PA is not a load-bearing force. The bone conduction is real and measured. The piezoelectricity is real and measured. The line drawn between them here is ours, and it is a rhyme. We would rather say so than let a nice sentence do the work of a mechanism.

Five The door is the argument What punk actually contributed was not a sound. It was a claim about who is allowed to make one. Marianne Elliott-Said went to see a band on her nineteenth birthday. They were badly rehearsed and playing to almost nobody, and what she took from the evening was not that they were good — it was that this was clearly doable. She formed X-Ray Spex and became Poly Styrene, and within a year a generation of women watching her on television were running the same calculation about themselves. The mechanism has a name in the education literature we work in: you build the thing because you have seen someone build the thing, and the someone has to be near enough to you to count. Which is also why the exclusions mattered so much, and why the corrections came from inside. The Riot Grrrl manifesto, published in Bikini Kill Zine 2 in 1991, is not a document written by people who found punk welcoming. It is a list of grievances against a subculture that told girls they could not play, and it says so in its own vocabulary — the manifesto's word for the thing in its way is beergutboyrock. Cripple punk arrived for the same reason a decade later: disabled punks were still being handed the inspirational role and refusing it, and the refusal had to be stated because the scene was not going to state it for them. When it works, the door test is very simple and very literal. In May 2021, four teenagers played a set in the Los Angeles Public Library for AAPI Heritage Month; the recording of Racist, Sexist Boy went everywhere, and The Linda Lindas had a record deal within days. It was a library. There was no stage worth the name. Somebody said yes and pointed a camera. What is a punk band, after all, but an affinity group with guitars? CrimethInc., Punk — Dangerous Utopia: Revisiting the Relationship between Punk and Anarchism That is the whole apparatus. A room, a few people who have agreed to be in it together, and no audition.

Six Everything brought to the front There is a sentence that has organised a great deal of our work: everything that was normally supposed to be hidden was brought to the front. It names a whole method in fifteen words. It is also, it turns out, a good lesson in how a phrase travels. We traced it. It circulates almost everywhere as a quotation credited to “punk subculture” with no author, and the trail leads to the Wikipedia article on punk subculture, where the sentence appears as unquoted prose footnoted to LeBlanc, 1999 — that is Lauraine LeBlanc, Pretty in Punk: Girls' Gender Resistance in a Boys' Subculture (Rutgers University Press, 1999), a study built on interviews with forty punk girls and women. So the idea has a real scholarly source, and the wording may not be hers. An encyclopaedia sentence summarising a book is not the same object as a line from the book, and we could not confirm which one this is. We are keeping the phrase, because it is ours by use and it is true; we are crediting LeBlanc for the argument; and we are recording plainly that we could not verify it as a verbatim quotation. See Too Good to Check for why this is exactly the shape of thing that gets past people. There is a second reason to be glad the trail led there. The sentence that names punk's central gesture comes out of a book about a boys' subculture, written to document the women who had to fight it for room. Bringing everything to the front was never a courtesy the scene extended. It was a demand made on it.
Accepted down to your star stuff

Seven Accepted down to your star stuff Here is the version of belonging this collection keeps arriving at, and punk states it better than we do, because punk states it as a door policy rather than a sentiment. You are not admitted on the condition that you turn out to be fine. Nobody checks first. The weird thing about you is not something the room agrees to overlook — it is roughly what the room is for. Come in stimming. Come in with the wheelchair, the cane, the AAC device, the ear defenders, the meltdown you had in the car park. Come in without the money for the door. Rejected by society is not a disqualification here; on the night the party got its name it was practically the entry requirement. That is what Love You Down To Your Star Stuff means when you take the words literally instead of tenderly. Not despite the difference and not because of it either — which is the other trap, the one where you get admired for your spikes and still not fed. All the way down, past the diagnosis and the file and the behaviour plan and the phenotype, into the elements, which were manufactured in stars, which do not sort their output into acceptable and unacceptable atoms. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Neither should the door. The house line, in punk register. And then the honest part, which we would rather say than have someone discover: a loud room is itself an access barrier. For a great many of us the gig described above is unsurvivable — sensory load, crowds, no exit, no quiet room, no seat. A scene that will let anybody in and then builds the only entrance out of volume has not finished the job. Acceptance is not the nature of any scene. It is a practice, re-won in every room, by whoever notices who is missing. Not: Not punk as an aesthetic with the politics removed. The clothes without the door policy is a costume, and costumes are cheap. Not the mosh pit as a model of access. Getting in free is one barrier. Volume, crowding, stairs, no seating and no quiet space are five more, and they are the ones nobody puts on the flyer. Not inspiration. We are not here to be anyone's evidence that attitude conquers all. Cripple punk exists specifically to refuse the good-cripple role, and we refuse it too. Not reclamation on someone else's behalf. Crip, mad, weird and stimpunk belong to the people doing the reclaiming. Reclaimed words are not handed out to bystanders. Not a golden age. Punk was racist and sexist and ableist in plenty of rooms, from the start, and the people who fixed it were the ones being excluded. Telling it as a fable would erase exactly the labour that makes it worth citing. Not physics as permission. Harmonics do not vote. The acoustics here are a rhyme with the argument, never a substitute for making it.

Things fall because of what they are

Athens · the fourth century BCE Things fall because of what they are Aristotle's physics explains motion by disposition. A stone falls because it is in the nature of heavy things to seek the centre; fire rises because it is in the nature of fire to seek the heights. Each body has a proper place and moves toward it. It comes with quantities, too. Heavier bodies fall faster, in proportion to their weight. And the denser the medium, the slower the fall. Now here is the thing that matters, and it is not that Aristotle was careless. Go outside and test it. Drop a stone and a leaf. The stone lands first. Drop the same stone in water and it sinks slowly. Every prediction checks out. It is not a stupid theory. It is an excellent description of falling in air, mistaken for a description of falling. why it lasted two thousand years The error is not in the observations. It is in where the explanation was put. Aristotle located the cause of the trajectory inside the object — in what kind of thing it was. The medium appeared in the theory only as a modifier, a resistance that slowed down what the object was going to do anyway. Everything that follows in this chain is about that choice of location, and about a very long argument over whether the reason a thing moves the way it does is in the thing or in what is acting on it. Physics took roughly two millennia to settle it.
