Padua and Florence · around 1600 Imagine the air away Galileo's decisive contribution was not an experiment. It was noticing that Aristotle's rule contradicts itself, and then doing something strange: reasoning about a world that does not exist. The argument, from Two New Sciences (1638). Suppose heavy bodies fall faster than light ones. Now tie a heavy body to a light one. The light one should hold the heavy one back, so the pair falls slower than the heavy body alone. But the pair is heavier than either, so it should fall faster. The same premise gives both answers. To get further he had to make the fall measurable, so he rolled balls down inclined planes — slowing the motion enough to time it, and finding that the distance goes as the square of the time regardless of the ball's weight. And then the move that this whole collection keeps circling: he imagined the medium away. Not "air resistance is small" but "consider a fall with no medium at all," a thing no one in 1638 had ever seen. The tower, and why it is marked contested. Everyone knows the story where Galileo drops two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa and settles it in front of witnesses. It is almost certainly not true. It appears in a biography by his assistant Vincenzo Viviani, written decades afterwards, and Galileo — who was not shy — never describes it in his own published work. The most famous experiment in physics is a story about an experiment. Which is precisely the kind of smoothing this collection exists to catch: the tidy public demonstration travels, the self-contradiction argument and the inclined planes do not. The idealization deserves one more note, because No. 39 is about it going wrong. Wells idealized the air away too, and got a threshold that was true only in a room nobody has. The tool is the same; what differs is whether you remember you used it. Galileo's idealization was a hypothesis awaiting a vacuum. 1687 · the deletion Character, removed Newton finished it. In the mechanics that followed, a body's motion is determined by the forces acting on it and by exactly one property of the body itself — a single number, its mass. Look at what disappeared. There is no heaviness-seeking. No proper place. No disposition, no tendency, no character. The object stops being the kind of thing that wants to go somewhere and becomes the kind of thing that is acted on. Arguably the single most productive move in the history of physical science was deleting character from the explanation. and it took two thousand years Be precise about what was not deleted, because the sloppy version of this argument is wrong in a way that matters. The body still has a property. Mass is real, it differs between objects, and it appears in the equation. Bodies are not interchangeable. What changed is that the property no longer explains the trajectory by itself. Ask why this object took that path and the answer is a description of its situation — what was pulling, pushing, resisting — with the object's own property entering as one term among several rather than as the story. That distinction is the whole of the second half of this zine. Nobody sensible claims children are identical. The hinge · our move, not physics' Now run it backwards Here is the claim this zine exists to make, stated plainly so it can be argued with. Deficit ideology is Aristotelian physics, applied to children. It explains a trajectory by an internal disposition: grit, mindset, resilience, motivation, character, self-esteem. The child's situation appears in the account the way the medium appeared in Aristotle's — as a modifier that slows down or speeds up what the child was going to do anyway. And it has the same evidential position that Aristotle's physics had. It fits ordinary observation closely. In any real school, some children do visibly persist longer, and their outcomes are visibly better. The correlation is right there. You can build an entire industry on it and every prediction will look confirmed. Ordinary observation of children, like ordinary observation of falling, happens in a medium — and the medium is doing a great deal of the work while remaining invisible. the hinge The medium here has a name in the literature: poverty, racism, ableism, hunger, housing, undiagnosed disability, a classroom built for one nervous system. This collection's first chain is largely a history of how it was made invisible. Marked contested, and here is precisely what is contested. Children are not projectiles. They have interiority, agency and preference; a stone does not decide anything, and any argument that treats a child as fully determined by circumstance is making the mirror-image error and is just as wrong. What we claim is narrower and, we think, defensible: an explanation that locates the cause of a trajectory inside the object, while the medium goes unmeasured, is the specific failure mode physics spent two thousand years escaping. That is a claim about the shape of an explanation, not about whether children are objects. The machinery arrives Behaviourism deleted the wrong thing There is an obvious objection at this point, and answering it is the most useful thing on this spread. Didn't behaviourism already make the Newtonian move? It threw out inner states, refused to talk about minds, insisted on observable behaviour and environmental contingencies. That sounds exactly like deleting disposition. It isn't, and the difference is the point. Newton moved the explanation outward and upward — from the object to the field it sits in, which means to a situation nobody owns and anybody can change. Behaviourism moved it outward and then put it straight back into a box around the individual. The "environment" in an operant account is the reinforcement schedule arranged around this one child: the tokens, the contingencies, the chart on the wall. Housing is not in it. Hunger is not in it. They checked first. Then they shipped it anyway.

California · 1986–1990 They checked first. Then they shipped it anyway. The self-esteem movement is usually told as a story about a culture that failed to check its evidence. That telling is too kind, and the truth is stranger. California established a Task Force to Promote Self-Esteem and Personal and Social Responsibility in 1986. To its credit, it commissioned academic work: a volume of research reviews from University of California scholars, published as The Social Importance of Self-Esteem (Mecca, Smelser & Vasconcellos, eds., University of California Press, 1989). That volume reported what the literature actually showed: "The news most consistently reported, however, is that the associations between self-esteem and its expected consequences are mixed, insignificant, or absent." Mecca, Smelser & Vasconcellos (eds.), The Social Importance of Self-Esteem, 1989 The Task Force's final report, Toward a State of Esteem, was published in 1990. This is not a failure to look. They looked, they paid for the looking, the answer came back negative, and it was printed — and the programme went out regardless, into a decade of school assemblies and worksheets and posters. Whatever governed that decision, it was not the evidence, because the evidence was in the room. Hold that alongside No. 40. There the problem was a threshold nobody had examined. Here the threshold was met, the answer was no, and it changed nothing. The originators objected. It kept selling.

The 2000s and 2010s The originators objected. It kept selling. Self-esteem gave way to grit and growth mindset — better research, genuinely more careful researchers, and the same location for the explanation. The meta-analysis is the one we already walked in No. 40. Macnamara and Burgoyne examined growth-mindset interventions across 63 studies and 97,672 participants and found publication bias, authors with a financial incentive to report positive effects more likely to report them, and major threats to internal validity. The finding to hold onto: 63 studies meta-analysed 97,672 participants ↓ higher-quality studies less likely to show benefit Better studies, smaller effect. That is the signature of something that is not there. And here is the part that separates this spread from a straightforward debunking. The researchers themselves said so. Carol Dweck has written at length about "false growth mindset" and about the concept being misused — including to explain why some students simply cannot learn, which is the precise inversion of what she proposed. Angela Duckworth has cautioned publicly against using grit measures for high-stakes school accountability. Now · the product Disposition, with a dashboard The last step is the one Aristotle could not have taken: making the disposition measurable, trackable and saleable in real time. Scarcity has a cognitive cost. Mullainathan and Shafir's work argues that being short of something — money, time, food — consumes mental bandwidth directly, degrading exactly the capacities that get read as character: planning, impulse control, follow-through. Their key term is slack: the margin that lets a small setback stay small. Privilege is largely slack, and slack is invisible to whoever has it. Read that against the falling feather and the shape is identical. The person without slack behaves differently in a way that looks dispositional and is medium-dependent. Change the medium and the behaviour changes, without anyone acquiring more grit. Linda Nathan names the assumptions this displaces, and they are the assumptions mindset marketing runs on: money doesn't matter; race doesn't matter; just work harder; everyone can go to college; beliefs make dreams true. Marked leap, and this is the one to watch. The seductive next sentence is remove the barriers and the difference vanishes, the way it vanished on the Moon. Worse, the strong version is dangerous in a familiar way: if you claim gaps vanish once barriers are removed, then a persisting gap becomes proof that the barriers are gone, which lands you back in deficit ideology by a longer road. When a feather falls slowly, look for the air

The turn When a feather falls slowly, look for the air You would not watch a feather drift down and conclude that it lacks determination. You would not design an intervention to build feather resilience. You would look for the air, because that is where the explanation is. That instinct is not soft-headedness. It is the single most productive habit physical science ever acquired, and it cost two thousand years, a self-contradiction argument, a set of inclined planes and eventually a man on the Moon with a hammer in one hand. So the argument of this zine is not that we should be kinder than science. It is that we should be as rigorous as it, and we are not. Deficit ideology is not a hard-headed alternative to structural analysis. It is the older, worse physics — the one that puts the cause inside the object and treats the medium as a footnote — kept alive in a domain where nobody thought to check. Fix injustice, not kids. Justice, not grit. Stimpunks And nobody built this road on purpose either. Aristotle described what he saw. The California task force commissioned research. Dweck and Duckworth did careful work and objected to its misuse. Teachers adopted programmes offered to them by people who believed in them. Every step was a competent local move, and the accumulation runs two thousand years in the right direction and forty in the wrong one. Which is the hopeful reading, and the reason this collection writes chains. The medium is the part you can change. That is what makes it the useful place to put the explanation — not because it is kinder, but because a room can be rebuilt and a nature cannot. Not:that children are objects. They have interiority and agency; a stone does not. An account that makes a child wholly a product of circumstance is the mirror error and just as wrong. Not:that difference isn't real. Mass survived Newton. Variation between people is real, is not a defect, and is the thing this whole site exists to defend. The claim is that it does not explain the trajectory by itself. Aristotle's account of natural motion — bodies moving toward their proper place, speed increasing with weight and decreasing with the density of the medium — is given from the standard reading of the Physics and On the Heavens rather than from a translation quoted here. Galileo's self-contradiction argument (tie a heavy body to a light one and the same premise predicts both faster and slower) is in Two New Sciences (1638), as is the inclined-plane work establishing that distance goes as the square of time independent of weight. The Leaning Tower demonstration is marked contested on its own spread: it comes from Vincenzo Viviani's biography, written decades after Galileo's death, and Galileo does not describe it in his own published work — the most famous experiment in physics is a story about an experiment, which is exactly the smoothing this collection exists to catch. Newtonian mechanics is described structurally rather than quoted. Apollo 15. On 2 August 1971, at the end of the final Hadley–Apennine moonwalk, commander David Scott released a geology hammer and a falcon feather simultaneously and they reached the surface together; the demonstration was televised and Scott remarked that it confirmed Galileo. His words are paraphrased rather than quoted here, having not been checked against the mission transcript. Self-esteem. The California Task Force to Promote Self-Esteem and Personal and Social Responsibility was established in 1986 and published Toward a State of Esteem in 1990. Its commissioned academic volume — Andrew Mecca, Neil J. Smelser & John Vasconcellos (eds.), The Social Importance of Self-Esteem, University of California Press, 1989 — reported that "the associations between self-esteem and its expected consequences are mixed, insignificant, or absent." Growth mindset. Brooke N. Macnamara & Alexander P. Burgoyne, "Do growth mindset interventions impact students' academic achievement? A systematic review and meta-analysis with recommendations for best practices," Psychological Bulletin (2023; online first 3 November 2022) — 63 studies, N = 97,672; publication bias, authors with financial incentives more likely to report positive effects, major internal-validity threats, and higher-quality studies less likely to show benefit. Carol Dweck's warnings about "false growth mindset" and its misuse, and Angela Duckworth's caution against grit measures in high-stakes accountability, are characterised rather than quoted; both are well documented in their public writing but were not read at source for this piece, and are flagged here as open. The Shorthands LYDTYSS is the full phrase — Love You Down To Your Star Stuff — and it carries everything. But it's a mouthful, and language that lives in community needs forms that fit in a text message, a sticker, a caption, a moment. These are the shorthands we use and what each one carries. LYDTYSS Love You Down To Your Star Stuff The source. Use it when you want the full weight of the phrase — in writing, in titles, in contexts where the whole arc matters. It's cumbersome on purpose in the same way a full name is: it holds the complete thing. LYSS Love You, Star Stuff The warmest shorthand. Pronounceable — it sounds like a name, like a term of endearment, which is exactly what it is. Use it the way you'd use love you — quick, direct, meant. The comma does quiet work: it addresses you as star stuff directly, not just describes you as containing it. LUSS Love U Star Stuff The punk version. The dropped vowel is deliberate — it leans into informal, texty, a little defiant. Where LYSS is tender, LUSS has an edge. Both are correct. Both are true. L★S Love ★ Star Stuff The most visual shorthand. The star does double duty — it is both the symbol of what we're made of and the punctuation that holds love and star stuff together. Works in print, on stickers, as a hashtag, as a signature. The star is load-bearing. ★stuff Star Stuff The noun on its own. Use it as an identity, a descriptor, a reclamation. We are ★stuff. It carries the Sagan lineage — the specific weight of that phrase — while making it communal and punk. When you see ★stuff, you are seeing the raw material named directly, without the love clause, because sometimes you just need to name what you are. Which register you reach for depends on the moment. LYSS for tenderness. LUSS for solidarity with an edge. L★S when the visual matters. ★stuff when you're naming the thing itself. LYDTYSS when you need the whole phrase to do its full work. We Are Star Stuff: Being Autistic, Ethodiversity and Cosmic Connection

We Are Star Stuff: Being Autistic, Ethodiversity and Cosmic Connection Some phrases arrive as slogans. This one arrived as a realization. The science has been settled for decades: we are, literally, made of star stuff. The six elements essential to life are woven through the Milky Way. A survey of 150,000 stars confirmed that humans and the galaxy share around 97% of the same kinds of atoms. We are not like the cosmos. We are continuous with it. For neurodivergent and disabled people — people who have spent their lives being told they are too much, not enough, wrong in some fundamental way — that continuity matters differently. The universe did not make one configuration of matter and call it correct. It made billions of years of variation, explosion, collapse, and emergence. Nearly every element heavier than helium was forged in violence and became something new. You are part of that lineage. LYDTYSS begins here. Not as comfort, but as cosmological argument: the problem was never you. The following reflection comes from Helen, Co-Creative Director at Stimpunks. Helen wrote it in direct response to first hearing the phrase "Love You Down To Your Star Stuff" — what it opened up, what it confirmed, what it made newly speakable about being Autistic and made of the same matter as everything else. I find it genuinely awe-inspiring to know that the atoms that make up your body, the oxygen in your lungs, the calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood were forged inside stars that died before our planet even existed. Not metaphorically, we are actually, literally, made of stars ! A 2017 survey of 150,000 stars confirmed that humans and our galaxy share around 97% of the same kinds of atoms, and that the six elements essential to life — carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulphur — are woven right through the Milky Way ( Howell, 2017 ). We are a living part of the cosmos. I have been thinking about this a lot, and what it may mean to us as Autistic people, and it is something that is evolving in conversations within the CASY Autistic Physics group and my recent collaborative work with Stimpunks . There is something about being made of stardust that resonates far deeper than a scientific fact for me. As an Autistic person, I have always felt that the boundaries between myself and the world are more porous than I was told they should be. Everything feels entangled, I am deeply influenced by my environment in ways that go beyond what neuronormative frameworks tend to account for. Time, my past and present merge and move together; my pull towards moss and mushrooms , and my interest in water, are more than a 'like' or form of regulation or sensory relief, they feel like I am becoming more attuned to something deeper and more essential, something I can only describe as parts of my soul recognising what they actually belong to. The elements in your body right now came into being through some of the most violent events in the universe. The iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones, the oxygen in every breath, were forged in the cores of massive stars and released in supernovae: entire stars compressing their whole lives into a single catastrophic release. In that rupture, what had been locked inside was scattered outward, making things possible that could never have existed before. We Are Star Stuff: Being Autistic, Ethodiversity and Cosmic Connection | More Realms

Resonance Helen ended with an image of rupture and release: entire stars compressing their whole lives into a single catastrophic event, scattering outward what had been locked inside, making things possible that could never have existed before. She was describing supernovae. She was also describing what it feels like to finally hear something that names you correctly. That is what resonance is. Not agreement with an idea, but recognition at a level below argument. The cards below trace why "Love You Down To Your Star Stuff" produces that recognition — in neurodivergent people especially, in people who have felt alien their whole lives, in anyone who has been told that the way they move through the world is the problem. Cosmology No hierarchy of matter The cosmos doesn't rank configurations of itself. Carbon in a star core and carbon in a human brain are the same carbon. There is no "wrong kind" of matter in the universe — no deficit, no pathology at the atomic level. For someone measured and found lacking their whole life, this is radically leveling. Language "Down to" does everything Love that reaches through every layer. "Down to" doesn't say you contain star stuff — it says love travels all the way through diagnosis, difference, difficulty, and keeps going to the atomic substrate. That's not conditional love. It cannot be cancelled by anything on the surface. Identity Alien → cosmic Feels like an outsider? You're looking the wrong direction. Many neurodivergent people describe feeling alien their whole lives. LYDTYSS doesn't correct that feeling — it elevates it. The distance isn't between you and other humans. It's between all of us and the stars we came from. That reframe shifts everything. Narrative Reclamatory cosmology Sagan's framing as counter-narrative to deficit. "Star stuff" carries Sagan's specific argument: not that humans are small, but that we are continuous with the universe. For people who have internalized a deficit story, this is a direct rewrite. Not a broken version of normal. A particular arrangement of the cosmos looking at itself. Philosophy True pluralism No configuration of star stuff is more star stuff. The phrase doesn't describe a type — it describes a shared origin that holds every variation inside it equally. There's no bell curve in stellar nucleosynthesis. Every possible mind, body, and way of being emerges from the same substrate. The universality is the point. Voice Intimate, not institutional "Love you" — not an affirmation program. It doesn't say "we affirm your neurodivergent identity" or "your differences are a gift." Just: love you. Down to your most fundamental level. That simplicity can reach people who have built defenses against therapeutic language, because it doesn't sound like a program. It sounds like someone means it. Belonging, Authenticity & Radical Inclusivity LYDTYSS is not just a phrase about cosmology. It is a signal — one that tells you this is a place where you do not have to perform your humanity to receive love. Belonging, authenticity, and radical inclusivity are not additions to the star-stuff idea. They are what it means in practice. Belonging A signal that you are home Belonging is wholeness. It is the experience of being at home in ourselves and in community. When someone who has spent their life feeling alien — too much, too different, not legible to the world around them — hears "Love You Down To Your Star Stuff," something specific happens. The phrase does not ask them to become more acceptable. It says: you are already loved, at the level of your matter. That is a belonging signal. It says: this is a place where you are personally accepted, respected, and valued — not despite your difference, but without condition. Belonging at Stimpunks is not a reward for fitting in. It is the starting point. Authenticity No masking required — love goes all the way down Authenticity is our purest freedom. Being true to yourself is not optional — it is the foundation of liberation. For neurodivergent and disabled people, inauthenticity is often a survival strategy. Masking — suppressing stims, flattening emotions, performing normality — is expensive. It consumes cognitive and emotional resources that belong to the person doing the work of being alive. LYDTYSS short-circuits that logic entirely. Love does not travel to the surface performance. It goes down — past diagnosis, past behavior, past legibility — to the atomic substrate. That is what authenticity as our purest freedom means in practice: you do not have to earn it. You already are it. Radical Inclusivity Inclusion grounded in the sole qualification of being Radical inclusion goes beyond tick-box accommodations. It dismantles systemic barriers and creates neuroqueer spaces where everyone has freedom to embrace cognitive and somatic liberty. Inclusion safety — the first stage of psychological safety — is species-based acceptance: if you have flesh and blood, we accept you. LYDTYSS goes even further. It grounds that acceptance not just in biological fact but in cosmological fact. You are not merely tolerated because you exist. You are loved , because at the level of your matter, you are made of the same stuff as everything else in the universe. That is radical inclusivity as a cosmological argument: there is no configuration of star stuff that is outside the circle. No mind, no body, no neurotype. The universe did not make exceptions. Neither do we.

Related Concepts The star-stuff insight — that we are made of the same matter as everything else in the universe, that there is no hierarchy of configurations, that love can reach all the way down to the atomic substrate — is not new. It has arrived independently across cultures, traditions, and centuries, in different vocabularies and for different purposes. What follows is not a claim that these traditions say the same thing. It is an acknowledgment that LYDTYSS is in conversation with something very old.

Tat tvam asi — Advaita Vedanta That thou art. One of the mahāvākyas — the great sayings — of the Upanishads. The teaching is that the self ( atman ) and the ground of all being ( Brahman ) are not separate. You are not a fragment of the universe looking at it from outside. You are it, expressing itself in this particular form. Advaita Vedanta, the non-dual school of Hindu philosophy, holds that the infinite diversity of existence is rooted in a single reality — and that each thing, living or not, is a unique manifestation of that one reality. Unique and universal at the same time. No configuration is more real than another. No configuration is outside the whole. The parallel with LYDTYSS: love that goes all the way down to your star stuff is love that reaches the level where you and the cosmos are not separate. It is not love despite your particularity. It is love through your particularity to the universal substrate you share with everything.

Esho funi — Buddhism Two but not two. The Buddhist principle that life and its environment are inseparable — not identical, but not separate either. The self does not end at the skin. The environment is not something outside the self. At a primal level of existence, there is no boundary between what you are and what surrounds you. This is not a metaphor in Buddhist teaching. It is a description of how existence actually works, obscured by the conventional perception of separation. For neurodivergent people who have always experienced the world as porous — who feel the environment deeply, whose boundaries between self and surroundings are less defended than neurotypical frameworks expect — esho funi offers a framework in which that porousness is not a deficit. It is a more accurate perception of how things are.

Waḥdat al-wujūd — Sufism Unity of Being. The teaching of the 13th century Sufi mystic Ibn Arabi: all existence is a single reality, and apparent multiplicity is the one reality appearing in different forms. The many are not separate from the One. They are the One, taking on particular shapes. Rumi's reed flute — cut from the reed bed, crying for reunion — is one of the most enduring images of this tradition. The longing is not pathology. It is the memory of original unity. The feeling of being cut off, of not belonging, of having come from somewhere else — in this reading, that feeling is not wrong. It is the accurate perception of a genuine separation, and the longing for return is sacred. For people who have spent their lives feeling alien, waḥdat al-wujūd offers a reframe: the alienation is real, but it points toward something, not away from it. You were not wrong to feel the distance. The distance is the distance from the reed bed. LYDTYSS is one way of saying: you were never actually cut off. The universe is still in you. You are still in it.

Interbeing — Thich Nhat Hanh Thich Nhat Hanh's term for the insight that nothing exists independently — that everything contains everything else, that to look deeply into anything is to find the whole cosmos inside it. A flower contains the cloud that rained on it, the sun that warmed it, the soil that held it, the person who will one day look at it. Interbeing is already present on this page in Thich Nhat Hanh's own words: "My physical body is your physical body... You are nothing less than myself." But the concept is worth naming directly: this is not sentiment. It is a systematic account of reality in which the boundaries between self and other, between one being and another, are real but not absolute — permeable at depth. The star-stuff argument is interbeing stated in the language of astrophysics.
Brahmacharya and the Animacy of Matter — Indigenous Cosmologies

Brahmacharya and the Animacy of Matter — Indigenous Cosmologies Many Indigenous traditions hold that humans are not made from the land, the sky, the stars — they are made of them, in an ongoing relational sense. Not past tense. Not metaphor. The elements do not stop being in relationship with their origins when they become part of a body. Robin Wall Kimmerer, Potawatomi botanist and author of Braiding Sweetgrass , writes of the grammar of animacy — Indigenous languages that treat the living world not as it but as he , she , they . To name something animate is to acknowledge it as a being in relationship with you, not a resource or a backdrop. When that grammar is applied to the elements in your body, the star-stuff argument becomes something warmer and more mutual: the cosmos is not just what you are made of. It is who you are in relationship with.

Song of Myself — Walt Whitman I am large, I contain multitudes. Whitman was writing in a tradition shaped by the Upanishads, filtered through Emerson's transcendentalism, and expressed in the most expansive poetic voice American literature had produced. Song of Myself is a sustained argument that the self is not a fixed, bounded, singular thing — that it contains contradiction, plurality, the whole of humanity, the whole of nature. For neurodivergent people who have been told their multiplicity is a disorder, their contradictions are dysfunction, their way of being too large for the rooms they're given — Whitman's embrace of largeness as the nature of the self, not a deviation from it, is kin to what LYDTYSS is doing. You do not need to resolve your contradictions to deserve love. You are large. You contain multitudes. You are ★stuff.

Transcendental Empiricism — Deleuze Deleuze's transcendental empiricism holds that experience is not filtered through pre-given categories — not sorted and stabilised before it reaches us — but encountered directly, in its raw difference and intensity. Where Kant asked what makes experience possible, Deleuze asked what experience actually is before it gets normalised. The answer: difference, variation, becoming. Not objects with fixed identities, but forces in flux. From this flows a constellation of concepts that Autistic thinkers have found genuinely resonant. The rhizome — as opposed to the root or the tree — is a model of connection with no fixed centre, no hierarchy, no single origin point. It spreads laterally, unexpectedly, making connections between heterogeneous things. The fold suggests that interiority is not sealed off from exteriority but continuous with it, always turning inside out, always folding deeper. The line of flight is a rupture in a fixed system — a movement that escapes the structures meant to contain it. Not destruction, but becoming something the structure couldn't predict. Helen Edgar has spent years exploring why these concepts resonate so specifically with neurodivergent experience. Her work suggests that Deleuzean philosophy does not merely describe neurodivergent minds from the outside — it maps the territory from within. A monotropic person's attention does not move through a tree-like hierarchy of priorities; it spreads rhizomatically, following the pull of a particular interest tunnel through unexpected connections. The fold describes what Helen calls the infinite nature of the bodymind: always a deeper cavern, always more interior to explore. The line of flight is what neuroqueering actually does — a departure from neuronormative structure that is not a failure to conform, but an opening into something new. The connection to LYDTYSS is structural, not decorative. Transcendental empiricism refuses the idea that there is one correct way to process the world. Difference is not a deviation from a norm — it is what exists, at every level of experience. The DSM assumes a tree: a single structure of typical development, from which some people branch incorrectly. Deleuze assumes a rhizome: no trunk, no correct branch, just the spread of actual experience in its heterogeneous reality. LYDTYSS makes the same move. The universe doesn't produce one kind of star, one kind of mind, one kind of knowing. It produces variation. You are one of the variations. You are loved all the way down to that level. For neurodivergent people who have found the rhizome, the fold, and the line of flight before they found the language for them — who have always known their attention moves differently, their time feels differently, their interiors have more caverns than the map shows — Deleuze offers philosophical scaffolding for something already lived. The fold is not only a philosophical concept here. It is also the physics of the body described in the Crystal Under Pressure section below — piezoelectric bone is literally folded crystalline matter that transduces exterior pressure into interior charge. The boundary between outside force and inside response is not a wall. It is a fold. Deleuze's bodymind and Yasuda's bone are the same argument in different vocabularies: the cosmos outside and the body inside are not separate things, but continuous, folded into each other. See Helen Edgar's work at Autistic Realms — including her explorations of Deleuzean time, the neuroqueering potential of the fold, and the rhizome as a model of Autistic community and belonging.

Spinoza's Pantheism Baruch Spinoza, 17th century philosopher, argued that God and nature are one and the same substance — that the finite things of the world are not separate from the whole but expressions of it, like modes or properties of a single infinite being. There is no hierarchy among modes. No configuration of the one substance is more legitimate than another. Spinoza was excommunicated for this. The idea that existence itself is sacred — not a fallen material world separate from a spiritual one, but one continuous substance that is both — was dangerous then. It remains radical now, in any system that ranks human beings by the legitimacy of their minds and bodies. LYDTYSS is, among other things, a Spinozist argument: there is one substance. You are made of it. That is enough.

A Note on This Constellation These traditions differ from each other in profound ways — in their metaphysics, their ethics, their relationship to self and cosmos. This is not a claim that they are saying the same thing, or that LYDTYSS is a synthesis of them. It is a recognition that the intuition underlying LYDTYSS — that at some deep level, the boundaries between self and universe are not absolute, that this has implications for how we treat each other, that no configuration of matter is outside the circle of what deserves love — is one that human beings have kept arriving at, across very different starting points, for a very long time. That is not proof. But it is not nothing.

The Cosmos is within us. The Cosmos is within us. We are made of star-stuff. We are a way for the Universe to know itself — in every color, key, and frequency of neurodiversity. Crystal Under Pressure A prose poem drawing on Dr. Iwao Yasuda's discovery of the piezoelectric properties of bone, the cosmological origins of the elements in our bodies, and the neurodiversity reframe. Our bones are not solid. They are piezoelectric crystals — the same principle as quartz watches, microphones, sonar — that generate measurable electricity every time we move. Dr. Iwao Yasuda discovered this in 1957. Our skeleton is not a coat hanger for our muscles. It is a chemical factory, an electrical generator, a living crystal lattice humming with charge. And it is made of star stuff. The phosphorus in those bones — 85% of your body's supply — was forged in a stellar core before Earth existed. The calcium. The magnesium. Scattered by supernovae, gathered by gravity, assembled over billions of years into something that can bend and generate light. The Cosmos is within us. Our bones are electrical crystals. Our neurons fire in patterns the DSM calls disorder and the stars call weather — solar flares, magnetic storms, plasma eruptions: dynamic systems doing what dynamic systems do, turbulence that belongs, variation that has never needed a diagnosis. We are a way for the Universe to know itself — chaotically, hyperfocusedly, nonlinearly, beautifully. LYSS. The body as fold. The crystal as transducer. Force from outside becomes charge from inside — which is also what Deleuze means by the fold: interiority is not sealed off from exteriority, but continuous with it, always turning inside out, always folding deeper. See Transcendental Empiricism — Deleuze in Related Concepts, and The Fold and the Crystal for the full exploration. Read Bone Song — the full prose poem in zine form, with diagrams tracing piezoelectric matter, star-forged calcium, and the universe that doesn't pathologize its own variation.

What LYDTYSS Is Not Not: your differences are a gift. That puts the burden back on you to be useful enough to deserve love. Not: everything happens for a reason. Your suffering does not need a purpose to be real, or to matter, or to stop. Not: you are special. Star stuff is not rare. It is everything. The phrase is about continuity, not exceptionalism. Not: love you despite your star stuff. The direction matters. Down to . All the way through. Not around. Not: a substitute for structural change. Loving someone cosmologically does not fix inaccessible systems. LYDTYSS knows this. It lives in the register of belonging, not policy. It does not pretend the two are the same. It is not inspiration porn . It does not say your suffering has a purpose, or that your neurology is a superpower, or that everything happens for a reason. It does not ask you to reframe your pain as a gift. It is not toxic positivity . It does not say everything is fine. It does not paper over the real costs of living in systems that were not built for you. It is not the "your differences are a gift" framework. That framing puts the burden back on the person — you must justify your existence by being useful, extraordinary, or instructive to neurotypicals. LYDTYSS asks nothing of you in return. It is not conditional. It does not say "love you for your star stuff" — as though the cosmic material is the lovable part and the rest of you is on probation. It says love goes down to that level. The direction matters. It is not a ceiling. It is a floor. It is not a metaphor for being special. Star stuff is not rare. It is everywhere. Every rock, every raindrop, every person who has ever made you feel like you were too much — also star stuff. The phrase is not about being chosen. It is about being continuous with everything that exists. It is not a substitute for structural change. Loving someone down to their star stuff does not fix inaccessible systems, underfunded support, or the violence of forced normalization. The phrase lives in the register of love and community, not policy. It does not pretend otherwise.

What LYDTYSS Is It is a cosmological argument stated as an act of love. It says: the matter you are made of was forged in stellar cores before Earth existed, scattered by supernovae, gathered by gravity, assembled over billions of years into something that can feel joy and grief and overstimulation in a fluorescent-lit room. That process did not produce a hierarchy. It produced variation. You are one of the variations. You are loved all the way down to that level. It is a belonging signal. When you hear it, it means: this is a place where you do not have to perform your humanity to receive care. The love is not conditional on your behavior, your productivity, your legibility, your diagnosis, or your ability to pass. It goes all the way down past all of that to the substrate. You are in. It is a refusal. A refusal to accept that there is a correct configuration of human being. A refusal to locate the problem in the person rather than in the systems that were not built for them. A refusal to rank matter. It is an affirmation that does not require you to be exceptional. You are not loved because your neurology is a superpower, or because your suffering has produced wisdom, or because you have overcome. You are loved because you exist. Because at the atomic level you are continuous with everything that has ever existed. That is the only qualification. It has never been in question. It is a phrase that travels. LYDTYSS in full when you need the whole weight of it. LYSS when you mean it tenderly. LUSS when you mean it with an edge. L★S when the symbol is enough. ★stuff when you are just naming what you are. The phrase scales because the love it describes scales — from the cosmic to the personal, from the philosophical to the text message. It is a community practice. Not just something said to individuals but something practiced collectively — in how Stimpunks builds spaces, funds access, holds people, refuses to make belonging conditional. LYDTYSS is the phrase. The practice is what happens when you take it seriously. It is, finally, an invitation. To let love reach that far. To stop defending the parts of yourself you have learned to hide. To belong somewhere at the level of your matter, not the level of your performance. Love you down to your star stuff. All the way down. LYSS. Read the Love You Down To Your Star Stuff Zine — the cosmology of care in six spreads. What Sagan said, what the elements are, what "down to" means as a direction, and affirmations across every register.

Reflection Ancient, Cosmic, Real The star stuff framing positions us as ancient, cosmic, made of real matter. Some prompts that fit that ethos: "You are made of exploded stars. What are you made of, emotionally, today?" "What in you feels elemental right now — fire, water, pressure, light?" "Name something you're carrying that's older than you." "What part of you is still forming?" "Where did you come from, and where are you going?" Belonging When have you felt personally accepted — not tolerated, not accommodated, but genuinely welcomed as yourself? What made that different from other spaces? Have you ever belonged somewhere only by performing a version of yourself that wasn't quite real? What did that cost you? Belonging is described as wholeness — being at home in yourself and in community. Which of those feels harder right now? What would it mean to belong somewhere the way matter belongs to the universe — not earned, not conditional, just intrinsic? Who in your life has made you feel like you didn't have to explain yourself to be loved? Authenticity What parts of yourself have you hidden or suppressed in order to survive a space? What would it feel like to stop? Authenticity is described as a precondition for psychological safety, not a luxury. Has there been a moment when you were allowed to be fully yourself and noticed the difference in how you could think, feel, or function? Masking is expensive. What cognitive and emotional bandwidth might become available to you if you didn't have to spend it on performing normalcy? What does your authentic self do, sound like, or need — that the world has most often asked you to hide? If love goes all the way down past performance to your atomic substrate — what would you stop apologizing for? Radical Inclusivity Radical inclusivity confronts normativity directly — it doesn't just tolerate difference, it dismantles the systems that treat difference as a problem. What norm have you been asked to conform to that you now recognize as arbitrary? Inclusion safety is described as acceptance based on the sole qualification of having flesh and blood. Have you ever been in a space that actually felt that way? What made it possible? The argument here is cosmological: no configuration of star stuff is outside the circle. Does that framing shift anything for you about who deserves care and belonging? Where in your life are you still waiting for permission to exist fully? What is the source of that permission, and is it legitimate? What would it look like to build a space — in your home, your classroom, your community — where no one has to mask to survive? Across all three LYDTYSS says love reaches all the way down to your star stuff. What is the deepest, most hidden version of yourself that you have not yet let be loved? If belonging, authenticity, and radical inclusivity are not additions to the star-stuff idea but what it means in practice — what does that ask of you as someone who receives that love? What does it ask of you as someone who gives it?

The phrase · its origin What Carl Sagan actually said He said it first in The Cosmic Connection (1973): "All of the rocky and metallic material we stand on, the iron in our blood, the calcium in our teeth, the carbon in our genes were produced billions of years ago in the interior of a red giant star. We are made of star-stuff." The line most of us know is the 1980 one, from Cosmos: "The nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, the carbon in our apple pies were made in the interiors of collapsing stars. We are made of star stuff." He said it many times, and he was not being metaphorical. He meant it literally — that essentially every atom heavier than helium in your body was forged in a star or in its death, and scattered across the galaxy. We are not like stars. We are not inspired by stars. We are made of them — their ash, their legacy, their long slow gift to whatever came next. The phrase · its meaning To say love you and then say down to your star stuff is to say: I love you at every scale. I love you all the way in. "Love you down to your star stuff" moves in one direction: inward and downward, through skin and blood and bone, through cell and molecule and atom, all the way to the stellar origin of each element. It doesn't stop at the visible. Most love stops at the surface — at behavior, at presentation, at the parts that are easy to love. This phrase names a love that doesn't stop. That goes past the parts that are hard, past the parts that are different, past the diagnosis and the accommodation and the sensory profile, all the way to the calcium in the bone — which came from a star. You can't pathologize star stuff. The universe made it. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. LYDTYSS · Stimpunks
Six elements. All of them stellar.

What you are made of Six elements. All of them stellar. Essentially every atom in your body heavier than helium has a stellar origin. These are the six that make you most distinctly you — the ones that show up in your bones, your blood, your breath, your brain. None of them were made on Earth. All of them arrived here the same way: scattered by supernovae, gathered by gravity, assembled by time into the improbable configuration that is a human nervous system. Your neurology is as old as the stars. The particular way your mind works — the frequency, the intensity, the pattern — is built from the same material as everything else the universe has ever made. It belongs here. HHydrogen The oldest element. Made in the Big Bang, 13.8 billion years ago. The water in your body. The original. CCarbon The backbone of every molecule that makes you alive. Forged in red giant stars through triple-alpha fusion. NNitrogen In your DNA. In every protein. Built by the CNO cycle inside stars — roughly half of it shed by ageing low- and intermediate-mass stars, the rest from massive ones. The language of your cells. OOxygen 65% of your body by mass. Made in massive stars through carbon and neon burning. Every breath is stellar. CaCalcium Your bones. Your teeth. Your nerve signals. Made in supernovae. The electric bone that Yasuda measured. FeIron The iron in your blood. The last rung of fusion in massive stars — and about half of it flung out by exploding white dwarfs. LYDTYSS · Stimpunks

What "down to" means Love at every scale The phrase moves through scales. "Down to your star stuff" is a direction — inward, deeper, smaller, older. It names every level at which you can be loved. Most love operates at the level of behavior and personality — the things that are visible, the parts that present themselves to the world. This phrase insists that love go all the way in. Past the mask, past the accommodation, past the things that are hard. Down to your star stuff means: I see you at the level where there is nothing left to pathologize. At the level of carbon and calcium and iron, you are simply matter that the universe made. And matter that the universe made belongs. The scales of love Cosmic The universe — 13.8 billion years of stellar evolution that produced every atom in your body. This is the outermost frame. Community The people around you — who see your whole self, not just the parts that are easy. Who don't ask you to be less. The body Your nervous system, your sensory profile, your way of moving through the world — the parts that get pathologized. Loved here too. The cell The biological substrate — where your neurology actually lives. The neurons and the synapses. Loved at this level too. The atom Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, calcium, iron — each one a stellar legacy. This is where the phrase lands. This is "star stuff." Star Stuff Manifesto On the cosmic origins of who we are, the science of how we carry the universe in our bones, and why neurodivergent and disabled people belong — not despite difference, but as difference. L ★ S · Love You, Star Stuff I · Origin
We are all made of exploded stars

We are all made of exploded stars Carl Sagan said it plainly: “The nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, the carbon in our apple pies were made in the interiors of collapsing stars” ( Cosmos , 1980, ch. 9). When those stars exhausted their fuel, they exploded across the cosmos. Their debris became clouds. The clouds collapsed into new systems, new planets, new oceans, new life. You. Stellar Nucleosynthesis Almost every atom heavier than helium was manufactured in stars. Carbon, oxygen, calcium, iron — the building blocks of every human body — were forged under conditions of unimaginable pressure and heat, then scattered across the galaxy when those stars died. (Three light elements are the honest exceptions: most lithium came from the Big Bang, and beryllium and boron are made almost entirely by cosmic rays shattering heavier nuclei out in interstellar space. Stars destroy all three rather than build them.) We are, in a literal chemical sense, the remnants of stellar death. This is not metaphor. It is the actual account of where you came from. And it matters — because a cosmology that grounds identity in the violent, generative creativity of the universe is a very different cosmology than one that locates value in conformity, productivity, or neurotypicality. ★ II · The Bones Remember

Your skeleton is piezoelectric In the 1950s, Japanese orthopedic surgeon Dr. Iwao Yasuda and physicist Eiichi Fukada established something remarkable: bone is piezoelectric. Under mechanical stress — compression, tension, bending — bone crystal generates its own electrical charge. This is not incidental. It is how bone knows to grow, where to strengthen, how to heal. The skeleton is a living signal processor, converting force into information. Piezoelectricity Piezo comes from the Greek piezein — to press, to squeeze. Certain materials generate an electric charge when their structure is deformed. In bone the effect comes chiefly from collagen — the protein scaffold, not the mineral — whose fibres are arranged without a centre of symmetry and slip past one another under shear. (Hydroxyapatite, the mineral that makes bone rigid, is symmetric in the way that rules out classical piezoelectricity; recent work gives it a role in bone's electrical environment, but the original effect Fukada and Yasuda measured was collagen's.) Every step you take, every breath, every impact — your bones are generating voltage. Responding. Adapting. Alive. We carry the electrical signature of the cosmos not just as metaphor but as mechanism. The universe built into the architecture of our bodies the same responsive-to-pressure principle it uses everywhere: force begets signal, signal begets change, change begets structure. We are responsive systems, not static ones. Every nervous system that processes the world differently is doing what responsive systems do — responding to the particular pressures of a particular life. "Your bones are piezoelectric. They generate charge under pressure. They respond. They adapt. They remember every load they've carried — and grow stronger at the point of stress. That is not a malfunction. That is the physics of survival written in calcium and light." — Stimpunks Foundation ★ III · The Neurodiversity Paradigm
The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation

The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation The neurodiversity paradigm holds that neurological difference is a natural, valuable form of human variation — not a deviation from a healthy norm to be corrected, but a dimension of the diversity that characterizes our species. Autism, ADHD, dyslexia, Tourette's, and the full range of neurological profiles are not disorders in the sense of broken-ness. They are differences in how nervous systems are organized. The universe is staggeringly, relentlessly various. Stars range from red dwarfs barely massive enough to fuse hydrogen, to hypergiants swollen past a thousand times the sun's radius, to blue monsters near two hundred times its mass. Galaxies spiral, ellipse, collide, merge, scatter. No two snowflakes, no two fingerprints, no two nervous systems. Variation is not the exception. It is the rule. It is the engine. Core Claim The same universe that forged every atom in your body also produced the nervous system you inhabit. There is no astrophysics of typicality. There is only the astonishing variety of what the cosmos can make — and we are part of that variety. The DSM is a human document written at a particular historical moment to describe patterns of distress and difference through a particular cultural lens. The cosmos has no DSM. Turbulence in fluid dynamics is not a pathology — it is a regime of behavior, one with its own laws, its own beauty, its own utility. The same is true of neurological variation. We reframe. Not to deny that neurodivergent and disabled people experience real challenges — many of which are compounded or entirely caused by environments built for a narrow range of bodies and minds — but to insist that the starting point is not deficit. The starting point is this: you came from the same place everything came from. Stars. ★ IV · Love You Down to Your Star Stuff
What it means to say L★S

What it means to say L★S Love You Down to Your Star Stuff — LYDTYSS, L★S — is not a slogan. It is a position. It is a way of saying: I see you at the level of your constituent matter. I love what you are made of. I love the process that made you. I love the particular, improbable, once-in-a-cosmos arrangement of atoms that is you, right now, reading this. This matters in community spaces built for neurodivergent and disabled people because so much of what those community members have been told — by schools, by clinics, by families who meant well — is a story of falling short. Not meeting the threshold. Not reaching the benchmark. Not being the version that fits the space that was already built without them in mind. What L★S says back The threshold is arbitrary. The benchmark is cultural. The space can change. But you — the specific arrangement of matter and electricity and history and nervous system that is you — you are not a problem to be solved. You are a thing the universe made. We love you for it. L★S is also punk. It refuses the frame in which some nervous systems are inherently more valuable than others. It refuses the medicalization of variation without consent. It refuses the premise that the burden of adaptation falls entirely on the person who diverges, rather than on the systems and structures that were built too narrow. It is gentle and it is fierce. It is Sagan's wonder and it is community rage at a world that keeps telling neurodivergent and disabled people they are too much, too little, too loud, too still, too slow, too scattered, too focused, too strange. L★S says: we were made by supernovae. We are not too much. We are exactly as much as we are. ★ V · What We Hold
Declarations of the Star Stuff community

Declarations of the Star Stuff community 01 We hold that every person is made of star stuff. Not metaphorically, but chemically. The iron in your blood was forged in a dying star. This is the baseline of your cosmic belonging, and no diagnosis, no deficit model, no exclusionary system can revoke it. 02 We hold that neurological variation is natural variation. The neurodiversity paradigm is not a denial of challenge. It is a refusal to locate the problem in the person rather than in the mismatch between person and environment. 03 We hold that disabled people belong — fully, without asterisk. Not despite their disabilities, but as people whose full humanity includes their disability experience, and whose knowledge from that experience has value. 04 We hold that your bones remember pressure and grow toward strength. The piezoelectric fact of bone is a reminder that living systems are adaptive. What you have carried has shaped you. That shaping is not damage — it is history, written in calcium. 05 We hold that the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. There is no correct galaxy, no normative star. The cosmos makes what it makes and none of it is a mistake. We extend this to people. 06 We hold that community is a mutual aid structure, not a charity transaction. We are not here to fix each other. We are here to share resources, to amplify each other's signal, to build environments where more kinds of people can be more fully themselves. 07 We hold that love operates at the level of constituent matter. L★S means: I love you down to the atoms. The specific improbable arrangement. Not a performance of you, not a corrected version — this one, as made, as present, as star-forged. 08 We hold that punk and wonder are not opposites. Rage at injustice and awe at the cosmos coexist. Stimpunks carries both. The same voice that says "we are made of exploded stars" also says "build better systems or we will build them ourselves." ★ VI · Carried in the Body
On piezoelectric bones and the neurodiversity paradigm

On piezoelectric bones and the neurodiversity paradigm Your bones are piezoelectric. Under pressure — literal, mechanical pressure — they generate voltage. Collagen fibres in compact bone, sheared against one another, convert load to charge. This is how bone remodels: stress signals the skeleton to grow where it is needed, to reinforce the places that carry load. It is not damage. It is response. It is the body's oldest and most literal act of knowing. Every step is a signal. Every weight you have carried has left its mark — not as fracture, but as architecture. The bone grew denser there. The body remembered. "The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation." — Stimpunks Foundation · Star Stuff Manifesto Neurodivergent nervous systems process signal differently. They amplify some frequencies and damp others. They notice what the typical processing filter removes. They fatigue under loads that weren't in the design spec — because the design spec was never written with them in mind. This is the social model of disability applied to nervous systems: the problem is not the nervous system. The problem is the mismatch. The too-loud room. The eye contact requirement. The assumption of one right rhythm. We carry our cosmology in our bodies: atoms forged in stars, bones that conduct electricity, nervous systems that are — each one — a distinct and unrepeatable way of encountering the world. The universe made all of it. The universe makes all of it still. We are not asking for tolerance. We are not asking to be included in a structure built to exclude us, as a favor, on the condition that we approximate the expected shape. We are saying: the structure was wrong about what shapes are possible. We are made of the same stuff as everything. And everything includes us. Colophon The Star Stuff Manifesto is the founding statement of this collection — the argument every zine, field guide and broadside here is a variation on. It braids two real findings with one paradigm, and the braid is a reading , not a proof. Sources below; corrections are logged publicly in the changelog . I · Origin Stellar nucleosynthesis is established science, traced to Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler & Hoyle, “Synthesis of the Elements in Stars” ( Reviews of Modern Physics 29, 1957) — the B²FH paper — and, for the modern accounting of which sites make which elements, Kobayashi, Karakas & Lugaro, “The Origin of Elements from Carbon to Uranium” ( ApJ 900:179, 2020). Hydrogen is primordial; carbon comes from the triple-alpha process in red giants; nitrogen roughly half from low- and intermediate-mass AGB stars via the CNO cycle; oxygen and calcium from massive stars and core-collapse supernovae; iron roughly half from Type Ia supernovae rather than massive stars alone; iodine and the other r-process elements from neutron-star mergers. Lithium, beryllium and boron are the honest exceptions named in the text — most lithium is Big Bang, beryllium and boron come almost entirely from cosmic-ray spallation in the interstellar medium, and stars destroy all three. The Sagan passage is quoted verbatim from Cosmos (1980), ch. 9, “The Lives of the Stars.” II & VI · The bones Bone piezoelectricity was established by Eiichi Fukada and Iwao Yasuda, “On the Piezoelectric Effect of Bone” ( Journal of the Physical Society of Japan 12:1158–1162, 1957), following Yasuda's earlier work; C. A. L. Bassett and colleagues extended it through the 1960s, and it supplies a mechanism for Wolff's law — that bone remodels along the loads it carries. The effect is collagen's: its fibres are arranged without a centre of symmetry and generate charge when sheared past one another. Hydroxyapatite, the mineral that makes bone rigid, is centrosymmetric, which rules out classical piezoelectricity; recent work gives it a role in bone's electrical environment, but the original measured effect was the protein's, not the mineral's. Greek piezein , “to press.” III · The paradigm The neurodiversity paradigm and the pathology paradigm it refuses are Nick Walker 's formulations, from “Throw Away the Master's Tools: Liberating Ourselves from the Pathology Paradigm” (written 2011; published 2012 in Loud Hands: Autistic People, Speaking ; revised 2013) and Neuroqueer Heresies (2021). Neurodiversity itself is not one person's coinage: per Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley & Walker, “The neurodiversity concept was developed collectively” ( Autism , 2024), “neurological diversity” and “neurodiversity” reached print in 1997 and 1998 through journalist Harvey Blume, who attributed them to the online Autistic community — the InLv list founded by Martijn Dekker in 1996, and the wider movement around Jim Sinclair and Autism Network International. Neurodivergent is Kassiane Asasumasu 's (2000). The mismatch framing is the social model of disability, from the disability rights movement. Stellar variety: red dwarfs outlive the present age of the universe; the largest hypergiants exceed a thousand solar radii ; the most massive star known, R136a1, is about 196 solar masses (169–230; Gemini South, 2022), against a theoretical ceiling near 300. Held honestly The science here is real, and it does not make our ethics true. “The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation” is a statement about us — about what we owe each other — dressed in cosmology because that is where it was easiest to see. The cosmos has no opinion, and deriving an ought from an is is a fallacy we would rather name than commit. Bone's piezoelectricity is a mechanism in a skeleton; it is an analogy for responsive nervous systems, not evidence about them. Nothing in stellar chemistry implies anything about how a school or a clinic should be run. What the science does is more modest and, we think, enough: it removes the excuse that difference is a defect, by showing that variation is the ordinary condition of everything we have ever looked at. As About puts it — we are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. upstream, once L★S · 004 The One-Way Trip Pacific salmon · Oncorhynchus natal river · magnetic imprint · no return It finds the one stream it was born in, across a whole ocean, partly by remembering the magnetic field it first felt — then spawns, dies, and carries the ocean up into the forest in its own body. natal hominggeomagnetic imprintsemelparousfeeds the forest ▸ Field notes Field notes · Pacific salmon · Oncorhynchus Pacific salmon return from the open ocean to the single stream they hatched in, using smell at close range and — the surprising part — the Earth's magnetic field at long range. The species' migration runs 5,000 to 10,000 km at a plodding 3 to 12 km a day. Every one of those crossings had been happening all along. The gap was in our observation, not in the eel. We think about this one a lot in relation to the parts of our own lives that go unwitnessed — the pain nobody sees, the work done at 3am, the effort that leaves no visible trace, the disability that no one believes because they cannot watch it. The evidence arriving late does not mean the thing started late. metres a year, for millennia L★S · 011 The Migration With No Legs Postglacial tree range shift tens to hundreds of metres a year Forests migrate. The gap between how far seeds fall and how fast forests moved is still called Reid's paradox; rare long-distance dispersal events, often by birds and rodents, are the leading explanation. An oak does not migrate. Oaks do. The unit that travels is the population, and the mechanism is entirely relay: one tree's whole contribution is a handful of acorns landing slightly further north than it stands. Alongside the monarch, this is the guide's second argument that the traveller and the journey need not be the same size — and its quiet argument that the work you can see from inside one lifetime is not the whole of what you are moving. The consequence is now standard: most stars in the solar neighbourhood were probably born at other radii and migrated here, and old stars formed near us have been scattered across a wide annulus of the disc. So the Sun is, in all likelihood, not from around here. The soil, the ocean, the calcium in your bones, the whole stage this catalogue is performed on — all of it moved, on a timescale that makes the tern's 71,000 km look like a step. There is no fixed address anywhere in this system. life builds the world 16 Niche Minor Worlds on niche construction, stimming, and how difference doesn't just see a world — it builds one L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Niche construction Organisms are not passive Since Darwin, we have pictured the environment as the fixed thing: it sets the test, and organisms adapt or die. But that is only half the loop. The beaver builds a dam and turns a stream into a pond. The spider spins a web; the bird weaves a nest; the earthworm rewrites the chemistry of the soil. Organisms are not passive. The environment is a product of organisms. Biologists call this niche construction (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman), and it runs as a second engine of evolution beside natural selection. It even has its own inheritance: descendants receive not only genes but the world their ancestors built — a beaver born into the pond its grandparents dug. So life does not only drift and sense. It builds — and the built world is handed on. Evolution has two engines: the genes you inherit, and the world your ancestors built. the beaver dam · pond the environment is a product of organisms back from the Council, and building the world remade, and inherited Minor Worlds · Stimpunks
Don't fix the head, change the world

fix the person bend the mind to the slot build the world shape the room to the mind two answers to a mind that doesn't fit change the room, not the head Positive niche construction Don't fix the head, change the world Here is what that means for us. The old model says that when a mind doesn't fit, you fix the mind — make it more like the standard one. Niche construction says the standard was never sacred. As Thomas Armstrong argues, there is no "normal" brain kept in a vat at the Smithsonian for all other brains to be measured against. So stop bending the person. Build the environment. This is not soft metaphor; it is how minds actually work. We ease a too-loud world by acting on it — dimming the light, finding the quiet room, laying the routine down like track. Cognitive science frames it as acting on the world to suit our own states; the plainer version is that the place itself helps us think. Cognition is spread across the room we arrange, not sealed in the skull. Change the world, and you change what a mind can do. Don't bend the mind to fit the room. Build a room the mind can think in. Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

A space of one's own Stimming is worldmaking Watch that building up close. The noise-cancelling headphones. The same walk, the same meal, the song on repeat. The desk set just so; the shelf that holds the whole special interest; the stone turned over and over in a hand. From outside, these get filed as symptoms to manage. From inside, they are worldmaking — the patient assembly of a few stable points a self can stand on. Stimming is niche construction at the scale of a body: movement that tunes the sensory field until it is livable. Ombre Tarragnat calls such movements ontological choreographies — dances that bring a small world into being. One Autistic writer describes their nest plainly: this is my space; it lets me hold one small part of a hard world. Own Sky left us inside a soap bubble — whole, but never guaranteed. Here is the reply to that precarity: we build the bubble ourselves, and we keep on rebuilding it. a world assembled from chosen things we build the bubble ourselves Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

the "Major" world small, real, and networked minor worlds, tended and shared small is not lesser Niche communities Minor worlds These worlds are small, and the smallness is the point. A corner, a routine, a fandom, a friendship, a special interest — none of them universal, every one of them real. Erin Manning calls this the minor: not lesser, only not pretending to be the whole. And we build them together. Autistic people all but invented fandom; we assemble niche communities out of necessity and because our ways of being are, frankly, weird (Devon Price). Some grow into NeurodiVentures — non-hierarchical groups run by neurodivergent people for collaborative niche construction, thickening over time into resilient little ecosystems. Small, local, tended by the people who need it — that is not a lesser world. That is a world. A world doesn't have to be universal to be real. It only has to be built, and shared. Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

Reconstruction, not accommodation Whose niche is the default? But not every niche admits that it was built. The hum of fluorescent light, the open-plan clatter, the crowded room — these get called neutral, just the conditions everyone works in. They are nothing of the sort. They are a niche too, built to suit one kind of mind and then renamed the default. Kadodia and Krueger call it the epistemic niche: our shared spaces quietly encode whose senses, whose pace, whose ways of knowing count, and reward the people they were built for. Which is why bolting an accommodation onto a hostile room is not the fix. The architecture itself has to change — reconstruction, not accommodation. There is no neutral sky and no neutral room. And as biodiversity toughens an ecosystem, a wider range of minds toughens a society's knowledge: the default was only ever one niche among the many we could build. Notan accommodation bolted onto a hostile room — reconstruction, not a ramp to nowhere. Nota "neutral" default — a default is just someone's niche, left unmarked. Notbending the person to the room — build a room more minds can think in. Nota world you're only allowed to visit — a world you get to help build. NEUTRAL light · noise · crowd built for one mind a default is someone's niche peel back "neutral" and find a niche, unmarked Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

human dog plant kin tools a niche is always made with we world each other into being The oldest work Worlding together The last thing to notice is that we never build alone. A niche is made with — with the people who share the fandom, the dog who sets the shape of the day, the plants on the sill, the tools on the belt. Donna Haraway calls these companion species: we world one another into being. Step back far enough and it is all one story. The beaver's pond, the spider's web, the quiet room, the niche community, the reconstructed school — every one of them is matter arranging itself into a place where life can hold. The universe builds itself into worlds, and it does it through us. We are star stuff, building — and to make one small, livable world, together, is the oldest work there is. We are star stuff, building. To make a world is the oldest thing matter does. Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

L★S We are star stuff, building. No niche is neutral, no world is lesser — and to make one, together, is the oldest thing matter does. No. 10 The Dead Stars Still Reach Us — starlight, ancestry & the work of memory No. 11 Why Difference Comes First — Helen Edgar (guest) No. 12 Turn and Face the Strange — David Bowie No. 13 Warriors and Weirdos — AURORA, the alien who came home No. 14 The Council of All Beings — multispecies justice & more-than-human kin No. 15 Every Creature's Own Sky — umwelt, attention-worlds & double empathy No. 16 Minor Worlds — niche construction & the building of livable worlds ← you are here Reflection What have you had to build for yourself to make a hard world livable? Which "neutral" rooms in your life are really built for one kind of mind? Whose niche gets called the default — and who has to keep visiting instead of building? Minor Worlds is the sixteenth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the third of a loose trilogy: how we treat other worlds (No. 14), how we sense them (No. 15), and — here — how we build them. It is the one where the cosmology comes home to the ground the Foundation stands on. Niche construction — organisms remaking their environments, and passing the remade world on as ecological inheritance — is from Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman (2003), after Lewontin; the beaver, spider, and nest are the textbook cases. Positive niche construction — change the environment, not the child; there is no "normal" brain in a vat — is Thomas Armstrong's (Neurodiversity in the Classroom). That we act on the world to suit our states, and that "the place itself helps us think," draw on active-inference research on Autistic cognition and Annie Murphy Paul's The Extended Mind. Stimming as worldmaking, and the precarious yet buildable bubble, draw on Ombre Tarragnat (Autistic worldings, ontological choreography) and Erin Manning (the minor, Autistic perception); the nest that holds "one small part of a hard world" is from Emergent Divergence. Niche communities and fandom are Devon Price (Unmasking Autism) and Steve Silberman (NeuroTribes); NeurodiVentures and collaborative niche construction are Jorn Bettin / Autistic Collaboration. The epistemic niche — "neutral" defaults built for one kind of mind, reconstruction over accommodation — is Kadodia & Krueger (2026). Companion species is Donna Haraway; "matter worlds" is Karen Barad. Monotropism carries over from No. 15. The reading — that no niche is neutral, no world is lesser, and that building them is the cosmos's oldest work — is ours. You were star stuff, building, all along. The rhizome Not a tree The usual picture of knowledge is a tree. One trunk, a few big branches, everything ranked and traceable back to a single root. To learn it you climb; to belong you find your place on the chart. Miss a branch and you're lost. Deleuze and Guattari offered another shape: the rhizome. Picture ginger root, or crabgrass, or fungal thread — no trunk, no first cause, no top. Any point can connect to any other. It is "a model perpetually in construction or collapsing," they wrote: a map you can enter from any edge, not a tree you must climb from the base. Cut a rhizome and it doesn't die — it regrows from anywhere. There is no root to ask permission of, because there is no root. A map you can enter from any edge — not a tree you must climb from the base. tree one root · a top rhizome any point to any point hierarchy vs network no root, no top A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks
