Neurodivergent knowledge is a rhizome you enter wherever your life opens a door. Come in at Spiky Profiles and you might follow a thread to Monotropism, and on to Deep Attention — or arrive from the far side entirely, through burnout, or a word that finally fit, or a problem in a classroom. No prerequisite. No gatekeeper checking you read the introduction first. No "you're not ready for this yet." The map has as many doors as there are people, and every door opens onto the whole. This matters most for minds that were told they'd learned things in the wrong order, or hadn't earned the next rung. In a rhizome there are no rungs — only the next connection that makes sense to you. No prerequisite. No gatekeeper. As many doors as there are people. A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks

The network flows The mycelium moves A rhizome is the shape; a mycelium is the life in it. Underground, fungal threads lace through the soil and trade with the roots they meet — water and scarce minerals for sugar made in the light. Whether those threads also wire whole forests together, elder tree feeding shaded seedling — the "wood wide web" (Simard) — is the contested part, and we hold it loosely (Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, 2023). And the network is not fixed. Where a path is useful, traffic thickens it; where it isn't, it quietly fades. A slime mold — one cell, no brain, no boss — grows across a map of scattered food and settles into almost exactly the rail network human engineers drew for Tokyo (Tero et al., 2010). Decentralised, and still smart. That's how care and knowledge move through our communities too: not issued from a head office, but flowing along the threads to wherever they're needed, strengthening whatever works. Not issued from a head office — flowing along the threads to wherever it's needed. the network learns plenty fed in the shade strong paths thicken · weak paths fade flow · redistribute · adapt smart without a boss A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks

same shape, different scale cosmic web mycelium neuron not a pyramid — a web supercluster · mushroom · synapse read the captions to tell them apart the universe's favourite shape Every scale The same shape everywhere Zoom all the way out and the shape returns. The cosmic web — the largest structure there is — is galaxies strung like dew along vast filaments of dark matter, with great voids between and no center anywhere. Matter drifts down the strands to the bright knots where filaments cross. Set a slice of the cosmic web beside a mycelial mat, beside a slime mold, beside a single neuron, and you have to read the captions to tell them apart. The universe keeps reaching for the same answer: not a pyramid, a web. So when we build without a throne at the top, we aren't failing to organise. We're organising the way the universe does at every scale. Decentralisation isn't disorder — it's the oldest structure there is. Not a pyramid. A web. The oldest structure there is. one shell arriveseveryone moves up at once L★S · 005 The Housing Queue Hermit crabs · Coenobita and Pagurus one shell arrives · a whole line rehouses A hermit crab builds nothing. When a single empty shell turns up, crabs gather beside it and line up by size — and when the largest moves in, every crab behind it moves up at once. owns nothingqueues by sizesynchronous chainsbenefits are distributed ▸ Field notes Field notes · Hermit crabs · Coenobita and Pagurus A hermit crab contributes no material to its home. Every shell it will ever occupy was made by a snail and vacated by circumstance. This looks, at first glance, like the least impressive entry in the guide. It is arguably the most interesting one. Chase, Weissburg and DeWitt described the vacancy chain in 1988: a vacant resource enters the population, an individual takes it and abandons its old one, which a second individual takes, and so on down. One new shell rehouses many crabs. In a synchronous chain, this happens as a piece of visible collective behaviour. Crabs assemble at a newly available shell and queue beside it in descending order of size. When the largest crab moves in, the next takes the shell it left, and the cascade runs down the line. In an asynchronous chain, a lone crab finds a shell and the animals never meet. Lewis and Rotjan tested the prediction that matters and found it held: vacancy chains provide aggregate benefits distributed across many participants, not just the first taker. Read that as a housing system and it is remarkable. Nobody can improve their situation until somebody above them does, so the arrival of one resource lifts a whole queue, and the animals wait for it rather than fight over it. The crab that waits is not being passive. It is standing in the only position from which the chain works. The insect injects signals that hijack the plant’s own development, and the plant grows a custom chamber — shaped to the insect’s specification, out of the tree’s tissue. plant tissue, insect designan extended phenotypespecies-specific shapesfeeds and shelters ▸ Field notes Field notes · Gall wasps and other gall inducers · Cynipidae and beyond This is the entry that broke the material sort. Ask what a gall is made of and the answer is oak. Ask whose it is and the answer is the wasp's. A gall-inducing insect lays into plant tissue and delivers effectors — including phytohormones — that redirect the host's developmental programme. The plant then grows a structure that shelters and feeds the larva, with tissue layers differentiated for the purpose, developing in step with the insect's own growth. The decisive evidence that this is the insect's design rather than the plant's reaction: different insect species induce distinctively different gall shapes on the very same host plant. The oak is not making a generic wound response. It is being made to build to spec. Which is why the literature reaches for Dawkins's term and calls a gall an extended phenotype of the insect — a body part expressed outside the body, in somebody else's tissue. Roughly 13,000 gall-inducing insect species are described, about 2% of insects, though global estimates run from 21,000 to 211,000, so we give it as a range. Set beside the hermit crab, this section stops looking like cheating. One animal spends its effort finding a home; this one spends it on instructions. Neither assembles anything. Both are housed, and both strategies are tens of millions of years old. The phylogeny says otherwise. Interspecific obligate brood parasitism — laying in another species' nest and leaving the rearing to them entirely — evolved independently at least seven times (Sorenson and Payne, 2002): three separate times among the cuckoos, once in the honeyguides, once in waterfowl (the black-headed duck, Heteronetta atricapilla), and twice among songbirds, in the African viduid finches and in the cowbirds. Seven independent origins is the signature of a solution that works. Evolution does not repeatedly stumble into the same catastrophic error in five families across the tree. Recent comparative genomics has gone looking for convergent adaptations across those origins and found them. We are not going to sentimentalise it. Brood parasitism is costly to hosts, and the arms race between parasite and host defence is one of the sharpest in behavioural ecology. The claim here is narrower and it is about our reading, not about the birds: not building is a strategy, not an absence of one. Of everything in this guide, this is the entry we would most like a reader to carry: the option you were told was the failure to do the thing properly may in fact be the thing, arrived at over and over by animals with no contact with each other. Where a weaver spends time and a hermit crab spends searching, a swiftlet spends body. And the entry does not end at the natural history, because it cannot honestly. Those nests are the bird's nest soup of the trade — harvested at industrial scale, farmed in purpose-built concrete houses across Southeast Asia, and among the most expensive animal products in the world. A structure an animal makes out of itself is also, here, a commodity. We are noting that rather than dressing it up. This guide is a catalogue of ways of having somewhere to be, and one of the ways that happens on Earth is that somebody comes and takes it. Every other entry in this guide has an object at the centre of it. This one has a posture. And the shelter that does the work is not built either: it is the huddle, thousands of birds pressed together, rotating slowly so that individuals cycle from the freezing edge to the warm interior and back. If somewhere-to-be requires a structure, the emperor penguin has nowhere and yet manifestly succeeds. The definition has to give. We would rather state the obvious than let it go unsaid: some of us have been housed by other people rather than by rooms, and it counted. A guide that only recognised objects would have missed the entire mechanism. 3 Field Guide A field guide to the Neurodiversity Paradigm What the paradigm actually claims. What it means to say variation instead of disorder. Why the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation — and why that matters. The paradigm, plainly stated Neurodiversity · InLv · Nick Walker open edition L★S
Two frameworks. One is a medical model. One is a paradigm.

Two ways of seeing · the same person Two frameworks. One is a medical model. One is a paradigm. The neurodiversity paradigm doesn't replace medicine. It changes the frame — what counts as a problem, who gets to define it, and what solutions are even on the table. Here are the two frameworks, side by side. Pathology Paradigm Neurodiversity Paradigm Neurological difference is a disorder — a deviation from normal functioning that needs to be identified and treated. Neurological difference is a form of natural variation — one point in the full range of human neurological experience. The goal is to identify what is wrong with the person and move them closer to a neurotypical standard. The goal is to understand the person's actual profile and create conditions where they can thrive as they are. Difficulty is located inside the person — as a deficit, a symptom, a dysfunction. Difficulty is located in the mismatch between the person and their environment — the environment is often the problem. Success means the person appears more neurotypical — masks better, behaves more normatively. Success means the person can live well as themselves — with support that fits their actual needs. The diagnostic manual defines the standard from which the person has deviated. The diagnostic manual is a tool for accessing support — useful but not definitive of who a person is. The person's way of being in the world is a problem to be solved. The person's way of being in the world is a valid mode of human existence. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks
Not a buzzword. A paradigm with a lineage.

The word · its history Not a buzzword. A paradigm with a lineage. The concept of neurodiversity emerged from the Autistic community in the 1990s — not from academia, not from clinicians, but from Autistic and neurodivergent people describing their own experience and organizing around it. The online community InLv (Independent Living on the Autistic Spectrum), founded by Martijn Dekker in 1996, was one of the primary spaces where this thinking developed. Jim Sinclair's foundational essay "Don't Mourn For Us" (1993) and the work of Autism Network International laid the groundwork. The ideas were built through collective lived experience — no single author, and no one handing them down. This history matters. The paradigm was not handed down from above. It was built from the inside — by the people it describes, from their own understanding of themselves. That is its authority. The definition · plainly stated Neurodiversity (the paradigm) Neurodiversity is the infinite variation in neurocognitive functioning within our species — the diversity of human minds. The paradigm holds that this variation is natural and valuable, that there is no one "normal" brain any more than there is one normal ethnicity, and that neurological differences — autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and others — are not deficits to be cured. Some of that divergence is innate; some is made by experience. Neither kind is an error. — after Nick Walker, Neuroqueer Heresies (2021) Neurodivergent Having a mind that functions in ways which diverge significantly from the dominant societal standards of "normal." Not a synonym for disabled — though many neurodivergent people are disabled. A description of neurological difference, not a diagnosis. — term coined by Kassiane Asasumasu (2000); definition after Nick Walker, Neuroqueer Heresies (2021) Neurotypical Having a neurological profile that aligns with dominant societal standards of "normal." Not a synonym for healthy or good — a description of one position in the neurological distribution. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks
The DSM is a tool. Not a truth.

Diagnosis · what it is and isn't The DSM is a tool. Not a truth. The neurodiversity paradigm is not anti-diagnosis. Diagnoses unlock support, accommodations, language, and community. For many people, getting a diagnosis is a profound relief — finally having a word for what their life has been. What the paradigm disputes is the idea that the DSM defines reality — that the categories it creates are natural kinds rather than constructed tools. Diagnostic criteria are written by committees, revised every decade or so, and shaped by cultural assumptions about what counts as "normal" functioning. The DSM describes what deviates from a norm. The paradigm asks: who sets the norm? Who benefits from it? What gets missed when the instrument is calibrated only to detect deviation? Common misreadings · corrected Myth "The neurodiversity paradigm says autism/ADHD isn't real." Fact The paradigm says neurological differences are real — and that framing them as disorders rather than variations changes what we see and what we do. Myth "It only applies to people who are 'mildly' affected." Fact The paradigm applies across the full range of neurological difference — including people with high support needs. Support needs and human value are separate questions. Myth "Neurodiversity means you can't acknowledge that things are hard." Fact The paradigm locates difficulty precisely — in the mismatch between a person and their environment, not in the person's existence. That's a more accurate and more useful place to intervene. Myth "It's just positive spin — trying to make people feel good about deficits." Fact It's a substantive claim about the nature of neurological variation, grounded in disability theory, lived experience, and increasingly, in neuroscience. The goal is accuracy, not reassurance. Myth "If we don't call it a disorder, people won't get help." Fact The paradigm fully supports appropriate support and accommodation — it changes the justification, not the outcome. You don't need to call someone broken to give them what they need. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks
The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation.

The core reframe The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. This is not a metaphor borrowed from cosmology for comfort. It is a precise statement about the relationship between variation and value. The universe produces variation at every scale — in stellar types, in orbital mechanics, in the distribution of matter, in the neurological profiles of its most complex structures. No variation in that distribution is intrinsically wrong. The concept of "disorder" requires a norm, and norms are always constructed by someone, for some purpose, from some position. When the calcium in your bones was forged in a dying star, the universe did not ask whether it was being made correctly. It was matter becoming what matter becomes. Your neurology is the same. It is the universe producing variation — which is what the universe does. The paradigm takes this seriously. It says: difference is not deficit. Variation is not disorder. The distribution is not a hierarchy. Five principles · the paradigm in practice Principle 01 Neurological variation is natural Human neurological profiles exist on a distribution. No point on that distribution is intrinsically correct. Autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and related profiles are not errors — they are positions in a natural range. Principle 02 Disability is often environmental Much of what makes neurodivergence disabling is the mismatch between a person's profile and an environment designed for a narrower range. Change the environment and you change the disability. Principle 03 Support needs don't determine worth Having high support needs is not a measure of human value. Every person, regardless of support needs, deserves to have those needs met and to be treated with full dignity. Principle 04 Autistic and neurodivergent people are the experts The people who live a neurological experience have knowledge about it that outside observers don't. The paradigm centers neurodivergent voices — particularly on questions about neurodivergent lives. Principle 05 Nothing about us without us Decisions about neurodivergent people should involve neurodivergent people. This applies to research, policy, education, clinical practice, and every other domain that shapes neurodivergent lives. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks

The paradigm applied · lived experience What this changes The paradigm isn't only theoretical. It has practical consequences for how neurodivergent people understand themselves and how the people around them should respond. When you adopt the neurodiversity paradigm, certain things shift. The question changes from "what is wrong with this person?" to "what does this person need, and what is the environment failing to provide?" That shift has consequences. It changes what interventions look like. It changes what success looks like. It changes whether the goal is making someone appear more normal or helping them live well as who they are. It also changes how neurodivergent people are allowed to understand themselves — not as broken versions of a normal person, but as one valid configuration of the remarkable variation the universe produces. Practical implications 🔬 In assessment: The goal shifts from identifying deficits to mapping a full profile — strengths, challenges, and what environments and supports allow the person to thrive. 🏫 In education: Accommodation isn't charity — it's the environment doing its job. Universal design benefits everyone. The Autistic student asking for written instructions improves outcomes for the whole class. 🩺 In healthcare: Clinicians learn to ask neurodivergent patients how they experience their symptoms rather than assuming a neurotypical baseline. Sensory needs, communication differences, and masking are taken seriously. 👥 In community: Stimming is welcome. Atypical communication is met with curiosity, not correction. People are not asked to perform neurotypicality as the price of belonging. 💛 In self-understanding: You are not a failed version of a normal person. You are a valid configuration of the variation the universe produces. Your neurology belongs here. L★S. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks

a few neighbours · no captain 22 Emergence No One Is the Leader on murmurations, emergence, and the whole that exceeds its parts — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

The murmuration No one is the leader At dusk, hundreds of thousands of starlings pour across the sky in one rolling, folding shape — splitting, pooling, turning inside out, all as if breathed by a single lung. Watch for an hour and you will never find the bird in charge, because there isn't one. The physics is almost unbearably simple. Each starling attends to only its six or seven nearest neighbours — not a fixed distance but a fixed few companions (Ballerini and the STARFLAG project, 2008). Match their heading, hold your spacing, turn when they turn. That local rule, run by every bird at once, is the entire program. From it: a whole that no bird intends, no bird can see, and no bird commands. Order without a ruler. This has a name — emergence — and once you have seen it, you start seeing it everywhere. Look for the bird giving orders. There is none. That absence is the miracle. one bird tracks seven — the sky moves as one seven neighbours, no captain local rules, global shape No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

the parts every rule, listed more something new knowing the parts does not rebuild the whole more is different the whole is not the sum reduction doesn't run backwards Anti-reductionism More is different In 1972 the physicist Philip Anderson gave this its clearest statement, in an essay called More Is Different. Take reality apart and you find simpler laws — atoms, then particles, all the way down. But the reverse fails: knowing every rule the parts obey does not let you predict, or rebuild, the whole they make. At each new level of scale, entirely new properties, patterns, and laws appear that simply aren't present in the parts. Wetness isn't in one water molecule. Life isn't in one atom. The murmuration isn't in one starling. You don't get them by adding; you get them by relating. Reductionism took the world apart to name it — and then handed us the pieces as if they were the thing. But the whole was never more of the parts. It was something different. The whole isn't more of the parts. It's different from them. — after P. W. Anderson, "More Is Different," 1972 No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

Structure formation The universe self-organised The largest structures there are did exactly the same thing. The infant universe was almost perfectly smooth — but not quite. Faint ripples of denser and emptier, printed into the cosmic microwave background, were the whole seed. Gravity did the rest. Denser patches pulled a little harder, drew in a little more, pulled harder still. Over billions of years matter drained out of the voids and strung itself along threads, until the whole cosmos had woven the cosmic web — galaxies beaded along filaments around enormous bubbles of empty space. No architect drew it. No first galaxy gave the order. Gravity plus a whisper of unevenness, run everywhere at once, was enough. The cosmic web is a murmuration written in gravity — turning so slowly we mistake it for a plan. No blueprint. No architect. Just gravity, a little unevenness, and time. void galaxies on filaments · voids between the cosmic web a flock frozen in gravity No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

the checklist deficits counted the whole the parts don't add up to you you exceed them a person is an emergence realer than the list The whole person You are not a checklist Here is the first thing the flock teaches. A diagnosis is a list of parts: traits itemised, deficits counted, boxes ticked against a baseline. Useful, sometimes. But you can no more rebuild a person from that list than rebuild a murmuration from one bird's rules. A person is what emerges — a whole that is different from, and realer than, the sum of the criteria. The checklist is the parts. You are the murmuration. This is difference first in a new key: not a defective version of a standard human, but a whole that no inventory of missing pieces could ever contain. When a system reduces you to a score, it has confused the feathers for the flight. More is different — and you are the more. A checklist of deficits is a pile of feathers. You are the flock in flight. No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks
A murmuration, not an org chart

no clock the universe keeps 19 Time No Universal Now on relativity, crip time, and the clock that was never the universe's — with a coda by Helen Edgar L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Relativity No master clock Newton assumed one universal time, ticking the same everywhere — a single clock the whole cosmos runs by. For two centuries it seemed obvious. It's also wrong. Einstein showed that simultaneity is relative: two events that happen "at the same time" for me can happen at different times for you, if we're moving differently. Worse for the master clock — time itself runs slower the faster you travel, and slower again the deeper you sit in gravity. This isn't a thought experiment: the GPS in your phone only works because engineers correct for the satellites' clocks ticking faster than clocks on the ground. There is no clock the universe checks against. Every clock keeps its own honest time. The universe keeps no master clock. Why should you? an event A · now B · now time ↑ two observers, two "nows" simultaneity is relative No Universal Now · Stimpunks
The clock is a human invention

9 · 10 · 11 · 12 stamped onto bodies & minds railway time · factory time a convention, not a law Standard time The clock is a human invention So if nature keeps no universal now, where did the one true clock come from? We built it. Synchronized clock time — the shared minute, the timetable, the standardized zones — is barely a century and a half old, an agreement stitched together for railways and factories so trains would not collide and shifts would start together. It is genuinely useful. But it is a convention, not a law of physics — and somewhere along the way we forgot we invented it and began treating it as reality itself, then measuring bodies and minds against it. Be productive on its schedule; wake, work, and rest on its count. The clock stopped being a tool and became a judge. You can't fail a law of nature. You can only fail to fit a rule someone wrote. We built the clock, then mistook it for the sky. No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Crip time Crip time bends the clock Disabled people have a name for living off that clock: crip time. Irving Zola and Carol Gill were among the first to write it into disability studies — a term already alive in the community; it means the extra time and the flexible time — arriving at various intervals, processing at various rates, needing more hours or fewer or simply other ones. The usual reading is that we are failing to keep up. Crip time says the opposite: the schedule was built narrow, and a body meeting it late is information about the schedule. As Alison Kafer puts it, rather than bend disabled minds and bodies to the clock, crip time bends the clock to meet disabled minds and bodies. Which is exactly the move of Minor Worlds: don't fix the person — change the thing around them. Here the thing is time itself. Rather than bend the body to the clock, bend the clock to the body. — after Alison Kafer bend the body to the clock bend the clock to the body room to move same body, two clocks flex time, exploded No Universal Now · Stimpunks

clock time spiral time a smell pulls a thread across decades not a line — a spiral time folds back on itself Monotropic time Spiral time, felt time For many neurodivergent people, time was never a line to begin with. In a monotropic attention tunnel it stretches and folds — an hour of flow vanishes; a bad ten minutes lasts a week. Memory works the same way: not a shelf of dated files but a spiral you re-navigate, where a smell tugs a thread across decades and yesterday can feel further off than childhood. Marta Rose named this spiral time; Helen Edgar, writing of felt time, describes how a moment from years ago might feel like now, while a conversation from yesterday feels distant. It's why "what did you do last weekend?" can land as a demand rather than a question. Not broken clock-reading — a different clock, measured in intensity, not minutes. Bergson called this lived duration; physics, in its own tongue, already agreed that duration bends. Remembering isn't recall. It's re-navigation. — Helen Edgar, More Realms No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Six ways of looking Time travel, broken time None of this is only lovely. Ellen Samuels, in Six Ways of Looking at Crip Time, holds the hard edges too. Crip time is time travel — a wormhole of jerky stops and starts that pulls you out of the tidy line of life-stages, so you meet the frailties of old age while young, or get treated as a child at any age. It is grief time and sick time: the days that swell around a loss, the strange arithmetic where you must earn the very hours in which to be ill. Capacity arrives and departs on its own schedule, and the clock offers no credit for it. So we hold both at once — the flexibility is a gift, and the brokenness is real. Naming it plainly is how we stop grading ourselves against a straight line we were never on. Notlate — keeping a different, honest time. Notbehind — we were never on your line. Notlazy or slow — running a clock the wall can't read. Nota schedule to be fixed to — a schedule that should bend to us. the expected line crip time stops · starts · loops · gaps a wormhole, not a timeline held: gift and grief at once No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Temperature, resistance, frequency — and nothing else

the formula · and what is not in it Temperature, resistance, frequency — and nothing else Nyquist's conclusion is worth quoting at its full width, because the last four words are the whole thing. "the electromotive force due to thermal agitation in conductors is a universal function of frequency, resistance and temperature and of these variables only" Nyquist 1928, p. 111 Not the metal. Not the wire's history, its purity, its manufacture, how much it cost or who made it. He says so outright: "no assumption has been made as to the nature of the two conductors. One may be made of silver and the other of lead, or one may be metallic and the other electrolytic." And the power, in a band: "The average power, transferred from each conductor to the line in the frequency interval dν … is therefore kT dν." Integrate over a bandwidth B and you have the sentence people quote without the paper: kTB. In volts across a resistor R, his equation (1): E² = 4RkT per unit bandwidth. So the floor is not a fault in a component. It is a property of being warm. Every resistor above absolute zero has one, the good ones and the bad ones alike, and there is no version you can buy that doesn't. documented the hiss → a universal quantity Noise power against temperature A straight line rising from the origin, showing available noise power proportional to absolute temperature; the origin is marked absolute zero and labelled unreachable. 0 K · unreachable temperature → noise power kTB no offset · no floor below the floor Figure 2 · the only way to zero is a temperature nobody reaches floor0 K 2 · kTB · a property of being warm The Noise Floor · Stimpunks
A silent resistor would be a perpetual-motion machine

why it cannot be engineered away A silent resistor would be a perpetual-motion machine Nyquist did not measure the floor. He deduced it — and the thing he deduced it from is the second law of thermodynamics. The argument fits in a paragraph. Wire two resistors together, both at the same temperature. Each one's thermal agitation drives a current through the other, so each heats the other, and at equal temperature the two flows must be exactly equal — otherwise heat moves from one body to another of the same temperature, for free. Now suppose that were only true overall, and that in some narrow band of frequencies one conductor gave more than it got. Nyquist's move: put a resonant circuit between them, tuned to that band. Now more power flows one way than the other, and heat has moved from one body to another at the same temperature with no work done. The second law says no. So the hiss is not permitted, it is required. Build a conductor that doesn't do it and you have built a machine that violates thermodynamics. what "you can't remove it" actually means This matters for everything after. The floor is not an unsolved problem. It is not waiting on a better material or a bigger budget. It is the same law that says you cannot un-stir the milk from the tea — and nobody files that under insufficient effort. documented the second law → the floor is compulsory Two resistors at the same temperature Two resistors connected in a loop, with arrows showing equal power flowing in each direction, labelled as required by the second law of thermodynamics. Then the floor became a limit on meaning

Bell System Technical Journal · 1948 Then the floor became a limit on meaning Twenty years on, in the same laboratory's journal, Claude Shannon took that floor and worked out what it costs you in understanding. "The capacity of a channel of band W perturbed by white thermal noise power N when the average transmitter power is limited to P is given by C = W log (P+N)/N" Shannon 1948, Theorem 17 — note "thermal", note it is the same N Rearranged the way it is usually written: C = B log₂(1 + S/N). And then the sentence that closes the door: "It is not possible to transmit at a higher rate by any encoding system without a definite positive frequency of errors." Not "we haven't found a way yet." Any encoding system. No cleverer code, no sharper filter, no more careful listening gets you past it. The noise is in the channel, so it is in the message, and the most you can ever do is trade — more power, more bandwidth, more time, fewer bits. You cannot filter your way to clarity. That is a theorem, and it is the hinge of this whole zine. documented thermal noise → a hard ceiling on communication Capacity against signal-to-noise ratio A logarithmic curve rising steeply then flattening, showing that each doubling of signal power buys a smaller and smaller gain in capacity. ×2 ×4 ×8 signal power → capacity Figure 4 · each doubling buys less than the last · the curve bends, and never turns vertical floor0 K 4 · Shannon · you cannot filter your way to clarity The Noise Floor · Stimpunks
So they stopped trying to delete it

what engineering did next So they stopped trying to delete it Here is the part that gets skipped, and it is the most useful part. Once the floor was proved compulsory, the entire profession changed the question. Nobody spent the next fifty years hunting for a resistor that doesn't hiss. They read the formula and noticed it has three handles on it, and every one of them is a thing you do to the situation rather than to the signal. cool it the noise is kT. Drop T and the floor drops with it — which is why the best receivers live in liquid helium. shield it the thermal floor is compulsory; everyone else's noise is not. Keep it out and only the floor is left. narrow it the noise is kTB. Listen to less of the spectrum and you admit less of the hiss. Notice what none of these is. None of them asks the signal to try harder, and none of them asks the receiver to be better than physics. All three change the conditions the listening happens in. The floor stayed exactly where it was. What moved was everything around it. the sentence this zine is walking toward documented a compulsory floor → design around it floor0 K 5 · cool it · shield it · narrow it The Noise Floor · Stimpunks
Two engineers built the quietest receiver in the world

Crawford Hill · Holmdel, New Jersey · 1964 Two engineers built the quietest receiver in the world Every one of those three moves, in one instrument, pointed at the sky. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson had a twenty-foot horn-reflector antenna and a radiometer built to be quieter than anything else on Earth. A travelling-wave maser — the lowest-noise amplifier then made — cooled by liquid helium to 4.2 K or less. A comparison switch of 0.027 dB loss. And a reference termination that was itself a microwave absorber sitting in liquid helium, twenty litres of it, good for about twenty hours a fill. They were not looking for the beginning of the universe. They were doing careful radio astronomy, and Wilson states the reason for all that helium plainly in his Nobel lecture: "A fundamental limit to the sensitivity of a radiometer is the fluctuation in the power level of this noise." R. W. Wilson, Nobel lecture, 8 December 1978 Read that against Nyquist and it is the same sentence in a different decade. They lowered their own floor on purpose, as far as money and cryogenics allowed, precisely so that anything still left over would have to be real. meanwhile · in the buildings Architecture already knows this Here is the rung that surprised us while we were checking it. The transfer from Shannon to a room is not ours. It is already in the standard, in the standard's own words. ANSI/ASA S12.60 caps background noise in a core learning space at 35 dBA and reverberation at 0.6 s. The Acoustical Society's guidance for architects explains why in a sentence that could have come off Shannon's page: you need an "average differential between speech level and background level (called signal to noise ratio) of about 15 dB, which means the A-weighted background noise level should not exceed about 35 dB." Fifty decibels of teacher, minus thirty-five of room, equals fifteen of margin. A classroom is specified as a channel. And note the profession's instruction about what to do with it: "Rather than boost the instructor's voice through electronic amplification … we have to work to keep the background noise level inside the unoccupied classroom from exceeding 35 dB." Lower the floor. Don't shout. The same story is in the lights and the offices, and the numbers exist: Flicker. Wilkins, Nimmo-Smith, Slater & Bedocs (1989) compared fluorescent tubes on magnetic ballasts — pulsating 43–49% at 100 Hz — against high-frequency electronic ballasts under 7%. Double-blind, crossed over. Headaches and eyestrain more than halved. Wilkins' own later note is the honest part: the effect is "attributable to a minority that is particularly affected." The room was not equally bad for everyone. It was catastrophic for some. Open plan. Kim & de Dear (2013), across a large occupant-survey database, found sound privacy the single largest source of dissatisfaction anywhere in the building: 59% dissatisfied in high-partitioned cubicles, 58% in low, 49% with no partitions — against 18% in private offices. And the thing open plan was sold for did not show up: satisfaction with ease of interaction was no higher than in private offices. We know how to lower a floor. We do it for microwave receivers, for classrooms, for concert halls. the joint that has to be marked Where this stops being physics This is the joint where a chain like this normally cheats, so we are going to stop and say the disanalogy out loud before we say anything else. Auditory filtering is not thermal noise. kTB is a floor set by temperature in a conductor. What happens when we try to follow one voice in a hard-surfaced room is a different phenomenon in a different substrate, and none of Nyquist's numbers carry over. There is no k for a nervous system. Anyone who tells you the physics proves something about an Autistic person's hearing is selling you the naturalistic fallacy with a formula attached, and this collection exists partly to refuse that move. What does carry across is smaller, and it is not a number. It is this: filtering is not free, and a limit is not a defect. Both of those are true in a circuit for reasons we can prove, and true in a room for reasons acousticians act on daily. Whether they are true in the same way for a person is a live research question, not a settled one. What the research says, carefully: Anna Remington and Jake Fairnie, in "A sound advantage: increased auditory capacity in autism" (Cognition, 2017), find that Autistic adults have a larger auditory perceptual capacity — and that this single fact predicts both results at once. We detect additional sounds others miss, which shows up as superior performance on the task we were asked to do and as greater distraction by the sounds nobody asked us to process. That is not a deficit account and it is not a superpower account. It is a capacity account, and it means the sound reaching us was already received. "Tuning it out" is not a filter placed before the input; it is work done after, on material that has already arrived. And acoustics has now gone and asked the question directly. María del Carmen Rosas-Pérez's 2026 doctoral thesis Disabling Acoustics surveyed 311 noise-sensitive people alongside interviews with twelve Autistic adults. Asked whether they can filter out irrelevant background sound, none of the Autistic participants said they find it easy — 96% could not do it or struggled, against 77% of the neurotypical respondents (χ²=25.08, p<.001). Read that second number carefully: everyone in this survey was already noise-sensitive, so it is a difference measured inside a sensitive sample, not a claim about the general population. The noise in the room does not become free by being ignored. Somebody pays for it, downstream, in a currency nobody is measuring. the honest version of the transfer Here is where the analogy actually breaks, and the break is worth more than the resemblance. Thermal noise is stationary: kTB is the same in the tenth hour as in the first, and a receiver that runs all day is no worse off at dusk. Rosas-Pérez found the opposite in people — no habituation, but an accumulation effect, with fatigue and distress building over the short and long term. So the floor in a room is crueller than the floor in a circuit, not merely similar to it. A resistor never gets tired of being warm. We mark this contested because it is: perceptual-capacity accounts are actively argued over, replication is ongoing, and no one study settles a population. We are not going to pretend otherwise to make a stronger ending. contested a floor in a channel → a capacity in a person floor0 K 11 · the transfer · marked contested The Noise Floor · Stimpunks
Nobody asks a receiver to be quieter than kTB

the endpoint Nobody asks a receiver to be quieter than kTB "Just tune it out." "It's not that loud." "You'll get used to it." Those are not our inventions. The first two are what Rosas-Pérez's interviewees reported being told, over and over, since childhood — a pattern her participants' accounts led her to name sensory gaslighting. One of them put the whole argument in a sentence: "The attitude that you often get is, ‘Well, it doesn't bother me and I can't see it, so it doesn't exist and I don't need to do anything about it.’" Participant 10, Disabling Acoustics (Rosas-Pérez, 2026) And "you'll get used to it" has an evidence base worth looking at. The idea that reducing exposure makes sensitivity worse — the reasoning behind telling people not to wear ear protection — traces to a study of five participants, none of them noise-sensitive, listening to two pure tones over two weeks. That is the foundation under advice given to people whose daily lives are nothing like it. Careful measurement, generalised past what it can carry, and handed back to us as a character note. Hold that next to the instrument at Holmdel. Penzias and Wilson had the quietest receiver on the planet and it still had a floor, and not one person in that building thought the floor was a character flaw. They cooled it. They shielded it. They narrowed the band. Then they measured what was left and published it. The move engineering made in 1928 was to stop demanding that the receiver be better than physics, and start changing the conditions the listening happened in. That move is what an accommodation is. Noise-cancelling headphones are shielding. A quiet room is a cooled load. A shorter meeting is a narrower band. None of it is special treatment; all of it is standard practice, applied to people. We are not asking to be exempted from a limit everyone else beats. Nobody beats it. We are asking for the thing every engineer already does when the floor is real: change the room, not the receiver. the argument, stated at its actual strength And we mark it leap, because it is one. The physics does not prove this. Thermal noise entails nothing whatsoever about who deserves a quiet room — that is a moral claim and it has to stand on its own feet. What the physics does is narrower and still worth having: it removes an excuse. It makes "just tune it out" visibly the wrong kind of request — one that no receiver ever built has been able to honour. Not:that thermal noise explains sensory experience. It does not, we say so twice, and the joint is marked. Not:that a sensory limit is a superpower. Remington and Fairnie found a larger capacity, not a gift, and it costs what capacity costs. Not:that the answer is resilience training. You cannot train a resistor below kTB, and nobody has ever tried. Not:that desensitisation is the fix. The measured pattern is accumulation, not habituation — so an intervention built on exposure is not merely useless, it runs the wrong way. Not:that noise is free because it is invisible on the budget. Somebody is paying for every decibel the room was allowed to keep. Not:that physics is the enemy. Every rung of this chain is careful measurement doing exactly what it should. leap change the conditions, not the receiver → accommodation floor0 K 12 · change the room · marked leap The Noise Floor · Stimpunks
Somebody already wrote down how to lower it

a coda, not a rung Somebody already wrote down how to lower it This zine is an argument, and an argument is the least useful thing in the room if you are the one in the room. So: everything above says the floor is set by the environment, therefore the environment is the unit of repair. The work of writing down how to actually do that has been done, by us and by people we learn from, and it is free. Sensory Access at Work is the one-page version for a workplace — ear protection as normal kit, cutting HVAC and open-plan chatter, and the rest of the senses nobody budgets for. Designing Sensory-Safe Spaces is the longer pattern for a room you can change. Neuroception and Sensory Load collects what our complex sensory experiences are actually like, in our own words rather than an observer's. And there is now an instrument. The third study in Disabling Acoustics builds AcoustInA, an Acoustical Inclusivity Assessment tool, tested by thirteen experts across twenty-one real spaces — which means the question how disabling is this room, and by how much has stopped being rhetorical and started being something you can go and score. And the frame that reaches furthest: Sensory Trauma, the name Autism Wellbeing gave to something Autistic people had been describing all along — that the events which harm us need not be the extreme ones, that they arrive through taking a shower or going shopping, and that our responses are proportionate to our genuine, lived experience even when they are mislabelled as something else. Sensory trauma "has been there all along, hiding in plain sight." The hiss at Holmdel had been arriving for thirteen billion years before anyone built an instrument quiet enough to notice it, and when they did they assumed for ten months it was a fault in the equipment. Being persistently told your reading is instrument error does not make it instrument error. floor0 K coda · the room is the unit of repair The Noise Floor · Stimpunks

Not a Line A spectrum was never a severity scale. Split a star's light and you get a fingerprint — the pattern of lines that tells you what it is made of, with no high end and no low end. The spiky profile A faint grid with a dashed horizontal baseline labelled "expected baseline". A jagged line crosses it, rising far above in speech, motor and social and falling far below in sensory, memory and planning — one person, one day, measured against a flat expectation. expected baseline speech sensory motor memory social planning This is the spiky profile — Damian Milton's, building on Francesca Happé — and it already beats what most people mean by spectrum : nobody is uniformly mild or uniformly severe. But look at what it keeps. A better chart is still a chart , drawn against a flat expected baseline, frozen at one moment of assessment. The reverse drops the grid. “Mild” Reports how much your difference costs the person describing it — and is usually written down on a good day, in a quiet room, about someone who was masking hard to be there at all. “High-functioning” Heard as a compliment, used as a refusal. It reads coping in one domain as proof that no support is needed in any other , and then withdraws it. Support needs are plural and specific, and they move by day, room and domain — one number cannot carry them, and the number is what gets budgeted. “A little bit on the spectrum” Treats the spectrum as a quantity of a thing. A spectrum is not a line

Spectroscopy A spectrum is not a line Split white light through a prism and you don't get a ranking from a bad end to a good end. You get a fan of every wavelength at once — red through violet, none higher or lower, just light spread out by colour. Now split the light of a star. Threaded through its spectrum are fine dark and bright lines — and here's the wonder: every element leaves its own exact pattern of them, a fingerprint. Hydrogen signs one way, helium another, iron another still. Reading those lines is the only way we know what the stars are made of. So a spectrum was never a scale of more-or-less. It is a signature of what something is made of. A spectrum doesn't rank a star. It tells you what the star is made of. every wavelength hydrogen iron each element, its own fingerprint a fan, then a signature this is how we read the stars Not a Line · Stimpunks

Not a Line is the twenty-first zine in the Stimpunks series, and it argues for the metaphor Star Stuff already runs on: the sky is organised by constellations, not lines. The credit Already load-bearing, never named We have cited Terry Pratchett three times, always as fiction, always as one turtle among several. Terry Pratchett, Wintersmith (2006) — quoted on stimpunks.org since 2024 That is this project's method. Not a resemblance to it — the thing itself, described better than we have ever managed. And it is not alone: Miss Level's “I store it in other people” carries our mutual-aid page, the neurodiversity-punk hedgehog mascot is named for Esmeralda Weatherwax, and the Librarian is in the Library. Narrativium is his. Lies-to-children is not.

Two lineages, one book Narrativium is his. Lies-to-children is not. Both coinages arrive in the same 1999 book. They come from opposite directions and have completely different parentage, and keeping them straight is the whole job of this spread. Narrativium is Pratchett's, and it is a joke with a knife in it. On the Disc it is an actual element — the substance that makes stories happen, so that the millionth-to-one chance works and the third son succeeds. It is built as a parody of phlogiston, the imaginary fire-stuff that eighteenth-century chemistry invented to explain burning and then had to abandon. The joke: we invent a substance to explain a pattern we have noticed, and sometimes the substance is fictional and the pattern is real. Lies-to-children is not his at all. Jack Cohen and Ian Stewart had been working the idea for years before Discworld carried it anywhere: where lies-to-children actually comes from year book what happens 1994 The Collapse of Chaos Cohen & Stewart discuss the thing: cultural lore passed on in a form that is sufficient but not completely true 1997 Figments of Reality elaborated, and the term used for the difficulty of reducing complex ideas for teaching 1999 The Science of Discworld reaches a mass audience — with a novelist's name on the spine A lie-to-children is the thing your physics teacher does when they tell you electrons orbit the nucleus like planets. It is false. It is also the only way to get you to the next rung, and the honest version of the practice says so out loud: this is a ladder, and you are not at the top of it. Every one of these zines is a lie-to-children. That is not the confession it sounds like — it is the job. The question is only whether we admit the next rung exists. which is the next spread Two lineages converging on 1999 Two tracks. The upper track is Pratchett's Discworld, arriving with narrativium, coined as a parody of phlogiston. The lower track runs from Cohen and Stewart's Collapse of Chaos in 1994 through Figments of Reality in 1997, carrying lies-to-children. Both meet at The Science of Discworld in 1999. The method, credited First Sight and Second Thoughts Here is the debt paid properly. Everything this site does procedurally is a witch's two-part discipline, and Pratchett named both halves better than our documentation does. First Sight is seeing what is actually in front of you — not what you expected, not what the story says should be there. It is harder than it sounds, because the expectation arrives first and feels like observation. Our whole Field Guides collection is First Sight as a form: seven of the twelve arrive independently at there is no standard one of these, which is what you find when you go and look instead of consulting the type specimen in your head. The wood wide web rhymes so beautifully with mutual aid that it got past us in three pieces before Karst, Jones and Hoeksema's 2023 review made us go back. First Sight is not scepticism. It is the refusal to let a lovely pattern do your looking for you. Second Thoughts are the thoughts that watch the first ones. Not doubt — supervision. The Industrial Revolution books A technology arrives. Who pays? There is a run of Discworld novels that all do the same trick: drop one modern innovation into a medieval city and then refuse to look away from the bill. The pattern is consistent enough to be a method. Moving Pictures gets cinema. The Truth gets the printing press and the newspaper. Going Postal gets the post — stamps, a network, a man made to run it. Making Money gets paper currency and modern banking. Raising Steam gets the railway. In each, the innovation genuinely works, genuinely delights, and genuinely costs somebody something, and the book stays in the room for the third part. That third part is rare. The default technology story has two acts — the invention, and the wonder — and stops before the bill arrives. Pratchett's have three, and the third is always about who was standing where the thing landed: the clacks workers on the towers, the golems who are property, the engravers whose craft the press makes worthless, the people the railway timetable now owns. The question is never “does it work?” It works. That is what makes the question interesting. the shape of an Industrial Revolution book Which lands squarely on techno-solutionism and on the Luddite Sensibilities Stimpunks argues for — and it is worth being precise, because the word gets used as an insult by people who do not know what it means. The Luddites were not against machines. They were skilled workers objecting to a specific arrangement in which the machine's gains went one way and its costs went another. They broke the frames of the employers cutting wages and left the others alone. That is not technophobia. That is a question about distribution, asked with a hammer. It is also the question this site keeps asking about a different set of machines. An assessment instrument works. A behaviour protocol works, for some value of works. Who pays? is the question How We Got Here exists to keep open, and Pratchett was running the experiment in a fantasy city for thirty years. Two acts or three The default technology story runs invention then wonder and stops. The Industrial Revolution novels add a third act asking who pays, with examples: the clacks workers, the golems who are property, the engravers the press displaced, and the people the timetable owns. the default story invention wonder stop what Pratchett does invention wonder who pays? clacks crew golems engravers timetabled it works. that is what makes it interesting the Luddites broke some frames, not all a question about distribution Figure 6 · the act most stories skip One Atom of Justice · Stimpunks

The clacks GNU In Going Postal there is a semaphore network across the continent — towers, shutters, a code, and crews who live up there. Early in the book a young man named John Dearheart dies on one. His father puts his name into the Overhead — the working channel the towers use to talk to each other, which no customer ever sees — with three letters in front of it. G: send it on. N: do not log it. U: at the end of the line, turn it around and send it back. GNU John Dearheart, up and down the towers, indefinitely, for as long as the network stands. A man's not dead while his name is still spoken. Terry Pratchett, Going Postal (2004) — see the colophon on wording Pratchett died on 12 March 2015. Within days, readers on the Discworld subreddit proposed doing the obvious thing to the network we actually have: put him in the Overhead. An HTTP response header, invisible in the page, carried on every request, logged by nobody, meaning nothing to any browser: X-Clacks-Overhead: GNU Terry Pratchett As of today, this site sends it. Every page you load from starstuff.earth carries that header. You can see it in your browser's network panel, under response headers, on this page or any other. It does nothing. That is the point — it is the exact structural joke, an unlogged message that costs one line of config and turns around at the end of the line. stated plainly This is a fan convention, not Pratchett's instruction. He did not ask for it, his estate did not originate it, and nobody should read the header as endorsement by anyone. It is a thing readers started doing in March 2015 because the book gave them a shape for grief and no better one has turned up since. It also belongs in this collection more exactly than anything else here. An easter egg on this site is a real piece behind a small door — and the smallest door we have is a header nobody has to read. GNU, turning around at the end of the line A row of clacks towers. A message travels left to right along the top, marked G for pass it on and N for not logged, then U turns it around at the last tower and it travels back along the bottom, repeating indefinitely. Posterior cortical atrophy The embuggerance In December 2007, at fifty-nine, Pratchett announced that he had posterior cortical atrophy. He gave it a word of his own almost immediately, and the word was not battle or journey. PCA is a rare presentation of Alzheimer's disease that attacks from the back of the brain forward. Because those posterior regions do visual and spatial processing, it takes the seeing before it takes the remembering — reading, judging where things are, recognising what your eyes are pointed at. It typically arrives earlier than typical Alzheimer's, in the mid-fifties or early sixties, which is exactly where it found him. He called it an embuggerance. A nuisance of an unusually total kind. Something in the way. Not a battle he was losing. Not a lesson. A thing that was in the way, named accurately, out loud, by the person it was in the way of. why the word matters here Then he kept writing, by changing the method rather than the ambition: dictating to his assistant Rob Wilkins, and using speech-recognition software. He was knighted in 2009. He went on publishing until he died on 12 March 2015. We are putting this in because Stimpunks is a disability organisation and this is what accommodation actually looks like from inside: the output was never the thing that had to change. The interface did. Dictation is not a lesser way of writing a book; it is a way of writing a book. That is the entire argument of the disability rights movement, demonstrated at length by a man producing novels while his occipital lobe went. What we are not doing with this. Not treating his diagnosis as inspiration, not describing him as brave for having a disease, and not diagnosing him with anything he did not name himself — including anything on our own side of the neurodivergence line. He told us what he had. That is the only source we need or should want. The method changed, the ambition did not Two rows. Before the diagnosis: typing, leading to novels. After: dictation and speech recognition software, leading to novels. Death's challenge One atom of justice Now the objection. In Hogfather, Death is explaining to his granddaughter why humans need to believe in things like the Hogfather. Susan pushes back — and he says the hardest thing anyone has said to this website. YOU THINK SO? THEN TAKE THE UNIVERSE AND GRIND IT DOWN TO THE FINEST POWDER AND SIEVE IT THROUGH THE FINEST SIEVE AND THEN SHOW ME ONE ATOM OF JUSTICE, ONE MOLECULE OF MERCY. AND YET—Death waved a hand. AND YET YOU ACT AS IF THERE IS SOME IDEAL ORDER IN THE WORLD, AS IF THERE IS SOME . . . SOME RIGHTNESS IN THE UNIVERSE BY WHICH IT MAY BE JUDGED. Death, in Hogfather (1996), verbatim — the capitals and the two italics are the novel's own. Checked against the book, not an aggregator. Read our signature phrase against that — Love you down to your star stuff, which is on thirty-five of these pages. The star stuff is nucleosynthesis and it is true. The loving is not in the atoms. You can grind this entire site down — every citation, every field guide, every carefully sourced figure — and sieve it, and there will be no molecule of and therefore you belong in the powder. We know. It is written into the house rules: no naturalistic fallacy, and the line that closes No. 35 — that variation persists in nature is not why difference deserves welcome. The physics does not entail the love. It never did. Anyone who tells you the universe validates your existence because carbon is common is selling you the same trick the eugenicists sold, with a nicer conclusion attached. So what is the second sentence doing there? Pratchett's answer arrives a few lines earlier in the same conversation, and it is the ladder from spread four in the novelist's half of the shop: YES. AS PRACTICE. YOU HAVE TO START OUT LEARNING TO BELIEVE THE LITTLE LIES. “So we can believe the big ones?” YES. JUSTICE. MERCY. DUTY. THAT SORT OF THING. Death and Susan, Hogfather (1996), verbatim That is lies-to-children, arrived at from the fiction side. Cohen and Stewart's ladder gets you from planetary electrons to quantum mechanics. Death's gets you from the tooth fairy to justice, mercy, duty — the big lies, which are not found in the powder either, and which exist anyway because enough people practised on the small ones and then acted as if the big ones were real. Susan makes exactly our objection — “people have got to believe that, or what's the point—” — and Death's reply is three words long and closes the argument: MY POINT EXACTLY. Death, Hogfather (1996) The point is not that it is out there. The point is that it has got to be believed. And a few lines later he says the other half, helping her onto the horse: NO. YOU NEED TO BELIEVE IN THINGS THAT AREN'T TRUE. HOW ELSE CAN THEY BECOME? Death, Hogfather (1996) — quoted at Stimpunks under Becoming, where the capitals and the italic on become had been lost How else can they become. Not a consolation — a construction schedule. Justice is not a discovery, it is a thing being built, and belief is the scaffolding you stand on while you build it. That is the same grammar as the falling angel meeting the rising ape: we are the animal that is on its way somewhere, in both directions at once, and the meeting place is made of things we decided to mean. And there is one more beat, which could have been written for this site specifically. Death points out that stars explode and worlds collide and there is almost nowhere in the universe a human can survive — and yet you believe that a bed is a normal thing. He calls it the most amazing talent, and then, being Death, calls it a very special kind of stupidity. Both of those are correct at once, which is the register this entire project is written in. The physics Only in relation A particle, on its own, doesn't quietly hoard its properties in private. In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics, a system's properties become definite only relative to another system it interacts with (Rovelli, 1996). There's no view from nowhere in which an electron already "has" its values, waiting to be read. What is real is what happens between systems. An honest caution before we go further: RQM is one interpretation of quantum theory among several, and physicists still argue it. We're not smuggling physics in to prove anything about people. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. "There is no absolute, observer-independent description of a person that tells the whole truth about themselves." — Helen Edgar, We Are Made of Relations (2026) the same particle, two situations in isolation ? no fact of the matter in relation ↑ definite — for that system a value is something two systems have between them not something one holds alone Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

count the outcomes two coins — distinct H H H T T H T T 4 two bosons — identical H H H T T T (H T = T H) 3 the missing 4th is the tell nature can't tell the two apart so it doesn't count them apart What is actually real Count the bosons Flip two coins and you get four outcomes — HH, HT, TH, TT — because the coins are distinct objects, so "heads-then-tails" and "tails-then-heads" are two different things. Do the same with two identical quantum particles — two bosons — and nature counts only three. The two mixed cases collapse into one, because there is no fact about which particle is which (Webster, 2026). That vanished fourth outcome is measurable, and it is the tell: what's fundamental isn't the standalone particle. It's the symmetry — the relation — that says these two can't be told apart. "What is fundamentally real are not particles as such, but rather the laws and symmetries … that govern their behaviour." — George Webster, IAI (2026) Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

Relation before relata Made of each other Entangled particles can't be described one at a time. The pair carries correlations the parts simply don't have on their own — measure one and you've said something about the other, however far apart they've drifted. The physicist-philosopher Karen Barad calls this intra-action: not the meeting of two things that already exist separately, but a relation out of which the parts come to be distinct at all (Barad, 2007). The relation is first. The "things" are what it leaves behind. There's a word for the human version, one Helen draws from Barad: intradependence — not two finished people who later depend on each other, but selves made of each other from the start. Deeper than interdependence. We don't arrive as sealed units who only later reach out. We are, from the start, relations wearing the shape of a person. inter- vs intra- inter-action two wholes, then a link intra-action one relation, then parts the bond is the origin, not the bridge the parts are what the relation leaves behind made of each other Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

what comes first difference · relation objects (late arrivals) first the differentiating, then the things the object is what got built The order of things Difference, then relation Reading the physics through Deleuze, George Webster puts the metaphysics plainly: "Objects do not come first and then differ; rather, objects emerge out of more fundamental processes of differentiation." — George Webster, reading Deleuze (2026) First there is difference and relation; the tidy, standalone object is the late arrival — the thing that gets built. It's the same move Star Stuff has made from the start in Why Difference Comes First: the measured, average "normal person" was never the ground floor. Difference is. Turn it one notch further and relation is. Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

What it means for us The gap is two-way When an Autistic person and a non-Autistic person misunderstand each other, the old story put the deficit in one of them — the Autistic one. Damian Milton named the truer picture: the double empathy problem. The misunderstanding runs both ways — a mismatch between two differently-built minds, not a fault inside one (Milton, 2012). Relational physics says: of course it does. The trouble was never sitting inside a single object. It lives in the relation. Helen widens double empathy into DEEP — Dynamic, Embodied, Ecological, Political — because the mismatch isn't a static glitch between two heads. It's alive, bodily, environmental, and shaped by power. Change the lighting, the pace, the assumptions, the room — and the "deficit" you were measuring moves. It was in the relation all along. where the gap lives one mind another mind not one side — the space between double empathy, made DEEP a mismatch is a property of the pair it has no single owner Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

the ARLES ladder Systems Environment Lived exp. Relational + Regulation Attention near the base — on purpose regulation lives inside the relational rung not a private skill Up the ladder Regulation is relational This is why, in Stimpunks' ARLES ladder, Relational sits near the base — and why Regulation lives inside it. Regulation isn't a skill you own privately and keep failing to deploy. We co-regulate: nervous systems settle, or don't, in relation to other bodies, other pacing, a room that holds us or doesn't. So the support that actually works doesn't try to repair an isolated person. It changes the relational field — the sensory environment, the pacing, the temporal texture, a community's capacity to hold different ways of being. If it's not working, it's not the person. It's the environment, the relationships, or the system. — Stimpunks · ARLES "We are not broken objects. We are relations, all of us still becoming." — Helen Edgar (2026) Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

Held with care What we are not saying Relational physics rhymes with how we already know support works. It is not a licence for the traps that show up whenever "quantum" meets "people." Notquantum mysticism. No "quantum consciousness," no mind magically collapsing reality. In physics the "observer" is any system at all — a speck of dust will do. Not"everything is connected" as a vibe. This is a specific claim about how properties come to be, not a warm fog. Notdissolution into sameness. Being a relation doesn't melt you. Where two rivers meet they run braided for miles — one current, still distinct. The spiky profile survives the merge. Notphysics proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. Our belonging stands on its own; the physics only rhymes with it. Nota duty to stay connected. Relational doesn't mean always available. Some of us need less contact, not more — and need is not a rank. the confluence, not the blur one channel · two waters · still distinct relation is not erasure difference survives belonging Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

The receipt There was never a No. 37 Count the zines on this site and you will find a hole. Nos. 36 and 38 sit next to each other with nothing in between. This is the page about the hole, and it has to start by correcting itself. We were going to tell you we skipped it by accident. That is not what happened, and it took about four minutes of reading our own notes to find out — which is roughly how long the check always takes, and roughly how often it gets skipped. What actually happened: on 11 August 2026 a zine about the last stage of a supernova remnant was drafted and given the next number in the sequence, No. 37. Then it stopped, because it leaned on Helen Edgar's writing closely enough that the honest thing was to ask her before building it. So it waited. And while it waited, seven other pieces were finished and took the next seven numbers. When it was finally built on 13 August it was No. 45 — The Cloud Phase. Our own decision log is blunt about what that means: The number moved 37 → 45 because seven pieces shipped while it sat — the number says when, and that gap is the rule working, not a renumbering. DECISIONS.md · 13 August 2026 So 37 is not a mistake. It is a receipt for a question asked rather than assumed. Which is a much better thing to find in your numbering than a tidy unbroken run, and it is why this page fills the slot without pretending to repair it. Why the false version mattered enough to catch. “We lost track and skipped one” is a smoother story than “we deferred a piece to ask someone, and the sequence recorded the wait.” Smoother stories travel further, which is exactly the failure Too Good to Check catalogues and the broadside hands out on a card. Shipping it here would have been this house committing its own named fault, in a piece about honesty, for a joke. The famous one Your temperature is not 37 The most famous 37 in the world is a body temperature, and it is out of date by about a century and a half. It comes from one man with a very long thermometer. Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich published Das Verhalten der Eigenwärme in Krankheiten in Leipzig in 1868, reporting over a million readings from roughly 25,000 patients. His instrument was about a foot long and had to sit in the armpit for twenty minutes. The mean of that vast, patient, hand-tallied dataset was 37 °C — 98.6 °F — and he called it the physiological point. It was a fine number. It is no longer our number. In 2020 Myroslava Protsiv and colleagues put three American datasets spanning 157 years side by side and found body temperature has been falling the whole time, monotonically, by about 0.03 °C per birth decade: decline in mean body temperature by birth cohort cohort span change men born 1800 → 1997 −0.59 °C women born 1890 → 1997 −0.32 °C both per birth decade −0.03 °C Modern adult oral means land nearer 36.6 °C. So 37 is not wrong the way a typo is wrong — it is an accurate 1868 average that got promoted to a constant and then quietly stopped describing anybody. Nobody lied. A number was measured carefully, published honestly, and then outlived the population it was measured on — and kept being taught. the failure mode, without a villain Our own field card calls this one the number that went stale, and it is the third of six ways a fact goes wrong. Worth sitting with, because it is the failure mode with no bad actor in it at all: the only way to catch it is to go back and measure again. How long to look Spend 37% not choosing There is a second 37, and this one is a theorem. It answers a question everybody actually has: how long should I keep looking before I commit? Set it up strictly. Options arrive one at a time, you can rank the ones you have seen, and every decision is final — no going back to number three. The optimal strategy has a shape that is not obvious: look at the first 1/e of them and reject every one, however good, then take the first option after that which beats everything you have seen. 1/e is 0.368. Roughly 37%. And the payoff is the strange part: It finds the single best option about 37% of the time — whether there are a hundred options or a hundred million. the 1/e law of best choice The number does not decay with scale. A third of a very long search is a lot of looking, and it is still the right amount. Which is where this zine's own subject walks back in. The Cloud Phase spent its looking time. It could have been built on 11 August with an assumption in it; instead it sat while a question went out, and the sequence recorded the waiting as an absence. The number of the wait, and the fraction of any search you are supposed to spend not choosing, are the same 37. And that is a coincidence. A delightful one, sitting right at the centre of this piece, with nothing behind it. The next spread is about not pretending otherwise — because this is exactly the moment a zine reaches for a mechanism it does not have. We will not solder these together

Three unrelated 37s We will not solder these together Here is the trap this whole zine is walking toward, and it is the most fun thing about the number, which is precisely why it is dangerous. Three 37s in a row. A body temperature. An optimal stopping fraction. And the number people apparently reach for when told to be random. Lay them beside each other and something in the head starts reaching for a because — as if the brain picks 37 because of something to do with 1/e, or as if 37 recurs because 37 is somehow special. They are not connected. Not loosely, not deeply, not at all: what each 37 actually is the 37 what kind of thing 37 °C a 19th-century arithmetic mean of armpits, in one unit 37% 1/e, rounded — a limit, in no unit at all “pick 37” a fact about people, in a base-ten range of 1–100 The 37 in the temperature is a decimal accident of the Celsius scale — in Fahrenheit the same fact is 98.6, and the coincidence evaporates. The 37 in the stopping rule is 36.79 rounded, and it is a percentage, not a count. The 37 people pick only exists because somebody offered them 1 to 100. A coincidence dressed as a mechanism is not a small mistake. It is the specific move that lets a real finding get pointed at people, and it is why this collection exists. the fault this piece was built to name This is the same shape as Five Sigma's complaint: keeping the authority of a number while dropping the practice that earned it. And it is why the joke here stops short of a punchline. Three 37s is a nice thing to notice and nothing to conclude from. We are allowed to enjoy it. We are not allowed to explain it. The genuinely lovely part Thirty-seven, honestly Strip out the coincidences and the number is still worth the apology. All of the following is checkable on paper in a couple of minutes, which is the nicest property a fact can have. It is the 12th prime. Reverse the digits and you get 73, which is also prime — and which is the 21st. The digits of the number reverse, and so do the digits of its position. That is not deep. It is just very pleasing, and it is exact. It is the third star number: 6n(n−1)+1 gives 1, 13, 37, 73 — so 37 and 73 are consecutive star numbers as well as digit reversals of one another. Which means a site built entirely out of starfields skipped the star number. It is also the fourth centered hexagonal number, 3n(n−1)+1: 1, 7, 19, 37. Triple it and you get 111, because 111 = 3 × 37. So 37 × 6 = 222, 37 × 9 = 333, and so on up — a repdigit machine hiding in a prime. And the biggest one: every positive whole number, without exception, is a sum of at most 37 fifth powers. Thirty-seven is exactly enough and no smaller number will do. That is the value of g(5) in Waring's problem, and Chen Jingrun nailed it down in 1964. Every number there has ever been, or will be, is thirty-seven fifth powers or fewer. It is a strange thing to be the exact size of. g(5) = 37 None of this makes 37 special in a way that means anything about anybody. It just makes it good company — which is all we promised it.
