Held loosely on purpose The number people reach for The third 37 is the one everybody wants to be true, and it is the one this zine holds at arm's length — which is the honest thing to do and also, awkwardly, the whole point of the site. Ask a lot of people to pick a random number from 1 to 100 and the answers are not flat. They avoid round numbers, avoid the ends, avoid the exact middle, avoid repeated digits — and they pile up on a few odd, prime-looking numbers. In a survey of roughly 200,000 responses run by Veritasium, 37 and 73 came out near the top, close to tied. We like this a great deal. We are still going to say what it is: Contested A large, self-published survey, not a refereed finding. The data is real and the effect is plausible, but we have not read a peer-reviewed paper reporting it, and every account of it we could reach is secondary. It is on this spread as somebody's experiment, never as a law about human beings. What the result would mean, if it holds, is nicer than the number anyway. Primes feel random to us because nothing divides them — no pattern to catch the eye, so the mind reads “no structure” and offers it up as randomness. But primes are the most rigidly determined objects in arithmetic. There is nothing arbitrary about 37 whatsoever. So the thing we reach for when we want to be unpredictable is one of the least arbitrary things there is. That is a fact about us, not about the number. if the finding holds Which is a familiar shape here. Something gets called disordered, or random, or arbitrary, because the person looking cannot see the rule it is running on. The Lines We Drew has the long version. Filed late This page is younger than No. 46 Now the part where this zine has to be honest about itself, because everything above was built on a rule it is currently breaking. On this site, the number records when. That is load-bearing and stated everywhere: the changelog is dated by number, the fact-check ledger is keyed by number, and pieces cite each other by number with no redirects. It is the reason the gap at 37 was information in the first place. And this page has 37 in the corner while being newer than No. 46. Its own number is the least reliable claim on it. Leap The number in the corner is not a date. Every other number on this site is. This one is a slot we went back and occupied, so the sequence now reads as though this arrived between Nos. 36 and 38, and it did not. Marked with How We Got Here's notation, borrowed for exactly one claim, because a piece about our own honesty cannot leave its weakest link unlabelled. Which is the oldest joke in time travel and also its actual structure: go back to repair the past and the repair becomes part of the past you were trying to fix. There is no version of this page that fills the gap and leaves the record of the gap intact. It has a building on it now, with a plaque explaining that the lot was empty for a reason. The sequence has a hole in it, and the sequence still works. Nothing about you needs to be contiguous in order to count. the only thing this zine actually wants to say Not:an accident. We did not lose track of a number. What this page costs, stated plainly Filling a deliberate gap is not free. Owed, Not Earned Inclusion safety is the first stage of psychological safety. It is not a reward for the worthy, and not a prize you win. It is the baseline we owe one another simply for being here. Be human. Be harmless. Meet both and you are in · that is the whole qualification 01 No litmus test Not your diagnosis, your speech, your output, your history, or how easily others can make sense of you. There is no audition at this threshold. 02 Worth, not worthiness Worth is a thing you have, entire, already. Worthiness is no one's to weigh at the door — and if it is ever anyone's business, it is not here. 03 The one disqualifier Acceptance is owed to everyone. So is safety from harm — and harm is the single thing that can cost you your place. Not your way of being. Only harm. “Inclusion safety is not earned but owed. Every human has title to it as a nonnegotiable right.” Timothy R. Inclusion is a judgment about your worth — which you have, entire, already — not a verdict on your worthiness, which is no one's to weigh at the door. iii · be human, be harmless What does it take to qualify? Two things. Meet both and you are in. We say the second part out loud, because a welcome that tolerated harm would betray the very people it exists to keep safe. iv · the binding thing Read Douglass for every characteristic, not race alone. When we include one another, we set our differences beneath a deeper, common thing — and agree that the common thing matters more. v · older than humanity The common thing beneath our differences is older than humanity. You, and we, and everyone at this door were made in the same stars — the same hydrogen from the same beginning, the same calcium and iron from the same dying giants. Kinship is not a courtesy we extend to you. It is the material you are made of. vi · come in So: if you have flesh and blood, we accept you. If you are made of stars — and you are — you are already one of us. Come in. Rest. You are owed this. “I know of no rights of race superior to the rights of humanity.” Frederick Douglass · Our Composite Nationality · Boston, 7 December 1869 The four doors Inclusion is the first of four. Beyond it lie the freedom to learn , to contribute , and to challenge the status quo — but none of them open until this one does. So we hold this one open first, and for everyone. Designing for Paper Notes & Rationale · how the broadsides are built Every number here was arrived at by printing something and finding out it was wrong. This page is the working — the spec, the inks, the gates, and the faults that no gate can see. Backing material for the Print collection , which argues what earns a sheet. This one covers how a sheet is made, and is deliberately outside the reading chain — it is reference, not a stop on the tour. For the site-wide visual language, see The Design System ; this page is only about the artifacts made for paper.

The format One fixed specification for every sheet. The point of a fixed format is that eight different arguments come off the printer as the same object — a rack, not a pile — and that a reader in any country gets the same artifact from the same file. 190 × 259 mm The intersection of A4 and US Letter. At 9 mm page margins, A4 gives a box of 192 × 279 mm and Letter gives 198 × 261 — so a sheet inside both is one file that prints uncropped in either country, with no “US version” to maintain and get out of sync. 9 mm margins, not 10 At 10 mm the Letter box is 259.4 mm against a 259 mm sheet. That 0.4 mm of slack was thin enough for sub-pixel rounding to tip the whole thing onto a third page . Found by printing to PDF and counting, not by reading the arithmetic — the arithmetic said it fit. Two sides, A and B Side A is the face; side B does the work. Enforced structurally: each side is a .sheet element with page-break-after on the first, so the file is two printed sides or it is broken. Breakpoint below 700 px The one that looks like a screen concern and isn't. Print media queries resolve against the page box, not the screen — and the narrowest real page box here is A4 less its margins, 192 mm, or about 726 px. A mobile breakpoint set at 820 px was therefore matching on paper , collapsing a two-column card into one 190 mm column at roughly 95 characters a line, long enough that side B overran and was silently clipped.
Ink on white, in both media

Ink on white, in both media The rest of the site is light on dark, and starstuff.css inverts it inside @media print so a zine survives being printed. The broadsides never enter that machinery: they are drawn as ink on white on screen and on paper, so what you see in a browser is a preview of the sheet rather than a different design that will be converted later. The reason is blunt. Browsers leave Background graphics off by default , so a light-on-dark page reaches paper blank — which is exactly what happened to 44 of the 46 pages on this site until somebody measured it. A broadside cannot depend on a reader finding a checkbox in a print dialog, because the whole premise is that it gets handed to people and photocopied by people who never saw the web page at all.

Borders, not backgrounds Same constraint, one level down. The registration bar across the top of each sheet is a border-top , not a background — because borders survive that checkbox and background colours do not. An earlier design put the cream stock in a background-color and a halftone in a background-image , and neither ever reached paper. What did print was the gold misregistration shadow, because it happened to be text: at 1.84:1 on white, a faint smudge. The reader got the flaw of the effect and none of its charm.

Type Atkinson Hyperlegible Next throughout , with Space Mono for labels and chrome. Atkinson was drawn by the Braille Institute for letterform distinction at exactly the small sizes a hand-out uses — the 6–9 pt range where a broadside does most of its work. No display serif. Fraunces was inherited from the earlier risograph costume and went with it. It is Bone Song 's editorial voice, not a broadside's, and more to the point it is a high-contrast serif whose hairlines are the first thing to drop out of a photocopy or a tired laser printer — which is most of a broadside's life. Worth recording that before this was fixed, the sheets loaded Atkinson and rendered 0% of their characters in it. The star is drawn, not typed. Atkinson has no U+2605 , so a typed ★ silently comes from whatever font the reader's system happens to supply — measurably so: the character rendered at exactly the generic-serif advance width. For a logotype on a sheet meant to print identically everywhere, that is not good enough, so the L★S mark is an SVG path with an inner radius 0.382 of the outer, filled currentColor so it inherits the surrounding ink.

Two spot inks An explicit exception to a house rule. starstuff.css flattens all five accents to near-black inside @media print on purpose — print is monochrome by default here. The broadsides keep two colours each, declared as literal hex rather than aliased to the --sp-* tokens, and forced through with print-color-adjust: exact . They have to be declared literally because the screen accents measure 1.6–2.7:1 on white and are unusable as paper ink. So each is the house hue darkened until it clears WCAG AA on white, and each sheet takes a different pair — which means the bar across the top tells you which sheet you are holding when five of them are face-down in a stack. That is the registration bar's real job. Gold · #92400e 7.1:1 · L★S & Elements faces Violet · #5b21b6 9.0:1 · Six Ways & BGUTI faces Pink · #9d174d 7.9:1 · Refuse face, Elements verso Green · #166534 7.1:1 · Owed face, Shared Air verso Cyan · #164e63 9.1:1 · Water & Air faces, BGUTI verso

What we check, and how For about a year, both of the original broadsides said “two-sided single sheet” in their own copy, and both were lying. Measured by printing to PDF and counting pages: the L★S sheet came out as three sides on US Letter and two on A4 — a different physical object depending on the reader's country — and Six Ways came out as four sides on both. Nothing in the repository could see it, because the checks that existed measured whether ink was legible, not whether it landed on the page. Three committed tools now run before a sheet ships. Each exists because something shipped broken in a way the others could not detect. tools/check-sheets.mjs Prints each sheet at both paper sizes and counts pages, and separately measures content height against the box. The separate measurement is the subtle part: a fixed-height sheet whose content overruns does not paginate — it is silently clipped — so a clean page count can still hide a cut-off final line. It measures at the real page-box width rather than a desktop viewport, for the breakpoint reason above. tools/check-contrast.mjs Composites every text element against its real ancestor background stack, on screen and under print emulation, at WCAG AA. It runs a separate pass for SVG text fills, because color never reaches fill and a CSS-only pass is structurally blind to diagrams. The print pass composites against the bare white sheet rather than trusting emulated print media, which still paints backgrounds a real reader will not get. tools/check-markup.mjs Reads source rather than the DOM, and that is the design: it catches markup the browser silently rewrites — nested or

Take it and reuse it The whole specification is four numbers and two rules: 190 × 259 mm at 9 mm margins , ink on white in both media, borders rather than backgrounds for anything that must survive to paper, and two inks darkened until they clear AA on white. Everything else is editorial. The sheets are CC BY-SA 4.0 , the tools are in tools/ , and the whole repository is public. If you make broadsides for your own community with this, that is the intended outcome, not a tolerated one — and you will not need our colours, only the method. The Quillery Eight Esmx · drawn for the sky Our mascot is a bundle of spikes whose tips come loose and drift, as if they are made of energy . This page takes that literally eight times over, and puts a source line under every one. Esmx the Porkypine — part pig, part porcupine — is the Stimpunks Foundation's community mascot, drawn by Kaya Oldaker and released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with an explicit invitation: feel free to customise, make variants of Esmx to represent your community. This is us taking that up. Star Stuff's community is a collection about what the sky is made of, so ours are eight Esmx pointed at the sky. What this is, and what it is not These are variants, not reproductions. Kaya's original artwork is not reproduced here and is not ours to redraw stroke for stroke; it lives at its own page , with a download of every official variant. What is on this page is Esmx built again from scratch in this site's line, the way the A'Tuin drawing and the twelve cosmic eggs were. The licence is share-alike , this whole site is already CC BY-SA 4.0, and the credit is at the foot of every drawing below. One figure, eight manes — and that is the design, not a shortcut. The official variant set works exactly this way: the same Esmx, recoloured, so a community can make one that looks like itself. The mane is where Esmx is meant to be remixed, so the mane is where all eight of these differ. It also keeps the promise the drawings make: if the figure were redrawn each time, a difference between two cards could be an accident of the pen rather than the thing the card is about. Every drawing carries alt text, because the source asked. Kaya's page ships alt text for each official variant with the instruction if you share these, include alt text . Honouring a licence is the easy half of honouring a maker. Each drawing below has a real description, not a filename.

The eight Esmx in Emission A drawing of Esmx — a porkypine, part pig, part porcupine, with a teal and pink colour scheme, an earring in one ear and a missing chunk in the other. Esmx's mane sweeps to the right and breaks apart into a row of separate vertical bright lines, like the emission spectrum of a star. One line, taller than the rest, is labelled helium, 587.6 nanometres. He · 587.6 nm found in the Sun first

Esmx in Emission No. 1 · the mane as a spectrum Split a star's light and it does not come out as a smear. It comes out as separate bright lines , at fixed places, and each set of lines belongs to one element and no other. It is the closest thing astronomy has to a signature: you can name what a thing is made of from a distance you will never cross, without touching it, without asking. On 18 August 1868 , watching a total eclipse from Guntur in India, Pierre Jules Janssen found a yellow line in the light of the Sun's prominences that sat where no known element sat. Norman Lockyer, working in London, reached the same line that October and named the thing behind it helium , for the Sun. Nobody found it on Earth for another twenty-seven years. An element was catalogued in a star before anyone had held it. Esmx's mane already does the thing the prism does: it starts as one mass and comes apart into discrete, separated, differently-coloured lines. That is not a metaphor we added. It is in the original design , and in the alt text — the spikes trail off and separate. Sources: Janssen's eclipse observation, 18 Aug 1868, and Lockyer's of 20 Oct 1868 — American Physical Society, This Month in Physics History . Terrestrial isolation: William Ramsay, 1895, from cleveite, with Per Teodor Cleve and Abraham Langlet independently. Related here: A Field Guide to the Elements , Not a Line (No. 21), which uses the same fingerprint fact. The Quill Is a Hair A drawing of Esmx the porkypine, with an earring in one ear and a missing chunk in the other. One spike of the mane runs off to the right and is drawn again, hugely magnified, as a single quill whose tip carries rows of tiny backward-pointing barbs. Arrows show that the barbs make the quill easy to push in and hard to pull out. in: easier out: harder keratin · the same protein as a fingernail

The Quill Is a Hair No. 2 · what a spike is made of A quill is not a thorn, not a bone, not a claw. It is a hair — a hair that grew stiff and hollow and enormous. It is made of keratin, the same protein as your fingernails and the hair on your head, and it grows from a follicle in skin the way any hair does. In 2012 a group at Harvard and MIT put the North American porcupine's quill under proper measurement and found the tip is not smooth. It carries rows of microscopic backward-facing barbs , and those barbs do two things at once. They make the quill harder to pull out , which everyone expected. They also make it easier to push in — the barbs concentrate stress along the tip and let it cut rather than shove, cutting the penetration force substantially. Both properties come from the same feature. We like this one because it refuses a tidy story. The thing that makes a spike good at going in is the same thing that makes it hard to take back. That is not a moral, and we are not going to make it one. Source: W. K. Cho, J. A. Ankrum, D. Guo, S. A. Chester, S. Y. Yang, A. Kashyap, G. A. Campbell, R. J. Wood, R. K. Rijal, R. Karnik, R. Langer & J. M. Karp, “Microstructured barbs on the North American porcupine quill enable easy tissue penetration and difficult removal,” PNAS 109 (52), 21289–21294 (2012), doi:10.1073/pnas.1216441109 . Quills as modified hairs: standard mammalogy. Esmx Does Not Shoot A drawing of Esmx the porkypine with a full mane. To the right, three dashed arcs show quills supposedly flying through the air; each arc is crossed out. Below them a solid line shows what actually happens: a quill leaves only where something touches it. never happens contact only the quill releases; the porcupine does not throw it

Esmx Does Not Shoot No. 3 · the popular verdict, corrected Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. They cannot throw them, fire them, or launch them. The quill is held in the skin by an attachment that gives way under a particular kind of push — so when something makes contact, the quill stays in the thing it touched rather than in the porcupine. An attacker has to come to it. The myth is easy to see the shape of: you find a predator studded with quills and no porcupine within reach, and the story writes itself backwards. It is also the exact fault this collection keeps finding — a mechanism invented to explain a coincidence , then repeated until it sounds like something everyone has always known. We are keeping this one at the front because our mascot is a porcupine and a spiky mascot invites precisely this reading: that the spikes are for attacking, that they go out looking. They do not. A quill is what happens at the boundary, and only there. The animal is never the punchline , and neither is the animal's armour. Source: Uldis Roze, Porcupines: The Animal Answer Guide (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2012) — Roze's own field work on the quill's release mechanism is the standard account. Related here: True Facts About True Facts (No. 47), A Field Guide to Watching Animals , whose reframe tables correct the popular verdict on the animal and nothing else. Spikes, Independently A drawing of Esmx the porkypine beside a simple branching tree. Four separate branch tips each end in a spiky silhouette — porcupine, hedgehog, tenrec and echidna — and the branches meet only far down at a common ancestor drawn with no spikes at all, showing that spines were arrived at four separate times. porcupine hedgehog tenrec echidna a common ancestor with no spines at all

Spikes, Independently No. 4 · there is no standard way to make a spike Porcupines have spines. So do hedgehogs, tenrecs, and echidnas. Take those four back down their branches and they do not meet at a spiky ancestor — they meet at an animal with ordinary fur, and in the echidna's case you have to go back past the split between egg-laying mammals and everything else. Spines were arrived at separately, four times, in four lineages that were not talking to each other. A hedgehog is not a small porcupine; it is not even a close relation. An echidna is not a porcupine that lays eggs. They are four independent answers, built from different starting material, to a problem that has more than one solution — which is what convergence keeps demonstrating and what a single standard keeps denying. Seven of our twelve field guides have arrived at some version of this sentence without being pointed at each other: there is no standard star, nervous system, migration, shark, turtle, tortoise, galaxy. Add spikes to the list. The universe keeps solving the same problem more than one way, and keeps declining to rank the answers. Related here: Five Times a Crab (No. 36), on carcinisation — where the real finding is that the crab shape was lost more often than it was gained; the Field Guides , where the no-standard sentence keeps recurring. The four lineages sit in four different mammal groups (Rodentia, Eulipotyphla, Afrosoricida, Monotremata), which is what makes the independence uncontroversial rather than a close call. Sulfur, and the Last Days A drawing of Esmx the porkypine whose mane spikes are drawn as chemical bonds: pairs of sulfur atoms joined by a short link, the disulfide bridges that make keratin stiff. Behind them, two oxygen nuclei collide and fuse into sulfur-32, labelled as oxygen burning in a massive star. S–S · what makes a quill stiff O O S oxygen burning a massive star, near the end

Sulfur, and the Last Days No. 5 · the whole argument, in one spike Keratin is a protein, and what makes the hard kind hard — quill, claw, horn, nail — is that its strands are stitched to each other by disulfide bridges : two sulfur atoms, from two cysteines, holding hands across the gap. Pull the sulfur out and a quill is a limp thread. The stiffness is not in the shape. It is in the bond. And sulfur is made in a specific place, at a specific point in a star's life. When a massive star has run through hydrogen, helium, carbon and neon, its core turns to burning oxygen — two oxygen nuclei fusing, throwing off products of which sulfur-32 is one of the most abundant . This is late. It is the accounting a big star does in its last stretch before the core gives way. So: the reason a porcupine's spike stands up is a bond made of an element assembled in the final days of a star that died before the Sun existed. Not a resemblance. Not a rhyme. The same atoms. This is the whole site in one drawing, and it is why Esmx belongs here at all — love you down to your star stuff reaches all the way down to the thing that makes a quill a quill. Sources: disulfide cross-linking in hard α-keratins — standard protein biochemistry. Sulfur's origin: all sulfur isotopes are synthesised in hydrostatic or explosive oxygen burning, which happens only in massive stars and Type Ia supernovae — Chin, Henkel et al. , “Interstellar sulfur isotopes and stellar oxygen burning,” A&A (1996), arXiv:astro-ph/9505067 . Related here: A Field Guide to the Elements , Bone Song (No. 1). Not a Chart A drawing of Esmx the porkypine. Behind the mane, a faint measuring grid with a dashed baseline and an axis fades out toward the right, while the mane's spikes carry on past the edge of the grid entirely. A note reads: no baseline, no axis, not one moment. baseline no baseline · no axis and not measured at one moment

Not a Chart No. 6 · the mascot outruns its own diagram Esmx's spikes are there for a reason: they evoke the spiky profile , the observation that a neurodivergent person's abilities are not one level but a range with real peaks and real troughs. The idea is Damian Milton's , building on Francesca Happé . It also turns up in the workplace literature, where a 2020 paper describes it as large, statistically-significant disparities between peaks and troughs of the profile and suggests it “may well emerge as the definitive expression of neurominority” — a study using the term, which is not the same thing as being where it came from. And we have already published the argument against it . No. 21 grants that the spiky profile beat the single severity dial, then names what it kept: it still plots you as distances from a flat expected baseline, still needs axes, and still freezes you at the one moment somebody assessed you. A better chart is still a chart. Which is exactly what makes the mascot better than the diagram it came from. Esmx's mane has no baseline. There is no zero line under it, no axis beside it, nothing it is a deviation from , and the tips keep going after the drawing stops. The same move the cosmic egg on our door makes: keep the jag, throw away the grid. Sources: the spiky profile is Damian Milton 's, building on Francesca Happé — the attribution this collection carries throughout. The two quoted phrases are from Nancy Doyle, “Neurodiversity at work: a biopsychosocial model and the impact on working adults,” British Medical Bulletin 135 (1), 108–125 (2020), doi:10.1093/bmb/ldaa021 , which is the wording Esmx's own page quotes; it is cited here as a use of the term in the workplace literature, not as its provenance . Related here: Not a Line (No. 21) and its broadside . The Trailing Spikes A drawing of Esmx the porkypine whose mane tips come loose and become the stars of a constellation, joined by faint lines into a figure. Underneath, a depth scale shows the same stars at wildly different distances from the viewer, so the figure exists only from here. nearer much farther the figure exists from here, and nowhere else

The Trailing Spikes No. 7 · a pattern is a place you are standing The best thing in Esmx's design is the part that comes apart. The mane does not end — the tips separate and drift , and Kaya's page says they can trail off and make patterns. Draw them far enough out and you have made a constellation, which means you have made the mistake this whole collection was built to notice. A constellation is a line of sight . The stars in one are, in the general case, nowhere near each other; they sit at wildly different distances and are held together by nothing but the angle you happen to be looking from. Move a long way sideways and the figure dissolves. It was never out there. It was a fact about your position, wearing the costume of a fact about the sky. Which is the friendliest possible warning about a mascot. Esmx's spikes make a pattern because we are standing here. That is a good enough reason to enjoy a pattern, and not a good enough reason to believe it is a structure. Related here: A Field Guide to Constellations ; The Lines We Drew (No. 9), which had to correct its own version of this — its depth argument originally ran on Orion's Belt, whose three stars turn out to be at essentially one distance and genuinely related. The general claim survives; the example did not. Esme A drawing of Esmx the porkypine. The tallest spike of the mane rises into the pointed silhouette of a witch's hat against a field of stars, and the letter x at the end of the name is drawn large beneath, marking the name Esmx as a variant of Esme. Esme → Esm x they / them

Esme No. 8 · where the name came from Esmx is named for Esme — for Esmeralda Weatherwax and the Witches of Discworld. The x is deliberate: it marks gender neutrality and fluidity, and Esmx's pronouns are they/them. Kaya's page adds that if you build your own variant from the blank template, you pick pronouns to fit what you made. That the name is a Discworld name is not a small coincidence for this particular collection. The Easter Eggs already hold No. 49 , a credit to Terry Pratchett that turned up three attribution corrections and ended by conceding that our own masthead is a promise rather than a finding. And the method it credits him for — First Sight and Second Thoughts , seeing what is actually in front of you and then watching yourself think about it — is Granny Weatherwax's inheritance more than anyone's. So the mascot was carrying a citation the whole time. Our porkypine is named after a witch who is famous for refusing to be fooled, including by herself. That is a better fit for a fact-checking collection than anything we would have arrived at on purpose. Source: the naming, the x , and the they/them are stated on Esmx's own page — primary, being the mascot's own account of itself. Related here: One Atom of Justice (No. 49); the Turtle at the foot of the collection.
What we left out, and one we nearly got wrong

What we left out, and one we nearly got wrong Notes The goblin stays in. Kaya's design notes name a bit of goblin in the mix, after goblin mode — refusing a social norm in order to be comfortable, and being frank about being weird. We have not drawn that as a feature because it is not a feature; it is the posture the whole character is standing in. It is also the closest thing Esmx has to a thesis, and it is the same one as Wyrd and Weird . We did not draw the pig. A porkypine is pig plus porcupine, and the temptation was to make something of the fact that porcupines are rodents and are not pigs at all — that the Latin behind the name calls it a spiny pig and the animal politely declines. We left it out because it is a joke about a word rather than a fact about an animal, and this page had eight better things to carry. It is written down here so the next person does not think we missed it. One distinction this page nearly got wrong, in the direction it warns about. A draft of card No. 6 cited the 2020 British Medical Bulletin paper as the source of the spiky profile , on the reasoning that it is the wording most often quoted and that its author's name appeared nowhere in this project. That is the error, not the fix. Using a term in a study is not being part of its provenance — a paper that defines a phrase in order to work with it is a use , and the citation belongs to whoever the idea came from, which here is Damian Milton building on Francesca Happé. Caught by Ryan Boren before it shipped. It is recorded because it is precisely the substitution Too Good to Check catalogues: the most quotable source standing in for the actual one, which is how a citation ends up pointing at the wrong person while looking more rigorous than the alternative. “Esmx” by Kaya Oldaker is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 · these eight variants likewise Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms stimpunks.org · morerealms.com · starstuff.earth open edition · print freely

no hub · no clock L★S · 001 The One With No Ledger Hydra · Hydra vulgaris a nerve net, no brain · a ~4-hour cycle, no clock A freshwater animal a centimetre or two long, related to jellyfish and coral, with no brain and no central nervous system — just a mesh of nerve cells with nothing anywhere gathering it into a decision-maker. It sleeps, and if you keep it awake its cells stop dividing properly. no brain at allno circadian rhythmrebound after deprivationsleep the cells need ▸ Field notes Field notes · Hydra · Hydra vulgaris Sleep is usually described as something a brain does. Hydra is the standing objection. It has neurons — a few thousand — but they form a nerve net with no centre, no ganglion, nothing that could be called an organ of control. And it sleeps. Kanaya and colleagues established it against the behavioural definition, which is the one that works across species that share no anatomy: the animal becomes quiescent, it is harder to rouse, and if you deprive it of the state it takes more of it afterwards and falls into it faster. That third criterion is the whole test. Being still is not sleep; being still and then owing stillness is. Two findings from the same paper make this the card the guide opens on. The first is that melatonin, GABA and the PRKG1 kinase all push Hydra towards sleep, exactly as they do in animals with brains — the machinery predates the organ. The second is what deprivation costs: cell proliferation falls off. Rest here is not a pause in the animal's real work. It is when a good deal of the building happens. And it keeps no time. Put Hydra in constant light or constant dark and its daily rhythm simply vanishes — there is no free-running circadian clock underneath. What remains is a cycle of roughly four hours, returning and returning. So the oldest resting animal available to us is not answering to a day at all. The authors call it a sleep-like state before they call it sleep, and that hedge is kept here. What is established is that it meets the criteria, not that a polyp experiences anything. The argument this card serves is No. 59: an account of rest as something earned needs a ledger to keep score in, and there is no ledger in a nerve net. Trait Sounds like Actually Has no brain, only a diffuse net too simple to sleep meets all three behavioural criteria for sleep Goes still for stretches inactivity, not sleep raised arousal threshold and rebound afterwards — which is the difference No day/night rhythm under constant light a broken clock no circadian clock to break; a roughly four-hour cycle instead Kept awake by shaking or by drugs merely disturbed the number of dividing cells drops measurably Its way rest with no clock to answer to · L★S 001

day · then nightfewer, longer gaps L★S · 002 The First One We Caught Upside-down jellyfish · Cassiopea sp. first brainless animal shown to sleep · 2017 A jellyfish that lies bell-down on the seafloor and pulses. In 2017 three graduate students established that it has a sleep state — the first animal without a centralised nervous system for which that was shown, which moved the root of sleep down below the brain on the tree of life. nerve net, no CNSpulses less at nightslow to right itselfsleep older than brains ▸ Field notes Field notes · Upside-down jellyfish · Cassiopea sp. Cassiopea lives upside down — bell on the sediment, tentacles up, farming photosynthetic symbionts in its own tissue. It pulses steadily, which makes it unusually easy to measure: you can count the pulses. At night the pulsing drops by about a third, and the gaps between pulses grow longer and more variable. On its own that proves nothing; plenty of things slow down at night. What made it sleep was the other two tests. Roused at night, the animal took longer to respond and longer to right itself. And when the researchers kept it awake with pulses of water through the dark hours, it was quieter the next day — it paid the loss back. This was the finding that reset the question. Before it, sleep was reasonably assumed to require a centralised nervous system, because every animal known to sleep had one. Cassiopea has a nerve net. Hydra followed three years later and pushed the same point further, since a hydra has no circadian rhythm either. The framing worth keeping is not even jellyfish sleep. It is that we had been reading a requirement off a coincidence: everything we had checked had a brain because we had only been checking animals with brains. Trait Sounds like Actually Pulses more slowly at night winding down, like a machine fewer pulses with longer and more variable gaps — a state, not a slope Slow to react in the dark hours sluggish a measurably raised arousal threshold, the second sleep criterion Disturbed all night no consequence it sleeps more the following day — homeostatic rebound Has no brain to be tired so this cannot be sleep so sleep is not a property of brains Its way the root moved down the tree · L★S 002

four stops, four moults302 neurons L★S · 003 Four Times, Before Each Change Nematode · Caenorhabditis elegans 302 neurons · 2–3 hours before each of four moults A worm a millimetre long with a completely mapped nervous system of 302 neurons. Before each of its four moults it stops — stops moving, stops feeding, stops responding much — for two or three hours. The state is called lethargus, and it satisfies the sleep criteria. every neuron mappedrest scheduled by developmentstops eating tooegl-4 / PKG ▸ Field notes Field notes · Nematode · Caenorhabditis elegans C. elegans is the animal whose nervous system we know completely — all 302 neurons and every connection between them. It is also, since 2008, an animal with a sleep-like state. Raizen and colleagues named it after a period already known to developmental biologists: lethargus, the two-to-three-hour quiet before each of the worm's four larval moults. What they showed was that it is not simply incapacity. It is reversible, it comes with reduced responsiveness and a characteristic posture, feeding ceases, and — the test that counts — the worm compensates if you deprive it. They also found a gene for it: egl-4, a cGMP-dependent protein kinase, acting in sensory neurons. What this card adds to the band is the timing. Hydra shows that rest is older than brains, and Cassiopea that it does not need a centre. The worm shows something else: its rest is scheduled by development. Four times in its life the animal has to rebuild its own cuticle, and four times it stops first. Which is a fact about worms, not a lesson. The Twenty Hours That Was One Warm Room

33 °C26 °C19.9 h · 11.0 h L★S · 011 The Twenty Hours That Was One Warm Room Little brown bat · Myotis lucifugus 19.9 h at 33 °C · 11.0 h at 26 °C The sleepiest mammal, in every table and every listicle, at just under twenty hours a day. It is about how a number becomes a fact. Everyone has met the sleepiest mammal. It appears in infographics, in trivia, in science journalism, and in the comparative databases those draw on, at 19.9 hours a day. Harding and colleagues went back to where the figure came from. Almost all of the extreme-bat-sleep record traces to two studies by Brebbia and co-workers in the 1960s and 70s, on Myotis lucifugus and Eptesicus fuscus. The 19.9-hour measurement specifically was taken at an ambient temperature of 33 °C, and it "rests on a single study using an unknown number of specimens." Then the finding that should be printed somewhere permanent: the same body of measurement gives 11.0 hours at 26 °C. The most-repeated sleep statistic about any mammal nearly halves depending on how warm the room was — which for a bat is not a detail, because a bat in a cool room enters torpor, and torpor is not sleep. Two fruit bat species measured properly come in at about 14.8 and 14.7 hours, comparable to a Syrian hamster, an animal that features in nobody's list of champion sleepers. The paper's wider argument is the one this band is built on. Roughly one per cent of mammal species have had their sleep measured at all; a great deal of the comparative record is decades old and was gathered under artificial conditions, notably social isolation and controlled temperature, which for many species is a description of stress rather than of life. The familiar giraffe and cat figures come out of the same thin literature, and the giraffe circulates at both 1.9 and 4.6 hours depending on which secondary source you land on — a factor of nearly two and a half, which is the tell. So this card carries no headline number of its own, and the missing bar in its diagram is deliberate: there is no honest single figure to draw. Which is why the guide's claim is what it is. There is no standard way to rest — and for most of the animals alive, there is not even a standard measurement of it. Its sleep has two modes. Hauled out on land it sleeps as a land mammal does: both hemispheres in slow-wave sleep together, with REM. In the water it converts to a largely unihemispheric pattern — one hemisphere in slow waves, the other awake — and REM sleep is profoundly reduced or eliminated. Kendall-Bar, Lyamin, Siegel and colleagues measured what the eyes do while this happens: the eye contralateral to the sleeping hemisphere stays closed about 99.4 per cent of the time, while the eye on the waking side opens in brief bouts averaging 1.9 seconds, around eight times a minute. Half the animal is watching, in glances. Then the result that gives the card its title. Lyamin and colleagues found fur seals suppress REM sleep for very long periods — weeks — without subsequent rebound. No catch-up. In most mammals REM deprivation produces a measurable debt that is paid back with interest, and it is one of the better arguments that REM does something necessary. A fur seal at sea appears to simply not owe it. This is not a licence to skip sleep, and the guide will not pretend otherwise: the seal is a specialist, and its physiology is not ours. But it belongs in a catalogue about rest because it breaks the tidiest available story. Sleep debt is not a universal law of animals with brains. It is how the accounting works in the species where it has been measured, and here is a species where it does not. Grutter and colleagues noted that the explanation had never actually been tested, and asked a different question. Coral reef fish are attacked by gnathiid isopods, small crustaceans that feed on blood. During the day, cleaner fish remove them. At night there are no cleaners, and it was unclear how anything on the reef avoided being fed on. So the researchers exposed Chlorurus sordidus overnight to gnathiids, with and without cocoons. Roughly 10 per cent of the cocooned fish were attacked. Virtually all of the uncocooned ones were. And by analysing the mucus they costed it: building one takes about 2.5 per cent of the fish's daily energy budget. The paper's own phrase for the thing is a mosquito net. Whether it works by masking the chemical cues gnathiids home in on, or as a physical barrier, or both, is not settled, and the card leaves it open. What earns it a place in this band is the shape of the solution. The fish is not more vigilant at night, and it has not evolved a tougher skin. It spends a small, fixed amount of energy on a structure outside its body, and then it can stop paying attention. That is what an accommodation looks like when it is working: cheap, external, and boring once installed. Tied To The Forest It Sustains

the kelp does the holding L★S · 015 Tied To The Forest It Sustains Sea otter · Enhydra lutris kelp-anchored rafting · spent in full in No. 58 Sea otters rest in rafts on the surface, often in kelp canopy, and wrap themselves in the kelp so that sleeping does not mean drifting. The holding is done by the forest — and the forest is there because the otters are, which makes this the tightest loop in the guide. rafting on the surfacewrapped in kelpthe kelp does the holdingand the otters sustain the kelp ▸ Field notes Field notes · Sea otter · Enhydra lutris This card is deliberately short, because the otter is spent properly elsewhere: The Stone You Keep (No. 58) is ten spreads on this animal, and repeating it here would be a second telling rather than an entry. What belongs in this guide is one structural point. Otters rest in rafts at the surface and wrap themselves in kelp, so that sleep does not carry them away. Notice what is doing the holding: not vigilance, not grip, not a sleeping animal working at staying put. The kelp holds it. The otter's whole contribution is to be somewhere that will hold it, and then to stop. And then the loop closes, which is why it is the last card in the band. Sea otters eat urchins; urchins eat kelp; remove the otters and the kelp forest becomes a barren of spines. So the forest that holds a resting otter is a forest that exists because otters are present. Not because they manage it, or intend it, or have earned it. Because they are there. One thing left out on purpose. You have seen the photograph of otters asleep holding hands, with a caption about love. Rafting is real and kelp-anchoring is real; the hand-holding romance is a story the internet tells about them. Being held by the forest you live in is the better fact anyway. no neurons at allquestion open L★S · 016 Nobody Knows Yet Sponges · Porifera · no neurons at all no reframe offered — there is no verdict to correct Sponges have no neurons whatsoever — not a net, not a ganglion, nothing. They do have documented daily rhythms of contraction and expansion. Whether any sponge rests in a way that would meet the sleep criteria is genuinely unknown, and this card carries no reframe table because there is nothing yet to reframe. no neurons of any kinddiurnal contraction rhythmsthe honest answer is openno reframe table ▸ Field notes Field notes · Sponges · Porifera · no neurons at all Every card above this one has three columns: a trait, what it sounds like, and what is actually the case. That apparatus exists because a verdict had been reached about an animal and the verdict was wrong. A bat's sleep was said to be twenty hours. A parrotfish's cocoon was said to be about predators. A vertically hanging whale looked like a whale in trouble. No verdict has been reached about sponges, and that is the entire content of this card. What is known: sponges are animals with no neurons at all — not the nerve net that Hydra and Cassiopea have, but no nervous system of any kind. They nonetheless detect changes around them and respond, they contract and expand, and in at least one species, the demosponge Tethya wilhelma, that contraction cycle has been shown to be diurnal and light-controlled. They filter enormous volumes of water and there is a reasonable suggestion that periods of quiescence let them do maintenance on their own cells. What is not known is whether any of that is rest in the sense the rest of this guide uses — because the sleep criteria are behavioural and two of the three are hard to apply here. You can ask whether a sponge becomes quiescent. Asking whether it is harder to rouse, and whether it rebounds after deprivation, requires knowing what rousing a sponge would even mean. So the column headed actually stays empty, and it stays empty on purpose. Writing actually over an open question is not rigour. It is bluff with a table around it. This is the rule Field Guide No. 10 set and No. 16 kept: a subject that cannot take the apparatus gets a different card, not a smaller one. openfoldednot sleep, and never claimed L★S · 017 The Word Was Borrowed, And They Said So Nyctinasty · Linnaeus’s Somnus Plantarum (1755) no reframe offered — the misnaming was ours Bean and pea and prayer-plant leaves fold at dusk and open at dawn, on a circadian clock, and the movement has been called the sleep of plants since Linnaeus. Here there is a common belief — that plants sleep — but it was never a verdict passed on plants. It was a convenience of ours, and it has been flagged as one by its own authors for two and a half centuries. The provenance is worth reading from the primary rather than from summaries of it, and the primary is out of copyright. In The Power of Movement in Plants (1880), Charles Darwin, assisted by his son Francis, writes that "the so-called sleep of leaves is so conspicuous a phenomenon that it was observed as early as the time of Pliny; and since Linnæus published his famous Essay, 'Somnus Plantarum,' it has been the subject" of continuing study. So: the phenomenon is ancient, the word is Linnaeus's, from a 1755 essay, and Darwin inherited it with visible reservations. He is blunter about the daytime version — "The leaves of some plants move during the day in a manner, which has improperly been called diurnal sleep" — and elsewhere says of it that "we believe it to be of an essentially different nature from the nocturnal movement." The modern name is nyctinasty: nastic leaf movement at the onset of darkness, driven by the circadian clock, documented from legumes to the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha. It is real, it is rhythmic, and it is not sleep by the three criteria this guide has used throughout — there is no arousal threshold to raise and no homeostatic rebound to measure. A plant deprived of its night-time leaf position does not fold harder the next evening. None of which is a deficit, and that is why there is no actually column. A reframe table corrects a misreading of an organism. Nothing here has misread the plant; a folk usage borrowed a good word for a movement that deserved one, and the borrowing was labelled from the start. Recording that is bookkeeping, not rescue. It sits at the end of the guide because it names the guide's own risk. Rest is a word we carry across enormous distances — to a polyp, to a nematode, to a bird asleep on one side — and every one of those carries is a judgement about whether the word still means anything. Linnaeus made one and Darwin queried it in print. The least we can do is say which ones we are making. No reframe offered no reframe offered · L★S —

Six Ways a Fact Goes Wrong

Six Ways a Fact Goes Wrong A story that fits gets less scrutiny, which is exactly when it needs more. Six shapes the failure takes — and the tell for each. 01 The quote nobody said What circulates is a compression — true in spirit, absent from the text. Tell More quotable than anything anyone says out loud. Do Search the actual book. 02 The number that went stale Measurements get superseded. The old value circulates for decades with nothing marking it expired. Tell Repeated everywhere, dated nowhere. Do Check the source you cited gives your number. 03 The story told backwards The facts survive the retelling and the emphasis doesn't, so the meaning inverts while every sentence stays defensible. Tell The paper's own hedge is missing. Do Read what the authors said they don't know. 04 The credit that drifted Attribution decays toward tidiness. A collective becomes a founder; a documenter becomes a coiner. Tell One name where a community was. Do Find the first printed instance, not the famous one. 05 The press release, not the paper A layer whose job is to make the finding interesting. Its output isn't a lie — it's a livelier verb. Tell The vivid verb is doing the work. Do Open the abstract. See which word the authors chose. 06 The finding that flatters you The other five are accidents. This one is an appetite, and it comes looking for you. Tell You wanted it true before you read it. Do Slow down here. The book, the paper, the talk. Aggregators and summaries are leads, not citations. Cite the source you actually read. If you haven't opened it, it doesn't go in the references. Read your own siblings. Check what you've already claimed about the same thing. When one source falls, re-check its relatives. Errors travel with their quotes. Quote or paraphrase — never dress one as the other. Verbatim and in marks, or in your own words with the idea attributed. Say what's still open. “Leading hypothesis, not a settled result” costs one sentence. Log the correction in public. With a date, and the name of whoever caught it. Measure rather than assume. A stated principle nobody checks is a wish. Five we got wrong The forest is wired together. Elders feeding shaded seedlings through the fungal network — in three of our pieces. Karst, Jones & Hoeksema (2023) find no published evidence for the elder-feeds-offspring claim. Mode 06. “We are star stuff harvesting sunlight.” Not in the book — but he said it aloud: “We are star stuff. Harvesting starlight .” Circulation changed one word. Developed collectively by the online Autistic community; reached print via Harvey Blume, who said so (Botha et al., 2024). Mode 04. Disgust is learned. Ours, and wrong as we stated it. Where we started The skeleton you were promised This whole collection opens with a bone. Bone Song starts where you'd expect: your calcium was forged in stars, and the skeleton it built is piezoelectric. Press on it and it makes voltage. Iwao Yasuda found that in the 1950s. Your bones are listening to how you move. That's the founding image here. Star-forged mineral, laid down in a living lattice, humming quietly under load. And then the ocean says: sure. Or don't. There is a whole class of vertebrates — sharks, rays, skates, the strange deep chimaeras — that never turns up to the bone. Same phylum. Same backbone-having club. No true bone anywhere in the body. Not a lesser version of yours. A different answer to the same question, and it has been working for a very long time. two vertebrates, two skeletons us mineralised bone press → voltage piezoelectric shark soft core cartilage + tiles bends, then springs no true bone both are vertebrates · neither is the draft same club, different build yasuda 1954–1957 · dean & summers 2006 Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
A mosaic where the bone would be

What's in there instead A mosaic where the bone would be "Cartilaginous" makes it sound floppy. It isn't. A shark's skeleton is cartilage with a mineral crust laid over it — thousands of small blocks, packed edge to edge like paving, sitting on top of an uncalcified core. The blocks are called tesserae, from the word for mosaic tiles, and that is exactly what they look like. Mason Dean and Adam Summers, reviewing the tissue in 2006, describe a skeleton whose mineralisation comes in distinct types — areolar, globular, prismatic — arranged differently depending on the animal's age, its species, where in the body you're looking, and how it feeds. The skeleton is tuned to the life. And the design does something bone can't. A tiled surface over a soft core bends further before it breaks, then springs back. It's lighter than bone. It doesn't need marrow cavities or a blood supply threaded all the way through. None of that is a workaround. It's a different set of trade-offs, chosen — over deep time — by an enormous number of successful animals. You were taught one skeleton and told it was the skeleton. There are others, and they are not rough drafts. tessellated cartilage, in section uncalcified cartilage core tesserae — mineral tiles, laid edge to edge the seams between tiles are where it flexes stiff enough to bite · springy enough to swim areolar · globular · prismatic — three ways to mineralise dean & summers 2006 · zoology a mosaic, tuned to the life it carries Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
They didn't miss it. They let it go

The part that changes the story They didn't miss it. They let it go For most of a century the shark was taught as the before picture. Cartilage first, bone later — sharks as a living snapshot of the stage vertebrates passed through on the way to becoming us. Primitive. Ancestral. Not there yet. The fossils stopped cooperating. In 2020 Martin Brazeau and colleagues described Minjinia turgenensis, an Early Devonian fish from Mongolia on the placoderm grade — close to the common ancestry of all jawed vertebrates — and it is full of endochondral bone. The kind sharks don't have. Which flips the sequence. If the shared ancestor already had bone, then the shark's bonelessness isn't something it never got round to. It is something its lineage gave up. A derived condition. A loss. We have run into this exact shape before, one zine ago. The crab body plan was gained five times and lost seven — leaving turned out to be the commoner event. Here it is again in the skeleton: subtraction is not the same as never having arrived. And whatever they traded away, they have been fine. The chondrichthyan record runs back to the early Silurian — call it 440 million years, on scales and teeth at first. Four mass extinctions. Still here. The animal you were told hadn't got there yet had been there, and chose otherwise. who had bone, and when shared ancestor HAS BONE Minjinia turgenensis early Devonian bony fishes → us kept the bone sharks & rays let the bone go loss derived, not primitive · brazeau et al. 2020 nature ecology & evolution, 2020 the before picture was never before Skipped Bone · Stimpunks

The word doing the damage "Primitive" is a verdict Watch how it works. Primitive has a technical meaning — a trait resembling an ancestral state — and it carries a second meaning it never declares: unfinished. lesser. earlier on the way to better. Both meanings ride in the same word. So a real observation ("this trait resembles the ancestral condition") arrives already sentenced. And here the technical meaning was also wrong. The shark skeleton isn't ancestral. It's a later change. The word was carrying a verdict it hadn't earned, about a fact that wasn't a fact. Our field guide to nervous systems flagged the same habit in neuroscience — jellyfish nets called primitive, worm brains called simple. Same move, different tissue. It's the move that gets made about us, too. Low-functioning. Developmentally delayed. Behind. Every one of them a measurement with a destination smuggled inside it, and the destination is always somebody else. one word, two cargoes "primitive" what it declares resembles the ancestral state what it smuggles unfinished · lesser · behind and for the shark skeleton: the declared meaning was false too a sentence, passed before the evidence the verdict inside the description low-functioning · delayed · behind Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
Then someone decided it was a cure

The turn Then someone decided it was a cure Here is what happened next to the skeleton we've just spent five pages admiring. Somewhere along the way a claim got loose: sharks don't get cancer. Cartilage has no blood vessels of its own; tumours need a blood supply to grow; therefore — the reasoning went — a shark must be carrying something that stops them. Grind it up. Take it as a powder. It became an industry. Capsules, powders, whole shelves of them, sold to people who had just been given the worst news of their lives and were looking anywhere at all. Notice the shape of the claim, because it is the important part. The animal is no longer an animal. Once you've decided a body contains the answer to your problem, the body stops being a life with its own reasons and becomes a supply. And then there's the small matter of whether it was true. the chain of reasoning cartilage has no vessels true so sharks don't get cancer false so grind them into pills didn't work one true premise does not carry a conclusion a body that contains an answer stops being read as a life the premise, the leap, the shelf an animal becomes a supply Skipped Bone · Stimpunks

The record Sharks get cancer They always did. Somebody just had to go and count. In 2004 Gary Ostrander and colleagues went through the literature and the Registry of Tumors in Lower Animals and found 42 documented tumours in cartilaginous fishes — across at least 21 species, in nine families and seven orders. Twenty-four in sharks, sixteen in skates and rays, two in chimaeras. Tumours of the nervous system, the gut, the skin, the blood-forming tissue, the reproductive organs, the endocrine system — and of the skeleton itself. At least fifteen were malignant, invading normal tissue. Their paper's title says the quiet part: Shark Cartilage, Cancer and the Growing Threat of Pseudoscience. Then it was tested properly. Charles Loprinzi and colleagues ran a randomised trial in patients with advanced cancer and reported in 2005: no difference in survival, no difference in quality of life, and side effects bad enough that people struggled to keep taking it. So: the premise was false, the product did nothing, and the animals were killed anyway. 42 documented tumours ≥ 21 species · 7 orders 0 benefit to survival or quality of life The claim was never checked because it was useful. That is usually the reason. 42 tumours, by group sharks 24 skates & rays 16 chimaeras 2 at least 15 malignant · invading normal tissue ostrander et al. 2004 · cancer research the count that was there all along nobody had asked Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
A body read as a cure gets harvested

The pattern underneath A body read as a cure gets harvested This is the sentence the zine exists for, so here it is plainly. The shark was not harmed because anyone hated it. It was harmed because somebody decided its body contained something useful, and once that decision is made, everything else follows without anyone needing to be cruel on purpose. You stop asking what the animal is doing with its own skeleton. You start asking what the skeleton can do for you. And then you go and get it. It is the same operation when it's aimed at people. We know this frame very well: the search for the cause, so there can be a cure. The interest in Autistic people that arrives only as what are they good at, could we use that. The inspiration story where a disabled life is raw material for somebody else's lesson. The research funding that goes to prevention rather than to the things we've actually asked for. All of it starts the same way — not with hatred, with usefulness. A body is read for what can be extracted, and the reading feels like appreciation right up until the moment it costs you something. Being valued for what can be taken out of you is not the same as being valued. two ways of looking at the same body read for what's in it the useful part leaves the body supply read as a life the useful part is doing a job here a life the difference is not kindness · it is direction extraction begins as appreciation and then it comes to collect Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
What the skeleton is actually for

Back to the animal What the skeleton is actually for It's for the shark. That's the whole answer, and it's worth sitting with, because it is the answer that got skipped. The tiled cartilage is doing a job every second of that animal's life. It holds a jaw that has to bite without shattering. It carries a body through water with the springy recoil that makes the swimming cheap. It grows with the animal, tuned — species by species, region by region, feeding style by feeding style — to the exact loads that particular life puts on it. It is not a message to us. It is not a resource with an animal wrapped round it. It is a body, solving the problem of being that body, in a way that has held up across four mass extinctions. Your skeleton is doing the same thing. Yasuda's finding wasn't that your bones are useful to somebody — it's that they're listening, minute by minute, to the life you are actually living. You don't owe anyone a reason

Closer to home You don't owe anyone a reason Everything in this zine turns on one question, and it's a question that gets asked about people constantly. What is it for? Asked of a shark's skeleton, it produced a shelf of pills that didn't work and a lot of dead animals. Asked of a person, it produces the same shape: what are you good for, what does your difference get us, where's the upside. You've probably been handed the flattering version. Autistic people are so detail-oriented — brilliant for quality assurance. It sounds like praise. It's a receipt. It says the welcome is conditional on the yield, and quietly hands you the bill if the yield stops. So here is the plain form of the refusal, which is the same one we'd make on the shark's behalf if it could be bothered to care what we think: The skeleton is for the animal. Your mind is for you. Not a resource. Not a lesson. Not a supply. A body doing the work of being itself, which is the only justification anything in this universe has ever had, and it has always been enough. Four hundred million years of no bone at all, and nobody down there is apologising. The tiles aren't a rough draft of a spine. You aren't a rough draft of anyone. the question, and the better question "what is it for?" answers that follow: supply · yield · upside · cure "what is it doing?" answers that follow: living · holding · swimming · being one asks for a receipt · one just looks change the question and the whole shelf empties Skipped Bone · Stimpunks

The Star Stuff You're Made Of Eight elements essential to your body, traced to where the universe forged them. Almost every atom heavier than helium was made in stars and their deaths — and none of it was made for you, which is somehow the better story. H Z 1 Hydrogen The First Light ~10% of you The Big Bang, ~13.8 billion years ago. No star ever made it — every other atom in you is younger. O Z 8 Oxygen The Weight of You ~65% of you Massive stars, scattered by core-collapse supernovae. Mostly the water you're built from, not the air. C Z 6 Carbon The Scaffold ~18% of you Aging stars, by the triple-alpha process — three helium nuclei fusing almost at once. N Z 7 Nitrogen The Borrowed Letters ~3% of you Dying stars, via the CNO cycle. You breathe it constantly and can't use a molecule of it raw. Ca Z 20 Calcium The Bone Note ~1.5% of you Massive stars and their supernovae. Your skeleton, and the spark behind every heartbeat. Fe Z 26 Iron The Death Rattle ~4 g · trace Two kinds of stellar death: roughly half from core-collapse supernovae, half from Type Ia. K Z 19 Potassium The Spark ~0.25% of you Explosive burning in supernovae. Every nerve signal you have ever had. A little of it is radioactive. I Z 53 Iodine The Rare Catastrophe ~15–20 mg · trace Colliding neutron stars, by the r-process.
