Star light Making in the open, in the shine of the cosmic latte This repository is public — every page, every tool, every error. The reason is one sentence of Brandeis's, and one colour that had to be corrected in public before anybody could use it. Average the light of two hundred thousand galaxies and you get a colour. It is a warm off-white, and somebody reading the newspaper over a coffee named it cosmic latte . That is the fact this page is named after, and it is not the interesting half. The interesting half is that the first answer was wrong, and the astronomers said so out loud.
The colour of the universe is a correction

The colour of the universe is a correction The colour was never the point. Ivan Baldry, Karl Glazebrook and the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey team were measuring the cosmic spectrum — the volume-averaged light of present-day galaxies — to constrain how fast the universe used to make stars. What colour that spectrum would look like to a human eye was a footnote . Footnote 3, to be exact, and you can still read the original on arXiv: “Integrating these through the cosmic spectrum we have computed RGB values of 0.269, 0.388, 0.342. This corresponds to a blue-green color, the closest match in standard RGB color lists… is ‘pale turquoise’.” Baldry, Glazebrook et al. · astro-ph/0110676 · footnote 3, as posted It travelled. The universe is turquoise is a lovely sentence and it went everywhere, which is how it reached Rochester, New York, and the desks of people who do colour for a living. They spotted the problem in the arithmetic that turns a spectrum into a colour: the software had been handed the wrong white point . A white point is the colour your eye has decided counts as white, and it is not a property of the light being measured — it is a property of where you are standing . Tungsten bulbs push it yellow. A monitor pushes it blue. The program had been set to a reddish white, and anything measured against a reddish white looks green by comparison. The galaxies had not moved. The observer had. Within weeks the team put out the correction themselves. Two sentences from Glazebrook in that announcement are the reason this page exists: “It's our fault for not taking the color science seriously enough. I'm very embarrassed.” “I don't like being wrong, but once I found out I was, I knew I had to get the word out.” Karl Glazebrook · Johns Hopkins University announcement, 13 March 2002 Corrected, the colour is a beige-white. NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day describes it with a care worth stealing: “a conditionally perceived shade of beige.” Not is beige. Conditionally perceived as beige — by an eye, adapted to a particular dark, standing somewhere. Then they ran a naming contest. Skyvory and univeige were among the entries. Cosmic latte won. The same spectrum, before and after the white point was corrected Two colour swatches side by side. On the left, the colour as first announced in January 2002: a pale turquoise, labelled with the paper's computed RGB values of 0.269, 0.388 and 0.342, and its footnote's name, pale turquoise. An arrow runs from left to right labelled "white point corrected", noting that the software had assumed a reddish white and that the galaxies did not move, the observer did. On the right, the colour as published in March 2002: a warm off-white, hex FFF8E7, named cosmic latte. Beneath both: same spectrum, same two hundred thousand galaxies, different observer. one spectrum, two white points announced · jan 2002 pale turquoise rgb 0.269 0.388 0.342 footnote 3, still on the preprint white point corrected the software assumed a reddish white published · mar 2002 cosmic latte #fff8e7 the correction, in public same spectrum. same 200,000 galaxies. the galaxies did not move. the observer did. a colour is a relation between light and somebody looking at it Figure 1 · the retracted colour and the published one, and the knob between them Marking the rung #FFF8E7 is not a constant of nature. It is one sRGB rendering of a colour that only exists relative to an observer — which is the same thing the astronomers said, in the words “conditionally perceived.” The sample is around two hundred thousand galaxies in one survey's volume, not every star there is. And the colour moves : APOD notes the cosmic spectrum has grown much less blue over the past ten billion years as redder stars became more common. We are painting this page in it anyway, and saying all of that out loud, because a simplification is honest exactly where it marks where it stops . So the most-shared fact about the colour of the universe is an erratum . The reason anyone can trust the number is that the people who got it wrong put the correction where the mistake had been, under their own names, before the journal version went out. It cost Glazebrook an afternoon of being embarrassed in public and it bought everyone since a usable answer. That is the entire argument for working in the open, and it happens to be lit in the exact colour we are borrowing.
“Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants”

“Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants” The line everybody quotes is Louis D. Brandeis's, from a Harper's Weekly essay of 20 December 1913 that became chapter five of Other People's Money and How the Bankers Use It . Two things go missing every time it is repeated, and both are worth having back. “Publicity is justly commended as a remedy for social and industrial diseases. Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants; electric light the most efficient policeman.” Louis D. Brandeis · “What Publicity Can Do” · Harper's Weekly, 20 December 1913 The first missing piece is the second clause. Sunlight and electric light are doing two different jobs — one kills what is already there, the other deters what would otherwise arrive. A public changelog is sunlight: it cleans up what we already got wrong. A public repository is the electric light: it changes what we are willing to write in the first place, because somebody can read the diff. The second missing piece is smaller and, for a project with a fact-checking ethic , more interesting. Brandeis did not write sunlight is the best of disinfectants . He wrote “is said to be.” He was passing on a proverb and marking it as one. The most quoted sentence in the literature of transparency is itself hedged by its author, and the hedge is the first thing a century of quoting filed off.

What “open” means here, in nouns Open is a word that survives being meant loosely, so here it is as a list of things that exist and can be checked. Every one of these is in the same public git repository as the pages themselves, at the same commit. the artifact, and where its working is kept what you can read where the working is 115 pages — zines, field guides, broadsides, essays the repository, and every revision of every one of them the claims FACTCHECK.md — 114 pieces logged, 122 items VERIFIED , 24 CORRECTED , 19 PLAUSIBLE , 1 REMOVED the errors the changelog — 21 dated releases, 169 entries, 50 of them fact-checks , each naming what was wrong, what is right, and who caught it the reasoning DECISIONS.md , plus the design system and the print rationale as public pages the checking tools/ — six gates, about 2,850 lines, runnable by anyone with a browser and Node the search search-index.json , a committed build artifact — 1,270 records across 114 pages the licence CC BY-SA 4.0. Print it, copy it, hand it to somebody One thing is deliberately closed, and it belongs in the same list. Search runs entirely in your browser against that committed index. There is no server to send a query to, no analytics on it, and no log of it anywhere. We are open about our work; we are not curious about yours. Openness that only ever flows one way — institutions private, readers observed — is the ordinary arrangement, and inverting it is the point.

The machines Six automated gates check this site. None of them was planned. Every one exists because something shipped broken and a person found it — which turns out to be the most important sentence in this section, and we will come back to it. six gates · what each asks, and what made it necessary the gate the question the fault that created it contrast check-contrast.mjs What colour is it — on screen, and on paper? Browsers leave background graphics off by default, so a light-on-dark page prints blank. 44 of 46 pages did. Nobody noticed until somebody pressed print. markup check-markup.mjs What shape is the tag tree? Four links nested inside a link on a collection page. Anchors cannot nest, so the parser closed the outer one early and the cards came apart on the live site. collision check-overlap.mjs Where is it? One zine shipped with three pieces of text sitting on top of other text. All five other gates passed it , and none of them was wrong to. sheets check-sheets.mjs Does it fit the paper? A broadside describing itself on its own face as “a two-sided single sheet” printed as three sides on US Letter. sitemap check-sitemap.mjs Does the sitemap agree with the filesystem? A live zine, linked from the front page, that had never been listed — uncrawlable for weeks — and a broadside listed twice. search index build-search-index.mjs Is every word findable? A page whose text was indexed at 12% and which passed the coverage check, because the check counted records instead of measuring words. The gates are only half the story. What each failure taught is the other half, and those lessons are now the operating rules of this repository.

Measure, don't count The search indexer used to check its own work by counting records: did this page produce at least as many chunks as it has sections? One page has exactly three of the blocks it was chunking on, produced three records, and shipped 12% of its own text into the index looking perfectly healthy. Now every page's records are measured against that page's actual words, and anything under 90% gets re-segmented and a remainder record appended. The run prints a percentage per page, because a page that indexes an eighth of itself looks exactly like a clean one if all you print is a count.
Wait on a condition, never a clock

Wait on a condition, never a clock Two of these tools drive a headless browser, and both used to wait a flat 1.3 seconds for a page to render before reading it. That makes every run a race. On 11 August the indexer lost it: one build produced 629 records where the builds either side produced 637 — eight records and fifteen kilobytes of text gone, with exit code 0 and no warning. Now both tools wait for the page to stop changing, then read it twice and require the two reads to agree, and a page that never settles is a hard error rather than a quiet truncation. Removing the sleep also made the whole run faster, which is the usual reward for replacing a guess with a question.
A tool's worst failure is the page it didn't look at

A tool's worst failure is the page it didn't look at Zero failures out of zero elements measured looks exactly like a clean page. Worse: when a page silently drops out of a sweep, its failures leave the total, so the number goes down and reads as progress. So the contrast checker reports any page it could not measure as UNREAD , never as ok , counts those separately from the failures, and fails on them on their own terms before contrast is even considered. The same instinct runs through the rest. Where a check genuinely cannot answer — a heading painted with a clipped gradient has no single pair of colours to compare — it says unmeasured, check by eye rather than guessing. A tool reporting “I can't check this” is reporting a gap, not clearing it. That list once ran to 196 entries and was being read as a footnote — while 90 elements across 45 pages printed invisibly, including the site's own wordmark, so the front page came off the printer with no title on it. The tool had been saying look here the whole time.

Keep every baseline at zero All six gates sit at a baseline of zero, and that is a maintenance decision rather than a compliment to the code. The contrast gate stood at 110 failures on the morning of 13 August and was cleared that day. A gate that reports “110, same as yesterday” requires a human to remember yesterday's number; a gate at zero requires nothing. A green number you have to read past stops being read. Two more rules earned the same way. A check that has to be rebuilt is a check nobody runs — the contrast tool was written three separate times as a throwaway scratch script before anyone committed it. And a comment is a note, not a control : one zine's source carries a warning that anything drawn past a certain coordinate lands on the words. The warning was accurate, it was correct, it was right there, and it did not stop the next page from doing it. That is the whole difference between documentation and a gate.
The first honest run is the argument for the gate

The first honest run is the argument for the gate The collision checker's first real run over the finished site found seven pre-existing defects nobody had seen — four covers with a caption printed over the title, an unbreakable label overflowing its column onto the body text, and a shipped page where a reader was being shown “ight-years.” None of these was subtle. All of them had been live for weeks, on a site with five other automated checks and a fact-check ledger, being read by people.
What machines are good at, and what they are not

What machines are good at, and what they are not There is a name for the method these gates implement, and it is not ours. The previous essay takes it from Terry Pratchett: First Sight is seeing what is actually in front of you rather than what you expected; Second Thoughts are the thoughts that watch the first ones. Not doubt — supervision. Second Thoughts can be built. First Sight cannot. Which is the honest shape of every tool in tools/ . Look again at the table above and notice what it is a list of: six faults that a person found first. Not one gate anticipated the fault that created it. The sequence is always the same, and it does not reverse. How every gate in this repository came to exist Four steps in a row. First, a fault ships and nothing sees it. Second, a person notices — marked as the only step that cannot be automated. Third, a gate is written. Fourth, the gate holds that ground on every run afterwards. A return arrow runs from the fourth step back to the second, labelled: attention freed for the next thing nobody has noticed yet. Beneath: machines hold ground, people take it. a fault ships nothing sees it a person notices first sight a gate is written second thoughts it holds that ground every run, forever attention freed for the next thing nobody has noticed yet machines hold ground. people take it. It is a precise one, and it is what makes the machines worth having: a gate never has to notice the same thing twice, which means the noticing can move on. A repo-wide sweep can touch 66 pages in one pass and check all of them Be embarrassed. Which is what Glazebrook was, and it is the mechanism — the correction was published by the feeling, not by the arithmetic Repeatable. The same question, asked identically, on every commit Decide what is worth making at all , or who it is for, or what this project owes the people in it

Generative AI, said plainly This is the first page on this site to state it, which is itself a small failure of the openness it is arguing for. Generative AI facilitates a great deal of the work here — drafting, the gates and their output, index and sitemap maintenance, the ledger, source legwork, and the sweeps that touch every page at once. Star Stuff is, among other things, an experiment in whether that can be done in service to accessibility, accuracy and transparency rather than at their expense. So, in nouns, on both sides. what it does here, and what it is never allowed to do does does not Draft, revise, and build pages against a written house style Decide what is worth making, or what this project believes Run and extend the six gates; rebuild the search index; keep the sitemap and the chain honest Stand as a citation for anything, ever Do the legwork of finding primaries — fetch the paper, grep the out-of-copyright book, pull the preprint Be the last check on a quotation. A person reads the primary before it ships Maintain FACTCHECK.md and write the public changelog entries, including the ones about its own errors Be trusted about anything it merely recalls The rules constraining it are the ordinary house rules, applied without an exemption: aggregators are leads, not citations ; a quotation is traced to the book, essay, paper or talk; a paraphrase is never dressed as a quote; the check is logged before the piece ships. With one addition that exists specifically because of the machine — your own summary is an aggregator. A model's account of a source is a secondary source about that source, and it is not exempt from the rule just because it is the thing writing the sentence. Why the rule is shaped that way One collection here exists to separate science from three things that wear its clothes: pseudo-science, scientism, and the smoothed popular retelling — the version with every hedge filed off, because the tidy version travels further. A language model is, structurally, a machine for producing the third one : the fluent, confident, average account, at scale. That is an odd thing to build a fact-checked site with, and the answer is not to trust it more carefully. It is to make everything it produces answerable to something that is not it — a primary source, a gate that measures, and a person who reads the paper. The smoothing is exactly why the machinery had to be built. And the mechanism has already failed here, in a way worth publishing. This repository keeps a working-notes file that tells the AI how the site works. A sign-off sentence in those notes got absorbed as house voice, promoted to “our masthead,” and shipped in a zine — where it was quoted with the three words that repaired it removed, and then argued against. It had never been the masthead. It was a colophon on one zine, and it had corrected itself in the next breath. Ryan Boren caught it , and both the essay and the notes now say the same thing: context is not evidence. Working notes are a lead about the site, exactly like any other aggregator. That is one of three attribution errors published in the last week alone. Another credited five neurodivergent love locutions to a single person on the strength of a citation chain that led, at every step, back to our own pages — a closed loop with no primary at the bottom of it, in which the aggregator being over-trusted was us. The third credited an organisation where it owed a person: Betsy Selvam's byline was on the essay the whole time. Each is in the changelog with what was wrong, what is right, and who caught it. None was caught by a gate.

A public entity There is a reason a foundation whose subject is learning builds in the open rather than merely publishing when finished. Seymour Papert and Idit Harel gave it a name: constructionism , which takes constructivism's idea of learning as building knowledge structures and adds one condition. “…this happens especially felicitously in a context where the learner is consciously engaged in constructing a public entity, whether it's a sand castle on the beach or a theory of the universe.” Seymour Papert & Idit Harel · “Situating Constructionism,” in Constructionism, 1991 A public entity. Not a finished one — a public one, while it is being made. That condition is the whole of this page: the repository, the ledger, the tools, the errata and the changelog are not documentation of the learning, they are it. It is what the Stimpunks Learning Space practices, and this site is the foundation eating its own cooking rather than recommending a recipe. And it is why the errors are the most valuable thing in the repository. A private error log teaches one person, once. Fifty published fact-checks are a curriculum — in what a closed citation loop looks like, in how a hedge goes missing, in why the tidiest version of a story is the one to distrust. We would not have any of that if we had waited to be right. A knowledge garden is how star stuff comes to know itself. It cannot do that behind a login. Which lands where the self-portrait already had it, and where the essay before last put the observer: there is no view from nowhere, only an unstated view from somewhere. The astronomers' white point makes that literal. Every measurement carries an observer, and the honest thing to do with an observer is name them and show your working — which is the same reason the changelog says who caught each error, and the same reason this page says how it was made. Not: Not a claim that open equals accountable. Publishing a correction does not un-publish the error. People read the misattributed quote, printed the blank page, followed the citation loop. Sunlight disinfects; it does not undo. Not a claim that the gates make the site correct. Six gates at zero, 122 verified items, and we shipped three attribution errors last week. The gates measure colour, structure, position, paper, coverage and completeness. None of them can read. Not an argument that transparency substitutes for structure. Brandeis was arguing for publicity alongside regulation, not instead of it, and the sentence is regularly quoted by people who want the first without the second. Not an advertisement for AI. The honest summary is that a language model is a smoothing machine pointed at a project built to resist smoothing, and it earns its place here only under constraints that a human maintains and enforces. Take the constraints away and you get a fluent, confident, well-formatted version of exactly what this site exists to argue against. Not a claim that the machines caught the interesting things. Every gate here is downstream of a person noticing. The gate's value is that the noticing never has to happen twice — not that it happened at all. Not open-washing. Open is a licence, a repository, a runnable toolchain and a published error log, or it is a word in a footer. If any of the four goes away, so does the claim. Not everything. Your search query is yours and never leaves your browser, and there is no personal data in this repository. Open about the work is not the same as open about the people, and the second one is somebody else's business model.

The shorter version The average colour of the light in this universe is a warm off-white, and the first published value for it was wrong. It got fixed because two astronomers put their own erratum where their mistake had been, and because colour scientists who had nothing to do with the paper could see enough of the working to spot the flaw in it. That is the arrangement we are copying. The pages, the tools, the reasoning, the ledger and the errors are all in one public place, at the same commit, under a licence that lets you take them. The machines here are second thoughts made durable — they hold ground that a person already took, so the person can go and look at something new. And the looking is still ours, because it has to be. Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants. We work by the light of a colour that had to be corrected — in public, by the people who got it wrong, with everything shown. Neither is doing charity — each is handing over what it has plenty of for what it lacks. Fungal threads do connect many plants at once, and the popular name for that is the "wood wide web" (Simard) — a sunlit elder feeding a seedling shaded on the forest floor. Be careful with this one: the root-to-fungus trade above is settled, but the forest-wide version is not. Reviewing the field studies, Karst, Jones & Hoeksema (Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023) found the evidence too thin to say shared networks are widespread or that they reliably help seedlings, and found no published evidence that elder trees preferentially feed their own offspring through them. The lesson we keep is the smaller, sturdier one: not charity from the strong, but partners each handing over what they have plenty of. Monotropa uniflora, the ghost pipe, is the honest exception. It makes no chlorophyll and does no photosynthesis; it glows waxy-white in deep shade, living entirely on carbon it siphons from mycorrhizal fungi that are themselves fed by trees. Botanists call it a myco-heterotroph, or epiparasite: a one-directional relationship, not a mutualism. Named plainly, it belongs here precisely because not every symbiosis is gentle, or even. But read it with care. That a living thing takes what it needs and returns nothing in kind is not a moral failing — it is how a forest floor works, and how mutual aid works too: to each according to need. Some seasons, some bodies, can only receive, and the network holds them anyway. No one earns belonging through output; no one is disposable for being, this season, a taker. There's a deeper rhyme, too. "Monotropa" means one turn — the same root as monotropism, the Autistic attention-style (Murray, Lesser & Lawson, 2005). Helen Edgar calls the ghost pipe "one of the most perfect botanical expressions of being monotropic": thriving in the dark others can't use, nourished through a hidden mycelial network of care. Her essay Monotropa uniflora and Monotropism is written in tribute to Dinah Murray, who named monotropism and spent her last years studying the very fungi that feed this ghost. Energy is only transformed, never gone. it falls back in 45 Star Stuff The Cloud Phase on the last stage of a supernova remnant, and how long the in-between actually lasts after Helen Edgar · a cloud, not a waiting room L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely

The cloud phase Astronomy already named it A big star does not simply stop. It explodes, and what is left is called a remnant — the star's own material, thrown outward at thousands of kilometres a second. The version most of us were handed ends about one step past that. The shell expands, thins, cools, and disperses into the interstellar medium. Fade out. The star is finished, and the sentence is finished with it. But the physics runs further than the sentence does, and there is another word waiting at the end of it. In 2024 Leonard Romano, Manuel Behrendt and Andreas Burkert followed remnants through their long cold decline in three-dimensional simulation. They found the late evolution divides into four stages — and the one at the end they call the cloud phase. Not the end phase. Not the dispersal phase. The cloud phase — a named, described, modelled stage of a remnant's life. Romano, Behrendt & Burkert · ApJ 965, 168 · 2024 That is the whole reason this zine exists. We did not go looking for a metaphor and bend the astronomy to fit it. The astronomers got there first and wrote the word down. What is left of a dead star is understood as a cloud, studied as a cloud, and given a stage of its own in the literature. Held as proposed, not as settled. Romano et al. is a 2024 hydrodynamic simulation study, not textbook consensus, and the four-stage subdivision is their result. It may be revised. We are flagging that here, in place, the way this collection flags the wood wide web — and nothing later in this zine leans on it. The argumentative weight sits on spread five, which is an observation. Where the usual story stops A remnant's life shown as four boxes — free expansion, Sedov-Taylor, radiative, cloud phase. A marker shows the popular account ending after the third box, while the literature carries on to the fourth. freeexpansion Sedov–Taylor radiative cloudphase where the retelling stops and it keeps going the last stage has a name Romano et al., 2024 · proposed Figure 1 · the word at the end of the sentence The Cloud Phase · Stimpunks

It falls back in The shell comes back The intuitive picture of a remnant is a bubble that just keeps growing until it is too thin to see. Outward, all the way down. That is not what the simulations do at the end. Romano and colleagues find four stages inside the radiative phase: the radiative phase, subdivided stage what happens pressure-driven snowplow the hot, overpressured bubble inside is evacuated and pushed into the cold shell momentum-conserving snowplow nothing is driving it any more; the shell coasts and broadens implosion cold material from the back of the shell floods into the central vacuum cloud phase the infalling gas settles as a central, compact overdensity The third stage is the turn. Once the shell is no longer being pushed from behind, and the pressure inside has fallen to match the pressure of the medium outside, nothing is holding the cavity open. So the remnant falls back into itself. The collapse inward is not the failure of the expansion. It is the next thing the remnant does. stage three of four And what settles in the middle is not thin leftover. In these simulations it is highly chemically enriched, can reach a thousand to ten thousand solar masses, and can become self-gravitating within a few million years — which the authors call an attractive, novel pathway for supernova-induced star and planet formation. The timescales are long. The implosion takes a few hundred thousand to a few million years to launch. The cloud takes a few million to about ten million more to form. Nothing here is quick, and nothing here is idle. Grains that did not exist before

The debris makes new material Grains that did not exist before On 23 February 1987 a star exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, close enough to see with the naked eye. It was the nearest supernova since 1604, and we have been watching it continuously ever since. In 2014 ALMA resolved the millimetre emission from the middle of that remnant and measured what was sitting there: at least 0.2 solar masses of dust — the largest mass then measured in any supernova remnant — concentrated at the centre, in the cold inner ejecta, not yet reached by the reverse shock. Later work with Herschel and further ALMA data puts the cold dust nearer half a solar mass. Here is the part worth sitting with. That dust is new. Silicate and carbon grains condensed out of the cooling wreckage, assembled from atoms forged in the star's last seconds and in the explosion itself. Before the star died, that material did not exist in that form anywhere. The debris field is not where things end up. It is where the next material gets made — not after the wreckage, but in it. SN 1987A, thirty-odd years in Dust is not incidental, either. It is what lets a cloud cool, what shields molecules from starlight, what eventually accretes into rock. The grains in your bones were made in places like this. Some fraction of them, in something's ejecta, in some galaxy's slow afterwards. What is contested here. The ≥0.2 M☉ measurement is the firm floor; the total, the composition, and the timing are still argued. Sarangi & Cherchneff and Dwek & Arendt find silicate-dominated dust forming early; Wesson et al. find carbon-dominated dust forming mostly after day 1500. And how much of it survives the reverse shock over the coming millennia is genuinely open. We are using the floor, not the ceiling. Most of a cloud never becomes a star

Ninety-two percent stays cloud Most of a cloud never becomes a star This is the middle of the argument, and it is not a simulation. It is a measurement. In 2011 Norman Murray took the thirteen most luminous free-free radio sources in the Galaxy — responsible for a third of the Milky Way's free-free emission — matched them to their host giant molecular clouds, and asked how much of each cloud had actually been turned into stars. The star formation efficiency ran from 0.002 to 0.2, with an ionizing-luminosity-weighted average of 0.08. Eight percent. In the most vigorously star-forming clouds in the Galaxy — the bright ones, the ones you would pick deliberately if you wanted star formation to look efficient — ninety-two percent of the cloud does not become a star. And that is the flattering figure. Murray gives the Galactic average efficiency as 0.005. Ninety-two percent is the number from the clouds chosen for being the most productive. Galaxy-wide, more than ninety-nine percent of a molecular cloud stays cloud. Murray · ApJ 729, 133 · 2011 Read that as a shortfall and you have read it wrong. There is no rate the cloud is failing to hit. Nobody set a target. There is no efficient cloud somewhere, meeting expectations, against which these are underperforming. Ninety-two percent is not what the cloud failed to do. It is what a cloud is. What a cloud turns into Two bars. The first, for the Milky Way's most productive clouds, shows eight percent becoming stars and ninety-two percent staying cloud. The second, the Galactic average, shows half a percent becoming stars. the most productive clouds 8% 92% stays cloud the Galactic average 0.5% 99.5% stays cloud gold is the part that lights Murray, ApJ 729, 133, 2011 Figure 4 · the argumentative centre The Cloud Phase · Stimpunks

So the in-between is not the short part The long condition The same paper measures the other half of it: how long a giant molecular cloud lasts. 27 ± 12 million years, at the mean mass of that sample — a bit less than three free-fall times. Tens of millions of years of being a cloud. And the bright episode inside that span is short, late, and terminal: Murray finds the luminous clusters in his sample are actively tearing their host clouds apart. The star formation does not crown the cloud's life. It ends it. So the arithmetic runs the opposite way from the story we get told. Put the two measurements side by side and the shape is unmistakable: The bright part is brief and it destroys the cloud. The cloud part is long, and it is nearly all of what there is. two numbers from one paper Which means the in-between is not the gap between the real states. It is the majority state — by mass, and by duration — and the luminous thing is the exception that terminates it. We are not offering that as consolation, and it would be a weaker piece if we were. It is simply what the measurements say. The refusal to rush this to a bright resolution is not editorial restraint. It is the data. A discrepancy worth naming. The arXiv preprint of Murray (2011) gives cloud lifetimes as 17 ± 4 Myr and “about two free-fall times”; the published ApJ version says 27 ± 12 Myr and “a bit less than three.” We cite the published paper, which is the version of record — and we are telling you the preprint disagrees, because you may go and find it. Remnants entangled in new ways Re-assembly, not return Helen Edgar names this stage from the inside, and she named it before we went looking for the physics. In My Monotropic Galaxy (More Realms, June 2026) she maps twenty constellations of her own Autistic self. The second one is Supernova Remnant, and it is burnout. The Supernova Remnant in my galaxy is like a new way of becoming that emerges after burnout, remnants of my old self entangled in new ways of being. Helen Edgar · My Monotropic Galaxy · More Realms, 2026 She is precise about the direction of travel: “Each significant burnout has remade me and formed new constellations.” Remade. Not restored, not repaired, not returned. The third part of her burnout series makes the word carry weight — Autistic Burnout Recovery as Ecological Re-assembly — where recovery is the rebuilding of relational and attentional systems rather than a journey back to a previous configuration. Which is exactly what a remnant does. The material persists; the arrangement does not. Every atom is still there, and not one of them is where it was, and the thing they now compose is not the star. Nothing goes back. That is not the tragedy of the remnant — it is the mechanism by which anything else is possible. the physics agreeing with the account So when we are asked to come back — the same output, the same tolerances, the same mask, the same person we were before we broke — we are being asked for a return that the physics of the thing does not contain. There is no configuration to go back to. There is only what assembles next, out of the same material, differently. Return versus re-assembly Two paths from a scattered set of points. One loops back to the original arrangement and is marked not available. What seeded us is unsettled Something nearby was freshly dead Our own solar system began in a cloud, and there is a fingerprint of what was in it. In 1976 Typhoon Lee, Dimitri Papanastassiou and Gerald Wasserburg found an excess of magnesium-26 in calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions in the Allende meteorite — the decay product of aluminium-26, which has a half-life of about 717,000 years. That half-life is the entire argument. 26Al is made in massive stars. For its decay product to be locked into the oldest solids in the solar system in that quantity, live 26Al had to arrive in our birth cloud within a few half-lives of those solids forming. Ombre Tarragnat calls this ethodiversity — the variety of "ways of being and behaving" across all animals — extending a term coined in ecology by Adolfo Cordero-Rivera. The migratory route, the dialect of a birdsong, the nocturnal life, the whole existential style of a creature. Its shadow is ethonormativity: the unwritten rule about which behaviours are allowed to count as acceptable. The horse who refuses the rider, the cat who won't be petted — abandoned, or worse, for departing from the expected script. A grid laid over a field that was already full of variation. The Dead Stars Still Reach Us is the tenth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the one about ancestry — the astronomy underneath our writing on memory and lineage. The astronomy is real, and worth stating precisely. Light travels at a finite speed, so we always see a star as it was when its light departed, never as it is now. It's often said that "the stars you see are already dead" — in truth, most naked-eye stars are still shining, because they sit tens to hundreds of light-years away, far less than a star's lifetime. The deeper, exact point is that we can never see any star's present, so we live by light from sources we cannot check — and some of them, especially distant ones, are indeed already gone. SN 1006 is the vivid case: observers worldwide recorded the supernova in the spring of 1006 CE; the star lay roughly 7,200 light-years off, so the explosion itself happened millennia before anyone on Earth saw it, and only its expanding remnant — and its scattered elements — remain (this is the "Liberating Star Stuff" image Stimpunks keeps). Betelgeuse, about 550 light-years away, will end as a supernova; if it exploded today we would not know for roughly five centuries, and it may already have gone. The ancestry is drawn from our own writing. The Highlander Folk School crosswalk reads the school (founded 1932 by Myles Horton; Septima Clark's citizenship schools; Rosa Parks, 1955; Aldon Morris's "movement halfway house") as ancestry rather than parallel — via Nico Slate's 2022 history. How knowledge grows The garden, not the stream Most of the web is a social stream: a feed of dated posts, sorted by an algorithm, urgent for a day and then washed away. A post starts decaying the moment it's published. You don't return to it; you scroll past it. A garden is the older idea. Mike Caulfield drew the line: the garden is the web as space, an arrangement you can walk. It's evergreen — you keep tending and refining the notes — and richly cross-linked, so that, as Maggie Appleton puts it, every walk creates new paths. You add things not in sequence but so they can form future, unpredicted relationships. The Star Stuff site is a garden. So is the whole knowledge garden it grew from. Not a feed to keep up with — a landscape to wander. A stream tells you what's new. A garden lets you wander what's true. hierarchy subjects → articles rhizome sideways, not up grown from lived experience a mesh, not a ladder roots down in real life Lived experience Grown from the ground up An encyclopedia grows downward from the top: subjects, then categories, then articles, handed down by an authority. A garden grows the other way. Ours climbs up from the soil of lived experience — from what a body knows, to a word for it, to a pattern, a recipe, an environment, a system. And it doesn't grow in straight lines. Its shape is a rhizome and a mycelial network (after Deleuze & Guattari): ideas spread sideways and underground, throwing up shoots where they connect, refusing the neat trunk-and-branches of the tree. Knowledge grown up from the ground of real neurodivergent and disabled life — not lowered down onto it. An encyclopedia is handed down from the top. A garden grows up from the ground. The cosmic turn Star stuff, knowing itself Here is the reason it's a garden and not a vault. Carl Sagan said we are a way for the cosmos to know itself. A knowledge garden is that sentence built into a thing you can walk through — and the method it uses is the cosmos's own. A star forges the elements in its core and then, dying, scatters them — a supernova is a seed-head bursting (the image on every Stimpunks page, SN 1006, is literally liberated iron). That scattered stuff settles into life; life grows minds; minds grow gardens of meaning that go to seed and grow new minds. Nucleosynthesis, then the periodic table — the first seed catalogue — then us. So the universe doesn't know itself as stored data. It knows itself as a garden — by growing, connecting, and seeding, over and over. The reflex It arrives before you do You know the feeling. It gets there ahead of you. Something on a screen, something in a jar, something in a documentary about the deep sea — and before a single thought has formed, the whole body has already voted. The face does its thing. The shoulders go up. Ugh. No. Get it away. And it doesn't feel like an opinion. That's the important part. It feels like perception — like you have simply noticed a property the thing has, the way you'd notice that it was blue. It isn't. There is no gross in the animal. There is no gross anywhere in the ocean. Gross is a reading, produced by a particular frame, in a particular animal, at a particular moment in its history — and this zine is about who ends up on the wrong side of it. Before we go any further Two icks, not one There is a distinction the research makes, and an earlier version of this zine walked straight past it. It matters enormously, so it goes here, before the argument. Paul Rozin's own framework separates two things that both feel like "ew." Distaste is sensory. It is a response to the actual properties of a thing — bitter, sour, slimy, sticky, cold and wet in the wrong way. And it is there from the beginning. Put something bitter on a newborn's tongue and you get the gape face: mouth open, upper lip pulled back, nose wrinkled, brow down. It is highly conserved across species. It has been observed in humans in utero. And then the finding that settles how deep it runs. In 1973 Jacob Steiner published observations of the gustofacial response in anencephalic newborns — infants born without most of the higher brain. They make the face too. The response does not require a cortex. It isn't a judgement, it isn't an attitude, and it cannot be a prejudice, because there is nothing there to hold one. Disgust proper is a different animal. Rozin calls it ideationally based and contamination-sensitive: you don't have to taste a cockroach to be disgusted by one. It attaches to ideas about things — where they have been, what they touched, what they count as. This zine is about the second one. Everything that follows — the borders, the projections, the sorting of bodies — is the ideational kind doing political work. The sensory kind is not a prejudice and never was. You were never a blank slate. You arrived with a body that already had positions on the world, and that gape is older than our species — history, carried in you. Which is, after all, the premise of this entire collection. The correction on this spread is Helen Edgar's, who taught children with profound and multiple learning disabilities for twenty years and pointed out that the first version of this zine presumed a thinking response to the ick — and that the babies and the young people she has worked with plainly have one without it. two responses, both called "ew" distaste the gape face present at birth no cortex needed disgust where has it been? ideational contamination-sensitive develops later not a prejudice never was does border work this zine is about this one rozin · steiner 1973 · gustofacial response distaste is bodily · disgust is ideational only one of them can be a prejudice The Ick · Stimpunks

Where it came from The second one gets taught The gape was there at birth. The contamination logic was not, and small children are famously unbothered by it. Paul Rozin and April Fallon, in a 1987 paper that still anchors the field, treat disgust as a food emotion at root — revulsion at the prospect of taking something into the mouth. Its objects are overwhelmingly of animal origin. And crucially, this kind develops, arriving across a child's first eight years or so rather than being present at the start. They also describe what it runs on. Disgust obeys the laws of sympathetic magic — including the law of contagion, under which contact transfers an essence. A cockroach touches your sandwich; the sandwich is now inedible. Not partly inedible where the legs went. All of it. Forever. Sit with that, because it's the whole argument in one move: the reaction is out of all proportion to any physical fact. No amount of chemistry explains the whole sandwich. What's operating is a rule about categories and contact — and rules about categories are things a culture teaches you. Which means the border can be redrawn. People do it constantly, in both directions, without noticing. Somebody, somewhere, feeds their child something you would gag on, and their child grows up finding it delicious and finding your dinner revolting. Both of you think you are perceiving. the law of contagion edible one touch ALL of it inedible and it arrives on a schedule birth ~4 yrs ~8 yrs unbothered fully installed rozin & fallon 1987 · it was taught a rule about categories not a measurement of danger The Ick · Stimpunks

Exhibit one The worm with no mouth In 2004 Greg Rouse, Shana Goffredi and Robert Vrijenhoek named a genus that shouldn't work. Osedax — the name means bone-devourer — lives on whale skeletons on the deep sea floor. The adult females have no mouth and no gut at all. What they have instead is a root system: a branching, blood-supplied network that grows down into the bone, carrying symbiotic bacteria that break the bone down from inside. The animal doesn't eat. It roots, like something between a worm and a small tree, into the skeleton of something enormous that died above it. And the males never grow up. Dozens of them — tiny, paedomorphic, arrested partway through development — live inside the female's own tube, doing the one job they are there for. Every clause of that is a small horror in English, and not one of it is a problem. It is a lineage that found a food source nobody else could reach, and built a body that could get at it. Read from inside, it's just competent. You are not looking at a violation. You are looking at somebody's job. What it costs to never let go

Exhibit two What it costs to never let go The deep-sea anglerfish is the one everybody has heard about, usually told as a joke. A male, far smaller than the female, finds her in the dark, bites on, and fuses. Tissues join. The two circulatory systems merge into one. He never leaves. It is the only case in nature of two vertebrates becoming, permanently, a single joined body. Here is the part that isn't a joke, and it is the reason this zine exists. In 2020 Jeremy Swann, Stephen Holland, Malte Petersen, Theodore Pietsch and Thomas Boehm looked at the genomes and found what the fusion cost. Species whose males attach temporarily have lost functional aicda — the gene behind antibody maturation. Species whose males attach permanently go further, some losing functional rag genes altogether, which abolishes the somatic shuffling of antigen receptors that is the defining hallmark of adaptive immunity. Your immune system's entire job is telling you from not-you, and rejecting the not-you. So: To be permanently joined to another body, they gave up the machinery that draws the line between self and other. They did not solve rejection. They dismantled the thing that rejects. The border you are so sure of is a piece of equipment. It can be traded. Somebody did. attachment, and what it costs temporary lost: aicda no antibody maturation permanent lost: aicda + rag no receptor shuffling — adaptive immunity gone the immune system's job: self | not-self to stay joined, they gave up the line swann, holland, petersen, pietsch & boehm 2020 science, 2020 · immunogenetics of sexual parasitism the price of never letting go The Ick · Stimpunks
A body that becomes a town

Exhibit three A body that becomes a town Nothing triggers the reflex like a corpse. So let's take the biggest one there is. A whale dies and sinks. Down there, food arrives as a slow drizzle of scraps from far above — and now, all at once, forty tonnes of it lands in one place. Craig Smith and Amy Baco, reviewing the whole field in 2003, put the scale plainly: the sediment beneath a sunken carcass gets an initial pulse of organic matter equivalent to roughly 2,000 years of the normal background supply. Then a town builds itself, in three overlapping stages. Months to years. The mobile scavengers — sleeper sharks, hagfish, rat-tails — strip soft tissue at 40 to 60 kilograms a day. Months to years. Enrichment opportunists move onto the enriched sediment and the exposed bones: dense assemblages of polychaetes and crustaceans, up to 40,000 animals per square metre. Decades. The sulphophilic stage. Bone lipids break down without oxygen and give off sulphide; bacteria make a living out of the sulphide; a large, trophically complex community assembles on top of that. Smith and Baco report a mean of 185 macrofaunal species on a large skeleton at this stage — higher local diversity than any other hard surface in the deep sea. Across the world's whale falls, 407 species. Twenty-one of them are known from nowhere else on Earth. The thing you were taught was the end of a body is, down there, one of the most generous events that ever happens. 185 mean macrofaunal species on one large skeleton 21 species known from nowhere else one carcass, three stages, decades 1 · mobile scavengers sleeper sharks · hagfish · rat-tails — 40–60 kg/day months–years 2 · enrichment opportunists polychaetes · crustaceans — up to 40,000 per m² months–years 3 · sulphophilic bone lipids → sulphide → chemoautotrophs mean 185 macrofaunal species DECADES ≈ 2,000 years of background food, at once smith & baco 2003 decay is a construction schedule the richest hard surface down there The Ick · Stimpunks
What the ick was actually measuring

The turn What the ick was actually measuring Go back over the three of them and ask what they had in common. It wasn't danger — none of them can hurt you. It wasn't dirt — the deep sea is one of the cleanest places on the planet. What they share is distance from one particular body plan. Mouths belong on faces. Bodies end at the skin. The dead are separate from the living. Eating is done with a gut. These aren't laws of nature. They are the specifications of one animal, generalised into a template — and the ick is what fires when something falls outside it. That template has two settings, and this collection has been picking at both: Anthronormative — the assumption that the human arrangement is the correct arrangement for a body. Neuronormative — the assumption that one kind of mind is the correct kind, and other kinds are that kind gone wrong. Same machine, two dials. Both take a local arrangement and file everything else as a deviation from it. distance from a template one template Osedax anglerfish whale fall the ick tracks radius · nothing else anthronormative one right body neuronormative one right mind same machine, two dials a local arrangement, promoted to a standard The Ick · Stimpunks
The same reflex, aimed at us

Where it lands The same reflex, aimed at us Now the part this zine was actually written for. That reflex — the one that fires at a rooted worm and a fused fish — does not stay in the ocean. It gets pointed at people, and it does an enormous amount of work. It fires at a feeding tube. At drooling. At an adult in incontinence pads. At a stim that isn't the socially cleared kind — the loud one, the wet one, the one with hands. At a communication device that speaks in a voice somebody decided was unpleasant. At bodies that need help with the parts of being alive that everyone has agreed to pretend are private. Nobody says disgusting out loud. They don't have to. The reflex does its work in the face, in the half-step back, in the seat that stays empty, in the invitation that doesn't come, in the tone of the assessment paperwork. Martha Nussbaum gave this its name in 2004: projective disgust. We take what we cannot stand about being animal — that we leak, decay, depend, and die — and we load it onto a group of people, who then function as a buffer between us and our own bodies. Push them out and the animal facts feel further away. Which is why the ick is not a matter of taste, and why we are not asking anyone to find worms charming. Disgust is how a border gets enforced without anyone having to defend it. It doesn't argue. It just refuses, and then it acts hurt if you ask it to explain. The reflex that ruled out the bone-eating worm is the reflex that empties the seat next to us. It never learned there was a difference. projective disgust, in one move what we can't stand about being animal: leaking · decaying · needing · dying loaded onto a group of people who then sit between us and the facts push them out → the animal feels further away it was never about them nussbaum, hiding from humanity, 2004 a buffer, made of people the ick is doing somebody's laundry The Ick · Stimpunks
Weird we took. Gross we haven't

Two words, two jobs Weird we took. Gross we haven't There's a word next door to this one, and it has already been reclaimed. In Wyrd & Weird, Helen Edgar follows weird back to Old English wyrd — becoming, fate, a web held from every side — and shows Autistic and disabled communities running the drift backwards, taking the word up as a name rather than a verdict. Weird is ours now. People wear it. Gross has not been taken, and it works differently. Weird is a judgement about categories: you don't fit the box. It can be answered with pride, because pride is also a claim about where you belong. Gross isn't a claim at all. It's a body refusing another body. You can't be proud at it, because it doesn't stay to listen — it has already turned away. So this one doesn't get reclaimed. It gets disarmed: shown to be learned, shown to be arbitrary, shown to be doing political work it never admitted to. You don't march under it. You just stop letting it decide who's in the room. two words, two jobs weird a claim about categories "you don't fit" answerable → RECLAIMED worn as a name gross a body refusing another body "get it away" unanswerable → DISARMED shown for what it is you can march under one of these the other you just take the keys off no. 28 took the first one this one gets disarmed instead The Ick · Stimpunks

Held with care What we are not saying This argument has several cheap versions. Naming them so we don't get mistaken for one. Not"actually it's beautiful." That just swaps one aesthetic verdict for another and keeps the judge's chair warm. The worm doesn't need to be pretty. It needs to be left alone. Not"gross but useful to humans." Hagfish slime is being studied for fibres; whale-fall bacteria for enzymes. Fine — but usefulness is the extraction frame, and the zine before this one is about where that leads. Notyour sensory aversion is a prejudice. If a texture, a smell, a sound or a wet thing on your hands sends you through the roof — that is distaste, it is bodily, and none of this argument is pointed at it. Autistic and otherwise neurodivergent sensory responses are real, they are not bigotry, and you do not owe anybody an apology or an exposure programme for them. Nota blank slate. We are not claiming you arrived with no positions on the world. You arrived with a nervous system that had plenty, and the oldest of them are older than our species. What is learned is the contamination logic laid over the top, not the body underneath it. Notdisgust is never useful. It plainly has a job — some of it tracks real contamination. The claim is narrower: its objects are learned, it overshoots wildly, and it should never be trusted as evidence about a person. Notyou're bad for feeling it. It was installed in you before you could consent. Nobody is guilty of a reflex. You are only answerable for what you do in the two seconds after. Notdisabled people are deep-sea creatures. We are not anyone's metaphor. The shared thing is the reflex and the border it draws — not the bodies on either side of it. Notbiology proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. That the ocean is full of arrangements we find upsetting is not why people deserve welcome. They would deserve it in an empty universe. the two seconds after the reflex not yours to choose not yours to be blamed for treat it as evidence → the seat stays empty treat it as weather → you stay in the room nobody is guilty of a flinch everyone is answerable for what comes next a rhyme, not a proof the flinch is not the failure what you do next is The Ick · Stimpunks

Look again Nothing down there has changed Go back to the worm. It is still rooted in the bone. It still has no mouth. The males are still small and still in her tube. Not one fact about it has moved since page four. If it reads differently now — and it might — then the thing that changed was on this side of the glass. That's the whole demonstration. The verdict was never in the water. It was in the frame, that part of the frame was learned, and a learned thing can be widened. Your body may still not want to touch it. That's allowed, and it always was — that part isn't the frame, it's you, and it has a history in it older than our species. Not wanting to touch something is not the same as ruling it out of the world. The whole argument is the gap between those two. And widening it is not a favour you do the deep sea. The deep sea is fine. It's a favour you do yourself, and everyone who has ever been on the far side of somebody's flinch — which, at some point, is everybody. Because here is the thing the reflex is actually protecting you from, and it's not the worm: you are an animal. You leak, you decay, you need enormous amounts of help, and one day you will be food for something. Every one of those is also true of the whale, and the whale's version fed a town for thirty years. The atoms doing all of this were made in stars. That part is true of the worm, the anglerfish, the whale, and you — the same calcium, the same carbon, the same everything, arranged into a few thousand ways of being alive, not one of which is the correct one. The Ick Is a Border is Zine No. 33 in the Stimpunks Star Stuff series. It is a house zine and a deliberate companion to Wyrd & Weird (28), Helen Edgar's guest zine on weird — the word this community did reclaim. Weird is hers and the reclamation is hers; this zine takes the neighbouring word, gross, which works differently and is disarmed rather than worn. It extends Every Nervous System (27) and The Council of All Beings (25) into the territory of disgust, and continues the account of constructed lines begun in The Lines We Drew (9). Written after The Skeleton That Skipped Bone (32), for the same young person, whose marine biology special interest is the reason both exist. Corrected after publication — and the correction is the important part. The first published version of this zine argued that the ick is learned, full stop. Helen Edgar, who taught children with profound and multiple learning disabilities for twenty years, read it and pointed out that it presumes a cognitive, intellectualising response — and that pre-term babies, and the young people she has worked with, plainly have an ick without one. She is right, and the literature is unambiguous. Rozin's own framework separates distaste — a chemosensory rejection tied to a thing's actual properties, producing the highly conserved "gape face," present at birth and observed in utero — from disgust proper, which Rozin describes as ideationally based and contamination-sensitive, and which you can feel about a cockroach without tasting one. The strongest evidence for how deep the first one runs is Jacob Steiner's (1973) observations of the gustofacial response in anencephalic newborns, who produce it without most of a higher brain: the response does not require a cortex, and therefore cannot be an opinion. Spread 3 now makes that distinction before the argument starts, and the argument is explicitly scoped to the ideational kind. Helen's second point is the one that goes deepest and is now in the zine's own voice: we are not blank slates — that is the point of star stuff; we have history in us. A response conserved across species and present before birth is exactly that history, and the earlier draft was, in effect, arguing against this collection's own premise. Autistic and otherwise neurodivergent sensory aversion is distaste, not prejudice, and spread 11 now says so in a refusal. Sources & notes. On the anglerfishes: Swann, J. B., Holland, S. J., Petersen, M., Pietsch, T. W. & Boehm, T. (2020). The immunogenetics of sexual parasitism. On whale falls: Smith, C. R. & Baco, A. R. (2003). Ecology of whale falls at the deep-sea floor. Oceanography and Marine Biology: An Annual Review, 41, 311–354 — read in the primary; source of the three successional stages and their durations, of the sleeper sharks, hagfish and rat-tails removing soft tissue at 40–60 kg per day, of the enrichment-opportunist densities (up to 40,000 m⁻²), of the sulphophilic stage lasting decades with a mean of 185 macrofaunal species (higher than any other deep-sea hard substratum community), of the 407 species globally and 21 known only from whale falls, and of the ~2,000-year equivalent pulse of background organic-carbon flux to the underlying sediments. Held honestly. Rozin and Fallon's account is a theory of disgust, not the only one, and the claim made here is the modest one their evidence supports: the objects of disgust are substantially learned and culturally variable, and the response overshoots any physical fact. That some disgust responses track genuine pathogen risk is not disputed. The whale-fall figures are means and estimates from a review of a small, poorly sampled set of sites — Smith and Baco say so themselves — and should be read as order-of-magnitude. The anglerfish immune losses vary by species and are not uniform across the group; "gave up the line between self and other" is our phrasing of a genetic finding, and adaptive immunity is not the whole of self/non-self discrimination. A note on a familiar quotation: "dirt is matter out of place" is widely attributed to Mary Douglas's Purity and Danger (1966), and she did make it famous — but it is not her coinage. It appears unreferenced in her first edition and is credited in later editions to Lord Chesterfield without a source; the earliest located use is an 1853 address by Lord Palmerston. We have not used the line as hers, and neither should anyone else. Finally: the ethics do not come from the biology. That the ocean is full of arrangements we find upsetting is not why anyone deserves welcome — as about.html puts it, we are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation — and it has never once found any of us disgusting. The Ladder We Don't Print ARLES is the Stimpunks Design Method — five layers of neurodivergent life in an order that has to hold. It is named here, and deliberately almost nowhere in the zines. A spread-by-spread map: the one piece built on the ladder on purpose, three that climb it without being built to, two that sit on a single rung and say so — and the four pieces that already name the method out loud, which is a fact this page has to hold rather than tidy away. What this is, and isn't This is a reading of our own work, and a reading can be argued with. Every rung label below was applied after the fact, by us, to pieces that were mostly not built with the ladder in hand. Nothing on this page was measured. The six gates in this repository can check a colour, a tag tree, a page count, a sitemap entry and a text collision; not one of them can check whether a spread is really about attention. The method was: read the spread eyebrows and headings of all sixty-two numbered zines , then read the candidates in full. That will have missed a piece that climbs quietly, and it may have over-read one that doesn't. If a mapping below looks wrong to you, it might be. Stimpunks crosswalks other people's frameworks against ARLES — the ecosystemic model of distress , and Jessica Dark's System-Level Organisational Design Framework . This page turns the same instrument on our own shelf, which is a much easier exercise and worth much less. Finding your own method in your own artifacts is the least surprising result available. What it is good for is legibility: it tells a reader why the zines keep arriving at the room instead of the person.

The ladder, named once ARLES names five layers through which neurodivergent life is structured, and the order in which environments have to be redesigned to support it. Each layer holds up the one above it. A · Attention How a mind focuses, processes, and forms meaning. Monotropism lives here. This is the floor. R · Relational (incl. Regulation) Communication, co-regulation , consent. Regulation is relational and environmental, not an individual skill. L · Lived Experience The sensory, emotional and cognitive realities of a day. What it actually feels like to be in the room. E · Environment The conditions that shape participation. A space either fits a bodymind or fights it. S · Systems The structures, norms and institutions that distribute opportunity and constraint. Upward it is a design order · downward it is a diagnosis Read upward , it is a sequence for design: begin with attention and nervous-system safety, build shared language and co-regulation, name what people actually experience, redesign the environment, and only then move to systems. Read downward , it is a sequence for diagnosis: a failing system points to the environment that produced it, the environment to the lived experience it ignored, and on down to the attention it never accounted for. Skip the lower layers and systems reform collapses. That sentence is the whole reason the order is load-bearing rather than decorative, and it is why most reform fails: it starts at the top, rewrites the policy, and then asks people to cope. ARLES and the design method it belongs to are Stimpunks' own, published in the open — the glossary entry is the short form and the design method the long one.
Why the word stays off the spreads
Why the word stays off the spreads Three reasons, in the order they matter.
One · A named framework asks for assent before the argument does

One · A named framework asks for assent before the argument does A zine here works by taking one settled, checkable fact and following it honestly until the belonging claim is already inside it. The Moon runs the tide because tidal force falls off with the cube of distance. A hammer and a feather land together in vacuum. Bone under load makes a charge. The reader is not asked to agree to anything; they are asked to look. An acronym reverses that. It asks the reader to accept a five-part model of neurodivergent life first , and then the fact arrives as an illustration of the model — which is exactly the demotion the collection exists to refuse. The fact stops doing the work the moment it becomes an example.
Two · The rungs already have plain words

Two · The rungs already have plain words Attention. The people near you. What the day actually feels like. The room. Who set the rules. Every rung has an ordinary-language form that costs a reader nothing, and the zines already use them. A piece that says the storm is in the weather, not the water has delivered the Environment rung to someone who will never need the label. A piece that says when a feather falls slowly, look for the air has delivered the downward read.
Three · It is already the standing rule, written into a colophon

Three · It is already the standing rule, written into a colophon No. 59, The Rest You Keep , is the one zine built on the ladder deliberately, and its own colophon states the rule: Internally this zine is built on the ARLES ladder — attention, relational, lived experience, environment, systems — which is deliberately not printed on the spreads; the argument should stand without the scaffold. One precision, because the sentence is slightly generous to itself. What is withheld is the acronym, the diagram and the order-claim . The rung words are not withheld: five of them are printed on No. 59 as spread eyebrows, one per spread. That is the line, and it is the right line. A reader meets Attention as a heading over an argument about attention and loses nothing. They never meet a ladder they have to buy into.
The one built on it: No. 59

The one built on it: No. 59 The Rest You Keep runs the full ladder in order, one rung per spread, with the acronym absent. Two that don't climb, and say so

Two that don't climb, and say so This is the part that keeps the page honest. A framework you can find everywhere is a framework that has stopped saying anything. No. 31, Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not occupies two rungs across ten spreads and states it in its own colophon: “In Stimpunks' ARLES terms, this zine lives at the top two rungs — Environment and Systems.” Convergence, attractors, Waddington's canalized landscape, the difference between a slope that was found and a wall that was poured. There is no ascent and there should not be. A zine about terrain has no business pretending to be about attention. No. 16, Minor Worlds runs the rungs badly out of order — Environment, Environment, Attention and Lived Experience together, Relational, Systems, Relational — and it is right to. Its claim is about the Environment rung: that the hum of the fluorescent light and the open-plan clatter are a built niche that got renamed the default. You cannot argue that from below. The rung under examination has to be on the table first. And then the majority. Most of the sixty-two numbered zines do not map onto this ladder at all, because most of them are not making a design argument — they are following a fact. No. 9 is about who holds the pen when a boundary gets drawn. No. 61 is about a ruler that would not travel one clade sideways. Those are arguments about measurement and authority, and forcing a rung onto them would tell you nothing about either.
Four pieces already say it out loud

Four pieces already say it out loud The rule at the top of this page is a rule going forward. It is not a description of the shelf, and the difference has to be published rather than smoothed over. Four pieces name the method on the page today: No. 17, The Nearest Body — spread 6's eyebrow reads Ecosystemic distress · ARLES , and the body spells out the downward read and links the glossary. Listed again in the colophon. No. 29, Only in Relation — spread 6 draws the ladder , all five rungs, and argues from it: Relational sits near the base, and Regulation lives inside it, because regulation is not a private skill. No. 31, Five Times a Crab — the two-rung placement in the colophon, plus the design-method line carried as an attributed quote. No. 59, The Rest You Keep — the colophon sentence quoted above, which is the rule stating itself. Nothing here proposes stripping them. No. 29's ladder is doing real work on that spread — the whole point of the piece is that regulation lives in the relation, and the diagram is what makes the placement visible. And a collection with a public error log cannot quietly delete an exception in order to make a rule look cleaner than it is. What the rule says is that a new zine does not become the fifth. Not Not a template. ARLES is a design order and a diagnostic order. It is not a story shape, and a zine built to hit five rungs in five spreads would be a framework deliverable with a starfield behind it. No. 59 earns its ladder by paying for every rung with an animal. Not a grading scheme. A one-rung zine is not a worse zine. No. 31 sits at the top of the ladder and never moves, and it is one of the most carefully sourced pieces here. Not a claim about intent. Three of the five maps above are retrospective. Saying this piece climbs the ladder is not saying anyone was holding the ladder at the time, and the two are easy to blur once a diagram exists. Not a private vocabulary. ARLES is published, in the open, and free to use with credit — the glossary and the method . It is kept off the spreads for the reader's sake, not for ours. Not evidence of anything. A house framework found in house artifacts is the least surprising result available, and this page would be worthless as a defence of ARLES. It is a legibility aid: it explains why these zines keep arriving at the room instead of the person.
