One axis, and we put ourselves at the top of it

The ladder One axis, and we put ourselves at the top of it Ask how smart an animal is and you have already agreed to something: that smart is a quantity, that it runs along one axis, and that every mind can be given a place on it. The axis needs a yardstick, so we have built several. Absolute brain mass. Brain mass against body mass. The encephalisation quotient. Cortical surface. Neuron counts. These are real measurements, taken carefully by careful people, and none of them is the problem. The problem is the ordering. A measurement tells you how much of something there is. It does not tell you that more of it is better, or that the creature with the most of it is the one the others are failing to be. And the ordering came first. We had the ladder long before we had the instruments, and then we went looking for the instrument that would show us on the top rung — which is a different activity from measuring. us apes monkeys the rest … more the shape of the assumption one axis · one winner a ladder, not a measurement The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Then somebody counted the pilot whale

The count Then somebody counted the pilot whale Neuron number is the yardstick that feels least arguable. Cells are countable. You can do the stereology and get a figure, and the figure does not care what you were hoping for. In 2014, Mortensen and colleagues did the counting on the neocortex of the long-finned pilot whale — a dolphin, despite the name. They found roughly 37.2 billion neocortical neurons, alongside some 127 billion glial cells. That is, in the paper's own words, almost twice as many neocortical neurons as humans. The first animal ever counted with more neocortical neurons than us, and it is a mid-sized dolphin that most people have never heard of. 37.2 ×10⁹ neocortical neurons long-finned pilot whale ≈ 2× the human count mortensen et al. 2014 Neuron density is lower in the whale; the total is higher because the brain is bigger. Both facts are in the paper, and both are worth keeping. 37.2 pilot whale ≈ half human neocortical neurons ×10⁹ the countable yardstick and it does not favour us mortensen et al. 2014 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
The measurement lost. The ranking survived it.

The part nobody quotes The measurement lost. The ranking survived it. Here is the sentence in that same paper. The absolute number of neurons in the human neocortex, the authors conclude, is not correlated with the superior cognitive abilities of humans — at least not compared with cetaceans — as had previously been hypothesised. Read it slowly. The yardstick was neuron count. The count came back against us. And the conclusion drawn is not perhaps the ranking is wrong. It is the count must not be the right yardstick. To be fair to the authors: as a narrow claim about neuroscience that is entirely defensible, and probably correct. Neuron number alone plainly does not explain human cognition. They are reporting an honest negative result. But look at what stayed fixed while everything else moved. Human superiority is not the thing being tested here. It is the thing the test is being fitted to. Which tells you something useful: the ranking was never resting on the count. So no count could ever disturb it. Another yardstick will be found, and if that one comes back wrong too, another will be found after it. the evidence whale us moved and yet the ranking us didn't it was never resting on the evidence a fixed point, dressed as a finding the yardstick is replaceable the conclusion is not The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
The input layer our textbooks call canonical is simply not there

No fourth layer The input layer our textbooks call canonical is simply not there Open a neuroscience textbook at the cortical column and you will find six layers, with layer IV as the front door: the granular layer where signals from the thalamus arrive before anything else happens to them. The cetacean neocortex does not have one. Not reduced in places — the whole sheet is agranular. The lamination, as the literature describes it, runs: a thick cellular layer I; a densely packed layer II whose neurons send dendrites up into layer I; a wide pyramidal layer III; an absent or underdeveloped layer IV; a magnocellular layer V of large pyramidal cells; and a heterogeneous layer VI. So where does the input go? The current reading is that layer I takes the job — that it is the main target for incoming subcortical neurons precisely because layer IV is absent, with layer II then relaying that information down to the lower layers. The front door moved upstairs. The result, in the words of the review that lays this out, is a very different connectivity scheme compared to more commonly studied species, like rats and macaque monkeys. Sit with that phrase — more commonly studied species. The canonical column is canonical because of who we happened to put on the microscope. Rats and macaques are the baseline for reasons of husbandry and history, not because evolution nominated them. And in layer V of the anterior cingulate, anterior insular and frontopolar cortices, the humpback whale turns out to carry large spindle cells — von Economo neurons — similar in shape and distribution to those described in hominids. Hof and Van der Gucht call it a likely case of parallel evolution. Same cell type, arrived at separately, in a cortex with no fourth layer to build it on. primate IIIIII IV VVI in front door: IV cetacean I IIIII IV VVI in relay front door: I IV: absent the job moved two routes into a cortex absent ≠ missing ≠ lacking hof & van der gucht 2007 · marino et al. 2008 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Difference read as deficit, in Biological Reviews, in 2006

The live argument Difference read as deficit, in Biological Reviews, in 2006 In 2006 Paul Manger published a long paper arguing that cetacean brains got big to make heat — thermogenesis against a cooling ocean — rather than to think. He argued further that cetaceans are considerably less intelligent than generally supposed. One of his three claims was this: there is no neural basis for complex cognition in cetaceans. Among the evidence offered were the indistinct lamination, the pyramidalised layer II, and the absence of layer IV. In 2008, sixteen authors replied. Those features, they answered, are one aspect of an unusual combination of conservative and derived traits — and cetacean brains, having diverged from our common ancestor more than 95 million years ago and arrived at high encephalisation entirely independently, in all likelihood represent a non-primate route to neuroanatomical (and cognitive) complexity. A brain organised unlike ours was read as a brain insufficient for mind. The reply did not say the difference wasn't real. It said the difference wasn't a deficit. You know this argument. It is the one made about us, in clinics and classrooms, in the same century. Here it is being had by neuroscientists, about whales, in a review journal — and the shape of the inference is identical. one observation no layer IV manger 2006 no neural basis for cognition marino et al. 2008 the input moved to layer I same slide different baseline the inference is a choice one fact, two readings deficit or design the data did not decide it The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
We are not telling you who won

Held with care We are not telling you who won It would be easy, and dishonest, to leave Manger as the villain of this zine. So: his thermogenesis hypothesis was a serious proposal, published in a serious journal, and it has not simply evaporated. Later work has found real thermogenic signatures in cetacean brains — uncoupling proteins expressed in cortical neurons and in glia, an increased density of noradrenergic boutons. A brain in cold water may well be doing heat work and thought work. Organs are not single-purpose. The reply from Marino and colleagues is also not neutral ground. It is an argued position by researchers with a stake in cetacean cognition, and calling a paper a claim in search of evidence in your own title is not a gesture of detachment. So we are not handing you a verdict. What we are pointing at is narrower and, we think, harder to wriggle out of: the direction the inference travelled by default. Given a cortex organised unlike the ones we had studied, the available readings included this brain is built differently and this brain is built worse. The second was reached quickly, defended at length, and required no additional evidence to feel reasonable — because the ladder was already there to catch it. That is the part that recurs. It recurs in the lines we drew around normal, and it is the mechanism the difference-first frame exists to interrupt. Not who was right about whales. Which reading you get for free. obs unlike ours built worse no extra evidence required built differently argued for at length both available one is downhill the gradient under the argument a rhyme, not a proof what you get for free is the finding The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
They had to borrow from music, because the shelf didn't fit

Rubato They had to borrow from music, because the shelf didn't fit Sperm whales talk in codas — short patterned bursts of clicks. For decades the Eastern Caribbean repertoire was described as around 21 discrete coda types. A modest vocabulary. Roughly what you would expect from a lesser mind. In 2024, a team analysed 8,719 codas from at least 60 whales recorded between 2005 and 2018, and found the repertoire was not a list at all. It has four features that combine freely: rhythm and tempo, which hold steady regardless of context, plus two they named rubato and ornamentation, which shift with the conversation going on around them. Combine those four and you get roughly 143 combinations actually in use — nearly an order of magnitude past the old count. Notice the naming. Rubato and ornamentation are borrowed from music, because the categories on the shelf did not have a slot for what the whales were doing. The vocabulary had to be built before the structure could be seen. Which is the quiet lesson of the whole zine. When your instrument has no category for a thing, the thing reads as absence. Twenty-one types was never what the whales had. It was what we could hear. rhythm tempo faster, same shape rubato stretched ornament +1 extra was: 21 types is: ≈143 combinations four features, freely combined context-sensitive · context-free sharma et al. 2024 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one

Only some of them Fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one In Shark Bay, Western Australia, some bottlenose dolphins break a marine sponge off the seafloor, wear it over the closed beak, and use it to probe the sediment for fish. It is called sponging. Not the dolphins. Some. Krützen and colleagues found it in 15 of 141 known mothers, and mitochondrial DNA put its transmission almost entirely down a single matriline — mother to daughter, learned rather than inherited. And spongers live differently. Compared with non-spongers in the same water, they are more solitary, work the deep channels, dive for longer, and spend more of the day foraging. So inside one population, sharing one gene pool and one bay, there is a minority with a different sensory route to food, a different social pattern, and a different shape of day — passed along a family line, by learning. We have a word for a profile with peaks and troughs rather than a single level: the spiky profile. And a word for surfacing and diving by capacity — dolphining, which we named after them before we knew this. 141 known mothers 15 spongers · one matriline variation inside one population not a species difference krützen et al. 2005 · mann et al. 2008 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks

The question, straight Is there neurodiversity among whales? We went looking, and here is the honest answer: there is no cetacean autism literature. No whale ADHD, no dolphin dyslexia, no diagnostic framework of any kind applied to a cetacean. We found none, and we are not going to invent one to make this zine land better. That absence is worth stating plainly, because the temptation runs the other way. It would be easy to write whales are neurodivergent too, and it would be false, and it would borrow legitimacy from a clinical apparatus we spend the rest of our time arguing with. But the question has a real answer, once you notice that the neurodiversity paradigm was never about diagnoses. It is about variation within a population, and whether the population is built so that variation survives. At that level the record is not empty at all. It is fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one, with a traced inheritance route. It is 143 combinations where we had heard 21. It is a cortex with no fourth layer, working. The frame that lets us say this without diagnosing anybody is ethodiversity — Ombre Tarragnat's extension of the neurodiversity paradigm, by way of ethology, to beings with nervous systems. It takes the part that travels (variation is normal, and it is not a defect) and leaves behind the part that shouldn't (the clinic, the diagnosis, the deficit). You do not need to find an Autistic whale. You need to stop requiring a diagnosis before variation counts. Not: whales are smarter than us. That is the same ladder with a new occupant. A body shaped differently, travelling with whales

Eight days off Pico A body shaped differently, travelling with whales In 2011, off the island of Pico in the Azores, two researchers watching sperm whales found something else in the group: an adult male bottlenose dolphin whose spine curved so severely that his rear half held an S shape. Over eight days he travelled with the whales, foraged with them, and played with the adults and their calves. When he rubbed his body against them, the rubs were sometimes returned. A dolphin with a spine that didn't work like other dolphins' spines was moving with a slower species that had room for him in it. Two things this is not. First, it is not an adoption. The paper is titled Repeated Non-Agonistic Interactions — careful, unglamorous, exactly as far as the evidence goes. "Adopted" is the press's word, not the researchers'. Second, we do not know why. The suggestion that other dolphins had harassed him and he sought refuge is a plausible guess offered to reporters — not a finding. It may be that a curved spine made sperm whale pace easier to keep than dolphin pace. We don't know. What is in the record is eight days, and the rubs coming back. That is enough. Douglas Adams got there first, and then the joke came due

So long Douglas Adams got there first, and then the joke came due In 1979, in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, Douglas Adams made this exact joke and made it better. On Earth, he wrote, humans had always assumed they were the most intelligent species on the planet — whereas in fact they were the third. Mice first. Dolphins second. Look at the mechanism. He does not overturn the ranking. He keeps its form perfectly intact and moves us down two rungs, and the whole apparatus collapses into absurdity, because a ladder that puts mice on top was never measuring anything. The dolphins, knowing what was coming, left. Their last message, mistaken for a stunt: So long, and thanks for all the fish. Then the bill arrived. In 1988 Adams travelled with the zoologist Mark Carwardine to find endangered species for Last Chance to See, and one of them was the baiji, the Yangtze river dolphin — a freshwater cetacean going deaf and blind in a river turned into an industrial corridor. In December 2006, a six-week survey of the Yangtze ended without a single sighting. Turvey and colleagues published it as, possibly, the first human-caused extinction of a cetacean species. A species actually said so long. Not as a punchline. The ranking was never a description of the world. The Light Arrived Before the Name

62 Star Stuff The Light Arrived Before the Name on light-travel time, the seventy-one years it took one description of us to reach English, and the difference between what a thing is and what it ends up called for everyone whose record says found in a year they know was late L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely

The fact this zine runs on Light carries no name Light moves at a finite speed, so every observation is an observation of the past. Sunlight reaching your face left the Sun about eight minutes and twenty seconds ago. The nearest star after ours, Proxima Centauri, is 4.2 light-years off, so its light is four years old when it gets here. The Andromeda Galaxy is roughly 2.5 million. That is settled, checkable, and taught to children. What gets taught less is the second half of it: the light leaves with nothing written on it. A photon carries a wavelength, a polarisation, a direction. It does not carry a discoverer. Everything a star will ever tell us about itself is packed at the moment of emission, complete, and then it crosses however far it has to cross — and the name gets attached at the far end, by whoever happens to be standing there with an instrument when it lands. Astronomy has a term for that landing. First light is the moment a new telescope opens its eye and returns its first image. Nobody has ever thought the telescope invented the galaxy in the frame. First light is a fact about us — about when we got there, and what we had built by then. So a name in astronomy is an arrival record. It is never an origin record. Those two things get printed on the same line in a textbook, which is how they get confused, and almost everything in this zine is that confusion happening to a person instead of a star. Priority is a rule about who was standing there

The rule as written Priority is a rule about who was standing there Priority is the convention that scientific credit belongs to whoever publishes a finding first. In astronomy it is not a sentiment, it is administration: a comet or a minor planet takes the name of whoever reports it to the right body first, and the paperwork settles it. Halley's Comet is a clean case. Edmond Halley used Newton's gravitation to work out that the bright comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object making return trips, and in 1705 he predicted it back for 1758. It came. The name is his, and by the rule it is his fairly — he did the thing the rule rewards. He also did not see it first, and nobody claims he did. Its returns had been recorded for more than two thousand years before him, the earliest firmly identified passage being the one Chinese astronomers logged in 240 BCE. Naming a thing and observing a thing were never the same act, even where we teach the history as though they were. Notice what the rule is honest about. Priority does not pretend to record when the comet started existing, or when a human first looked at it. It records who filed. Everyone involved knows that, and the convention runs cleanly because nobody mistakes the register for the sky. The trouble is not the rule. The trouble is what happens when the filing system loses its own honesty and starts being read as a record of origin — because then whoever was late, or far away, or writing in the wrong language, stops looking late and starts looking absent. And a register does not lose its honesty on its own. It is kept by people. Committees, editors, prize panels, the handful of journals that got read and the two or three languages they got read in — and in the 1920s the people holding all of that were overwhelmingly white, Western and men. That is what does the accounting. So be exact about what the physics is for here. Light-travel time gives you the shape of the error — a thing complete at one end, named at the other, with a measurable gap between. It does not give you the cause. The cause is bias, and bias is not a property of light. It has names, addresses and letterheads, and it decides where the receiver points. The Light Arrived Before the Name · Stimpunks

One year, two continents 1925, twice So here is that accounting, twice over, in one year. Two women finished work in 1925 that their fields would be built on. Both were talked into sounding less certain than they were. Neither name arrived with the finding. In Cambridge, Massachusetts, Cecilia Payne submitted Stellar Atmospheres — the thesis showing that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, which is the single most consequential fact about what the universe is made of. Henry Norris Russell, a senior man in American astrophysics, told her the result was clearly impossible. She published anyway, with a line in it saying the enormous abundance of hydrogen and helium was “almost certainly not real.” Russell restated the same conclusion in 1929. Otto Struve later called her thesis “undoubtedly the most brilliant Ph.D. thesis ever written in astronomy.” In Moscow, Grunya Efimovna Sukhareva finished a clinical description of six boys who had spent about two years at the hospital-school she had founded in 1921. She was a Jewish woman, working in Soviet institutions, publishing in Russian. Every one of those facts is in the account of why you have not heard of her, and none of them is a shortfall in her. She recorded the aloneness, the flattened expression, the narrow blazing interests — and the giftedness running underneath. It is now widely read as the first clinical account of autism, eighteen years before Kanner and nineteen before Asperger. She published in Russian, then in German the following year so more of the world could read it. The English translation arrived in 1996 — seventy-one years later, and half a century after the two men's names were fixed to the thing she had described. A note on Moscow, kept on the page. An earlier draft of this zine placed her in Kiev, following a shorthand that circulates in the secondary literature — Manouilenko and Bejerot's 2015 paper calls her “Kiev-based.” She was born in Kiev in 1891 and moved to Moscow in 1921, where the hospital-school and the 1925 observations were. A zine about miscrediting that quietly repaired its own propagated error would be doing the smoothing it is complaining about, so the error is logged here and in the changelog rather than swept. Neither woman was wrong. Both were made to sound less certain than they were, by men whose certainty was not asked to justify itself in the same way. The finding, in each case, was already complete and already in flight. The Light Arrived Before the Name · Stimpunks

The name for late naming arrived late

A hundred and twenty-three years The name for late naming arrived late In 1993 the historian of science Margaret W. Rossiter published a paper called The Matthew Matilda Effect in Science, and gave the pattern in this zine a name it could be cited by. She was answering Robert Merton's Matthew effect — that credit accumulates on scientists who already have it, so the famous get more and the obscure get less. Rossiter's addition was the mirror: women's work is minimised, misattributed, or folded into a nearby man's name, and the two effects are the same accounting error seen from opposite ends. Here is the part that belongs in this zine rather than a general one about sexism in science. Rossiter did not name it for herself, and she did not name it for a scientist. She named it for Matilda Joslyn Gage, a suffragist and abolitionist who had already mapped the whole mechanism in a pamphlet in 1870 — Woman as Inventor, expanded thirteen years later for the North American Review. The pattern was described in 1870. It got a citable name in 1993. The concept of the late name was itself a hundred and twenty-three years late. That delay is the argument's best evidence. If the effect were rare, the description of it would have travelled at the ordinary speed of a good idea. Instead the description sat, in a nineteenth-century pamphlet by a woman outside the academy, doing exactly what it described — waiting for somebody with enough standing to be standing there when it landed. And when somebody was, she did the one thing the pattern does not do by itself: she looked back down the beam and put the earlier name on it. The Light Arrived Before the Name · Stimpunks
The signal had been arriving the whole time

Ninety-six feet a day The signal had been arriving the whole time In 1967 Jocelyn Bell was a graduate student working through the output of a radio telescope she had helped build, reading roughly 96 feet of chart paper a day by hand. She found something occupying about a quarter of an inch of it: a signal too regular to be noise. Her supervisor thought it was interference. She kept pulling the thread, and it was a pulsar — a rotating neutron star, sweeping a beam past us with a period the discovery paper gives as 1.3372795 seconds, stable to within two ten-millionths. Take the fact from spread two seriously for a moment. Those pulses had been arriving before anyone was there to receive them. The star had been doing this the entire time; the regularity was not created by the observation. What changed in 1967 was that somebody built a receiver and then read every foot of what came out of it. She is the second author on the paper that reports it — Hewish, Bell, Pilkington, Scott and Collins, Nature 217, 709 (1968). This is worth stating precisely, because the shorthand version of the story gets it wrong in both directions. She was not written out of the paper. She was written out of the prize: the 1974 Nobel in Physics went to Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, and not to the author standing second on the discovery. She has said since that she is not bitter, and that in 1974 students simply were not who prize committees looked at. That is a description of the instrument, not an absolution of it. A committee that cannot see a graduate student is a receiver with a known blind spot, and the signal it misses was never faint. Sukhareva spent her career on the other side of a comparable blind spot, and it is worth naming the blind spot rather than what she supposedly lacked. She was a woman. She was Jewish. She published in Russian and German, from the Soviet Union. Not one of those is a deficiency in her. Each is something the committees of the period were built not to see. The refusals What this does not say Six women, one pattern, and six quite different situations. Flattening them into a single shape would be the second erasure, so here is what is deliberately not being claimed. Not:that gender explains Sukhareva. Sher and Gibson give four reasons together, and rank none of them: her gender, her Jewish identity, her Russian nationality, and publication in Russian and German — which they call, plainly, not an efficacious recipe for worldwide attention in the 1920s. They also raise the possibility that Asperger omitted her deliberately under Nazi-era antisemitism. Her erasure was Jewish and Soviet as much as it was gendered, and a zine that files her under “women in science” and stops has taken three quarters of the mechanism out. Not:that a missed prize and state violence are the same harm. They are not, and the difference is not one of degree. Sukhareva was attacked at the 1951 Pavlovian Sessions for “anti-Marxist views” and self-censored the bibliography of her 1955 work; colleagues around her lost careers and lives. Nobody's life was at stake in a committee room in Stockholm. Both belong on the page; they do not belong on the same axis. Not:that every woman here was silenced the same way. Annie Jump Cannon built the stellar classification scheme still in use and was honoured in her lifetime: first woman to take the National Academy of Sciences' Henry Draper Medal, 1931. And she joined the Harvard College Observatory in 1896 and got no regular Harvard appointment until 1938. Honoured from outside, unpromoted at home, for forty-two years. She is the exception and she is forty-two years of the rule, which is why she is on this page rather than left off it. Not:that recognition and justice are the same thing. Getting the medal is not getting the job, the salary, the students, or the right to point the telescope. Caroline Herschel took the Gold Medal in 1828 and was still her brother's assistant on the payroll. A prize is an arrival record too. Not:that these men stole, or conspired. Russell cited Payne and reported “very gratifying agreement” with her results. Sometimes it is an editor; sometimes a translation that takes seventy years; sometimes a committee with a written rule about students. The mechanism varies every time. The direction does not. That is what makes it a pattern rather than a set of anecdotes. Not:an argument against priority, citation, or evidence. Spread three is the opposite: the naming conventions work precisely when they stay honest about recording who filed. We are asking the register to keep saying what it is a register of. Not:the naturalistic fallacy. No fact about light-travel time makes anybody worth loving. The physics never carried that claim and does not carry it here — see A Promise, Not a Finding. We are not new. Our records are

Which brings it to us We are not new. Our records are The six children Sukhareva wrote down in 1925 were Autistic. So were Autistic children in 1895, and in 1795, and every year in between that nobody was taking notes. 1925 is not when we started. It is when somebody was standing there with an instrument. This is the whole of spread two, arriving at a person. A diagnosis is an arrival record. It is a dated statement about when a clinician, working in a particular decade, in a particular language, using a particular set of criteria, first wrote something down. It is not, and has never claimed to be, a record of when the thing began. The criteria say so out loud. The DSM-5's third criterion for autism requires that symptoms “must be present in the early developmental period” — and then adds, in the same breath, that they “may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life.” The manual is describing light-travel time. It is telling you the emission was early and the detection can be decades late, and that the delay lives in the demands and the masking, not in the person. Somebody diagnosed at forty-seven has not been Autistic since they were forty-seven. The paperwork is forty-seven years old and the light is not. Many of us know this in the body, because we have had a version of it said to us: you can't have been, you'd have been picked up. That sentence quietly makes the record the origin. It says that whether we existed depends on whether the receiver was switched on, in our town, in our decade, for a child who looked like us. Girls, and Black and brown children, and anyone whose flavour of it stayed indoors, got the receiver switched on late or never. And it runs the other way too, which is the part that stings. The names on our diagnoses are Kanner's and Asperger's because of when translations happened. Sukhareva's account was eighteen years earlier and seventy-one years from English. There is a version of this history in which the first thing anybody read about us was written by a woman who noticed the giftedness in the same paragraph as the difficulty — because she did, in 1925, and it just did not arrive in time to set the tone. We are not asking to be discovered. We were never undiscovered. We are asking the record to be read for what it is: a log of when the looking happened, kept by the people who were doing the looking. Two lines that are not the same line One line runs the whole width: what was always the case. A second, shorter line begins only part way along: what the paperwork records. Made of the same star stuff, unsigned

The last crossing Made of the same star stuff, unsigned One more thing that crossed a great distance without a name on it, and it is the reason this piece is in this collection rather than a history-of-science shelf. Payne's thesis said the stars are hydrogen and helium. Everything heavier than those two was cooked afterwards, inside stars, and scattered when they died — the carbon in your cells, the oxygen in your blood, the calcium in the bone your hand is resting on. Those atoms crossed interstellar space and several billion years to get into you, and not one of them arrived with a discoverer's name attached. They did not need one. The calcium works whether or not Cecilia Payne was believed in 1925. The hydrogen did not become more abundant when Russell restated it in 1929, and it was not less abundant during the four years in between, while the most consequential fact about the universe sat in a Harvard thesis with a hedge in it that its author had been talked into. That is the whole premise of this collection put as plainly as it goes. Belonging runs underneath the record. The record is a human artefact — late, partial, in whichever languages the committees happened to read, and revisable. The thing it is a record of is not. She is not a footnote version of herself, waiting for us to notice. She was the whole star the entire time. We are only now getting the light. Which is the honest scale of what a correction can do. Publishing Sukhareva's name does not give her back the credit; she died in 1981 and nothing here reaches her. It fixes our instrument — the one we are using right now, on each other, on the next person whose account arrives in the wrong language or the wrong decade or the wrong body. And there is one thing available to us that is not repair. Her atoms are still in circulation; that is chemistry, not consolation. What we can carry forward is not her credit, which was never ours to hand back — it is her method. Notice closely. Write the giftedness down in the same paragraph as the difficulty. Then turn the instrument toward whoever is arriving right now in the wrong language, the wrong decade or the wrong body, and be the one who is standing there. So: love you down to your star stuff — and note the grammar, because it is doing the work. Down to is how far the loving reaches, never why it is owed. Not because you were recognised. Not because the record caught up. Down to the atoms, which crossed everything to get here and never once needed to be named to be yours. The bell curve is a vantage point

The same trick, on us The bell curve is a vantage point The curve that sorts us into normal and abnormal began in astronomy. It was the "error curve" — the math for how repeated measurements of a star's position scatter around its true one. In the 1800s, Adolphe Quetelet — an astronomer — turned that instrument on people, and invented l'homme moyen, the average man. What had described the error in a measurement now described the ideal human, with everyone else scattered around it as deviation. Francis Galton took the next step, reading the curve as a ranking, and built eugenics on it. So the tool that mapped the indifferent stars got turned on our minds — and the average, a made-up midpoint, was handed to us as the shape we were supposed to be. The Lines We Drew is the ninth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the companion argument to Field Guide No. 1 — where that guide redraws the constellations, this one is about why redrawing is legitimate at all. The astronomy moved, and this page moved with it. An earlier version of this zine said the belt was a line-of-sight accident — Alnitak ~740 light-years, Mintaka ~690, Alnilam ~2,000, "nearly three times farther." That was wrong, and we have corrected it. Those were Hipparcos-era parallaxes, and Hipparcos measured these bright, distant, multiple O and B stars badly: its parallax for Mintaka (212 ± 30 pc) is about half the figure that spectroscopy, cluster membership and Gaia DR3 now agree on, and both Hipparcos reductions of Alnilam proved incorrect. Current distances put all three at essentially the same depth — Alnitak 1,260 ± 180 ly (387 ± 54 pc), Alnilam 1,250 ± 26 ly (384 ± 8 pc, from VLTI interferometry: Oplištilová, Brož, Hummel, Harmanec & Barlow, "VLTI observations of the Orion Belt stars: I. ε Orionis," Astronomy & Astrophysics 704, A204, 2025), and Mintaka ~1,240 ly (381 ± 8 pc, Gaia DR3). All three belong to the Orion OB1b association, and the ε Ori paper places its star at that association's median distance: they are siblings from one cloud, not strangers in a row. APOD, cited in our earlier draft, likewise gives the three as a group "about 1,500 light-years away" — it never supported the numbers we hung on it. The depth is real; it is just in the figure rather than the belt. Bellatrix lies 250 ± 10 ly away, Betelgeuse about 548 (uncertain by as much as 100), Saiph 650 ± 30, Rigel about 863, and the belt near 1,250 — so the hunter is assembled from stars strung across roughly a thousand light-years. We think the correction improves the zine. A page arguing that confident lines get mistaken for facts of the sky had drawn one of its own, in depth, from superseded data — and better instruments moved it. That is the argument arriving uninvited, and it now runs on the spread. The lineage from stars to people is real and well documented. The bell curve entered science as the astronomer's "law of error": in his Theoria Motus (1809), Gauss used it to model how imperfect measurements scatter around a celestial body's true position — the same method that recovered the lost asteroid Ceres — with Legendre and Laplace close behind. Adolphe Quetelet, who directed the Brussels observatory, carried that error law from the sky to the census in his Essai de physique sociale (1835), inventing l'homme moyen, "the average man" — and, crucially, treating the average not as merely typical but as an ideal from which real people "deviate." Francis Galton kept Quetelet's curve but flipped its meaning: in Hereditary Genius (1869) he ranked human ability along what he called the "law of deviation from the average" and graded groups above and below the line. He coined the word eugenics later, in Inquiries into Human Faculty and Its Development (1883), where a footnote to the introduction proposes it for "the science of improving stock." His protégé Karl Pearson gave the field its machinery — the standard deviation (1894) and the correlation coefficient — in the Mathematical Contributions to the Theory of Evolution series, and was later appointed the first Galton Professor of Eugenics at University College London (1911–1933); the mathematics came first, the chair after. The statistical sense of the word "normal" arrives in the 1870s alongside all of this — used apparently independently by C. S. Peirce (1873), Galton, and Wilhelm Lexis (1877), with "normal distribution" settling into place in Pearson's writing by 1897. The sleight of hand was never the curve — some traits really are close to normally distributed — but the leap from deviation-as-measurement-error to deviation-as-human-defect, and the mistaking of a made-up midpoint for a law about how a person ought to be. Robert Chapman's Empire of Normality (2023) follows this same thread forward, into psychiatry and capitalism. On Chapman's account, Galton reframed the statistical centre as mere mediocrity rather than an ideal — so that deviation above it read as superiority and deviation below as defect — founding the frame that, carried through Kraepelin into the DSM, the neurodiversity movement later arose to name and refuse. That frame's name — the pathology paradigm, and its counterpart the neurodiversity paradigm — is Nick Walker's, articulated in "Throw Away the Master's Tools: Liberating Ourselves from the Pathology Paradigm" (written 2011; published 2012 in Loud Hands: Autistic People, Speaking; revised 2013), not Chapman's; Chapman works with the terms rather than coining them. The "normal" mind, in other words, has a history — and a contestable one. The border really does move: the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from the DSM beginning in 1973; Asperger's disorder was added in DSM-IV (1994) and merged into Autism Spectrum Disorder in DSM-5 (2013). "Epistemic injustice," with its testimonial and hermeneutical forms, is Miranda Fricker's (2007). "Neurodiversity" is not one person's coinage, though it is often credited to Judy Singer (1998). Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley & Walker, "The neurodiversity concept was developed collectively: An overdue correction on the origins of neurodiversity theory" (Autism, 2024), show that "neurological diversity" and "neurodiversity" reached print in 1997 and 1998 in the work of journalist Harvey Blume, who attributed them to the online Autistic community — and that the concept and its theory were developed collectively by neurodivergent people. We follow that correction here. The neurodivergent / neurodivergence coinage is Kassiane Asasumasu's (2000), as logged for Zine No. 3; the paradigm's articulation is Nick Walker's and the wider community's. The reading is ours: that the constructed line was never the sky, and so is ours to redraw. (2022); and, for a general reader, Todd Rose, The End of Average (2016). Online: Fergus Murray, "Weird vs. Normal" (Weird Pride Day). Tidal force The near body wins The tide is the ocean answering to the sky. The Moon pulls hardest on the water directly beneath it, a little less on the rock of the Earth, less still on the far ocean — and that difference in pull, stretched across the planet, lifts a bulge on each side. Two bulges, turning under us: two high tides a day. Here is the strange part. The Sun is 27 million times more massive than the Moon, and it hauls on the Earth with over 170 times the raw force. Yet the Moon runs the tide. Tidal force falls off not with distance but with distance cubed — so the small, close body overwhelms the vast, far one. Distance matters more than mass. You are pulled most by what is nearest — not by what is largest. The Sun is 27 million times heavier. The Moon still owns the tide. Nearness beats mass. a safe-enough body your nervous system pull across the gap gravity acts at a distance the moon never touches the sea Co-regulation · polyvagal Co-regulation is gravity Now read yourself as the water. Co-regulation is what it feels like when a safe-enough nervous system comes near: soft gaze, an unhurried voice, a steady heartbeat — and yours begins to fall into time with it. You don't settle by force of will. You are pulled into rhythm by a nearby body. Polyvagal theory offers a name for it: resonance with another regulated nervous system as the deepest safety signal there is, letting your body drop into a calm, social, at-ease state. (Polyvagal's finer physiology is contested; the settling you feel in safe company is not.) And gravity crosses a gap. Being with someone can be a felt presence, not a hand on the shoulder: a shared game, music in a chat, someone in the next room. Near enough to pull; not so near it overwhelms. You do not have to be touched to be moved. The moon never touches the sea. It only has to be near enough to pull. The Nearest Body · Stimpunks

Spring & neap · parallel presence Two high tides No body of water answers to a single pull. The Sun tugs too — and when Sun and Moon line up, their pulls add into a spring tide: high highs, low lows, a deep and easy rhythm. When they sit at right angles, the pulls half-cancel into a neap tide — flat, muddled, hard to read. So it is with us. When your people, your places, and your routines are all in safe mode at once, regulation comes easy; everything is pulling the same way. When they pull against each other, you go slack and confused, no tide to speak of. And two bodies can settle into one rhythm without ever merging. The Moon turns once for every orbit, forever showing the Earth a single face — tidally locked. That is parallel presence and body doubling: two people in one orbit, each a steady face for the other, together and separate at once. Aligned, the pulls add. Crossed, they cancel. We regulate best when our moons agree. SPRING · aligned pulls add → big tide NEAP · crossed half-cancel flat tide aligned moons deepen the tide crossed pulls flatten it The Nearest Body · Stimpunks

No steady pull to organize it, so it heaves every direction at once, hunting for anything to lock onto. Autistic and AuDHD folks know this state: meerkat mode — up on the hind legs, scanning for threat, unable to settle or focus, an overwhelmed monotropic mind desperate for a hook into flow. It gets misread as clinginess, as over-attachment, as too much need. It is none of those. It is a nervous system starved of a moon. The constant reaching for a safe person isn't a flaw in the water — it's a tide with nothing to answer to. You do not settle a churning sea by ordering the waves to stop. You restore its moon. A churning sea isn't broken. It's a tide that lost its moon. The Nearest Body · Stimpunks
The storm is in the weather

Ecosystemic distress · ARLES The storm is in the weather When the sea won't settle, we go looking for the fault in the water. But water has no weather of its own. The storm comes from the system overhead; the flooding comes from where someone built the seawall too low, dredged the channel, paved the marsh that used to drink the surge. Stimpunks calls this the ecosystemic model of distress: dysregulation lives in the relationship between a bodymind and its environment, not inside the person. Read ARLES downward and a failing system points to the environment that made it, the environment to the lived experience it ignored, and down to the attention and the nervous system it never once accounted for. Broken systems, not broken people. Nota broken nervous system — a body of water doing exactly what water does near a storm. Notover-attachment or "too needy" — a tide reaching for the moon it was starved of. Notlimerence: co-regulation is mutual and safe; limerence is one-sided and uncertain. Not every strong pull regulates you; some only pull you under. Notcalm-down-by-willpower — you settle a sea by restoring its moon, not by scolding the waves. What does your tide table look like, and who keeps asking you to run on someone else's? When the water churns, where is the storm actually coming from? The Nearest Body is the seventeenth zine in the Stimpunks series. After the more-than-human trilogy (Nos. 14–16), it picks the water back up and turns it inward: from a council of beings dissolving into flow, to the single body of water pulled by the bodies nearest it. The science is settled and citable. Tides are the ocean answering to the difference in gravity across the Earth, raising a bulge on each side — two high tides a lunar day. The Sun out-masses the Moon roughly 27 million times and out-pulls it more than 170-fold, yet the Moon raises the larger tide, because tide-generating force falls off as the cube of distance rather than the square: distance matters more than mass (NOAA Ocean Service; Stanford Solar Center). Aligned Sun and Moon make spring tides; crossed, neap tides. The Moon is tidally locked, turning once per orbit to show one face. The reading is Stimpunks' own vocabulary. Co-regulation — completing the stress cycle with a safe-enough person, and "being with" as felt presence — draws on Trauma Geek (Janae Elisabeth) and Autistic Realms (Helen Edgar); polyvagal theory is Stephen Porges — an influential but scientifically contested framework; the co-regulation it describes is well-supported independently. no brain. it sleeps anyway. 59 Rest The Rest You Keep on Autistic rest, monotropism, burnout — and the ledger that was never there L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff with Helen Edgar · open edition · print freely

The finding Nobody files a report Hydra is a real animal, not a thought experiment. A freshwater creature a centimetre or two long, related to jellyfish and coral, usually found clinging by its foot to a pond plant with a ring of tentacles at the other end. It has no brain. No central nervous system at all — just a loose mesh of nerve cells spread through the body, with nothing anywhere gathering that mesh into a decision-maker. And Hydra sleeps. It goes still. It is harder to rouse. Keep it awake and it sleeps longer afterwards to make up the debt, and falls asleep quicker when you let it — which is the homeostatic signature, the thing that separates sleep from merely sitting there. Keep it awake long enough and the number of dividing cells drops off. So rest is not a bonus feature bolted onto a body's real work. In an animal with no brain to argue the point, rest is part of how the body gets built and stays working at all. Which puts the usual story in a strange position. The assumption that rest must be earned — tracked, justified, released once enough has been put in — requires something keeping score. A ledger. An account with a balance. Hydra has no ledger. It rests anyway. Held honestly, and early. This is not the argument that Hydra rests, therefore your rest is natural, therefore it is allowed. Using natural to mean permitted is its own trap, and this collection refuses it everywhere else — the universe does not owe us a precedent, and a resemblance is a rhyme, not a proof. Hydra is not evidence that you are allowed to rest. Hydra is evidence that the thing you were asking permission from was never there. one animal · no brain · three criteria Hydra vulgaris nerve net · no centre 1 · goes quiescent 2 · harder to rouse 3 · rebounds after loss all three · met dividing cells slept deprived rest is when the building happens Kanaya et al. 2020 · Science Advances a sleep-like state, in an animal with no brain The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Attention The tunnel, not the line One more thing about Hydra, because it is the hinge. Put it in constant light or constant dark and its daily rhythm vanishes — it has no circadian clock to free-run. What is left is a cycle of roughly four hours, returning and returning. So the oldest resting animal we can point to is not keeping time against a day. It rests on a rhythm of its own that comes back around. Which is the shape a lot of us already know. Autistic attention often does not spread thinly across many things at once; it pools, and goes deep into a few. That is monotropism — Dinah Murray, Mike Lesser and Wenn Lawson, 2005 — and time inside that kind of focus has its own shape. Not slower or faster. Helen Edgar calls it spiral time: not a line you are falling behind on, but a spiral you are moving through, returning to the same place on purpose. Now the consequence, which is the whole reason this spread exists. If rest is offered by pulling that attention away — the meditation app, the walk, the gentle activity, when what the mind actually wants is stillness with the interest still in view — then it is not rest. It is another demand, wearing a rest costume. Rest that fights your attention is not rest. Helen Edgar · Reclaiming Rest (2025) For attention that works this way, rest often means staying in the tunnel. Going further into the one thing. Not being pulled out of it and told to relax. What this is not. Hydra's four-hour cycle is not monotropic time, and no shared mechanism is being claimed — one is a cnidarian ultradian rhythm and the other is how human attention is organised. The rhyme is worth noticing and it is not evidence. The monotropic account stands on its own literature, and on us. two shapes of time the line you fall behind on one direction · no returning the spiral you move through returning is the method attention, not exhaustion Murray, Lesser & Lawson 2005 · Edgar on monotropic time deeper in is a direction, not a retreat The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks
Rest is not the opposite of motion

On the wing Rest is not the opposite of motion A great frigatebird can stay in the air for up to two months without landing. Weimerskirch and colleagues tracked them across the Indian Ocean, riding thermals up and gliding down in a roller-coaster that costs them almost nothing. That is one study, and it is about where the birds go. A different team asked a different question of the same species: what is the brain doing up there? They fitted EEG recorders and followed non-stop foraging flights of up to ten days and three thousand kilometres — different birds on different trips, not the two-month records. Over those flights the birds slept an average of 42 minutes a day. Back on land: over twelve hours. The detail that matters is how. Slow-wave sleep arrived in bouts that could run several minutes; the REM episodes lasted only seconds. It was more often one hemisphere at a time in the air than it ever is on land, with the open eye generally facing the direction of the turn — though both hemispheres did sometimes go under together, so half a brain awake is not a requirement for staying up. And it happened while the birds soared on rising air, never while they flapped. So rest here did not require stillness. It required a system that could rest part of itself while another part kept working — and a glide, rather than a wingbeat, to do it in. It slept in the glide. Nothing stopped. Two studies, two claims, and not a target. The two-month figure and the 42-minute figure come from different work and are not one finding; the sleep study's own flights ran up to ten days. And 42 minutes is sleep restriction, not an achievement — the birds catch up on land, and nothing here suggests a body thrives on less. The point is narrower: rest was possible mid-flight, in pieces, without the motion stopping. one bird · two hemispheres asleep awake · watching more often aloft than ashore sleep per day 42 min in flight 12+ hrs on land it slept in the glide Rattenborg et al. 2016 · Weimerskirch et al. 2016 part of a system rests while the rest keeps flying The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Relational Partial presence is real presence Lurking in a group chat without posting. Camera off. Texting instead of calling. Reading every message and answering none of them today. Being in the room with the sound down. None of that is absence. What gets counted in each of those cases is output — messages sent, words spoken, a face on screen. But absence is a claim about somebody not being there, and not one of those is that. They are all being there, with the output turned down. Every Saturday the Stimpunks Solidarity Session leaves an otter cam running while the conversation drifts in and out. Some cameras on, most off. Some people speaking, some in text, some just there. Nobody has to watch it. That is the part that makes it work — and the reason it works is that the room does not price presence by output. Because a relationship that only holds when everyone shows up at full intensity was never built to hold a nervous system that varies. And they all vary. Ours vary visibly, which is a difference in legibility, not in kind. Presence does not need full output to count as presence. No animal on this spread, on purpose. Every other spread here has one, and the obvious move was to set the frigatebird's half-lit brain beside a camera-off Saturday and let the resemblance carry the claim. That is the metaphor this zine refuses five spreads later — and it would misdescribe the bird, which sleeps about 42 minutes a day in short bouts inside its glides, never while flapping, and is awake for the rest of the flight rather than cruising along permanently half-lit. The distinction is Helen Edgar's, from No. 58: the otters are evidence; we are testimony. This spread is testimony. It does not need a bird standing behind it. one room · four ways of being in it camera on in text only lurking stepped out still connected no mode outranks another presence without performance Solidarity Sesh · the low-demand shared watch a reason to stay in the room The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Lived experience No ramp, just the edge Interoception is the sense that reports the inside of your own body. Hunger. Heartbeat. Thirst. Tiredness arriving. For a lot of us that signal comes through quiet, or late, or in a shape that is hard to read. Which means the depletion does not announce itself while it builds. You feel fine. Then you do not. There is often no slope in between. Meltdown and shutdown live at that edge. They are not chosen and they are not a rest strategy — they are what a nervous system does when the cost has already been accumulating and no warning arrived in time to spend it differently. An emergency stop, where a signal should have come first. It would be easy to read that as proof that rest is optional if you are only careful enough — that with better monitoring you could time it precisely. It is proof of the opposite. Missing the signal costs too much. Rest cannot wait for a warning that may never come. Said plainly, because the framing gets this wrong. This zine does not call meltdown or shutdown a form of rest. Describing them as enforced rest makes an injury sound like a strategy, and then makes the person responsible for having needed it. They are the cost of rest having been unavailable. Everything else in here is about the rest that gets chosen, before the edge. what the signal does not do the ramp you were promised warning the edge you get “fine” emergency stop not a strategy · a cost interoception · and what it does not report the flat line is not the same as capacity The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Six months, no load The bear's bone Bone answers to load. That is why this whole collection opens with Iwao Yasuda's finding that a bone under pressure generates a charge — a skeleton is not scaffolding, it is a tissue that reads what is being asked of it and rebuilds accordingly. Which sets up a problem. Take the load away and bone is supposed to go. Put a person on months of bed rest, or in orbit, and it does: resorption outruns formation and the skeleton thins measurably. A hibernating bear goes roughly six months with no walking, no weight-bearing, none of the loading that is supposed to keep a skeleton honest. It loses no bone. Researchers compared hibernating and active grizzlies and black bears and found no difference in bone volume fraction or mineral density. Cellular activity dropped — but resorption and formation dropped together, staying balanced. The bear does not out-work the problem. It turns the remodelling down at both ends and comes out in spring with its skeleton intact. Long rest cost this animal nothing structural. So the loss is not a law. A bear is not a person, and this is not advice. Humans do lose bone in prolonged disuse; nothing here suggests skipping movement, and the researchers study bears precisely because we cannot do what they do. The claim is narrow and it is about the rule, not the routine: there exists a physiology in which half a year of stillness is not paid for in skeleton. What looked like an inevitable trade is a fact about particular bodies in particular arrangements. six months of disuse · two outcomes a person on bed rest loss a bear in the den held bone volume & mineral density · unchanged remodelling, turned down at both ends formation resorption balanced McGee-Lawrence et al. 2009 · Bone not pushing through — turning it down evenly The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks
Rest is a property of an arrangement

Environment Rest is a property of an arrangement The bear's skeleton is doing its own work from the inside. The den is doing a different job, and that one is measurable in the energy budget. A hibernating black bear drops its metabolic rate to about a quarter of basal while its core temperature falls only five or six degrees, and its heart runs as low as nine beats a minute. That is the striking part of Tøien's work: the metabolic suppression is largely uncoupled from the cooling. Deep rest here is not the body going cold and switching off. Holding that state still costs something, and the den is what lowers the bill. Bears select dens for insulation — buried, snow-covered, sheltered from wind and disturbance — and a well-insulated den measurably reduces what has to be spent on staying warm. The animal's contribution is to be somewhere that will hold the conditions steady, and then to stop. So rest is not only a capacity a body either has or lacks. It is what happens when a body and its surroundings are arranged so that resting is possible without effort being spent on making it possible. Temperature. Darkness. Safety. Nobody needing anything right now. Change the surroundings and the same body can no longer do what it just did. Two findings, deliberately not merged. The den lowers the energy cost of hibernating; the preserved bone is an internal remodelling result. Nobody has shown that a worse den costs a bear its skeleton, and this spread does not imply it — the bone would likely hold in a poor den and the animal would simply pay more to be there. Keeping them apart is the honest version, and it is the stronger one: the body and the room are each carrying a documented share. the room, doing the holding safety no demand insulation metabolism falls · temperature barely does ~25% basal −5–6°C only deep rest is not going cold Tøien et al. 2011 · Science · den microclimate literature the arrangement carries part of the cost The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks
The debt that was never owed

Systems The debt that was never owed Underneath most of how rest gets talked about sits an earning frame: rest as something released after enough output. A balance paid down. Never quite yet. Tricia Hersey, who founded The Nap Ministry, names what that frame is doing: Rest is a form of resistance because it disrupts and pushes back against capitalism and white supremacy. Tricia Hersey · Rest Is Resistance: A Manifesto (2022) Her ground is specific and it is not ours to blur: rest stolen from Black people under slavery and its long afterlives, and a grind culture that reads bodies as machinery. She names what the machinery story is: Rest pushes back and disrupts a system that views human bodies as a tool for production and labor. It is a counter narrative. We know that we are not machines. Tricia Hersey · The Nap Ministry, 21 February 2022 A counter narrative. That is the precise word for it, because the earning story is a narrative and not a measurement — and the argument is a Black liberationist one before it is anything else. What it hands us is the shape of the accounting. If rest must be earned, someone is holding the ledger, and whoever holds it decides who is behind. That is a mechanism for withholding, and it works best on people whose output is already read as suspect — which is to say, on us, routinely, from the first time a report card described us as not applying ourselves. And this is where Hydra comes back. There is no ledger in a nerve net. The debt was not discovered in the body; it was issued — and a debt that was issued can be refused. Not flattened into wellness. Hersey's rest is a demand made from inside Black liberation struggle, not a self-care tip and not a general theory we get to lift clean. We cite her because the accounting she describes is the same accounting we are handed, not because our situation is hers. two accounts of the same body earned · owed · behind issued, not found baseline no balance to clear a ledger is a tool for withholding and it is used hardest on whoever is already read as not trying a debt issued can be refused Hersey 2022 · The Nap Ministry rest as refusal, not as recovery time The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Held honestly What this zine refuses Every piece in this series ends by naming what it will not claim. The refusals are load-bearing: a zine about rest is unusually easy to turn into its opposite, and most of the ways that happens are kind-sounding. Rest gets recommended to us constantly. Almost none of it survives contact with how our attention actually works, and a surprising amount of it arrives as one more thing to do properly. If it needs to be justified afterwards, it was not rest. It was unpaid work with the lights off. Not:Rest so you can produce. Hydra is not recharging in order to divide more efficiently on Monday. Rest is not a maintenance interval on a working machine, and framing it that way just moves the ledger. Not:An animal metaphor for people. The bear is not a model of who to become and the frigatebird is not an instruction. They are kin, doing their own thing, in bodies that are not ours. Not:“Just relax.” Offered as advice it is usually a demand — for stillness that fits somebody else's nervous system, delivered to someone with no spare capacity to perform it. Not:Rest as a project. Optimised, tracked, done correctly, reviewed. That is the grind with a softer noun on it. Not:Meltdown as rest. Calling a shutdown enforced rest turns an injury into a strategy, and then hands the person the bill for having needed it. Not:Natural, therefore allowed. The animals are not a permission slip. Nature grants nobody anything, and a belonging claim resting on biology can be revoked by the next paper. Not:The smoothed version. The hedges in here are not padding — no circadian rhythm in Hydra, two months and 42 minutes from two different studies, a bear that is not a person. The true versions are stranger and they are enough. The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

L★S Rest is older than the brain, older than the ledger, and older than anyone's opinion of how much you have done today. An animal with no nervous centre sleeps, and its cells divide because it did. Nothing was ever owed. Love you down to your star stuff — and down to the rest you keep. What would it mean to let rest happen there, instead of somewhere more respectable? What is the den you would need — the arrangement, not the willpower — for your body to hold steady the way the bear's does? What debt have you been paying down that was never actually owed? Who issued it, and when did you start believing the balance? When did you last rest without preparing an account of why you were entitled to? The Rest You Keep was built with Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), from her essay Reclaiming Rest: Autistic Burnout, Monotropism, and Resistance and its companion Going Deeper: Rest, Burnout, and Monotropic Flow. The structure of this zine is hers; the inversion at its centre — that rest which fights your attention is not rest, and that recovery for monotropic people often means going deeper rather than switching off — is hers, and it is the reason the piece exists. The animal-rest framing follows Otters Already Know How to Rest (Stimpunks, 2026). It is a companion to The Stone You Keep (58), which takes the same Saturday room and follows the otters, and sits alongside Every Nervous System (27) and Minor Worlds (16). Monotropism is Murray, Lesser & Lawson (2005); monotropic and spiral time as used here are Helen Edgar's; stimming, body doubling, bodymind and caves, campfires and watering holes are Stimpunks'; rest as resistance is Tricia Hersey and The Nap Ministry. Internally this zine is built on the ARLES ladder — attention, relational, lived experience, environment, systems — which is deliberately not printed on the spreads; the argument should stand without the scaffold. Science, 331(6019), 906–909 — metabolism suppressed to about 25% of basal with core temperature regulated between roughly 30 and 36°C in multi-day cycles, and heart rate falling from 55 to as few as 9 beats per minute. Hersey, T. (2022). Rest Is Resistance: A Manifesto. Little, Brown Spark. (1950s), on the piezoelectric behaviour of bone under load; and Bassett, C. A. L., et al., on the same. Honesty notes. Four things this zine holds loosely, and one correction. First: the authors title Hydra's state a sleep-like state before calling it sleep, and that hedge is kept here — what is established is that it meets the behavioural criteria, not that a polyp experiences anything. Second: Hydra's four-hour rhythm is not monotropic time and no shared mechanism is claimed; the resemblance is a rhyme, not a proof. Third: the two frigatebird figures come from two separate studies and are not one result — the two-month flights are Weimerskirch, the 42 minutes is Rattenborg over flights of up to ten days — and 42 minutes a day is sleep restriction the birds recover from on land, not a standard to admire. Corrected after shipping: spread 4 first said about seven in ten in-flight bouts were asymmetric. That number came from a search summary rather than a paper and appears in neither Rattenborg source — the 2019 review says nearly half of the asymmetric sleep passed the unihemispheric threshold, a different claim over a different denominator. The page now states only what the authors state, and the flapping detail is added because that review is Rattenborg reviewing his own data. Fourth: a bear is not a person. Humans do lose bone during prolonged disuse, which is exactly why bears are studied; the claim made here is that the loss is not a universal law, not that anyone should stop moving. Relatedly, the den's documented job is reducing the energy cost of hibernating — no one has shown that den quality affects the bone result, and the two findings are kept apart on spreads 7 and 8 rather than merged into a tidier story. The corrections, and there are two, both about where a real Hersey sentence actually lives. Rest disrupting capitalism and white supremacy is widely cited — and was cited to us — as We Will Rest! (2024). It is in Rest Is Resistance: A Manifesto (2022), in the passage naming Rest Is Resistance the Nap Ministry’s tagline and mantra. The counter narrative passage on spread 9 was attributed to the 2024 book too; it is in neither book, but in a Nap Ministry post of 21 February 2022 — two years before We Will Rest! existed. Both were settled by opening the sources rather than by finding a third site that agreed. The circulated form of that second passage also drops two sentences without marking the omission — It is a counter narrative and We are divine — and the first of those turns out to be the load-bearing one, so it is quoted here whole. And nothing here claims the animals' arrangements justify ours — the universe does not owe us a precedent. The belonging claim does not rest on Hydra. It rests on us, and it reaches all the way down. You are not behind. There was no schedule. Rest, and keep resting. Love you down to your star stuff. liquid ice same molecules · two states 20 Water The Same Water on phase transitions, fluctuating capacity, and why "you could do it yesterday" was never the point L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Phase transitions Water doesn't get gradually stiffer Cool a glass of water and it does not slowly thicken toward solid. It stays liquid, liquid, liquid — and then, at a single temperature, it flips all at once into ice. Not a gradual stiffening; a sudden change of state. It is the same H₂O on both sides — the very same molecules, only rearranged. Physicists call this a phase transition: a substance holding steady until a threshold in its conditions is crossed, then reorganising completely — solid, liquid, gas — with nothing added and nothing taken away. Nothing about the water got better or worse. It crossed a line. Nothing about the water changed. It crossed a line. state colder → liquid ice 0°C not a ramp — a cliff the flip happens all at once The Same Water · Stimpunks

pressure temperature → solid liquid gas one substance, many states the conditions decide The phase diagram The conditions, not the substance Whether that water shows up as ice, liquid, or steam depends entirely on the conditions around it — temperature and pressure. Scientists chart it on a phase diagram: a map with a region for each state and lines where one becomes another. Read it and the point lands quietly. Ice is not defective water; steam is not water trying harder. There is no best state and no failed state — only one substance, and the conditions it happens to be in. So if you want a different state, you change the conditions, not the substance. We said this once about rooms and minds. Here it is again, about states. Ice isn't broken water. It's water somewhere colder. The Same Water · Stimpunks
Why could you do it yesterday?

Fluctuating capacity Why could you do it yesterday? Here is the question so many of us brace for: why could you do it yesterday and not today? However kindly it's meant, it lands like a charge of inconsistency — as if yesterday proved today is a choice. The phase answer is simple. Capacity is a state, not a trait — and you were near a boundary. A little less sleep, one extra transition, a degree more noise, and the conditions tip. The same person crosses from managing to not managing, the way the same water crosses from liquid to ice on one degree of difference. Not unreliable. Not lazy. Not putting it on. The same you, in changed conditions. You are not inconsistent. You were near a boundary. coping overload + load one degree of difference same person, tipped by conditions a state, not a trait The Same Water · Stimpunks

calm calm the crossing turbulent right at the edge calm, then the boundary, then calm the edge is where it churns Thresholds The hardest part is the crossing There's a reason the change itself is the hard part. the horizon the shadow 2.6× wider 48 Star Stuff The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing on the black hole nobody photographed, and what can only be known by its effect on everything else Eight telescopes · six sites · 3.5 petabytes · one dark circle · a rhyme, not a proof L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely
Nobody has photographed a black hole

The honest problem Nobody has photographed a black hole Start with the thing everyone gets wrong, including most of the headlines in April 2019. A camera works by catching light that left the subject. That is the whole mechanism — the apple sends photons at your eye, and you see an apple. A black hole sends nothing. Not a little. Not faintly. The event horizon is the surface where the geometry has tipped so far that every path leading outward has stopped existing; there is no direction that is away. Light does not struggle out slowly. It does not get out. So the ordinary way of knowing about a thing is simply unavailable, and no better camera will fix it. This is not a limit of our instruments. It is a fact about what the object is. There is no picture of a black hole and there never will be. What exists is a picture of everything else, arranged by one. the situation, stated plainly Which sounds like the end of the enquiry, and is instead the beginning of it. Because a thing that emits nothing still does a great deal — to gas, to stars, to the paths of passing light — and all of that is visible. The rest of this zine is about what you can learn from the second-best option, and about the one number that makes it dangerous. The second-best option Only what bends around it Gas falling toward a black hole does not go quietly. It compresses, shears against itself, and gets hot enough to shine — so the object that emits nothing is generally surrounded by something that emits a great deal. Now put that glow behind a lens made of gravity. Light travelling near a massive body does not go straight; its path bends, and the closer it passes the harder it bends. At a particular radius the bending becomes exactly enough to curve a beam right around into a circle — the photon sphere, at three GM/c² from the centre. Light there is orbiting. So what arrives at a telescope on Earth sorts itself into two kinds. Light that passed far enough out escaped and reached you. Light that came in closer than the critical approach spiralled in and never left. The result is a bright ring around a dark middle — and the dark middle is not an object. It is the set of directions in which any light you might have received went into the hole instead. You are not looking at a black hole. You are looking at the shape of a hole in everything else. what the image actually is The astronomers' word for that dark middle is the shadow, and the word is well chosen — a shadow is defined entirely by what it happens to, never by itself. The shadow is bigger than the thing

3√3 against 2 The shadow is bigger than the thing Here is the fact this zine is built on, and it is a piece of exact geometry rather than an impression. For a non-spinning black hole, all the relevant radii can be written in one unit — GM/c², which is just the object's mass expressed as a length: radii, for a non-spinning black hole, in units of GM/c² radius what sits there 2 the event horizon — the actual boundary of the actual object 3 the photon sphere, where light can orbit 3√3 ≈ 5.196 the edge of the shadow — what a distant observer sees Divide the last by the first. 3√3 / 2 ≈ 2.598. The dark circle in the picture is about two and a half times wider than the object casting it. Gravity does not merely hide the black hole; it magnifies the hiding, throwing the darkness outward well past the horizon's true edge. The shadow overstates its cause by a factor of about 2.6 — and it does so consistently, which is the only reason anyone can work backwards from it. the number the whole piece turns on One more thing makes this usable, and it is close to a fluke. Real black holes spin, and spin drags spacetime around with it — so you would expect the shadow's size to depend on how fast it turns and how it is tilted toward you. It barely does. Across the whole range of spins and viewing angles, the shadow's angular radius stays at 5 ± 0.2 GM/Dc² — a spread of about four percent, with the non-spinning case (3√3 ≈ 5.196) sitting near the top of it. That near-constancy is a quirk of the equations rather than a principle, and it is what turns a dark smudge into a measurement: if the shadow's size is fixed by mass over distance and almost nothing else, then measuring it tests the geometry itself. 10 April 2019 · M87* Forty-two microarcseconds The first one they got was not the nearest. It was the one whose shadow happened to be biggest in our sky. M87* sits at the heart of a giant elliptical galaxy about 55 million light years away, and it is enormous — the ring measurement implies a mass of 6.5 ± 0.7 billion suns. Distance shrinks it; size restores it. The two nearly cancel, and what is left is a ring 42 ± 3 microarcseconds across. A microarcsecond is a millionth of a second of arc, and a second of arc is already a 3,600th of a degree. Put it in terms of a thing: Forty-two microarcseconds is roughly the angle subtended by an orange, sitting on the Moon. our own arithmetic — see the sources note Nothing on Earth resolves that. A telescope's sharpness is set by the wavelength it works at divided by the width of the dish, and to see 42 µas at the 1.3 mm the hot gas shines at, the dish would have to be about as wide as the planet. So they used the planet. That is spread seven. The image released on 10 April 2019 came from data taken two years earlier, over six nights in April 2017 — the gap is not delay, it is the checking. And what the checking looked like is the next spread, because it is the most quietly admirable thing in the whole story.
