Too Good to Check How a story gets smoother than the science, and what reading the primary source puts back. Six ways a fact goes wrong, and seventeen worked corrections — most of them ours, published, dated, and fixed in public. Everybody knows the forest is wired together. Fungal threads under the soil, trees trading sugar and warnings across a shared network, an old tree in the sunlight feeding a seedling stuck in the shade. It is one of the loveliest facts of the last thirty years, and we put it in three pieces without checking it. We should not have. In 2023, Karst, Jones and Hoeksema went through the citation record and found the evidence insufficient that these common mycorrhizal networks are widespread in forests, insufficient that transfer through them reliably helps seedlings, and — this is the part that stung — no published evidence at all that mature trees preferentially feed their own offspring. The trade between a root and its fungus is settled science and always was. The forest-wide story is a different claim, and it had been growing by citation rather than by evidence. We corrected it on 3 August 2026 , across No. 5 , No. 26 , and Field Guide No. 6 . And the reason it got past us is not that we were careless. It is that it rhymed with everything we believe . A collection arguing for interdependence and mutual aid met a finding that said the forest is a mutual-aid society, and did not ask it a single hard question. A story that fits gets less scrutiny, which is exactly when it needs more. This page is about that failure and its relatives. It is written from inside the problem rather than above it: nearly every example below is one we shipped, or nearly shipped, and had to go back and fix. That is the only honest place to write it from. It is also the reader-facing front door to our fact-check ledger and our public changelog , which have been quietly accumulating this material for a year.

Why the smooth version wins Misconceptions do not spread because people are stupid. They spread because the retellable version out-competes the accurate one , and the competition is not close. A paper is hedged, conditional, and boring on purpose. It says in this system, under these conditions, we observed . The retelling drops the conditions, because the conditions are what make it hard to remember. Each hop smooths a little more: the hedge goes, then the sample size, then the species, then the name of the person who found it. What arrives at the other end is a clean sentence that anyone can repeat and nobody can source. The trap underneath is that repetition feels like verification . When you have met a claim in six places, it has the texture of a well-established fact — but if all six were downstream of the same press release, you have met it once, six times. Our own house rule exists because of this: aggregators and summaries are leads, not citations . A quote site, an encyclopedia, our own glossary, an AI summary — any of them can point you at a source. None of them can be one. The citation trail, and the hop that never happens A left-to-right chain of five boxes: the paper, the press release, the popular article, the summary, and our page. Arrows run rightward between them. Only the first arrow touches the evidence; the rest copy the copy. A dashed arc runs from our page all the way back to the paper, labelled as the one hop that actually checks anything. THE PAPER hedged, dated PRESS RELEASE hedge drops THE ARTICLE verb gets livelier THE SUMMARY name falls off YOUR PAGE stated as fact four hops. only the first one ever touched the evidence. THE ONE HOP THAT CHECKS ANYTHING meeting a claim in six places is not six confirmations if all six are downstream of the same release Figure 1 · Every arrow feels like corroboration from inside the chain. Only the dashed one leaves it.
Six ways a fact goes wrong

Six ways a fact goes wrong Sorting a year of our own corrections, they fall into six shapes. The value of a taxonomy over a list of trivia is that you can point it at a claim nobody has written about yet — including one of your own.

01 The quote nobody said The most quotable version of a thought is usually not the one a person actually produced, because people speak in clauses and circumlocutions and the culture files off the corners afterwards. What circulates is a compression — accurate in spirit, unfindable in the text. “We are star stuff harvesting sunlight” is Sagan's most-shared line, and what is actually wrong with it is more interesting than either the popular version or our own first correction. It is not in Cosmos the book. Searching all thirteen chapters turns up two separate sentences in chapter 9 — one about farming as the methodical harvesting of sunlight, and, elsewhere, “We are made of starstuff.” We concluded the one-liner was a compression nobody had said, marked it as ours in No. 6 , and moved on. That was an overcorrection, and it is the best example on this page. Sagan did say it — aloud, on camera, in the television series: “We are star stuff. Harvesting starlight.” What circulation did was smaller and more specific than invention. It changed starlight to sunlight , ran two sentences into one, and then cited the book, where the line has never been. So the quote is altered, and our correction — having checked only the page and never the broadcast — called a real spoken sentence an invention. Both errors have the same root: checking one medium and concluding about all of them . A book search cannot settle what a man said out loud. A debunking can be a misconception , which is why that refusal is further down this page and why this entry now carries the correction rather than the tidy version. Caught by Ryan Boren , against Sagan's own voice in the footage, 2026-08-11. Brian Eno's definition of scenius has the same shape. The version everywhere — including in five places in our own knowledge garden — reads “the intelligence and the intuition of a whole cultural scene… the communal form of the concept of the genius.” That wording entered circulation through Kevin Kelly in 2008. Eno's own sentence, in A Year with Swollen Appendices (1996), does not have those articles in it. A small difference, and it means the line has been quoted as his for eighteen years in a form he did not write. And sometimes the wrong name is on it. “We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality” shipped in our Symbioses field guide credited to James Baldwin. It is Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from Birmingham Jail , 1963. Helen Edgar caught it. The tell It is more quotable than anything anyone says out loud. Search the actual book, not the web.

02 The number that went stale A measurement can be wrong simply by being old. The literature moves; museum placards, planetarium scripts and popular astronomy do not, and the superseded value keeps circulating for decades with nothing to mark it as expired. No. 9 built a whole spread on Orion's Belt being an accident of sightline — Alnitak about 740 light-years out, Mintaka 690, Alnilam nearly 2,000, one star three times farther than its neighbours. Those are Hipparcos-era parallaxes, and Hipparcos measured bright, distant, multiple O and B stars badly. Current values from VLTI interferometry and Gaia put all three at essentially one depth, around 1,240–1,260 light-years, all of them in the Orion OB1b association. They are not a coincidence. They are siblings from one cloud. Two things should have caught it sooner, and both are worth stealing as habits. The zine's own colophon cited an astronomy-picture-of-the-day page that gives the three as a group at about 1,500 light-years and never supported our figures — we cited a source we had not read closely . And Field Guide No. 1 , the companion piece, already said it correctly. The collection had been contradicting itself in public for weeks. The tell You can find the figure repeated everywhere and dated nowhere. Check the source you cited actually gives your number.

03 The story told backwards Sometimes the facts survive the retelling and the emphasis does not, which inverts the meaning while leaving every individual sentence defensible. Everybody knows everything evolves into a crab. The paper behind that meme — Wolfe, Luque and Bracken-Grissom, 2021 — does say the crab-like body plan has arisen at least five times. It also says it has been lost at least seven times , that the reasons for the repetition “remain a mystery,” and that the authors do not know whether they are looking at true convergence or at deep homology. Three facts that cut against the meme, none of which travel with it. No. 31 is built on the ones that got left behind. Same shape in No. 32 : the shark's cartilage skeleton is routinely called primitive, as though bone had not been invented yet. Minjinia turgenensis , described in 2020, preserves endochondral bone deeper in the tree — so the chondrichthyan condition is a secondary loss . Derived, not primitive. The textbook reading is upside down, and the loaded word turns out to be factually wrong as well as rude. And in No. 35 : the turtle shell is not armour that evolved for protection. Broadened ribs came first as an adaptation for digging, and Lyson and colleagues note they “provide little protection” while costing the animal in locomotion and breathing. The protection is an exaptation — a later use for a structure built for something else. The tell The paper's own hedge is missing, and every fact that complicates the punchline dropped out together.

04 The credit that drifted Attribution decays toward tidiness. A collective becomes a founder; a documenter becomes a coiner; the person with the most citable book absorbs the idea of everyone around them. This one matters more than the others, because it is not only inaccurate — it takes something from people. The clearest case is in our own field. Neurodiversity was coined by Judy Singer in 1998 is repeated everywhere, including in places that should know better. Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley and Walker published the correction in Autism in 2024: the concept was developed collectively by the online Autistic community, and reached print in 1997 and 1998 through the journalist Harvey Blume, who attributed it to that community. Neurodivergent is Kassiane Asasumasu's, from 2000. The pathology paradigm is Nick Walker's, not Robert Chapman's, who works with the term. Crip time was documented by Zola and Gill, not coined by them. We had two of those wrong in No. 9 and No. 19 . It happens outside our field too, in both directions. Galton did not coin eugenics in Hereditary Genius (1869); he coined it in Inquiries into Human Faculty (1883), in a footnote. “Dirt is matter out of place” is credited to Mary Douglas so reliably that it reads as hers, and it appears unreferenced in Purity and Danger ; the earliest instance we could locate is an 1853 address by Lord Palmerston. “Turtles all the way down” is attributed to William James, whose 1882 essay uses rocks ; the turtle punchline was attached to him in a 1967 doctoral thesis. The tell One name sits where a community was, or a famous name sits where an obscure one belongs.

05 The press release, not the paper Between the finding and the public there is a layer whose job is to make the finding interesting, and it is very good at its job. Its output is not a lie; it is a livelier verb. While building No. 36 we nearly used the story of the bottlenose dolphin that adopted a sperm whale calf. The paper — Wilson and Krause, 2013 — reports “repeated non-agonistic interactions.” “Adopted” is the press's word, not the researchers'. And the explanation everyone repeats, that the dolphin had been harassed by its own kind, is a researcher's suggestion to reporters, not a finding in the paper. The zine says the motive is unknown, because it is. The costly version of this mode is shark cartilage. A popular book, a market, and decades of belief that sharks don't get cancer — against 42 documented tumours across at least 21 chondrichthyan species, and a clinical trial that found no difference in survival or quality of life. A false premise, industrialised. The tell The vivid verb is doing the work. Find the abstract and see which word the authors chose.

06 The finding that flatters you The last one is the wood wide web, and it is the dangerous one, because the others are accidents and this one is an appetite. Our worst instance was not a fact we imported but an argument we made. No. 33 argued that disgust is learned — a claim that suited us, since the zine is about how revulsion gets recruited into prejudice. Helen Edgar , who taught children with profound and multiple learning disabilities for twenty years, said plainly that this was wrong: pre-term babies have an ick without any capacity to have been taught one. She was right, and Rozin's own framework already carried the distinction we had collapsed. Distaste is chemosensory rejection, present at birth — Steiner's 1973 work found anencephalic newborns produce the gustofacial response, so it cannot be an opinion. Disgust proper is ideational and contamination-sensitive, and that is the only kind our argument was ever about. We added a spread rather than a footnote, because as published a reader with sensory processing differences could reasonably have understood the zine to be telling them their aversions were prejudice to get over. Aimed at our own community, that would have done harm. And Helen's underlying point is the better framing and now sits in the zine's voice: we are not blank slates — that is the whole point of star stuff. We have history in us. A response conserved across species and present before birth is that history. We had been arguing against this collection's founding premise without noticing. The tell You wanted it to be true before you read it. That is the moment to slow down, not speed up. Six failure modes and their tells A reference card of six boxes in two columns. One: the quote nobody said — more quotable than real speech. Two: the number that went stale — repeated everywhere, dated nowhere. Three: the story told backwards — the paper's hedge is missing. Four: the credit that drifted — one name where a community was. Five: the press release not the paper — the verb is livelier than the finding. That card exists as a two-sided printable sheet — the six modes and their tells on the face, the habits and the refusals on the reverse. Print it, pin it up, hand it to someone.

What actually works None of this needs a laboratory. It needs a handful of stubborn habits, each of which we adopted because something went wrong without it. Trace it to the primary. The book, the paper, the essay, the talk. Not a quote site, not an encyclopedia, not our own glossary, not a search summary. Those are leads. Cite the source you actually read. The Orion error survived because a colophon named a page that never said what we said. If you have not opened it, it does not go in the references. Read your own siblings. Field Guide No. 1 had the belt right while No. 9 had it wrong. Before shipping, check what the collection has already claimed about the same thing. When one source falls, re-check its relatives. One 2023 paper on mycorrhizal networks meant re-opening three pieces, not one. Errors travel with their quotes. Distinguish a quote from a paraphrase. Verbatim and in quotation marks, or in your own words with the idea attributed. Never dress the second as the first. Say what is still open. “This is the leading hypothesis, not a settled result” costs one sentence and is the difference between a claim and an overclaim. Log the correction in public, with a date and a name. A living document that never shows a correction is just a document making a claim about itself. Measure rather than assume. The same discipline applies to the artifact and not only to its facts — we discovered 44 of our pages printed blank because “prints fine” had been a belief and not a measurement. A stated principle nobody checks is a wish.

Not “do your own research” There is a version of everything above that curdles, and it is worth naming precisely, because it wears the same clothes. “Go to the primary source” is one short step from “do your own research,” a phrase that has been thoroughly captured and now mostly means trust no one who knows more than you . The difference is not attitude, it is direction. Tracing a claim moves toward the evidence and ends somewhere checkable, with a citation you can hand to someone else. The captured version moves away from it and ends in a place where nothing can be checked at all, because every institution that could check it has been disqualified in advance. One of them can be wrong and be shown to be wrong. The other cannot, which is the whole appeal. Debunking has its own failure mode, and it is the mirror image of the one this page is about. Carol Black's essay Science / Fiction describes it exactly: the reverse strategy of asserting “there is scientific consensus where there is no such thing, that an open, ongoing area of scientific inquiry has reached a settled conclusion,” and that anyone disagreeing is “as irrational and ‘anti-science’ as a climate denier.” Her worked example is the wave of LEARNING STYLES ARE A MYTH headlines, which take a narrow experimental result about one simplistic model and inflate it into a verdict on how human beings learn. A debunking can be a misconception. The Myth! headline is as smooth and as retellable as the thing it debunks, which should make you just as suspicious of it.

The refusals Not: Not “do your own research.” Tracing a claim toward its evidence is the opposite move from refusing everyone who has any. Not science literacy as a gate. Nobody owes anybody a reading list before they are allowed to speak about their own life. Not the pleasure of the debunk. If correcting people feels good, that is the appetite from mode six wearing a lab coat. Not contempt for the people who repeat the story. We repeated it. In three pieces. Not a claim to be finished. This page will need corrections, and the ledger it links to has open items in it today. Not certainty as the goal. The goal is knowing which things we have checked and which we haven't, and saying so out loud.
The primary source for a life

The primary source for a life Here is why a fact-checking page belongs in a collection about belonging. The deficit story told about neurodivergent and disabled people has exactly the citation structure described above. It is smooth, endlessly retellable, and repeated until repetition passes for evidence. Its hedges have fallen off. Its credit has drifted onto the people who wrote about us rather than the people who are us. And it flatters the teller, which is why it gets so little scrutiny from the people doing the telling. Autistic people lack empathy is the wood wide web of our field: a claim that grew by citation, and that Damian Milton's double empathy problem (2012) corrected by going back and looking — the breakdown is mutual, a difference in shared understanding between two parties rather than a deficit in one of them. Neurodiversity was coined by one author in 1998 is the credit that drifted, and it took a 2024 paper by six researchers to put a community's name back on its own idea. The primary source for an Autistic life is an Autistic person. That is not a metaphor and it is not a softening. It is the same rule as the rest of this page, applied where it costs something. Miranda Fricker's testimonial injustice names what happens when it is broken — a speaker's account is discounted because of who is speaking — and disability studies has had the shorter version since long before the philosophy arrived: nothing about us without us . Going to the source, here, means asking the person, and then believing the answer enough to let it change what you were going to write. Which is precisely what happened with the disgust zine. The correction came from a member of our own community with two decades of direct experience, arriving after publication, contradicting the argument we had just made. That is a primary source. We rewrote the piece.

Tending the garden No. 18 describes this project as a knowledge garden: evergreen, cross-linked, grown rather than filed. Gardens have weeds. The interesting property of a garden is not that nothing unwanted grows in it — it is that someone walks the beds , and a bed nobody walks looks perfectly healthy from the path right up until it isn't. So the corrections run both ways, which is the cosmic connections point. Checking the scenius quote for No. 31 found the altered wording in five places on stimpunks.org and in none of them the sentence Eno wrote — an error discovered here that has to be fixed upstream. Fact-checking one of Helen's zines surfaced a citation-year discrepancy that neither site can settle alone. This traffic is the part that makes a web of sites worth more than three sites. Two places hold the record. The fact-check ledger is the working file — every piece, every check, every open item, in the detail needed to re-derive a decision a year later. The changelog is the public version: what we got wrong, what's right, who caught it. Neither is an embarrassment to be managed. They are the only thing that makes the rest of the collection worth believing. Only ideational disgust is substantially learned. Caught by Helen Edgar; the zine gained a spread No. 33 Held honestly This is our ledger, not a survey of science communication. These are not the seventeen most important misconceptions in circulation — they are seventeen we can show our full working on, which is a different and much narrower claim. A page about verification has no business asserting anything it hasn't verified. Several rows rest on findings that are themselves live rather than closed. The secondary-loss reading of the chondrichthyan skeleton is where current evidence points, not a settled matter. Rozin and Fallon's is one theory of disgust among several, and that some disgust tracks real pathogen risk is not disputed. Karst and colleagues' paper is an argued position in an active dispute, not a final verdict — which is exactly the hedge the popular version dropped, so we are not dropping it in the other direction either. And the ledger has open items right now. A Carol Black quotation in No. 8 is marked plausible rather than verified. A Deleuze line reaching No. 29 by way of a paywalled article still needs primary confirmation. Five instances of the altered Eno wording remain live on stimpunks.org. Publishing the open items is part of the method, not a lapse in it. None of this makes us reliable. It makes us checkable , which is the only thing anyone can honestly offer. Read the receipts, follow them back, and tell us where we're wrong — open an issue or write to us. Two of the corrections on this page exist because somebody did. The forest is not wired together the way we wanted it to be. Fungus and root still trade, nine in ten land plants still depend on the arrangement, and the ordinary version is astonishing on its own. Popular accounts have said for decades that the pancake tortoise inflates itself inside the crevice to lock in place, chuckwalla-style. That claim is now believed to be untrue. The wedging is done with the limbs. We are keeping the correction visible because it is the more interesting fact. A charismatic mechanism got attached to a real animal and travelled for years on how good it sounded. The tortoise is remarkable either way. The story just wasn't ours to keep telling. Second, Jonathan is old in the way old animals are: he lost his sight to cataracts and has no sense of smell, and he is hand-fed to make sure he gets enough. Support is what makes a long life liveable, and that is true across species. We give that as the standard account rather than as a finding we can point you to a test for. What is not in doubt is the trade. Between 2000 and 2015, more than 34,000 live star tortoises were reported confiscated, over 21,300 of them within India. The thing that makes an animal wanted is not a compliment to it. The star tortoise is being removed from the world at scale precisely because it is beautiful and small and slow and easy to carry — every quality that reads as charming in a caption is, at volume, the mechanism. A pattern that hides you in grass does not hide you from a market. Fernandina is an active volcano; much of it is raw lava, and the pockets of vegetation between the flows are genuinely difficult to reach. In 2019 an expedition found an adult female in one of those pockets. In 2022, genome sequencing by researchers at Princeton, Yale and Ecuadorian institutions, published in Communications Biology, established that she is genetically and morphologically distinct from every other Galápagos tortoise species and closely related to the 1906 male. She is called Fernanda, she is now at the Galápagos National Park breeding centre, and searches for others continue — there is scat and there are tracks that are not hers. Put this entry next to the one before it and hold both. Lonesome George is what it looks like when the answer is no. Fernanda is what it looks like when the answer was never actually taken. A hundred and thirteen years of "extinct" turned out to mean "nobody had climbed that lava field." Absence of evidence had been doing a great deal of quiet work. The One Doing a Dead Tortoise's Job

gonebrought inthe job, not the animal529 hatchlings in 11 years L★S · 012 The One Doing a Dead Tortoise's Job Aldabra giant tortoise · Île aux Aigrettes, Mauritius 26 introduced · 529 hatchlings in 11 years Mauritius lost its own giant tortoises centuries ago, and the plants that depended on them stalled. Aldabra tortoises were brought in to do the missing job. It is working. ecological replacementseed dispersal529 hatchlingscontested practice ▸ Field notes Field notes · Aldabra giant tortoise · Île aux Aigrettes, Mauritius When Mauritius lost Cylindraspis inepta and its relatives, it did not only lose tortoises. It lost the thing they did: eating large fruit and moving big seeds around, and grazing hard enough to keep open ground open. Native hardwoods and screw-pines and palms were left with fruit and nowhere for it to go. Between 2000 and 2011, 26 Aldabra giant tortoises were introduced to Île aux Aigrettes as ecological replacements — not to be the lost species, but to perform its function. They ate the fallen fruit. The seeds that passed through them germinated and grew better than the ones that didn't. Grazed clearings came back, colonised by a native tussock grass the tortoises won't eat. Mortality stayed low, and in eleven years the programme recorded a minimum of 529 hatchlings. We are ending the guide here, and flagging the obvious objection rather than dodging it. Introducing a large non-native animal to an island is how a great deal of this damage was done in the first place, and ecological replacement is contested practice, not settled policy. This is one well-documented case, monitored for two decades, and it is not a general licence. But it is a real answer to a real question, and the question is the one this guide has been circling since spread one: what do you do when the thing that was holding a system together is gone? Sometimes the answer is that the job is more portable than the animal — and somebody else, from another ocean entirely, can be supported to do it. Which is, more or less, what accommodation is. Not restoring what was lost. Finding another way for the function to happen, and then checking whether it worked. A comedy channel in the ancestry

The credit A comedy channel in the ancestry Six of the zines here and three of the field guides exist because of a YouTube series about animals with jokes in it. Until this page, its author's name appeared nowhere in this project at all. Ze Frank makes True Facts — nature documentary footage, narrated straight into absurdity, about echidnas and pangolins and anglerfish and mantis shrimp. Ryan watched it with a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks, now studying to be a marine biologist. Out of that watching came No. 32, No. 34 and Field Guide No. 9, which already say who they were written for — and behind them the whole Kin collection, which is the citation-dense natural history end of this site. A shark catalogue, a Greenland shark's 156-year childhood, a skeleton that skipped bone. None of those get written by someone who was not already watching animal videos with somebody they love. where Kin actually comes from So why was the credit missing? Because it does not look like a source. We are careful to the point of tedium about citing papers, and there is a whole page — Cosmic Connections — arguing that nothing here comes from nowhere. But the thing that made us want to write about sharks was not a paper. It was a bloke doing a voice over some footage of a fish, and that kind of debt slips through, because the citation habit is pointed at claims rather than at causes. This page is the correction. It is filed as an easter egg rather than on the front page for one honest reason, which spread seven deals with directly: the tone does not port. That is not a criticism, and it is not a hedge either. It is the actual situation, and saying it plainly is more respectful than a credit that pretends we are doing the same thing. What the watching produced A chain running from the True Facts series, through watching it together, to the pieces it produced: zines 32 and 34, field guide 9, and the wider Kin collection of six zines. The animal is never the punchline

Where the joke lands The animal is never the punchline What we took from True Facts is not that it makes science fun. Plenty of things make science fun. It is something narrower and much harder, and it took us a while to see it. Watch where the comedy actually points. It lands on the narrator — his own bafflement, his own voice, his willingness to be the idiot in the room. It lands on human expectation — what we assumed an animal was for. It lands on language — the ridiculous names we gave things. And in our reading it does not land, at any point, on the organism for being a defective version of something else. That is the same move this site makes, arrived at from the opposite end. Every field guide here has a “sounds like / actually” table, and its whole job is to catch a verdict somebody already handed down — the failed brown dwarf, the primitive shark, the simple nervous system — and take it back. Our tables correct a verdict. True Facts just never issues one. It is the same destination and it arrives without needing the apparatus, which is a slightly annoying thing to discover about your own method. the honest version of the comparison And it is not that the animals are treated reverently — they absolutely are not. They get called ridiculous, they get compared to household objects, the delivery is relentless. But ridiculous is not the same as deficient. You can find a creature hilarious and still describe, accurately and at length, exactly what it is extremely good at. The two things sit together the whole way through, which is the part worth stealing. Stated as a reading, not a finding. This is our interpretation of a body of work, not a claim we can measure. Somebody could go through the catalogue and argue the opposite. We think the pattern holds; we are not pretending it is a result. Two routes to the same refusal Two columns. On the left, the field guide route: a verdict is issued, then corrected by a sounds-like-actually table. On the right, the True Facts route: no verdict is ever issued. Both arrive at the same place. field guides True Facts verdict handed down table takes it back no verdict issued (nothing to take back) the animal is not deficient ridiculous is not deficient our reading, not a measurement Figure 2 · same destination, one of us needs a table True Facts · Stimpunks

His own words Flawed and wonderful Asked what he is doing, in an interview with Pamela Hill Nettleton for U.S. Catholic in 2021, Ze Frank gave an answer that could be lifted straight onto this site's masthead. I like reminding people that we are flawed and wonderful. I like helping people feel less alone. Ze Frank, interviewed by Pamela Hill Nettleton · U.S. Catholic 86:7, July 2021 Flawed and wonderful, in the same breath, with no ranking between them. Not flawed but wonderful, which would make the wonder a consolation. Not wonderful despite. Both at once, as a single description — which is very close to what the neurodiversity paradigm says about human variation, and it arrived here from a man narrating footage of a sea slug. He is not making a claim about neurodiversity, and we are not putting one in his mouth. He is talking about people watching videos on the internet. But the shape of the sentence is the shape of the argument, and this collection is built on noticing when a shape turns up somewhere it was not aimed. Nettleton's own framing in that piece is the sharpest thing written about him. Her words, not his: Frank is a kind of Mister Rogers of the internet for grown-ups. He makes good stuff that makes people remember how good they are too. Pamela Hill Nettleton · U.S. Catholic, 2021 — her characterisation, not his And she catches the thing about the series that most coverage misses: it honours scientists — people generally ignored by most media — and the arcane subjects they spend their lives on. It got more rigorous, not less

The unusual direction It got more rigorous, not less Here is the part that made us pay proper attention, because it runs against the way everything on the internet normally goes. The early videos were jokes with animals in them. Sheela Clary, profiling him for SUCCESS in 2022, is blunt about the first one: it “included neither truth nor facts.” Spliced clips, a voice, a punchline. Still here from before your country was

The animal Still here from before your country was Somewhere in the Arctic dark right now, four hundred metres down, there is a shark that was already alive when Napoleon was. The Greenland shark, Somniosus microcephalus. It lives in water near freezing — down to about −1.8 °C — and has been recorded to depths of around 2,647 metres. It grows less than a centimetre a year. In 2016 Julius Nielsen and colleagues published the ages of 28 of them in Science. The results were not what anyone expected. A life span of at least 272 years. The largest animal in the study, five metres long, came out at 392 ± 120 years old. That makes it the longest-lived vertebrate known — longer than the bowhead whale, longer than anything else with a backbone. And the number that this zine is really about, the one that stopped everybody: They don't reach sexual maturity until roughly 156 years old. A century and a half. They read it in the eye

How anyone could possibly know They read it in the eye You cannot age a Greenland shark the usual way. It has no bone to lay down rings in — see the zine before last — and its vertebrae are too poorly calcified to count. So the researchers used the one tissue in a vertebrate body that never updates itself. At the very centre of the eye lens is a core of crystallin proteins laid down before the animal is born, and then left alone. No turnover. No replacement. Whatever carbon was around when that lens formed is still sitting there, decades or centuries later. The eye carries its own birth certificate. Then the second trick, and it is a strange one. Between the mid-1950s and the early 1960s, atmospheric nuclear testing spiked the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere worldwide — a sharp, dated, globally shared marker scientists call the bomb pulse. It works out to a timestamp printed across the whole planet. Find that spike in the lens core, and you know the animal was born after it. Don't find it, and you know it was born before — and how much ¹⁴C is there tells you roughly how long before. The oldest animals in the study were born before the pulse. Before the industrial revolution finished. Some of them, before the United States. We found out how old they were by looking for fallout from our own bombs in the middle of their eyes. the bomb pulse, and the lens that caught it lens core formed before birth never replaced ¹⁴C bomb pulse born before born after 19001960now no spike in the core → born before the tests nielsen et al. 2016 · eye lens radiocarbon the one tissue that never updates a birth certificate in protein Two Hundred Years · Stimpunks
"Late" is a comparison, not a measurement

The hinge "Late" is a comparison, not a measurement Here is the thing worth carrying out of this zine. A Greenland shark that reaches maturity at 156 is not late. It is not behind. It has not fallen off a track. It is exactly on time — for a Greenland shark. The word late only means something once you've picked a calendar, and the calendar always comes from somewhere. Pick a herring's, and every Greenland shark that ever lived is a catastrophic failure. Pick the Greenland shark's, and the herring is gone before the shark has opened its eyes properly. Neither calendar is the true one. There isn't a true one. There are just organisms and the rates they run at, and a ruler somebody laid alongside them afterwards. We do this to people constantly, and we do it with enormous confidence. Delayed. Behind. Not age-appropriate. Should have been doing this by now. Each one sounds like an observation about a child. Every one of them is a comparison to a schedule, and the schedule was made by averaging other people. Our zine on the invention of "normal" is about where those averages came from and what they were built to do. This is the same argument, in an animal that makes it impossible to miss. The shark isn't slow. The slowest fish in the sea eats seals

And yet The slowest fish in the sea eats seals In 2012 Yuuki Watanabe and colleagues put data loggers on six free-swimming Greenland sharks and measured how fast they actually go. Cruising speed: 0.34 metres per second. That is about one kilometre an hour. A slow walk. Tail-beat frequency: 0.15 Hz — one sweep of the tail roughly every seven seconds. Both figures were the lowest recorded for any fish of that size. The paper is titled, plainly, The slowest fish. Which sets up a genuine puzzle, because their stomachs contain seal. Watanabe's team found seal tissue in a substantial share of the guts they examined. And a seal, in water, is faster than this shark by an enormous margin. It is not close. The shark cannot chase anything. So it doesn't. The proposal in the paper is that the sharks take seals while the seals are asleep — creeping up on animals that have to rest in the water, and arriving before they wake. Read that again, because it isn't a consolation prize. This animal is not succeeding despite being slow. Silence is only possible at that speed. The strategy requires the trait. Nobody outswam anybody. It just found the part of the world where being unhurried is the whole advantage. the mismatch, and why it doesn't matter shark 0.34 m/s seal much faster a chase is not available. so there is no chase. what happens instead z z z quiet enough to arrive first the strategy needs the trait · watanabe et al. 2012 j. exp. mar. biol. ecol., 2012 not succeeding despite — succeeding by Two Hundred Years · Stimpunks
Nearly blind, and it doesn't signify

The eye again Nearly blind, and it doesn't signify There is a copepod called Ommatokoita elongata, a couple of centimetres of crustacean, and it spends its adult life clamped to the cornea of a Greenland shark's eye. In the study that documented the damage — Borucinska, Benz and Whiteley, 1998 — every shark they examined was carrying one. The parasite anchors itself with a structure called a bulla, and around each anchor the cornea goes opaque, ulcerated, scarred. By any ordinary reading, these animals are severely visually impaired, and it is close to universal in the population. And it appears to cost them approximately nothing. Four hundred metres down in the Arctic, in water that is dark most of the year and black below, vision is not the sense that matters. They have smell, they have a lateral line, they have electroreception. The environment never asks the question that the eye would answer. An impairment is a relation, not a property. Take the same eye and put it on an animal that hunts by sight in bright water, and it is a catastrophe. Down there it barely registers. same eye, two environments sunlit, hunts by sight catastrophic 400 m down, dark barely registers the eye is identical in both boxes only the demand changed impairment is a relation not a property of the body borucinska, benz & whiteley 1998 a deficit needs somewhere to be a deficit the environment asks, or it doesn't Two Hundred Years · Stimpunks
This is not a zine about slow being beautiful

The turn — and this one is not comfortable This is not a zine about slow being beautiful It would be easy to stop here, and it would be a lie. Read the last line of Nielsen's abstract. Having established the longest vertebrate life span ever measured, the authors do not celebrate. They raise concerns about species conservation. Here's why. An animal that takes about 156 years to reproduce even once has almost no capacity to replace losses. Kill a thousand of them and you are not waiting a decade for the population to recover — you are waiting longer than the modern world has existed. Every Greenland shark caught as bycatch today is an animal whose replacement will not be mature until well after everyone reading this is dead. They were hunted for liver oil for a long time, in very large numbers. They still turn up in trawls. The IUCN lists the species as Vulnerable. So slowness is not a superpower. It is a strategy with a bill attached. It is superbly adapted to an environment that stayed roughly the same for millions of years, and it is nearly defenceless against one that changes in decades. And that is the honest shape of the thing, for sharks and for us. A pace is not good or bad on its own. It is survivable or it isn't, and what decides that is the world around it. 156 years to replace a single animal VU iucn red list vulnerable a loss, and the time to make it back pop. fast breeder: back in years Greenland shark: still down pressure 050 yrs100150 slow is fragile against fast change schematic · not measured data the bill attached to the strategy iucn: vulnerable Two Hundred Years · Stimpunks

What follows from that The environment decides Put the last three spreads together and you get a single claim, and it is the one this whole collection keeps arriving at. A ruined cornea is a disaster in bright water and nothing at 400 metres. A 156-year childhood works fine in an ocean that holds still and is fatal in one full of trawlers. A one-kilometre-an-hour cruising speed is useless in a chase and perfect for arriving quietly. None of those outcomes is a fact about the shark. Every one is a fact about the shark and the world it is in — and when the outcome is bad, the thing that changed was almost never the animal. Disabled people have a name for this. It's the social model of disability: the distinction between a body's actual condition and the disabling produced by environments and expectations built as though that condition didn't exist. Stairs disable a wheelchair user. Open-plan offices and fluorescent light disable us. The pace of a school day disables a kid who needs longer. Which turns the question around. Not how do we get this child up to speed — but what is this environment demanding, who chose that, and what would it cost to stop? That is what a Cavendish Space is for, and it is why Stimpunks argues for slow pedagogy — unhurried time, room to revisit, the present moment treated as though it counted. Not as an indulgence for slow children. As a design change that stops manufacturing failure. You cannot tell whether a pace is a problem by looking at the creature. The defence of the clock Better get used to it Ask for a slower pace and you will meet one particular answer so often that it has an acronym. Alfie Kohn named it in Education Week in 2005: what he calls the BGUTI principle — Better Get Used To It. You have heard every version. Homework in the early years because there's homework later. Grades young because there are grades eventually. Sitting still now because a job will demand it. No accommodation at school because the real world won't accommodate you. The logic is always the same: life will be hard later, so hardship now is preparation. Kohn's sentence about this is the one that belongs in this zine, and it is exact: Almost by definition, the BGUTI defense ignores developmental differences. Alfie Kohn, "Getting Hit on the Head Lessons," Education Week, 7 September 2005 It has to ignore them, or it stops working. The whole argument treats the timetable as the fixed thing and the child as the adjustable thing. But if children arrive at things at genuinely different rates — and they do — then "everyone gets this at this age" guarantees that some of them are being handed something they cannot yet use. BGUTI doesn't overlook developmental difference by accident. It cannot survive noticing it. And the claim underneath is not even true. Kohn again: people don't really get better at coping with unhappiness because they were deliberately made unhappy when they were young. Early adversity is not a vaccine. It mostly just teaches you that adults will do this to you. This is where behaviorism does its worst work. A model that watches compliance and reaches for consequences has no way to represent a child who needs longer — so needing longer shows up as refusing, and refusing gets a consequence. The consequence never changes the pace. It only adds fear to it. Stimpunks' version is blunter, and we'll stand on it: we don't prepare students for a world of potential oppression by oppressing them. the BGUTI chain, and where it breaks life is hard later so make it hard now child becomes ready not what happens and for the chain to hold at all: timetable FIXED child THE VARIABLE developmental difference makes that incoherent "almost by definition, the BGUTI defense ignores developmental differences" alfie kohn · education week, 2005 it cannot survive noticing them Two Hundred Years · Stimpunks

Not"you're secretly a Greenland shark." You are not an Arctic shark and your life is not 400 years long. The shared thing is the logic of the ruler, not the animal. Noteveryone just needs more time. Not"but the real world won't wait." Sometimes true, and it still doesn't license BGUTI. That a hardship exists later is not evidence that inflicting it earlier prepares anyone — and the "real world" is not a fixed object either. It is also built, also by someone, also changeable. Nobody asked the shark to hurry

Closer to home Nobody asked the shark to hurry If you have been on the receiving end of a developmental timetable, you already know the whole of this zine in your body. The chart on the wall at the clinic. The milestone that didn't get met. The report that said working below age-related expectations. The reading level, the year group, the "should be able to by now." The particular quiet of being the last one still doing the thing everybody else finished. None of that measured you. All of it measured a gap between you and an average — and the average was assembled from other people, for reasons that had a lot to do with sorting and not much to do with you. Some things do take you longer. That's true and it doesn't need softening. What isn't true is the part that got smuggled in with it: that taking longer is a defect, that the schedule is a law of nature, and that being behind on it means being behind at living. There is an animal in the Arctic that spends a century and a half growing up, and no one has informed it that this is a delay. It is not lagging. It is not a slow version of a faster animal. It is simply what it is, at the rate it does it, and it was doing that before every schedule any of us has ever been measured against was invented. You are made of the same star stuff as that shark: the same carbon, the same calcium, forged in the same kind of dying star. Two arrangements of it, running at completely different speeds, and the universe has never once indicated a preference. Take the time it takes. Then ask who built the clock, and whether it can be moved. You were never late. You were being timed by somebody else's watch. two questions you can ask a schedule "why am I behind?" assumes the clock · looks for the fault in you "who set this clock?" makes the schedule a decision · decisions can change only one of these has an answer you can act on change the question and the fault moves off you Two Hundred Years · Stimpunks

The three of them One clade, three refusals This is the last of three zines built out of one young person's special interest, and they turn out to make one argument in three moves. No. 32 refused the word primitive. Sharks didn't fail to invent bone — their lineage had it and let it go. What was read as an earlier stage was a later change, and the reading was a verdict wearing a description's coat. No. 33 refused the word gross. Disgust isn't information about an animal; it's information about a frame, learned young, and it does border work on bodies — theirs and ours. No. 34 refuses the word late. There is no lateness without a calendar, and someone always brought the calendar. Three words that feel like observations and are all three verdicts. Primitive. Gross. Late. Each one describes a relationship between a thing and a standard, while sounding like a fact about the thing. And the sharks did not know they were carrying any of it. They were only ever doing the thing they do — slowly, in the cold, in the dark — while a species with a very short life and a very fast clock swam past and filed them. The animal is never the argument. Held honestly. The Nielsen figures are estimates with real uncertainty and the paper states them as such: 272 years is a minimum, and the headline 392 carries ±120. Age at maturity is given as "at least" 156 ± 22 and is inferred from body length, not observed directly. Borucinska and colleagues examined six sharks and found the copepod on all of them; very high prevalence is widely reported for this species, but "essentially all of them" rests on small samples, and we have not put a population percentage in the prose. That the sharks don't need their eyes is a well-supported inference from their habitat and their other senses rather than a directly measured finding — the honest version is that vision appears not to be load-bearing for them, not that blindness has been shown to be costless. The recovery curves on spread 7 are labelled on the figure as schematic, not measured data; they illustrate a mechanism the conservation literature describes and are not plotted from a population model. And the ethics do not come from the biology. That an animal thrives at its own pace is not why a person's pace deserves respect — as about.html puts it, we are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. Four hundred years in the cold and the dark, at one kilometre an hour. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation, and it has never once told anybody to hurry up. The oldest anarchist in the room

The mycelial network The oldest anarchist in the room Beneath the forest floor runs a living web of fungal threads — mycelium — laced through the soil and trading nutrients with the roots it meets. That trade is well established; how far the shared networks reach, and how much moves tree to tree through them, is still argued over by the people who dig them up. It has no head office. It grows in every direction at once, feeds its neighbors, and asks no one's permission. Its intelligence is distributed: problems get solved, paths get reinforced, weak connections fade — all with no commanding center telling each thread what to do. We know this shape, because it is how we try to hold each other. A competency network — everyone knowing something, sharing it with whoever needs it. Mutual aid — resources moving to where the need is greatest, not up a hierarchy to be rationed back down. Zero hierarchy is not a slogan we impose on the network. It is the shape the network takes when we stop forcing it into a chain of command. The mycelium never needed a manager. Neither, it turns out, do we — we need interdependence, which is a very different thing. no center trade distributed network · no commanding center hyphae · nodes · nutrient trade · reinforcing paths Underground · Stimpunks
Nothing is wasted. Only waiting to be metabolized.

star · C forged falls soil uptake the loop carbon: forged above, metabolized below star → soil → hyphae → uptake → and back Decomposition · bricolage Nothing is wasted. Only waiting to be metabolized. Decomposition has an image problem. We hear the word and think of rot and loss. But fungi reframe it: they break the toughest structures — rock, oil, a fallen tree — back down into materials life can use again. Rock becomes soil. A dead trunk becomes a nursery. The star-forged carbon of Bone Song does not stop at the skeleton. It falls, becomes soil, is taken up by the network, and passed along — star stuff all the way down, and up again through the ground. Then comes the leap from biology to politics: we can enlist those powers on the hard structures too. The pathology paradigm that files us as broken. The deficit framing. The systems built hostile toward the people who most need them. We do not argue with the rock. We grow into its cracks and, over time, turn it into ground. Composting is not destruction. It is how a commons renews itself. Underground · Stimpunks

The poem Beneath the forest, a network with no name is doing the work. No head office. No throne. No plan on file. It grows in every direction at once, feeds its neighbors, and breaks the dead down into the living — underground, unseen, asking no one's permission. We know this shape. It is how we try to hold each other: no one at the center, resources moving to wherever the need is, everyone teaching, everyone learning, growth in every direction at once. Decomposition is not the end. Rock becomes soil. A fallen tree becomes a nursery. Nothing is wasted here — only waiting to be metabolized into whatever comes next. The carbon in you was forged in a star. It fell. It became soil. The network took it up and passed it on, and some of it became you. Star stuff, all the way down, and up again through the ground. The realest work happens in the dark, where no one is watching, where the metrics never reach. Do not mistake invisibility for absence. The network is busiest exactly where you cannot see it. We are not admiring a clever organism. We are kin, recognizing a relative. We look for ourselves in the fungi and we find us there: mischief with a purpose, refusing the world as given, making new possibilities while composting the old. We love you down to your star stuff — and up again through the soil. To the thread. To the trade. To the dark. To the network that occasionally surfaces and is busiest when it does not. L★S. The work that changes everything is the work no one is watching

The quiet and the dark The work that changes everything is the work no one is watching In a world of influencers and incessant self-promotion, mycelial networks engineer whole ecosystems in the quiet and the dark. The most transformative work is often the most invisible. There is deep resonance here for anyone told to be louder, more visible, more legibly productive to count. So much of what holds us together is quiet crip labor — unglamorous, unposted, done where the metrics never reach. Unmasking is often a retreat from the stage lights into a truer, quieter mode. Monotropism — sinking all the way down into a single interest — needs exactly what the mycelium thrives in: undisturbed, unhurried, unsurveilled depth. This is what a cave is for. We do not mistake invisibility for absence. Mischief · punk Fungi gleefully defy well-established assumptions, making new possibilities while decomposing old ones. Mycologists call this punk science. Read the description back without the word fungi and it is a description of us: crossing boundaries, refusing the world as given, rooting the work in creativity. To neuroqueer a space is a punk act. To imagine a livable, interdependent future built by and for the people this world discards is punk aimed at the horizon. Nota tidy metaphor for teamwork. This is kinship and a critique of hierarchy, not a synergy poster. Notyour pain was worth it because it composts. Composting does not justify the harm — the hostile structure should never have been built. Notbe invisible and grateful. Quiet crip labor deserves resourcing, not romanticized erasure. Nota substitute for redistribution. Loving the network does not feed anyone; mutual aid does. We are not a hierarchy that occasionally cooperates. We are a network that occasionally surfaces. Underground is the fifth zine in the Stimpunks series — the below to Bone Song's above. It is offered freely, to be printed and folded and handed to someone who needs it. It draws on two Stimpunks pieces, "A Mycelium and a Rhizome" and "The Mycelial Worldview Is Punk," and on the sources they build from: the MOTH collective's essay "Punk Law: Lessons from Fungi," Toby Kiers and SPUN on "punk science," and the documentary Allpa Ukundi, Ñukanchi Pura (Kichwa for "underground, around, and among us"), made with the Kichwa people of Sarayaku in the Ecuadorian Amazon together with the Fungi Foundation and SPUN. The One We Drew Upside Down

righted, then turned around L★S · 001 The One We Drew Upside Down Hallucigenia sparsa wrong on two axes · 1977 → 1991 → 2015 Revised A Cambrian animal a few centimetres long, from the Burgess Shale. Described in 1977 walking on its spines with tentacles waving above it. Both of those were the wrong way round, and it took two separate corrections, thirty-eight years apart, to get the animal the right way up and the right way round. upside down for 14 yearsback-to-front for 24 morethe blob was not the headcorrected twice ▸ Field notes Field notes · Hallucigenia sparsa Simon Conway Morris described Hallucigenia sparsa in Palaeontology in 1977, and the name is a fair record of how the animal struck him: something hallucinatory, hard to place among living things. His reconstruction gave it seven pairs of stiff spines pointing down, as legs, and seven soft tentacle-like appendages pointing up. The first correction came in 1991. Ramsköld and Hou, working with better material from China, turned it over: the spines are armour along the back, and the soft appendages are the legs — clawed legs, which is what placed the animal near the living velvet worms rather than nowhere at all. Fourteen years upside down. Then the second correction, twenty-four years after that. Even right side up, the animal was still being drawn facing the wrong way. There was a dark blob at one end that everybody read as a head. Smith and Caron, in Nature in 2015, found the actual head at the other end — with a pair of simple eyes, a ring around the mouth, and a throat lined with tiny teeth. The blob was something else entirely, possibly decay fluid squeezed out of the body. So the record was wrong on one axis for fourteen years and on the other for twenty-four more, and each fix was published under names in a journal anybody can look up. That is the whole reason we can tell you about it. What is worth holding onto is why it was hard. This animal is a smear a few centimetres long, flattened in shale for half a billion years. Reading it at all is an achievement. The error was never in the observing — every spine Conway Morris drew is really there. The error was in the arrangement he brought to it, which is the thing an assembly error always is. The companion argument is in No. 61: what makes this a good record rather than a bad one is not that it was right first time. It is that each wrong version is still citable. The One That Was Three Animals

three, then one, then two L★S · 002 The One That Was Three Animals Anomalocaris canadensis three animals, three groups · united 1985 · partly re-split 2012 Revised For most of a century the largest known Cambrian predator was catalogued as three unrelated creatures: a shrimp-like animal, a jellyfish, and a sponge. They were a feeding appendage, a mouth, and a body — all from the same animal. And when that was finally sorted out in 1985, part of the fix had to be undone again in 2012. a shrimp that was an arma jellyfish that was a moutha sponge that was a bodythe correction got corrected ▸ Field notes Field notes · Anomalocaris canadensis This is the best case on the page for how far an assembly error can go, because the pieces were not just arranged wrongly — they were filed in three different groups of the animal kingdom. The first piece, named in 1892, was a curved segmented thing that looked like the abdomen of a shrimp. It got the name Anomalocaris — the odd shrimp. The second, a circular ring of overlapping plates, was described as a jellyfish and named Peytoia. The third, a large soft flattened mass, was called a sponge and named Laggania. Whittington and Briggs put them together in 1985, in a paper in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society. The decisive specimens showed the “shrimps” attached in pairs to the head of a large body, with the “jellyfish” sitting where the mouth should be. What had been three fossils in three phyla was one predator, and a big one for its world. And then the correction was itself corrected. In 2012 Daley and Bergström looked again at the oral cone and found that Anomalocaris's mouth has three large plates, not the four-part arrangement of the ring originally called Peytoia. So the two are not the same animal after all: Peytoia is a valid genus again, with Laggania as its junior synonym. The 1985 paper was right that the pieces went together; it was wrong about which pieces went with which. That second move is why this card is here rather than in the tidy-story band. The famous version of this anecdote stops in 1985 with a satisfying reveal. The real record kept going, and kept going in public, and a reader in 2026 can follow every step of it. One further layer, mentioned rather than tabled: the animal's reputation as an armour-cracking shell-crusher has also been questioned on functional grounds. The oral cone looks better suited to suction than to biting. The One With Its Head On Its Tail

and the anecdote too L★S · 003 The One With Its Head On Its Tail Elasmosaurus platyurus skull at the wrong end · 1868, corrected 1870 Revised Edward Drinker Cope reconstructed a long-necked marine reptile in 1868 with the skull mounted on the end of what was actually its neck — reading the neck as a tail. The error is real and famous. The story everybody tells about who caught it is wrong. neck read as a tailcorrected by Leidy, 1870Marsh claimed it 20 years laterand the count was revised again in 2013 ▸ Field notes Field notes · Elasmosaurus platyurus In 1868 Cope described Elasmosaurus platyurus from Kansas and restored it with the skull at the wrong end of the animal, on what was in fact the neck. He had a reason: jaw material had been found at that end of the skeleton. What he had not weighted properly was that the opposite end terminated in the atlas and axis — the first two vertebrae of a neck, which do not occur in a tail. The correction came in 1870, and it was Joseph Leidy's. Leidy made the point in Remarks on Elasmosaurus platyurus at a meeting of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia on 8 March 1870. Cope moved quickly: he issued a corrected version and tried to recall the preprints, and argued that he had been misled in part by an earlier reversal of Leidy's own. Now the part this guide is really for. The version of this story that circulates has Marsh catching Cope out, humiliating him, and lighting the fuse of the Bone Wars. That is not what the record shows. Marsh was present at the March 1870 meeting where Leidy made the correction. His claim to have discovered the error himself surfaces in a newspaper article roughly twenty years later, and it is that late, self-reported version that got into general circulation. So the animal was reconstructed wrongly, and then the story of its correction was also reconstructed wrongly, in a way that flattered the person telling it. Two errors, and the second one is the more instructive. A retelling that improves with age is the shape described in Too Good to Check. And the animal is still being revised: Sachs, Kear and Everhart published a corrected vertebral count in 2013, a hundred and forty-five years after the original description. Even the number of bones in the longest neck known is not a closed question. The One With A Thumb On Its Nose

a thumb, not a horn L★S · 004 The One With A Thumb On Its Nose Iguanodon a thumb read as a horn · 1825, corrected 1882 Revised One of the first dinosaurs ever named, from teeth that resembled an iguana’s. Among the fragments was a conical bone, and Gideon Mantell put it on the animal’s snout as a horn. It is a thumb. The correction waited fifty-seven years for a complete skeleton. named from teeth, 1825horn on the noseit is the first digitBernissart settled it ▸ Field notes Field notes · Iguanodon Gideon Mantell named Iguanodon in 1825, on teeth that looked like a scaled-up iguana's. It is one of the founding names of the whole subject, and the reasoning behind it — these are reptile teeth, but enormous — was sound for what was known. Among the associated material was a conical, pointed bone. Mantell reasoned by the nearest available analogy and put it on the animal's snout as a horn, in the manner of a rhinoceros. Every early reconstruction and sculpture inherited it. The correction is Louis Dollo's, and it needed an unusual piece of luck. In 1878 coal miners at Bernissart in Belgium cut into a fissure packed with near-complete Iguanodon skeletons. With whole hands articulated in place, the conical bone turned out to be the first digit — a thumb, modified into a spike. Dollo reconstructed and mounted the skeletons, and they went on display from 1882. Note what actually resolved it. Not a better argument; not a re-examination of the original fragments. It took thirty-odd whole animals. That is the honest lesson of the fragment: while the evidence is a handful of pieces, a wrong reading and a right reading can be equally consistent with everything you have, and no amount of care distinguishes them. Which is why this guide's second band exists at all. The gap gets filled by whatever you brought with you, and the only reliable cure is more animal. The One That Was Only Arms

44 years of unplaced L★S · 005 The One That Was Only Arms Deinocheirus mirificus two arms for 44 years · 1970 → 2014 Revised Two enormous forelimbs came out of the Gobi in 1965 — nearly two and a half metres each, with great curved claws, and no other part of the animal. They were named in 1970 as terrible hand, unusual, and for forty-four years that was the whole animal. It turned out to be a humpbacked, duck-billed plant-and-fish eater. found 9 July 1965named 1970, from armsunplaceable for 44 yearsthe guesses were all wrong ▸ Field notes Field notes · Deinocheirus mirificus On 9 July 1965, the Polish–Mongolian palaeontological expedition — led by Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska — recovered a pair of gigantic forelimbs at Altan Ula III in the Gobi. Halszka Osmólska and Ewa Roniewicz named the animal Deinocheirus mirificus in 1970: terrible hand, unusual. And then, for forty-four years, that was it. Two arms, a shoulder girdle, some ribs and vertebrae. Over the decades the animal was assigned to one group of theropods and then another — an ornithomimosaur, a therizinosaur, something requiring a clade of its own — and none of the assignments could be settled, because you cannot settle a body plan from a forelimb. In 2014, Lee and colleagues published two near-complete skeletons in Nature. The animal was not a predator. It is the largest ornithomimosaur known: a humped back, a long duck-like skull with no teeth, a wide flat bill, and gut contents including fish scales and gastroliths. An omnivore in a wet environment. The great claws are not for killing. What this card is doing in a guide about errors is worth being precise about. The reconstructions in circulation during those forty-four years were often wrong — but the published position for most of that time was closer to we do not know what this is, and that is not an error. It is a record correctly reporting the size of its own gap. That is rarer than it sounds, and it is the standard the companion zine asks for. No. 61's complaint is not that categories get things wrong; it is that they so seldom say how much they do not know. A name that sat honestly unplaced for four decades is the good version. Worth naming, too, that the expeditions which found and named this animal were led by women, at a time when very few were, and that the original describers are on the paper. no type left to check L★S · 006 The One Whose Holotype Burned Spinosaurus aegyptiacus type destroyed 24–25 April 1944 Contested Described in 1915 from Egyptian material. The original specimen — the physical standard the whole species is anchored to — was destroyed in the bombing of Munich in 1944, after its describer’s requests to move the collection were refused. Every reconstruction since has argued from photographs and drawings. described 1915holotype burned 1944the warnings were ignoredstill contested ▸ Field notes Field notes · Spinosaurus aegyptiacus Ernst Stromer described Spinosaurus aegyptiacus in 1915, from material collected at Bahariya in Egypt in 1912. The bones went to the palaeontological collection in Munich. On the night of 24–25 April 1944, Allied bombing destroyed them. Stromer had asked, more than once, for the collection to be moved somewhere safer, and the requests were not acted on. The animal now exists as his published figures and descriptions and as photographs. That is a different epistemic situation from every other card on this page. Elsewhere, a reconstruction can be checked against a specimen in a drawer. Here there is nothing to go back to. When Nizar Ibrahim and colleagues argued in 2014 for a very different Spinosaurus — short-legged, dense-boned, at home in water — and again in 2020 for a tail built for propulsion, the 1915 material could only take part as an image. The card is marked contested, and it stays that way. The aquatic interpretation is disputed in print on several grounds, including how much of the reconstruction is composite and whether the animal could really swim after prey. We are not adjudicating it here. What belongs in this guide is the structural fact: this is what a record looks like when the thing it refers to is gone. There is a modest, uncomfortable point in it about custody. A type specimen is a promise that a claim can be re-checked. Keeping that promise is somebody's job, and here it was somebody's job that did not get done — and the person who saw it coming had no power to act. lower jaw, whole arch L★S · 007 The One With The Spiral Helicoprion davisii whorl placed four ways · settled 2013 Revised A Palaeozoic relative of sharks and rays, known almost entirely from a spiral of teeth. With no skull preserved around it, the whorl was reconstructed on the snout, on the upper jaw, on the back, and on the tail. A CT scan in 2013 found it in the lower jaw, where it fills the entire arch. a whorl with no skullplaced on snout, back, tailCT scan, 2013the specimen sat since 1950 ▸ Field notes Field notes · Helicoprion davisii Helicoprion is a chondrichthyan — the group that includes sharks, rays and chimaeras — and like its relatives it had a skeleton mostly of cartilage, which rarely survives. What survives, in numbers, is a tightly coiled spiral of teeth. A whorl on its own does not tell you where on the animal it sat. So the published reconstructions put it in several places: extending from the upper jaw, as paired upper and lower elements, out on the snout like a bandsaw, and even as denticles on the pectoral region or the tail. One influential 1960s version put it at the tip of the lower jaw, working like a circular saw. Every one of these was consistent with the fossil. The resolution came from an instrument rather than an argument. Tapanila and colleagues published CT imaging of specimen IMNH 37899 — known as “Idaho 4”, collected in 1950 — in Biology Letters in 2013. The scan revealed a nearly complete jaw apparatus, preserved in three dimensions and articulated in the closed position. The whorl is supported at the symphysis, the midline of the lower jaw, and it occupies the entire mandibular arch. The detail worth sitting with is the date on the specimen. The fossil that settled a century-old argument had been in a collection since 1950. It was not a new discovery; it was the same evidence, read with a tool that had not existed. Which means some unknown number of currently open questions on this page are already answered by material somebody has, unimaged. That cuts both ways for this guide's argument, and honestly. A record that keeps being re-read gets better. A record nobody re-reads just gets older. The One That Got Its Name Back

thirteen changes apart L★S · 008 The One That Got Its Name Back Brontosaurus excelsus merged 1903 · separated again 2015 Contested Named in 1879, folded into Apatosaurus in 1903 on differences called insufficient, and separated out again in 2015 by a 298-page analysis that published the exact threshold it used. A hundred and twelve years of children being told they had the name wrong. The argument is still live. named 1879merged 1903separated 2015argument still open ▸ Field notes Field notes · Brontosaurus excelsus The short version of No. 61, which this guide accompanies. Othniel Charles Marsh named Apatosaurus ajax in 1877 and Brontosaurus excelsus in 1879. In 1903 Elmer Riggs folded the second into the first, on differences that were usually considered insufficient to justify generic distinction. Insufficient by what measure? None existed. In 2015 somebody built one. Tschopp, Mateus and Benson published a 298-page, open-access revision of Diplodocidae, scoring 81 specimens against 477 characters — and rather than assert a judgement, they published the calibration. They counted the differences between pairs everybody already agreed were a single genus, got twelve and eleven, and set the bar one step past: a minimum of thirteen character changes for a genus, six for a species. Then the move that makes it exemplary rather than merely convenient: they wrote that the numbers cannot be applied to any other analysis, even of the same clade. A threshold that declares its own range of validity. And it is still contested, which is why the chip says so. Their own abstract hedges: Brontosaurus is considered valid by our quantitative approach. Donald Prothero published a dissent four months later under his own name. There is no consensus, and this guide is not going to invent one. The other half of the story is in the zine and belongs here in one line: the same authors petitioned the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature over a separate problem with Diplodocus, and lost, in a numbered published Opinion in 2018. A field where the revisers can be refused in print is a field worth trusting. The One That May Be A Grown-Up

one genus or two · open L★S · 009 The One That May Be A Grown-Up Torosaurus latus merge proposed 2010 · rejected 2012 · unresolved Contested A large horned dinosaur with holes in its frill. In 2010 two researchers argued it is not a separate genus at all but simply a fully mature Triceratops. In 2012 others answered that the growth evidence does not support it. More than a decade on, there is no consensus — and this is the mirror image of the Brontosaurus case. merge proposed, not a splitgrowth stage or genusanswered in 2012no consensus ▸ Field notes Field notes · Torosaurus latus In 2010 John Scannella and Jack Horner argued in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology that Torosaurus Marsh, 1891 is Triceratops Marsh, 1889 — synonymy through ontogeny. Their case: cranial change in Triceratops continues late and fast, the parietal fenestrae open and the squamosals lengthen at the very end of growth, and the result is exactly what has been catalogued as Torosaurus. No juvenile Torosaurus has ever been found, which is what you would expect if they are the oldest individuals of something else. In 2012 Nicholas Longrich and Daniel Field answered, in PLOS ONE, that the growth evidence does not carry it — looking at epoccipital development and fusion, the closing of skull sutures, and bone surface texture, and clustering specimens by developmental sequence rather than by size. Their conclusion: Torosaurus is a valid, distinct genus. More than a decade later there is no settled answer. Several rounds of publication have sharpened what is actually being disagreed about without resolving it. Put this card beside Brontosaurus and something useful appears. That one is a proposed split; this is a proposed merge. They are the same operation run in opposite directions, and they have had opposite fates — the split is broadly (not universally) taken up; the merge is broadly (not universally) rejected. The direction of a proposal has no bearing on whether it is right, and a field that can take one and refuse the other on the evidence is doing the thing correctly. There is also a plain lesson about growth. Two very different-looking skulls can be one animal at two ages. How different does something have to look before it is a different kind of thing? is not a question anatomy answers on its own, which is the whole subject of the companion zine.
